tool.heroTitle: The Ancient World Behind the Text
tool.heroSubtitle: Pick a passage anywhere in the New Testament. See the customs and ideas a first reader knew without being told.

footer.text: The method. This covers the whole New Testament, Gospels to Revelation. Each passage lists the customs and ideas at work in it, in the order you meet them. Each idea is written once, in its own card, and every passage that uses it links to the same card.

entries.title: Matthew 1:1-17, The family tree
entries.summary: Matthew opens with Jesus' ancestry from Abraham through David and the exile, in three sets of fourteen generations, and names four women along the way.
entries.plain: Before any story, Matthew sets out a list: Abraham to David, David to the exile in Babylon, the exile to Jesus. It runs through the kings of Judah and so makes a claim to David's throne. Four women appear in it, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah, and the list ends with Joseph, the husband of Mary.
entries.note: The three sets of fourteen do not come out exactly even, and Matthew skips some generations; Keener reads fourteen as a rounded number marking the great turning points, and notes that the Hebrew letters of David's name add up to fourteen, which some scholars call coincidence. Wright counts the list as "six groups of seven names," so that Jesus opens the seventh seven. Whether Tamar was a Canaanite, as Keener's notes and the CSB Study Bible say, or an Aramean, as Bailey argues from Jubilees, is itself debated. The book names no author. Carson, Moo and Morris note that the early church named the apostle Matthew, the tax collector of 10:3, without dissent, and find the case that the title is early "very strong, even if not unassailable"; most scholars put Matthew between AD 80 and 100, after Mark and after Jerusalem's fall; Carson, Moo and Morris argue for the sixties, before 70, and Wilkins, following Irenaeus, for the late fifties or early sixties. Most place it in Syria, perhaps Antioch, where Ignatius is the first writer clearly to use it; the church fathers assumed Palestine, and Carson, Moo and Morris say the place cannot be known for certain.

ideas.s: Lists of ancestors that proved who you were: a true Israelite, a priest, an heir of David. Matthew opens with one. Some teachers also spun stories and family trees out of the Bible's lists, which 1 Timothy calls myths and endless genealogies.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Matthew 1:18-25, Joseph and the betrothal
entries.summary: Mary is found pregnant while betrothed to Joseph. He plans a quiet divorce until an angel in a dream tells him to take her as his wife and name the child Jesus.
entries.plain: Mary and Joseph are pledged but not yet living together when she is found to be with child. Joseph, a just man, decides to end the betrothal privately. An angel tells him in a dream that the child is from the Holy Spirit and that he is to name him Jesus, and Joseph takes Mary home as his wife.
entries.note: A divorce before elders in a court could have let Joseph keep money and would have exposed Mary's shame; a private divorce needed only a certificate and two or three witnesses (Keener's notes). Keener's background commentary adds that by this time the death penalty for unfaithfulness in betrothal was rarely if ever carried out, and his notes say Rome did not let subject peoples execute without permission; Bailey writes of forces that no doubt wanted her stoned. The name Jesus is the Hebrew Joshua, God saves, and Bailey points out the wordplay in Hebrew between the name and the verb to save. Wilkins adds that among many Jewish groups divorce for adultery was required, not optional, and that in Galilee, unlike Judea, sexual relations between betrothed partners were not tolerated and the girl stayed with her own family.

ideas.s: A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.

A Jewish husband ended a marriage, or a betrothal, by handing his wife a written certificate before witnesses that left her free to marry again, and the teachers argued over the grounds. In Greek and Roman law either partner could end a marriage by leaving.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Matthew 2:1-12, Magi at Herod's court
entries.summary: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking for the newborn king of the Jews. Herod consults his scholars, sends the visitors to Bethlehem, and they go home another way.
entries.plain: Foreign visitors arrive in Jerusalem looking for a newborn king, and the news unsettles Herod and the whole city. The temple experts know from Micah where such a ruler should be born, yet it is the outsiders who travel to Bethlehem and pay him homage with costly gifts. Warned in a dream, they slip home without reporting to Herod. From the very start the child is set up as a rival to the reigning king.
entries.note: Bowing low was how Persians honored kings and gods, and the gifts recall Isaiah 60:6 and Psalm 72:10, where the nations bring gifts; Bailey reads the scene as moving the glory promised to Jerusalem onto the child. Wright calls the story political: "What he tells us is political dynamite." Wilkins gives a reason for Herod's alarm: after earlier invasions from the east he had ringed his eastern border with fortress palaces, and a large party of easterners could look like a threat. Carson, Moo and Morris put Herod's death in late March or early April of 4 BC, so the birth fell before that, probably between 6 and 4 BC. The star has been matched with a comet reported in 5 BC and with a conjunction of planets in 7 to 6 BC; Carson, Moo and Morris think neither identification certain, and doubt that a star which went ahead of the magi and stopped over the place was a natural phenomenon at all. Wilkins adds the views that it was a new star recorded by Chinese and Korean astronomers, a supernatural light, or an angel.

ideas.s: Eastern astrologers and dream readers, respected across the empire for reading the sky. A star that meant a new king meant danger for the old one.
Rome's king of Judea from 37 to 4 BC: an Idumean, a great builder, and a ruler who killed anyone he saw as a threat, his own family included.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Matthew 2:13-23, Refugees in Egypt, home to Nazareth
entries.summary: Joseph takes the family to Egypt by night. Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem, and after his death the family settles in Nazareth to stay clear of his son Archelaus.
entries.plain: Warned in a dream, Joseph flees with Mary and the child to Egypt. Herod, tricked by the magi, orders every boy two and under in and around Bethlehem killed, and Matthew hears Rachel weeping for her children. After Herod dies, Joseph is afraid of Archelaus, now ruling Judea, and takes the family to Nazareth in Galilee.
entries.note: Egypt held a large Jewish community; perhaps a third of Alexandria was Jewish (Keener). Bethlehem was small, and estimates of the boys killed run from about 20 (Keener's notes) to between 10 and 30 (the ESV Study Bible). Josephus reports that Archelaus' horsemen killed about three thousand people at the Passover just after Herod's death, and that Caesar later banished him to Gaul. Wright sums up the child's position: "he was a homeless refugee with a price on his head." The saying that he would be called a Nazarene has no single source text; most sources read a play on the Hebrew netser, branch (Isaiah 11:1), and some mention the Nazirites, a link the ESV Study Bible rejects. Nazareth is not mentioned in the Old Testament, the Talmud or Josephus (the Zondervan Bible Dictionary). The plural of 2:20, those who sought the child's life, may mean Herod and his son Antipater, executed five days before him (the Zondervan archaeology handbook).

ideas.s: Rome's king of Judea from 37 to 4 BC: an Idumean, a great builder, and a ruler who killed anyone he saw as a threat, his own family included.

Small farming and fishing villages, ringed by Greek cities, with two new royal towns that the Gospels never say Jesus entered. Most of Jesus' story happens in places of a few hundred to a few thousand people.

entries.title: Matthew 3:1-12, John at the Jordan
entries.summary: John preaches repentance in the Judean wilderness because the kingdom of heaven has come near. He calls Pharisees and Sadducees a brood of vipers and warns of the winnowing fork.
entries.plain: John appears in the wilderness in camel hair and a leather belt, eating locusts and wild honey, and crowds come to be baptized in the Jordan. When Pharisees and Sadducees come, he warns them not to rely on having Abraham as their father, since God can raise children for Abraham from stones. One is coming after him who will clear his threshing floor and burn the chaff.
entries.note: Many people believed vipers ate their way out of their mothers, so calling someone a brood of vipers was close to calling them parent-murderers (Keener). Children and stones sound alike in Hebrew and Aramaic, a wordplay of the kind the prophets used. Keener's notes add that real chaff burns too fast to be good fuel; this fire is unquenchable. Josephus spent three years with a desert teacher, Banus, who "used no other clothing than grew upon trees," and Keener compares John to him. Wilkins explains the brood of vipers another way, as the dozen or more small, dangerous snakes born at once from a mother snake. The cultural backgrounds article on Jesus' baptism notes that the Qumran sect taught repentance and washing too; Wilkins thinks it doubtful John was ever one of them, since he called the whole nation instead of withdrawing from it.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 3:1-2, 3:7, 3:9 and 3:12
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 3:1, 3:4, 3:7, 3:9 and 3:12

ideas.s: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.
The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.

entries.title: Matthew 3:13-4:11, Baptism and the test in the desert
entries.summary: Jesus is baptized and hears the voice from heaven, then is led into the wilderness for forty days, where the devil tests him three times.
entries.plain: John hesitates to baptize Jesus but does it, and a voice from heaven calls him the beloved Son. The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, where after forty days of fasting the devil challenges him to turn stones into bread, to throw himself from the temple, and to worship him in exchange for the kingdoms of the world. Jesus answers each time from Deuteronomy, and angels come and serve him.
entries.note: All three of Jesus' answers come from Deuteronomy's account of Israel tested in the wilderness for forty years (Keener). People credited magicians with turning stones into bread, and many hoped for a new Moses who would bring new manna. The highest point of the temple may be the southeast corner above the Kidron valley, where a fall meant certain death. Later rabbis called a voice from heaven the bat qol and ranked it below prophecy (Keener's notes). The cultural backgrounds article on Jesus' baptism and temptation sets the scene in an unsettled time, when Pilate's arrival as governor in place of Gratus in AD 26 stirred unrest, and places the baptism at Bethany on the far side of the Jordan (John 1:28); many put John's baptizing at a natural ford on the middle Jordan, near Tel Shalem. Wilkins puts the drop from the southeast corner at about 450 feet, or takes the pinnacle as a high temple gate, and the second-century writer Hegesippus said James the Just was thrown from the pinnacle (the Zondervan archaeology handbook).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 3:17, 4:1-11, 4:3, 4:5-6 and 4:8-9
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 3:17, 4:3, 4:4, 4:5, 4:7 and 4:10
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article Jesus' Baptism and Temptation
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 4:5
J. Randall Price and H. Wayne House, Zondervan Handbook of Biblical Archaeology, Matthew 4:5 The Pinnacle of the Temple

ideas.s: Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: Matthew 4:12-25, Capernaum, fishermen and crowds
entries.summary: Jesus moves to Capernaum, Galilee of the Gentiles, announces the kingdom of heaven, calls four fishermen, and draws crowds from Galilee, the Ten Towns, Jerusalem and beyond the Jordan.
entries.plain: With John in prison, Jesus moves his base from Nazareth to Capernaum on the lake, and Matthew sees in this Isaiah's promise of light for Galilee. His message is that God's reign is close at hand. He calls two pairs of fishing brothers away from their nets and their father, and news of his teaching and healing pulls in people from across the region. In a land run by Rome's appointed rulers, talk of God's kingdom was loaded language.
entries.note: Keener notes that disciples normally chose their teachers, and that teachers rarely called disciples. Fishermen were better off than most peasants, and leaving a father and a family business risked dishonor. Crowds at hot springs such as those near Tiberias show how many people sought cures (Keener). Wright reminds readers that Rome had set up Herod and then his sons as its puppets, so talk of God's kingdom meant revolution. The cultural backgrounds article on the kingdom adds that the word meant reign, and that many took Daniel's fourth and final kingdom to be Rome, the empire God's own kingdom was to overthrow. Wilkins puts Galilee at about 45 by 25 miles with some 300,000 people in two hundred or more villages, and Capernaum at about a thousand, with a waterfront of piers. Its customs post sat on the International Route because Philip's territory lay just across the Jordan (the Zondervan Atlas).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 4:12-13, 4:14-16, 4:18, 4:19-20, 4:21-22 and 4:24

ideas.s: Small farming and fishing villages, ringed by Greek cities, with two new royal towns that the Gospels never say Jesus entered. Most of Jesus' story happens in places of a few hundred to a few thousand people.
Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: Matthew 5:1-12, The Beatitudes
entries.summary: Jesus sits on a mountain to teach and pronounces God's blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers and the persecuted.
entries.plain: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up a mountain and sits down, and his disciples come to him. He begins with blessings: on the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those hungry for justice, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for doing right. He ends by telling his hearers they will be insulted as the prophets were.
entries.note: Teachers sat to expound Scripture with disciples at their feet, and many compare the mountain to Sinai (Keener and the CSB Study Bible). The kingdom of heaven at 5:3 and 5:10 brackets the blessings. Bailey argues that the word blessed, Hebrew ashre, describes a happy state already given, not a reward for behavior. Keener sets the meek, the merciful and the peacemakers against hopes that the kingdom would come by war with Rome; on inheriting the earth, Keener notes that Jews expected God's people to rule the whole earth, while Bailey argues Jesus meant the land of Israel, open to the meek and not to the violent. Tradition and most scholars place the mountain on the ridge above Tabgha, by the Seven Springs (Wilkins).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 5:1-2, 5:3, 5:5, 5:9 and 5:10-12

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.

entries.title: Matthew 5:21-32, Anger, lust and divorce
entries.summary: Jesus takes the commands against murder and adultery to the heart, warns of the fire of Gehenna, and speaks against divorce except for sexual immorality.
entries.plain: Jesus takes familiar commands on murder, adultery and divorce and presses each one back to the heart. Contempt for a brother already sits on the road to killing, so mending the quarrel comes before worship. Desire that treats a woman as something to take is already adultery, and he narrows divorce to the single case of a wife's unfaithfulness. He speaks as one with the right to say what the law was always after.
entries.note: Raca is Aramaic for empty-headed, and the judgment, the council and the fire may all refer to God's heavenly court, which Jewish texts pictured as a supreme council (Keener). Debt prison was a Gentile custom Jewish hearers knew of, and the last small coin was worth a few minutes' wages. Keener also notes that the word Jesus uses for lust is the verb of the tenth commandment in the Greek Old Testament, you shall not desire your neighbor's wife. The last penny of 5:26 is the Roman quadrans, about a sixty-fourth of a denarius (Wilkins), and Mark values it at two lepta, the smallest bronze coin (the Zondervan Bible Dictionary). Wilkins adds that the valley of Hinnom was later used to burn Jerusalem's refuse.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 5:21-22, 5:23-24, 5:25-26, 5:27-28 and 5:31-32

ideas.s: The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

A Jewish husband ended a marriage, or a betrothal, by handing his wife a written certificate before witnesses that left her free to marry again, and the teachers argued over the grounds. In Greek and Roman law either partner could end a marriage by leaving.

entries.title: Matthew 5:33-48, No oaths, the other cheek, the second mile
entries.summary: Jesus tells his hearers not to swear at all, not to resist an evildoer, to go a second mile with a soldier who forces one, and to love their enemies.
entries.plain: Instead of oaths by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or your own head, let yes mean yes and no mean no. Against an eye for an eye, Jesus speaks of turning the other cheek, giving the cloak as well as the tunic, and going two miles with someone who forces you to go one. He ends with love for enemies, since God sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust.
entries.note: An eye for an eye was a rule for courts, not private revenge (Keener). Keener's notes say, "The backhanded blow on the right cheek was meant primarily as an insult." A creditor could not keep a poor man's outer cloak overnight (Exodus 22:26-27), so giving it up surrenders a case the law would win. Roman soldiers could press local people's labor or animals into service, as with Simon of Cyrene (Keener). Wright says a soldier could "force civilians to carry their equipment for one mile"; the CSB Study Bible replies that "no surviving text establishes this as law." Hate your enemy is not in Scripture; Josephus says the Essene entry oath included a vow always to hate the wicked. The Qumran Rule of the Community tells members to hate all the sons of darkness (1QS 1.9-11; Wilkins).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 5:33-37, 5:38, 5:39, 5:40, 5:41 and 5:43-44

ideas.s: Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.

entries.title: Matthew 6:1-18, Alms, prayer and fasting in secret
entries.summary: Jesus warns against doing acts of piety to be seen, and teaches his disciples the Lord's Prayer.
entries.plain: Giving to the poor, praying and fasting are each done for the Father who sees in secret, not for an audience. Do not sound a trumpet when you give, pray standing on street corners, or put on a gloomy face when you fast. Jesus gives a short prayer that asks for God's name to be hallowed, his kingdom to come, daily bread, forgiveness of debts as we forgive our debtors, and rescue from the evil one.
entries.note: Jewish teaching called sins debts before God, and one Aramaic word served for both; Bailey names it khoba (Keener and Bailey). The law cancelled debts every seventh and fiftieth year, though lawyers had found ways round the release so that lending could go on (Keener). Keener's background commentary reads lead us not into temptation as a prayer not to fall when tested, and Bailey reads it the same way. On their reward, Keener notes the phrase is the wording of a business receipt. Wilkins mentions the view that the trumpets were the trumpet-shaped chests in the temple where coins were dropped, though he reads the phrase as irony, and notes that the Didache (8.2-3) has Christians saying this prayer three times a day by the end of the first century.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 6:1, 6:2-4, 6:5-6, 6:7, 6:9-10, 6:12, 6:13 and 6:16-18
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 6:2, 6:6, 6:7, 6:9-10, 6:12, 6:13, 6:14 and 6:17

ideas.s: Giving to the needy was one of the three pillars of Jewish piety, with prayer and fasting. Greeks and Romans had nothing quite like it.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
Going without food, and often washing and oil, as a sign of mourning, penitence and longing. The law required one fast a year; the devout kept many more.

entries.title: Matthew 7:13-29, Two ways, false prophets, two builders
entries.summary: Jesus ends his sermon with the narrow gate, a warning about false prophets known by their fruit, and two houses built on rock and on sand. The crowd is struck by his authority.
entries.plain: Jesus closes the sermon with a set of choices: a narrow way or a broad one, true teachers or false ones known by what they produce, a house on rock or a house on sand. Calling him Lord counts for nothing without doing what he says. The crowds notice that he teaches on his own authority instead of leaning on others, as their scribes did.
entries.note: Two roads were a common picture in Greek, Roman and Jewish writing, and the idea that few are saved appears in 4 Ezra (Keener). A later rabbinic saying builds the wise man's house on the Torah; Jesus puts his own words in that place. Bailey explains that villagers build in summer, when clay ground is hard as bronze, so a lazy builder can set his walls on the surface instead of digging to rock, and the winter rains turn it to mud. Blomberg treats the story as a parable with two main points. Wilkins sets the builders on the lakeshore instead, where alluvial sand is hard in summer and the wise builder digs down, sometimes ten feet, to bedrock.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 7:13-14, 7:15, 7:24-27 and 7:28-29

ideas.s: Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.

entries.title: Matthew 8:1-17, A leper, a centurion and a mother-in-law
entries.summary: Coming down the mountain, Jesus touches and heals a leper, heals a centurion's servant from a distance, and heals Peter's mother-in-law and many others.
entries.plain: Jesus touches a man with a skin disease and makes him clean, then heals the servant of a Roman officer who trusts that a word spoken at a distance is enough. Jesus says he has found no such trust in Israel and pictures outsiders from every direction feasting with the patriarchs while those born to the promise are shut out. Back at Peter's house he heals Peter's mother-in-law and, by evening, crowds of the sick and possessed. A Gentile soldier held up as the model of faith would jolt a Jewish hearer.
entries.note: Centurions led sixty to eighty men, not a hundred, and were the backbone of the army (Keener), though Wilkins's table of Roman units gives a century as a hundred men. Pious Jews did not normally enter Gentile homes, and healings at a distance were rare and thought extraordinary. Exorcists of the day used incantations, Solomon's name or foul-smelling roots; Josephus says he saw a Jew named Eleazar, before Vespasian, draw a demon out through a man's nose with a ring holding a root that Solomon had prescribed. Excavations near Capernaum's synagogue uncovered single-story basalt houses around a shared courtyard. The largest had plastered walls covered with inscriptions, mostly short prayers to Christ and some naming Peter, so it was venerated in antiquity as Peter's house (the cultural backgrounds article on houses). Wilkins adds that it served as a family home from about 63 BC until about AD 50, then as a place of Christian worship. The excavators read its relaid floors and plastered walls as veneration from the first century on, though Kathleen Kenyon doubted the identification (the Zondervan archaeology handbook).

ideas.s: Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

ideas.n: The banquet of the age to come
ideas.s: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.

entries.title: Matthew 8:18-34, Let the dead bury their dead, the storm and Gadara
entries.summary: Jesus answers two would-be followers, calms a storm on the lake, and frees two men possessed by demons in the region of the Gadarenes.
entries.plain: Two men offer to follow Jesus; he warns the first that he has no home of his own and tells the second that following him comes before even a father's burial. Out on the lake a storm hits while he sleeps, and he silences it, leaving the disciples asking what kind of man this is. On the eastern shore he frees two violent men living among the tombs, the demons go into a herd of pigs, and the townspeople beg him to go. The cost of following him and his power over sea and spirits sit side by side.
entries.note: Burying a father was a son's highest duty, and Wright calls Jesus' answer "This is, quite frankly, outrageous." What the man asks for is debated. Keener notes that bones were gathered into an ossuary a year after death, so he "could thus be asking for as much as a year's delay"; Bailey, citing Middle Eastern commentators, takes to bury one's father as an idiom for staying home until the parents die, perhaps for years; Keener's notes mention both views. Matthew names Gadara, about six miles from the lake and much nearer than Mark's Gerasa (Keener). Wilkins puts Gadara about five miles southeast of the lake and takes Gerasa as the small lakeside village of Khersa or Kursi inside Gadara's region, the traditional site; Gadara's coins sometimes showed ships (the Zondervan archaeology handbook). Tombs were unclean and thought haunted, and before the time means before the day of judgment. The Mishnah released a man whose dead lay unburied from reciting the Shema, from prayer and from wearing phylacteries (m. Berakhot 3:1; Wilkins), which shows how far the duty to bury reached.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 8:19-20, 8:21-22, 8:23-27, 8:28 and 8:29

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.
Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.

entries.title: Matthew 9:1-17, A paralyzed man, Matthew's table and the wedding guests
entries.summary: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, calls Matthew from the tax booth and eats with tax collectors and sinners, and is asked why his disciples do not fast.
entries.plain: Jesus tells a paralyzed man his sins are forgiven, and when scribes take it as blasphemy he heals the man to show he has the right to forgive. He calls Matthew away from collecting taxes and shares a meal with tax collectors and other outcasts, pointing objectors to Hosea on mercy over sacrifice. Asked why his followers skip the fasts, he says guests do not mourn at a wedding while the groom is present. Each scene shows him claiming a place and a freedom that unsettled the religious experts.
entries.note: Priests might declare God's forgiveness after a sacrifice, but there is no sacrifice here (Keener). Matthew was probably a customs agent at Capernaum, on a trade route, with a secure and well-paid job to leave. Go and learn was a teacher's way of sending a pupil to a proof text. Wedding feasts lasted seven days and suspended fasting and mourning, and new wine would burst old skins already stretched by fermenting (Keener). Wilkins places the booth on the Via Maris, collecting tolls or a tax on fish, and notes that tax collectors were also counted ritually unclean through contact with Gentiles.

ideas.s: Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
Going without food, and often washing and oil, as a sign of mourning, penitence and longing. The law required one fast a year; the devout kept many more.
A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.

entries.title: Matthew 9:18-34, A ruler's daughter, a bleeding woman, the blind and the mute
entries.summary: A synagogue ruler asks Jesus to raise his daughter; on the way a woman touches the fringe of his cloak. Then two blind men call him Son of David, and a mute man speaks.
entries.plain: A leader comes to say his daughter has just died. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches the edge of Jesus' cloak and is healed. At the house he sends out the flute players and the noisy crowd and takes the girl by the hand. Two blind men call out Son of David and receive their sight, a man who cannot speak is freed from a demon, and the Pharisees say he drives out demons by the prince of demons.
entries.note: The edge of the cloak was probably one of the tassels on the four corners of the outer garment that the law required, with blue and white cords (Numbers 15:38-41; Keener and the ESV Study Bible). Flute players led the mourning, and Keener notes that even the poorest family had to hire women to wail at a funeral. Son of David was a royal title, and most expected a warrior king, not a healer. Sorcery was a capital charge, and Keener notes that critics in the second century still granted the miracles but called them sorcery. The rule Keener has in view is Rabbi Judah's: even the poorest man was to hire "not less than two flutes and one wailing woman" (Wilkins). The word for the woman's bleeding is the one the Greek Leviticus uses for menstruation (15:33), so Wilkins reads a prolonged menstrual flow.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 9:18-19, 9:20-21, 9:23-24, 9:25-26, 9:27-31 and 12:24

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Matthew 9:35-10:15, The Twelve sent with nothing
entries.summary: Seeing the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, Jesus sends twelve apostles to the lost sheep of Israel, with no money, bag or staff, to stay with whoever will have them.
entries.plain: Moved by crowds who are like sheep with no shepherd, Jesus names twelve followers and sends them out to do what he has been doing: announce God's reign and heal. For now they go only to Israel's scattered people, not to Gentile or Samaritan towns. They travel without money or spare gear, live on the hospitality of whoever takes them in, and leave a town that turns them away with a public sign of protest. They go as his agents, carrying his authority.
entries.note: Keener notes that an apostle was a sent agent who carried the authority of the one who sent him, the same idea used for business agents. Peasants, Cynic philosophers and prophets all traveled light, though a Cynic's bag was for begging (Keener). The way of the Gentiles was probably a road into a pagan city. Matthew forbids the staff that Mark allows; the CSB Study Bible offers ways to harmonize them, and Keener's notes say ancient readers expected such variation in retellings. Rabbi Tarfon's saying about the day short, the work great and the laborers idle is a later Jewish harvest parallel (m. Avot 2.15; Wilkins). The Cananaean of 10:4 is probably an Aramaic word for zealot, used before the word named a revolutionary party (the Zondervan Bible Dictionary).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 9:35-36, 10:1-4, 10:5, 10:9-10, 10:11-13 and 10:14-15

ideas.s: Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.
The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.
Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.

entries.title: Matthew 10:16-42, Wolves, floggings, a sword and a cup of water
entries.summary: Jesus warns the Twelve of councils, floggings in synagogues and trials before governors and kings, of family turned against family, and promises that whoever receives them receives him.
entries.plain: Jesus warns the Twelve that their mission will bring arrests, beatings in synagogues and trials before rulers, and that families will split over him. They need not fear people who can only end a life; the one to fear is the one who decides a person's final fate. Loyalty to Jesus must outrank loyalty to parents and children and be ready for a cross. Yet even the smallest kindness shown to his messengers will be rewarded.
entries.note: Local courts were run by elders or priests, and synagogues, as places of public assembly, were the natural site for discipline; second-century rules prescribed thirteen strokes on the chest and twenty-six on the back (Keener). Flat roofs made good places to shout news. Sparrows were probably the cheapest meat in the market. Micah 7:6, family turned against family, was read as a sign of the end, and Wright reads 10:34-37 with 8:22 as Jesus forming an alternative family. Wilkins gives the later Mishnah procedure: three judges, the offender's hands tied to a pillar, the synagogue attendant striking from a stone with a calf-leather strap of four thongs while Deuteronomy 28:58-59 was read aloud.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 10:17, 10:18, 10:26-27, 10:28, 10:29-31, 10:35-36, 10:38 and 10:40-42

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

entries.title: Matthew 11:2-30, John's question, children in the square, an easy yoke
entries.summary: John asks from prison whether Jesus is the one to come. Jesus praises John, compares his generation to sulking children, pronounces woes on the lake towns, and offers rest under his yoke.
entries.plain: From prison John sends to ask whether Jesus is the one they have been waiting for, and Jesus points to the healings and to good news reaching the poor. He then praises John to the crowd as no wavering, finely dressed courtier but the promised Elijah figure, more than a prophet. His own generation, he says, is like sulky children who reject both John's fasting and his own feasting. After warning the lake towns that saw his miracles and did not change, he invites the worn out to take on his yoke and find rest.
entries.note: Josephus names Antipas' fortress of Machaerus as John's prison. The reed was the emblem on Antipas' coins and a picture of weakness, and a tetrarch's palaces were the nearest thing to royal splendor Galileans saw (Keener). Children played weddings and funerals in the square, and bystanders were expected to join a procession. Jewish teachers spoke of taking up the yoke of the law and of the kingdom; Keener describes it as "carrying the yoke of God's law and the yoke of his kingdom," Sirach offers wisdom's yoke and rest, and rest for your souls comes from Jeremiah 6:16. Machaerus was built by Alexander Jannaeus, destroyed by the Romans and rebuilt by Herod (Wilkins). Korazin lay about two and a half miles north of Capernaum, and most of its visible ruins are later (Wilkins; the Zondervan archaeology handbook). Bethsaida, which Philip raised to a city and renamed Julias, is placed at the mound of et-Tell or, after recent digging, at el-Araj; the sources differ on whether Julias honored Augustus's wife (the archaeology handbook) or his daughter (the Zondervan Atlas and Bible Dictionary).

ideas.s: Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

Small farming and fishing villages, ringed by Greek cities, with two new royal towns that the Gospels never say Jesus entered. Most of Jesus' story happens in places of a few hundred to a few thousand people.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: Matthew 12:1-14, Grain on the Sabbath, a withered hand
entries.summary: Pharisees object when the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath. Jesus answers with David, the priests in the temple and mercy, then heals a withered hand in the synagogue.
entries.plain: When Pharisees object to his hungry disciples picking grain on the Sabbath, Jesus answers from Scripture: David ate bread reserved for priests, and priests work in the temple on the Sabbath without guilt. He claims that something more important than the temple is present, and that God wants mercy. In a synagogue he heals a man's crippled hand, arguing that doing good on the Sabbath is lawful, and the Pharisees begin to plan his death. The quarrel is over who has the right to say what the Sabbath is for.
entries.note: Matthew adds an argument from the law itself, since the law commanded priests to work on the Sabbath (Numbers 28:10), and a lesser-to-greater argument; Keener notes that most Jewish ears would have found a man greater than the temple presumptuous. The Essenes forbade lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath, while most Pharisees allowed it. Keener adds that Pharisees lacked the power to execute anyone. The Mishnah lists thirty-nine main kinds of forbidden work, reaping and threshing among them, and the Qumran rule forbade even lowering a ladder or rope to pull a man out of water on the Sabbath (CD 11:16-17; Wilkins).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 12:1, 12:2, 12:5-6, 12:9-10, 12:11 and 12:13-14
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 12:1, 12:5, 12:11, 12:12 and 12:14
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 12:2 and 12:10-11

ideas.s: The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

entries.title: Matthew 12:22-50, Beelzebul, the strong man, Jonah and his true family
entries.summary: When Jesus heals a blind and mute man, the crowds wonder if he is the Son of David and the Pharisees say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus answers with the strong man, refuses a sign except Jonah's, and names his true family.
entries.plain: After Jesus heals a blind and mute man, the crowd wonders if he is David's promised son, while the Pharisees claim he gets his power from the ruler of demons. Jesus replies that Satan would not fight himself, and that freeing captives shows their strong master has already been tied up. He warns that slander against the Spirit's work cannot be forgiven, refuses any sign except Jonah's, and says pagans who repented will condemn his generation. When his family comes looking for him, he names those who do God's will as his true relatives.
entries.note: Keener points out that David was the only exorcist in the Old Testament, when he played for Saul, which fits the crowd's question. Your sons means members of your own group, who also drove out spirits (Keener). Repentant Gentiles testifying against the unrepentant at the judgment was a known theme, and the desert was a familiar haunt of demons. The name Beelzebul is read as master of the house (Keener), lord of the flies (Wright) or, from the Ugaritic title, prince Baal of the underworld (Heiser), and Heiser grants that scholars disagree on its origin; Wilkins adds a link with Baal Shamayim, whose worship Antiochus IV brought into the temple, and notes that the Testament of Solomon calls Beelzeboul ruler of the demons. On three days and three nights, the rabbis counted part of a day and night as the whole (Wilkins).

ideas.s: Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Matthew 13:1-23, The sower
entries.summary: From a boat Jesus tells the parable of the sower to the crowd on the shore, explains why he speaks in parables, and interprets the story for his disciples.
entries.plain: A sower scatters seed that lands on the path, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil, which yields thirty, sixty or a hundredfold. The disciples ask why he speaks to the crowds in parables, and he answers with Isaiah's words about people who look but do not see. Then he explains the soils as different ways of hearing the word of the kingdom.
entries.note: A boat in a cove near Capernaum would carry the voice to a crowd on the slope (Keener). Blomberg notes that God as sower and his people as soil were standard Jewish images. Wright places the explanation in the Jewish tradition of a symbolic vision followed by its interpretation, as in Daniel 7. The traditional Cove of the Parables, about a mile southwest of Capernaum, is a natural amphitheater whose acoustics have been tested (Wilkins; the Zondervan Atlas). In Jubilees the prince of evil spirits sends crows to eat the seed, a picture close to the birds of 13:19 (Wilkins).

Carl G. Rasmussen, Zondervan Atlas of the Bible, The Life of Christ

ideas.s: Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.
The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.

entries.title: Matthew 13:24-52, Darnel, mustard, yeast, treasure and a net
entries.summary: More parables of the kingdom: weeds sown among wheat, a mustard seed, yeast in flour, treasure in a field, a pearl, and a dragnet, with the weeds and the net explained as the judgment at the end of the age.
entries.plain: Jesus tells a string of short stories about God's reign. Weeds and wheat grow together until harvest, and a net hauls in good and bad fish to be sorted later, and he explains both as the judgment at the close of history. A tiny seed and a little yeast show small beginnings that end large, and a hidden treasure and a fine pearl show something worth giving up everything to have. He ends by comparing a teacher trained for the kingdom to a householder bringing out things both new and old.
entries.note: The mustard seed was proverbially small, the smallest seed Jews regularly planted, Blomberg says, and the shrub usually grew to about four feet, sometimes more. Three measures of flour would feed about a hundred people (Keener). Treasures were often buried for safekeeping (Keener), and Blomberg says burying treasure in hopes of reclaiming it "was a common enough practice"; commentators disagree about the ethics of the finder hiding it and buying the field. A dragnet strung between two boats caught clean and unclean fish alike. The furnace and the righteous shining like the sun echo 1 Enoch, 4 Ezra and Daniel 12:3 (Keener). The Copper Scroll from Qumran lists sixty-four hiding places for treasure, and a dragnet could stretch 750 to 1,000 feet (Wilkins).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 13:24, 13:25-27, 13:30, 13:31-32, 13:33, 13:36-43, 13:44, 13:45-46, 13:47-50 and 13:51-52
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 13:24, 13:31, 13:33, 13:44, 13:45, 13:47 and 13:52
Craig L. Blomberg, Interpreting the Parables, 6.7 The Wheat and the Tares, 8.2.1 The Hidden Treasure and the Pearl, and 8.2.3 The Mustard Seed and the Leaven
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 13:31-32
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 13:44 and 13:47

ideas.s: The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

entries.title: Matthew 13:53-58, No honor in Nazareth
entries.summary: Teaching in his hometown synagogue, Jesus is dismissed as the carpenter's son whose family everyone knows, and he says a prophet is not without honor except at home.
entries.plain: Jesus teaches in the synagogue at Nazareth, and the people are astonished but take offense. They know his father's trade, his mother Mary, his brothers and his sisters. Jesus answers that a prophet is honored everywhere except in his hometown and his own house, and he does few mighty works there because of their unbelief.
entries.note: Sepphoris, about four miles from Nazareth, had been burned and its people enslaved when Jesus was a child; Antipas rebuilt it, and carpenters, who worked stone as well as wood, would have found work there (Keener). Mary was the most common Jewish woman's name of the period, and the brothers' names were common too (Keener's notes). Antipas rebuilt Sepphoris between 3 BC and AD 10 as his first capital, the largest city in Galilee (the Zondervan Atlas). Estimates of Nazareth's size differ: Wilkins gives about five hundred people, Garland 150 to 200.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 13:53-58
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 13:55 and 13:57
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 13:57
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 17.10.9 and 18.2.1, trans. William Whiston
