David E. Garland, Mark, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Mark 6:1

ideas.s: Small farming and fishing villages, ringed by Greek cities, with two new royal towns that the Gospels never say Jesus entered. Most of Jesus' story happens in places of a few hundred to a few thousand people.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

entries.title: Matthew 14:1-12, John beheaded at a birthday feast
entries.summary: Herod the tetrarch hears about Jesus and thinks John has risen. Matthew tells how Herod, bound by an oath at his birthday, had John beheaded.
entries.plain: Herod Antipas hears the reports and tells his servants that John has been raised. Matthew explains that Herod had imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to Herodias, but feared the crowd, who held John a prophet. At his birthday, Herodias' daughter dances, Herod swears to give her whatever she asks, and she asks for John's head on a platter. John's disciples bury the body and tell Jesus.
entries.note: Matthew uses the correct title, tetrarch (Keener). Birthday celebrations were a Gentile custom, and Keener notes Josephus says Jews were forbidden to celebrate them. Beheading with a sword was a Greek and Roman penalty, not a Jewish one, and here there is no trial. Josephus gives his own reason for the killing: Herod feared that "the great influence John had over the people might put it into his power and inclination to raise a rebellion." The sources differ on where the feast was held. Wilkins and the Zondervan Bible Dictionary set it at Machaerus, where excavators found a colonnaded court leading to a banquet hall; the Zondervan Atlas doubts Josephus and thinks a birthday banquet likelier at Antipas's palace in Tiberias. Herodias's first husband was a half brother living privately in Rome, not Philip the tetrarch (the Bible Dictionary).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 14:1, 14:5-6, 14:8-9, 14:10-11 and 14:12
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 14:1, 14:6, 14:7, 14:10 and 14:12
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 18.5.1-2, trans. William Whiston
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 14:6
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Herod
Carl G. Rasmussen, Zondervan Atlas of the Bible, The Life of Christ

ideas.s: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Matthew 14:13-36, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
entries.summary: Jesus feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, in a deserted place, then comes to the disciples walking on the lake, and Peter tries to walk to him.
entries.plain: Jesus tries to withdraw after John's death, but the crowds follow, and he heals them and feeds thousands from five loaves and two fish, with baskets of scraps left over. That night he walks across the lake to the disciples' storm-tossed boat, and Peter starts out to meet him on the water before fear makes him sink. The disciples worship him as God's Son, and at Gennesaret the sick are healed by touching his clothes. In Israel's Scriptures it is God who treads on the waters, which is why the scene ends in worship.
entries.note: Villages of a few hundred to a few thousand people could not feed such a crowd, and Keener notes that teachers rarely fed even their disciples. The fourth watch on the Roman scheme ran from about three to six in the morning. Belief in ghosts was popular despite mainstream Jewish teaching, and Keener notes that in the Old Testament only God treads on the waters. Josephus describes the plain of Gennesaret as thirty furlongs long and twenty wide, watered by a spring the locals called Capharnaum. Tradition puts the feeding at Tabgha, where the pilgrim Egeria saw the stone in the fourth century (Wilkins), while the Zondervan Atlas thinks it probably took place northeast of the lake. The baskets were the kophinos, a basket Jews used for carrying their own food (Wilkins). The Zondervan Bible Dictionary makes the plain of Gennesaret less than four miles long and about a mile wide.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 14:13-21, 14:16, 14:21, 14:22-33, 14:25, 14:26 and 14:34-36
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 14:15, 14:19, 14:21, 14:25, 14:26, 14:27 and 14:34
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 14:15-21
Josephus, The Wars of the Jews 3.10.8, trans. William Whiston
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 14:13 and 14:20
Carl G. Rasmussen, Zondervan Atlas of the Bible, The Life of Christ
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Gennesaret

ideas.s: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

ideas.n: The banquet of the age to come
ideas.s: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: Matthew 15:21-28, A Canaanite mother and the dogs
entries.summary: In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman begs the Son of David to free her daughter. Jesus is silent, then speaks of bread and dogs, and her answer wins him over.
entries.plain: In Gentile territory on the Phoenician coast, a local Canaanite mother begs Jesus to free her daughter from a demon. He first says nothing, then tells her his mission is to Israel and that the children's food should not go to dogs. She turns his own picture back on him, asking only for the scraps, and he praises her faith and heals her daughter. Readers have long disputed how harsh his words were meant to sound.
entries.note: Matthew's word Canaanite names the people the Old Testament most despised; yet a widow from this same region had once received food and healing for her child through Elijah (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). By calling Jesus Son of David she recognizes him as Israel's rightful king (the cultural backgrounds notes). Whether the word dogs was softened is disputed. The cultural backgrounds notes say "Gentiles sometimes raised dogs as pets" and could feed them scraps, though dog used as a label was a harsh insult; the ESV Study Bible reads the diminutive as affectionate and says "Jesus is not insulting the woman but testing her faith." Bailey answers that in the Middle East "Dogs are never pets," and reads the exchange as a test staged for the disciples, voicing their prejudice so that the woman can expose it. Wright says she accepts the label and argues from Israel's own calling that its Messiah must bless the world. Wilkins rejects the affectionate reading: the diminutive pairs with the children's bread and means a dog in the house but "nonetheless still a dog"; against Bailey he notes that some dogs were kept as household watchdogs and fed indoors.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 15:21, 15:22 and 15:25-28
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 15:21, 15:22, 15:26 and 15:27
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 15:26-27
Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, ch. 16, The Syro-Phoenician Woman
N. T. Wright, Matthew for Everyone, Part One, comment on Matthew 15:21-28
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 15:26 and 15:27

ideas.s: Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Matthew 16:13-28, The rock, the keys and the cross
entries.summary: At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and is called the rock and given the keys. When Jesus speaks of his death, Peter rebukes him and is called Satan.
entries.plain: Far north at Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks his disciples who he is, and Peter declares him the Messiah and God's Son. Jesus blesses him, plays on his name as a rock on which he will build his community, and gives him the keys of the kingdom; what the rock means is disputed. When Jesus then explains that he must suffer and die in Jerusalem, Peter objects and is sharply rebuked. Following Jesus, he tells them, means taking up a cross.
entries.note: Wright notes that Caesarea Philippi lay well outside Herod Antipas's territory, a wise place to raise a question that drew the authorities' hostility. Herod the Great had built a white marble temple to Augustus near the grotto of Pan at the Jordan's source, and Philip made the town his capital (Wilkins; the Zondervan Bible Dictionary). Son of the living God fits the king of David's line, whom God calls his son (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), as a Qumran commentary also saw (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Peter and rock are the same word in Aramaic and were used interchangeably in Greek (Keener), and church translates the Greek Bible's word for Israel's assembly. The sources disagree about the rock: the ESV Study Bible favors Peter himself; Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes read Peter in his role as the one who confessed Jesus; the CSB Study Bible points to Peter and the apostles' preaching; Heiser reads a double meaning with the rocky mountain of Hermon above them. Peter then breaks what Keener calls one of the first rules of discipleship: "Never criticize the teacher, especially publicly."
sources: N. T. Wright, Matthew for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Matthew 16:13-20
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 16:13, 16:15-16, 16:18, 16:19, 16:22 and 16:24
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 16:16, 16:18, 16:22, 16:23 and 16:24
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 16:18
CSB Study Bible, notes on Matthew 16:13 and 16:17-18
Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm, ch. 32, Preeminent Domain
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, sidebar Herod Philip the Tetrarch and Caesarea Philippi
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Caesarea Philippi

ideas.s: Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

In a king's house a senior official carried the keys and decided who came in. Teachers spoke of binding and loosing for forbidding and permitting, and a court bound or loosed when it condemned or released.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

entries.title: Matthew 17:24-27, The coin in the fish's mouth
entries.summary: Collectors of the two-drachma temple tax ask Peter whether his teacher pays. Jesus says the king's sons are free, then sends Peter to find a coin in a fish to pay for them both.
entries.plain: In Capernaum the men collecting the temple tax ask Peter if his teacher pays it, and Peter says yes. Jesus asks him whether earthly kings take tolls and taxes from their own sons or from others; from others, says Peter, and Jesus answers that the sons are free. So as not to give offense, he tells Peter to catch a fish and pay for both of them with the coin in its mouth.
entries.note: Collectors did not make those who lived on charity or beggars pay, and may have wondered where a traveling teacher stood (Keener). The coin was a stater, worth four drachmas, enough for two men (Keener). Jewish teachers told stories of God rewarding faithful Jews with gems found in fish, though their date is uncertain, and some fish in the lake had mouths large enough to hold such a coin (Keener; the CSB Study Bible). The CSB Study Bible notes that only Matthew records the story and takes it as a sign that the Gospel was written before AD 70. Carson, Moo and Morris press the same point: before 70 the story read as solidarity with Israel, but after 70, when Jews paid the tax toward the temple of Jupiter in Rome, it might suggest solidarity with idolatry, and they doubt Matthew would have let that stand without comment. Wilkins adds that the tax may have been a live question, since some at Qumran held it was owed only once in a lifetime, and that Peter's fish was more likely a barbel, which takes bait, than the plankton-eating musht now sold as Saint Peter's fish.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 17:24 and 17:27
CSB Study Bible, notes on Matthew 17:24 and 17:27
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, note on Matthew 17:25-26
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 2, Matthew, section Date
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 17:24 and 17:27

ideas.s: Every year free adult Jewish men across the empire paid two drachmas toward the temple in Jerusalem. After AD 70 Rome went on collecting the same sum for a pagan temple.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Matthew 18:1-14, Little ones, a millstone and their angels
entries.summary: Asked who is greatest in the kingdom, Jesus stands a child among the disciples. He warns against causing little ones to stumble, speaks of their angels, and tells of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep.
entries.plain: When the disciples ask about rank in the kingdom, Jesus puts a child in front of them and says they must become humble like children to enter at all. Welcoming such little ones is welcoming him, and leading one of them astray deserves a fate worse than drowning. Their angels have access to God, and God, like a shepherd who goes after one stray sheep, does not want any of them lost.
entries.note: The millstone meant is the heavy kind turned by a donkey, not a woman's hand mill (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Romans sometimes drowned the worst criminals tied to a heavy weight, and Jewish people thought the punishment too inhumane for themselves, which makes the image more dreadful (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). One hundred was an average flock, and a shepherd who went after a stray could leave his flock with the other shepherds working nearby (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Millstones were a local product: the basalt around the lake was worked into commercial grinders (the Zondervan Atlas).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 18:1, 18:2-4, 18:6, 18:10 and 18:12-14
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 18:2, 18:3, 18:6, 18:10 and 18:12
ESV Study Bible, study notes on Matthew 18:2-4 and 18:10
CSB Study Bible, note on Matthew 18:10
Carl G. Rasmussen, Zondervan Atlas of the Bible, Sea of Galilee

ideas.s: Children in the ancient world were loved but powerless. Status came with age, and a child had no rights or voice apart from the adults who provided for them.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: Matthew 18:15-20, Two or three witnesses and the assembly
entries.summary: Jesus sets out how to deal with a brother who sins: privately, then with witnesses, then before the church. What they bind on earth is bound in heaven, and he is present where two or three gather in his name.
entries.plain: Jesus sets out steps for dealing with a fellow believer who wrongs you: speak to him privately first, then bring a witness or two, then take it to the whole community. If he refuses even then, he is to be treated as an outsider. The community's decisions carry heaven's backing, and Jesus promises to be present even when only a handful meet in his name. Private correction before public action was already Jewish practice, and Jesus builds on it.
entries.note: Private reproof first was standard Jewish practice, found in the Dead Sea Scrolls and among the rabbis, and shaming someone needlessly was counted a sin (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Tax collectors were seen as agents of a pagan government and, like pagans, were excluded from the community's religious life (Keener). Ten men made a synagogue's quorum, but a familiar saying held that God's presence was among even two or three who studied his law (Mishnah Avot 3:2), and Jesus puts himself in that place (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener gives two readings of the prayer of the two or three: a curse spoken at excommunication, or prayer for the offender's repentance.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 18:15, 18:16, 18:17, 18:18 and 18:19-20
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 18:15, 18:16, 18:17, 18:18 and 18:20
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 18:18

ideas.s: Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.

In a king's house a senior official carried the keys and decided who came in. Teachers spoke of binding and loosing for forbidding and permitting, and a court bound or loosed when it condemned or released.

entries.title: Matthew 18:21-35, Ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii
entries.summary: Peter asks whether forgiving seven times is enough. Jesus tells of a king who cancels an impossible debt, and of the forgiven servant who then chokes a colleague over a small one.
entries.plain: Peter offers to forgive a brother up to seven times, and Jesus says seventy-seven times. Then he tells of a king settling accounts with a servant who owes ten thousand talents; when the man begs for time, the king cancels the whole debt. The same servant seizes a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii and has him jailed, and the king, hearing of it, hands him over to the torturers until he pays all he owes.
entries.note: Some later rabbis limited forgiveness for a deliberate sin to three times, so Peter's seven looked generous (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). The king is a Gentile, perhaps like the Greek rulers of Egypt, and the servants are probably his tax farmers settling accounts; Jesus uses a Gentile court because the selling and torture would not fit a Jewish setting (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Ten thousand talents was more than such a king's yearly income, and ten thousand was the largest number in Greek (Keener; the CSB Study Bible). Sold as a slave, the man would not recover even a thousandth of it (Keener). A king who forgave would at least win a name for kindness, and the servant's harshness spoiled it (the cultural backgrounds notes). Blomberg warns that the king is not a simple picture of God, since God does not torture. Wilkins sets the sum beside Josephus's figures for the yearly revenue of Herod's three heirs, nine hundred talents in all; the debt was more than ten times that.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 18:21-22, 18:23, 18:24, 18:25, 18:31-33 and 18:34
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 18:21, 18:23, 18:24, 18:27 and 18:34
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 18:21-22
CSB Study Bible, note on Matthew 18:23-27
Craig L. Blomberg, Interpreting the Parables, 7.6 The Unforgiving Servant
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 18:24

ideas.s: A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

entries.title: Matthew 19:1-15, Any and every reason, and the children
entries.summary: Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife for any and every reason. Jesus answers from creation, the disciples wonder whether it is better not to marry, and children are brought for his blessing.
entries.plain: Pharisees test Jesus on a live debate: may a man divorce his wife for any reason at all? He goes back behind Moses to creation, where God made man and woman to be joined as one, and says Moses allowed divorce only as a concession, which Jesus permits only in the case of unfaithfulness. The disciples think that makes marriage too risky, and Jesus speaks of some who stay unmarried for the kingdom. Then he welcomes children his disciples tried to turn away, saying the kingdom belongs to people like them.
entries.note: The question names the live debate between the Pharisaic schools: Shammai allowed divorce only for unfaithfulness, Hillel for almost any cause, even burnt food, and a later rabbi added finding someone more attractive (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). The sources differ on which school then had the upper hand: the cultural backgrounds notes say the Shammaites outnumbered the Hillelites, and Keener calls Shammai's school predominant in Jesus' day, with Hillel's winning out later. Josephus states the law as a man divorcing his wife "for any cause." Since only husbands could divorce at will, Jesus' stand also protected married women, and with parents arranging marriages, a marriage with no way out frightened the disciples (Keener). Eunuchs were excluded from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1) and mocked by Greeks, and most Jews treated marriage and children as a duty (the cultural backgrounds notes). Wilkins notes substantial evidence that some Essenes were celibate, a live example beside 19:12.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 19:1-3, 19:9, 19:10, 19:11-12 and 19:13-15
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 19:3, 19:10, 19:12 and 19:13
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 19:3
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 4.8.23, trans. William Whiston
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 19:12

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.

A Jewish husband ended a marriage, or a betrothal, by handing his wife a written certificate before witnesses that left her free to marry again, and the teachers argued over the grounds. In Greek and Roman law either partner could end a marriage by leaving.
Children in the ancient world were loved but powerless. Status came with age, and a child had no rights or voice apart from the adults who provided for them.

entries.title: Matthew 20:1-16, A day's wage for an hour's work
entries.summary: A landowner hires laborers for his vineyard at dawn and again through the day, then pays everyone a full denarius, starting with the last. Those hired first complain.
entries.plain: Jesus tells of a vineyard owner who hires workers at dawn and keeps hiring through the day, the last only an hour before quitting time. At payday everyone gets a full day's wage, and those who worked all day complain. The owner replies that he has cheated no one and is free to be generous with his own money. The story upends ideas of earning, ending with the order of last and first reversed.
entries.note: The grumblers speak to the landowner without a title, and few in their position would speak so rudely to a man whose favor they needed (the cultural backgrounds notes). The rich were praised for generosity to the poor, and calling such a benefactor stingy, the evil eye of 20:15, was a humiliating insult that the landowner turns back on them (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); the notes sum up: "Grace is not fair; it is generous." A later rabbinic parable told the same story to the opposite effect, with Israel, the hard worker, paid more than the Gentiles (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The working day ran from about six in the morning to six at night, so the eleventh hour was about five, and a man hired then could expect a twelfth of a denarius (Wilkins); a denarius was also a Roman soldier's daily pay (the Zondervan Bible Dictionary).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 20:11-12, 20:13-15 and 20:16
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 20:9-15
Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, ch. 28, The Parable of the Compassionate Employer
Craig L. Blomberg, Interpreting the Parables, 7.2 The Laborers in the Vineyard
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 20:3 and 20:6
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry money

ideas.s: Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.
The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

entries.title: Matthew 21:1-11, A donkey, a colt and the Hallel
entries.summary: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt, rides into Jerusalem as Zechariah foretold, and the pilgrim crowds spread cloaks and branches, crying Hosanna to the Son of David.
entries.plain: Approaching Jerusalem, Jesus has his disciples fetch a donkey and its colt, and Matthew reads the ride as Zechariah's gentle king arriving. Pilgrims carpet the road with cloaks and branches and greet him with festival shouts from Psalm 118, hailing him as David's son. The city is stirred, and the crowds identify him as the prophet from Nazareth. It is a royal entry, staged in humility.
entries.note: Following a common Jewish habit of reading the Hebrew text for all it held, Matthew takes Zechariah 9:9 to mean two animals; colts not yet ridden sometimes went with their mothers (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The owner may have seen the loan as royal impressment, as hospitality to festival visitors, or as the honor of helping a famous rabbi (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Hosanna means save, and the cry comes from Psalm 118, part of the Hallel sung through the Passover season (Keener). Jesus was better known in Galilee than in Judea, and most of those who knew him in the crowd were Galileans (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Wright hears in the branches the welcome given to Judas Maccabaeus (2 Maccabees 10:7). Bethphage means house of unripe figs, and rabbinic texts treat it as the limit of Jerusalem's confines; palm branches appear on many coins of the period (Wilkins).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 21:1-3, 21:4-7, 21:9 and 21:10-11
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 21:3, 21:5-7, 21:8, 21:9 and 21:11
N. T. Wright, Matthew for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Matthew 21:1-11
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 21:1 and 21:8

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Matthew 21:12-22, Tables, the blind and the lame, and a fig tree
entries.summary: Jesus drives out the sellers and overturns the money changers' tables, heals the blind and the lame in the temple courts, and the next morning curses a leafy fig tree that withers at once.
entries.plain: In the temple courts Jesus throws out the traders, upends the tables used for changing money and selling doves, and charges that a place meant for prayer has become a hideout for thieves, drawing on Isaiah and Jeremiah. He heals blind and lame people who come to him there, and children's shouts in his honor anger the priests. The next morning he curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit, and it withers. He tells the amazed disciples that faith can move mountains.
entries.note: Pilgrims had to buy sacrifices and change money in Jerusalem, so the sellers were needed; the question was where the trade took place (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Wilkins puts the market in the Royal Stoa on the south side of the temple courts, where pilgrims changed money into Tyrian shekels. Prophesying the temple's fall could be fatal, as Jeremiah 26 shows and as Josephus reports of a later prophet (the cultural backgrounds notes). Blind and lame priests could not serve in the sanctuary, and the rule was in time widened to exclude all the blind and lame, so healing them in the courts made a statement (Keener); the Herod's Temple article places the blind and lame begging in the court of the Gentiles. The Sadducean priests who ran the temple were not looking for a Messiah, and spoke Greek as their first language, which is why Jesus quotes Psalm 8 in Greek (Keener). The sources read this mountain differently: Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes take moving mountains as a figure for the impossible, with the Mount of Olives in view, while Wright argues that the phrase, spoken in Jerusalem, "would naturally refer to the Temple mount."
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 21:12-17, 21:12, 21:14, 21:15-17, 21:19-20 and 21:21-22
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 21:12, 21:14, 21:16 and 21:21
N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God, ch. 9, section (iii) Jesus' Action in the Temple
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 21:12 and 21:14
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article Herod's Temple

ideas.s: Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.

entries.title: Matthew 21:23-46, By what authority, two sons and the tenants
entries.summary: The chief priests and elders demand to know Jesus' authority. He answers with a question about John, then with two parables: a son who says no and goes, and tenants who kill the owner's son.
entries.plain: The temple leaders demand to know who gave Jesus the right to act as he does, and he answers with a question about John's baptism that they dare not answer. He then tells of two sons, one who refuses his father but later obeys and one who agrees but never goes, and says outcasts are entering God's kingdom ahead of the leaders. In a second story, tenants of a vineyard abuse the owner's servants and kill his son, and Jesus applies Psalm 118's rejected stone to himself. The leaders see that the stories are aimed at them.
entries.note: Answering a question with a question was standard Jewish debate, and Jesus' reply rests on the principle that a commissioned messenger carries the full authority of the one who sent him (Keener). A son who promised and did not go was worse than one who refused, since sons were bound to obey and honor their fathers (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The vineyard follows Isaiah 5:1-7, where the vineyard is Israel; Bailey notes that Jesus adds what Isaiah does not have, an absent owner and tenants. Killing unarmed messengers was treachery everywhere in antiquity, and hearers would think of the persecuted prophets (the cultural backgrounds notes). Hearers would also wonder why the owner had not acted sooner; aristocrats would have thought him naive (Keener). The stone of Psalm 118:22 is joined to other stone texts by shared key words, and a later rabbi warned that whether the pot falls on the rock or the rock on the pot, woe to the pot (Keener). Large estates owned by foreigners or rich Jews were leased to poor tenants, and many absentee landlords were known for harsh treatment (Wilkins).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 21:23-27, 21:28-30, 21:33-46, 21:40-41 and 21:44

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

The prophets and psalms pictured Israel as God's vine or vineyard, planted and tended by him and judged when it bore no fruit. A golden vine over the temple gate kept the picture in front of every worshiper.

entries.title: Matthew 22:1-14, The king's wedding feast
entries.summary: A king's invited guests refuse to come to his son's wedding and kill his messengers. He burns their city, fills the hall with people from the roads, and throws out a guest without wedding clothes.
entries.plain: Jesus compares the kingdom to a king who gives a wedding feast for his son. The invited guests will not come when called; some go off to their farms and businesses, others seize and kill the king's servants, and the king sends troops to destroy them and burn their city. He then has his servants bring in everyone they find, good and bad, but when he sees a man without wedding clothes he has him bound and thrown into the outer darkness: many are called, but few are chosen.
entries.note: In rabbinic parables God was often a king whose son stood for Israel, and the setting was often the son's wedding feast (Keener). The guests had already accepted the first invitation, so refusing the second call was a deliberate insult, and in the cultural backgrounds notes' words, "Refusal to accept a banquet invitation insulted the inviter; insulting a king was treason." The meat was already killed and would spoil (the cultural backgrounds notes; Bailey). Messengers were protected by universal custom, and a king's servants stood for his person, so abusing them was a declaration of revolt (Keener). The burned city probably alludes to Jerusalem in AD 70 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Carson, Moo and Morris answer that burning a city is the standard language, in the Old Testament and the Roman world, of punitive expeditions against rebellious cities, so the verse need not show knowledge of what happened in 70; refusing such a king's invitation, they add, smacked of rebellion. Blomberg defends the story as coherent and realistic, though many read it as Matthew's reworking of the banquet parable in Luke 14. There is some evidence of kings supplying festal clothes to guests (Genesis 45:22; Esther 6:8-9; Wilkins).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 22:1-2, 22:3, 22:5, 22:6, 22:7 and 22:11-13

ideas.s: A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

ideas.n: The banquet of the age to come
ideas.s: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.

ideas.n: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
ideas.s: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.

entries.title: Matthew 22:15-22, Caesar's coin
entries.summary: Pharisees and Herodians ask Jesus whether it is lawful to pay the poll tax to Caesar. He asks for the coin, asks whose image is on it, and tells them to give Caesar and God what is theirs.
entries.plain: Disciples of the Pharisees and supporters of Herod team up to trap Jesus with a question about paying Rome's tax: yes would anger the people, and no would sound like treason. He asks for a coin, points out that it carries the emperor's portrait and title, and tells them to give the emperor his due and God his. They leave astonished, unable to fault him.
entries.note: Pharisees tended to be nationalists and Herodians were clients of Herod's family, so they worked together only in unusual cases; the Herodians hoped for Herodian rule in Judea and feared messianic movements that would bring tighter Roman control (Keener). The denarius bore Tiberius' image and the title son of the divine Augustus, while Judean copper coins left the image off; Jerusalemites had told Pilate they would rather die than let images of Caesar into the city (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Wright puts the danger plainly: "Tell people they shouldn't pay, and you might end up on a cross." Keener notes that if the questioners objected to Roman taxes, they ought not to have been carrying the coin at all. The cultural backgrounds chart of Jewish sects describes the Zealots as opposing taxes to a pagan emperor because allegiance was due to God alone. The word for the tax, kensos, is the Roman poll tax (the Zondervan Bible Dictionary), and Wilkins cites an estimate that families paid about 49 percent of their income in Roman and Jewish taxes together.

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

entries.title: Matthew 22:23-33, Seven brothers and one bride
entries.summary: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a riddle about a woman married in turn to seven brothers. Jesus answers that the raised do not marry, and that God is the God of the living.
entries.plain: Sadducees, who deny any resurrection, try to make it look absurd with the case of a widow married in turn to seven brothers under the law of levirate marriage. Jesus says they misunderstand both Scripture and God's power: the raised do not marry, and live instead like the angels. He then argues from God's words to Moses at the burning bush that the patriarchs are still alive to God. He answers from the books of Moses, as Pharisees did when debating Sadducees.
entries.note: The law of the brother-in-law marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5) protected widows who could not earn a living and kept the dead man's line alive (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright). The riddle borrows the plot of Tobit, where Sarah's seven husbands die one after another, and the Sadducees were known for posing such conundrums (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Marry refers to the groom and be given in marriage to the bride given by her father (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Jesus argues from the books of Moses, as Pharisees did when facing Sadducees, and the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob was the God named in one of the most common prayers of the day (Keener). The cultural backgrounds chart of Jewish sects says the Sadducees accepted only the books of Moses as Scripture, and rejected belief in angels and demons as well as the resurrection. The Zondervan Bible Dictionary calls that inference about Scripture unnecessary and puts the dispute in the Sadducees' rejection of the oral traditions.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 22:24, 22:25-27 and 22:29-33
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 22:24, 22:28, 22:29 and 22:30
N. T. Wright, Matthew for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Matthew 22:23-33
Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm, ch. 23, Giant Problems
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article Jewish Sects
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Sadducee

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

A Jewish husband ended a marriage, or a betrothal, by handing his wife a written certificate before witnesses that left her free to marry again, and the teachers argued over the grounds. In Greek and Roman law either partner could end a marriage by leaving.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Matthew 23:1-12, Moses' seat, wide phylacteries, the best seats
entries.summary: Jesus tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach but not what they do, and mocks their wide phylacteries, long tassels, best seats and love of the title rabbi.
entries.plain: Jesus tells the crowds and his disciples to follow what the scribes and Pharisees teach from Moses, but not to copy how they live. He mocks their show of piety, from oversized prayer boxes and tassels to their love of honored seats and respectful titles. His own followers are to refuse such titles, since God alone is their Father and Christ their only teacher, and the greatest among them must serve. The warning is about status-seeking, aimed as much at the disciples as at their rivals.
entries.note: Moses' seat may be a real stone seat known from ancient synagogues or a figure for Moses' successors; the cultural backgrounds notes give both views, while Keener takes it figuratively. Wilkins favors a literal chair, from a marble seat in the synagogue on Delos as early as the first century BC to later stone seats at Hammat Tiberias, Chorazin and En Gedi, and the Zondervan archaeology handbook notes the Chorazin seat. Phylacteries were small boxes holding Scripture verses, strapped to the head and arm for prayer, and such boxes have been found (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The honored seats were probably near the bema, the platform for reading the Law, while many hearers sat on mats on the floor (Keener). Inferiors were expected to greet superiors first, rabbi meant my master, and disciples called their rabbis father (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Two leather phylactery cases were found in Qumran Cave 1 (Wilkins).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 23:1-2, 23:4-5, 23:6, 23:7-8 and 23:9-11
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 23:2, 23:5, 23:6, 23:7-8 and 23:9
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 23:2
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, sidebars The Seat of Moses and Phylacteries at Qumran
J. Randall Price and H. Wayne House, Zondervan Handbook of Biblical Archaeology, Matthew 23:2 The Seat of Moses

ideas.s: Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: Matthew 23:13-28, Oaths, mint, gnats and whitewashed tombs
entries.summary: Jesus pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees: they shut the kingdom, play games with oaths, tithe herbs while neglecting justice, strain gnats and swallow camels, and look clean outside like whitewashed tombs.
entries.plain: Jesus pronounces a series of woes on the scribes and Pharisees, calling them actors whose religion is for show. He attacks rules that let people slip out of oaths, careful tithing of garden herbs alongside neglect of justice and mercy, and fussing over tiny matters while swallowing huge ones. Their outward purity, he says, hides greed inside, like tombs painted bright while full of decay. Later rabbis criticized bad Pharisees in similar terms.
entries.note: Hypocrite first meant an actor (Keener). Later rabbis, who saw themselves as the Pharisees' heirs, criticized bad Pharisees of their own, and Keener notes that most of Jesus' moral teaching would have won agreement from the very people he opposed. The golden vine on the temple had gold added to it each year (the cultural backgrounds notes). A drink in which something died was unclean (Leviticus 11:32-33); Pharisees exempted creatures as small as a gnat, and in Aramaic the words for gnat and camel sound alike (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Shammai's and Hillel's schools argued over whether to clean the inside or the outside of a cup first, and Jesus' wording sides with Hillel (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Tombs were whitewashed before Passover to warn pilgrims away, since even a shadow touching a grave was thought to defile; the cultural backgrounds notes add that here Jesus uses whitewash as a beautifier covering decay. In Jerusalem tombs were whitewashed on the fifteenth of Adar, ahead of Passover (Wilkins). For converts, Wilkins points to Josephus on the wives of Damascus and Queen Helena of Adiabene, and notes that scholars debate how actively Judaism sought them.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 23:13-28, 23:15, 23:16-22, 23:23, 23:24, 23:25-26 and 23:27-28
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 23:15, 23:16, 23:24, 23:25-26 and 23:27
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 23:16-19
Michael J. Wilkins, Matthew, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Matthew 23:15 and 23:27

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Matthew 24:1-14, Stones, birth pangs and false messiahs
entries.summary: As the disciples admire the temple, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he warns of false messiahs, wars and persecution, the beginning of the birth pangs.
entries.plain: As they leave the temple, Jesus tells his disciples that its great buildings will be torn down stone by stone. Later, on the Mount of Olives, they ask when this will be and what will mark his coming and the close of the age. He warns of pretend messiahs, wars, famines and earthquakes that are only the first pains of labor, and of persecution and failing love among his followers. Before the end, the message of God's reign must reach every nation.
entries.note: The temple seemed strong and invincible, one of the most splendid buildings in the ancient world (Keener). Josephus describes stones forty-five cubits long, and the cultural backgrounds notes mention one block nearly forty feet long. Whether not one stone left standing is hyperbole is debated: Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes point out that some stones remain, as in part of one wall, but the temple was almost entirely demolished in AD 70; the ESV Study Bible gives both readings. Apocalyptic writers expected the nations to persecute God's people, but did not expect a great turning of Gentiles to God before the end, which makes 24:14 unexpected (Keener). The Zondervan archaeology handbook argues that these things meant the temple buildings, not the retaining walls of the platform, and that Herodian stones of two to four tons still lie where the Romans threw them onto the street below.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 24:1, 24:2, 24:4-5, 24:6-8 and 24:9-14
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Matthew 24:2 and 24:6-14
ESV Study Bible, study note on Matthew 24:2

N. T. Wright, Matthew for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Matthew 24:1-14
J. Randall Price and H. Wayne House, Zondervan Handbook of Biblical Archaeology, Matthew 24:1-2 The Destruction of the Temple Mount

ideas.s: Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

entries.title: Matthew 24:15-28, The desolating sacrilege and the flight
entries.summary: When the desolating sacrilege spoken of by Daniel stands in the holy place, those in Judea must flee to the mountains at once. False messiahs will say he is in the wilderness, but his coming will be like lightning.
entries.plain: Jesus tells his followers that when they see the desecration Daniel foresaw set up in the holy place, people in Judea must run for the hills at once, without stopping for anything. The flight will be hardest on pregnant and nursing women and worse in winter or on a Sabbath, and the suffering will be unmatched. They are not to believe reports that the Messiah is hiding somewhere, since his coming will be as obvious as lightning. A pagan threat to the temple was real for first readers, as Caligula's plan for his statue showed within a decade.
entries.note: Roofs were flat, used for drying vegetables and prayer, and reached by an outside stair, so a man could come down and run without going into the house (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Workers left their cloaks at the edge of the field as the day warmed; the cloak doubled as a blanket and was the one thing a creditor could not keep overnight (the cultural backgrounds notes). In winter the wadis and the Jordan flooded, and Josephus tells of fugitives trapped by the Jordan in 68 and slaughtered. On the Sabbath riding and long walks were forbidden, so passage would be hard to find (Keener). Wright writes that in AD 40 the emperor Gaius Caligula tried to put a statue of himself in the temple, the pagan invasion this warning had in view nearly coming within ten years. Carson, Moo and Morris count the Sabbath set beside winter in 24:20 among the details that suggest Matthew wrote before 70. Wilkins adds that Pilate's standards in AD 26 also brought Daniel to mind, and that Caligula was dissuaded by Agrippa I and died in 41 before his statue was set up.

ideas.n: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
ideas.s: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

entries.title: Matthew 24:29-51, The Son of Man on the clouds and the slave in charge
entries.summary: After the distress, sun, moon and stars fail and the Son of Man comes on the clouds to gather his chosen. No one knows the day, so the household must stay ready, like a slave left in charge.
entries.plain: Jesus describes the sky going dark and the Son of Man arriving on the clouds with angels and a trumpet to gather his people, language the prophets used for God's judgment on empires. He says his own generation will see these events, yet no one but the Father knows the exact day. People will be caught off guard as in Noah's flood, so his followers must stay ready, like a trusted servant found doing his job when the master returns. What the coming on the clouds refers to is disputed.
entries.note: Falling stars and a darkened sun were the prophets' language for God's judgment on empires (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4), and people expected signs in the sky before disasters like Jerusalem's fall (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). A regularly recited Jewish prayer looked for a trumpet to gather Israel at the end (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The temple fell about forty years after Jesus spoke, the rough length of a biblical generation, and the Dead Sea Scrolls expected a final forty-year generation (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Women ground grain together at a shared mill, and thieves broke in by digging through the clay walls of an ordinary house (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). On the coming on the clouds the sources part ways: the ESV Study Bible reads end-time language for Jesus' return, and Keener treats the sign of the Son of Man as the ultimate sign of his coming, while Wright argues that in Daniel the figure goes up to God, so the coming means "It is his ascension, his vindication." Wilkins notes the War Scroll's battle banners (1QM 3-4) as one proposed background for the sign.

God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: Matthew 25:1-13, Ten young women and the bridegroom
entries.summary: Ten young women wait with their lights for a bridegroom who comes late at night. Five brought extra oil and go in to the feast; five go to buy oil and find the door shut.
entries.plain: Jesus compares the kingdom to ten virgins who take their lamps to meet the bridegroom. Five are foolish and bring no extra oil; when he is delayed, all of them sleep, and at midnight the cry goes up that he is coming. The wise will not share their oil and send the others to buy some; while they are gone the bridegroom arrives, the ready go in to the wedding feast and the door is shut, and to the latecomers he says that he does not know them.
entries.note: Being a bridesmaid was a great honor, and being shut out unprepared was the stuff of young women's nightmares (Keener). Grooms were often late, and their coming was announced again and again until they arrived (Keener). The door could be bolted against the latecomers, and I do not know you was a form of repudiation, treating them as strangers (the cultural backgrounds notes). The sources disagree on whether oil could be bought at midnight: Keener thinks dealers would be hard to find, Blomberg says shops would stay open for a festival, and Bailey says in a village everyone knows everyone, so oil would not be hard to get. Bailey adds, "But women, young and old, always carry lamps." Wilkins takes the lamps as torches, oil-soaked rags in a holder that burned for hours if refilled, not small house lamps.

ideas.s: A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

entries.title: Matthew 25:14-30, Five, two and one talent
entries.summary: A man going abroad entrusts his property to three slaves. Two double what they were given and are rewarded; the third buries his talent and is thrown out.
entries.plain: Before a long journey a man hands his slaves five talents, two talents and one, each according to his ability. The first two trade with the money and double it, while the third digs a hole and hides his. When the master returns he praises the first two and gives them more; the third says he knew his master was a hard man and was afraid, and the master answers that he should at least have put the money with the bankers to earn interest, takes his talent and has him thrown into the outer darkness.
entries.note: Keener reckons the five talents at about fifty thousand denarii, the two at twenty thousand and the one at ten thousand, a small matter only to a very rich master; Wilkins values a silver talent at about seventy-five pounds and six thousand denarii, which would make them thirty thousand, twelve thousand and six thousand. Doubling an investment was normal, and the master threw a feast on his return and honored the servants who had helped him (Keener). You have what is yours was the phrase used in Jewish transactions to mean that one was no longer responsible (Keener). Wright reads the story, like other stories of a master and his slaves, as one Jesus' hearers would take as being about God and Israel, and sees the leaders of Matthew 23 in the slave who hid the money. There were no banks in the modern sense: people buried valuables or left them with a neighbor, and the bankers of 25:27 are probably money changers at their tables (Wilkins).

A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

entries.title: Matthew 25:31-46, Sheep, goats and the least of these
entries.summary: The Son of Man comes in glory with his angels, gathers the nations, and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, judging them by how they treated the least of his brothers and sisters.
entries.plain: Jesus pictures the Son of Man coming as king to judge all the nations, dividing them as a shepherd parts a mixed flock. Those placed on the honored side are welcomed because they fed, clothed, sheltered and visited him when he was hungry, a stranger, sick or in prison; surprised, they learn that what they did for the least of his family they did for him. The others, who neglected such people, are sent to the punishment made for the devil, while the first group goes to life without end. Who counts as the least of these is disputed.
entries.note: Judging all the nations belonged to God in Jewish expectation, so the scene gives Jesus God's place (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Blomberg notes that "Shepherds in Israel often herded mixed flocks" and parted them at night, since goats need warmth and sheep prefer the open air; sheep were also worth more (the cultural backgrounds notes). The right side was the honored side (the cultural backgrounds notes). Prisoners depended on friends or family for food and could die without them, so visiting prisoners was costly help (the cultural backgrounds notes). The sources differ on who the least of these are: Keener reads Jesus' messengers, and the cultural backgrounds notes lean the same way; the ESV Study Bible, the CSB Study Bible and Blomberg read needy disciples; Wright reads people outside the circle of followers judged by how they treated Jesus' family. Wilkins adds that about seventy percent of the Old Testament's goats are sacrificial animals.

ideas.s: Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.

entries.title: Matthew 26:1-16, Perfume at Bethany and thirty pieces of silver
entries.summary: The chief priests meet at Caiaphas's house to plot Jesus' arrest away from the festival crowds. At Bethany a woman pours costly perfume on his head, and Judas sells him for thirty pieces of silver.
entries.plain: As Passover nears, the chief priests and elders meet at Caiaphas's house and plan to seize Jesus quietly, away from the festival crowds. In Bethany a woman pours a jar of costly perfume over his head; the disciples call it waste, but Jesus says she has anointed him ahead of his burial and will be remembered for it. Judas then goes to the priests and agrees to betray him for thirty silver coins. Her lavish gift stands beside his cheap sale.
entries.note: Planning in the high priest's home instead of the council's usual meeting place broke accepted rules of justice (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). A Roman governor appointed Joseph Caiaphas, who held the office from AD 18 to 36, and an ossuary inscribed for a Joseph son of Caiaphas has been found (the ESV Study Bible; the cultural backgrounds notes); Josephus names Joseph Caiaphas as the governor Gratus's appointee. Crowds swelled fivefold at Passover, and riots at earlier festivals had killed many in the crush (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation the law set for a slave's death (Exodus 21:32) and the wage paid to the shepherd in Zechariah 11:12-13, more than a hundred days' pay (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The Caiaphas ossuary was found in 1990 in Jerusalem's Peace Park, with the bones of six people including a man of about sixty, and Vitellius deposed Caiaphas in AD 36 (Wilkins). During the feasts Roman guards walked the roofs of the temple porches (the Zondervan Bible Dictionary).

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Matthew 26:17-30, The Passover and the cup
entries.summary: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve in the city, names the one who dips with him as his betrayer, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and vows not to drink wine again until the kingdom.
entries.plain: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve in Jerusalem and warns that one of them, sharing the dish with him, will betray him. Over the bread and the cup he gives the meal new meaning, speaking of his body and of his blood sealing a covenant for the forgiveness of sins. He says he will abstain from wine until God's reign arrives, and after a hymn they leave for the Mount of Olives.
entries.note: The Passover had to be eaten inside the city walls, after sundown and before midnight, with at least ten people to a lamb, so most homes took in guests that night (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener compares the Passover liturgy, which identified the bread on the table with the bread of affliction eaten in Egypt; Jesus' words over the bread were no more literal than that. Vows of abstinence, I will not eat or drink this until that happens, were common, and since the fourth cup came after the closing hymn, the cup here was probably the third (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). After the meal the rest of the Hallel was sung (the cultural backgrounds notes). Matthew, Mark and Luke make this a Passover meal, so that Jesus died on Nisan 15, while one reading of John 18:28 puts his death on Nisan 14; Carson, Moo and Morris leave the day open and name Friday, April 7, AD 30, and Friday, April 3, AD 33, as the two likeliest dates. Wilkins sets out two ways of reconciling them: a different calendar or way of counting the day, or John's Passover meaning the whole festival week.

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

ideas.n: The banquet of the age to come
ideas.s: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.

entries.title: Matthew 26:47-75, Arrest, twelve legions, the council and the rooster
entries.summary: Judas comes with an armed crowd and a kiss. Jesus refuses the sword and the twelve legions of angels, is tried at night before Caiaphas, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter swears he never knew him.
entries.plain: Judas leads an armed party from the chief priests to Jesus and singles him out with a kiss. Jesus stops a follower's sword, saying he could call on armies of angels if he chose, and lets himself be taken. Before Caiaphas and the council, witnesses claim he threatened the temple, and when Jesus speaks of the Son of Man seated beside God, the high priest declares it blasphemy and the council calls for his death. Meanwhile in the courtyard Peter, given away by his Galilean accent, denies knowing Jesus three times before the rooster crows.
entries.note: The armed band sent by the city's leaders was probably the temple guard (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Wilkins thinks its best-armed men were Roman soldiers Pilate had assigned to the temple, alongside Levite police with clubs. A kiss was a sign of affection between family, close friends, or a disciple and his teacher, which made Judas's kiss a special act of hypocrisy (Keener). By later Pharisaic rules a night trial in a private house, with no day between hearing and verdict, was illegal on every count (Keener). The cultural backgrounds article on Jesus' trial adds that the rabbinic rules come from well over a century later, while the Gospel accounts fit the first-century evidence, and that the night hearing may have been meant only to frame a charge for Pilate. By the Mishnah's later rule a blasphemer was guilty only if he pronounced the divine Name itself (m. Sanhedrin 7:5; Wilkins). Galileans were careless with their vowels and gutturals (Keener). The sources differ on Judean prejudice: the cultural backgrounds notes say Judeans looked down on Galileans as backward, while Keener calls the evidence that they linked Galileans with revolutionaries ambiguous at best.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Matthew 26:47, 26:48-50, 26:52, 26:53-54, 26:57, 26:63, 26:65, 26:73 and 26:74

ideas.s: God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

entries.title: Matthew 27:1-26, Blood money, Pilate and Barabbas
entries.summary: At dawn the council hands Jesus to Pilate. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself, the priests buy a potter's field, and Pilate, warned by his wife's dream, releases Barabbas and washes his hands.
entries.plain: At dawn the council hands Jesus over to Pilate, the Roman governor. Judas, full of regret, flings the silver back in the temple and hangs himself, and the priests use the money to buy a burial field for foreigners. Pilate questions Jesus about being king of the Jews, ignores a warning from his wife's dream, and, with the crowd demanding Barabbas, washes his hands publicly and has Jesus flogged and sent to be crucified. To Roman ears a claim to be king was treason.
entries.note: For Rome king of the Jews meant treason, since only the emperor could grant the title (the cultural backgrounds notes). Pilate had begun his rule by bringing the standards into Jerusalem by night and backing down before the crowds (Josephus; the cultural backgrounds notes), and an inscription found at Caesarea calls him prefect, showing that the title procurator is an anachronism for his day (the Zondervan archaeology handbook). Dreams were taken seriously as revelation across the Mediterranean (Keener). In the usual ancient view, hanging himself inside the temple would have defiled it, and burying strangers who had no one else was an act of piety (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The traditional Field of Blood held tombs of Jerusalem's aristocracy, not strangers, so most scholars doubt the identification (Wilkins; the archaeology handbook). Washing the hands disclaimed innocent blood (Deuteronomy 21:6-7), though Keener notes it no more freed Pilate than the priests' words freed them. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes take the crowd's cry about blood on their children as fulfilled in AD 70, and Keener warns against the anti-Jewish use later made of the verse. Origen implies that most manuscripts of his day named the prisoner Jesus Barabbas (Wilkins).

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

entries.title: Matthew 27:27-56, Mock king, the cross and the torn curtain
entries.summary: Soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king. He is crucified as king of the Jews between two rebels, cries out in the words of Psalm 22 and dies; the curtain tears, the earth shakes, and women watch from a distance.
entries.plain: Roman soldiers dress Jesus up as a mock king and abuse him, and Simon of Cyrene is forced to carry his cross to Golgotha. Jesus is crucified between two rebels under a notice naming him king of the Jews, while passers-by and leaders jeer. After hours of darkness he cries out in the opening words of Psalm 22 and dies, and the temple curtain splits, the ground shakes and a centurion calls him God's Son. A group of Galilean women who had travelled with him watch from a distance.
entries.note: Soldiers wore red cloaks, which faded could pass for royal purple, and their kneeling parodied homage to the rulers of the Greek East (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Most scholars put Pilate's headquarters at Herod's palace, not the Antonia, whose pavement was laid after AD 70 (the Zondervan Bible Dictionary). The word for the two men crucified with Jesus was Josephus's usual term for revolutionaries (Keener). Matthew gives the cry in Hebrew, Eli, which explains the mishearing as Elijah, and some rabbis held that Elijah, who never died, ran errands like an angel to help the pious (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The darkness was no eclipse, since Passover fell at full moon (Wilkins), and stories were told of portents at the deaths of great rabbis (Keener). The sources read the torn curtain two ways: Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes think it more likely signals God leaving the temple ahead of its fall, while the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible read new access to God. Keener thinks the centurion may have meant a semi-divine hero, the cultural backgrounds notes the son of Israel's one God.
