ideas.s: A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.

entries.title: Matthew 27:57-66, Joseph's tomb and the sealed stone
entries.summary: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for the body and lays it in his own new tomb. The next day the chief priests get a guard and a seal on the stone.
entries.plain: That evening Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy follower, gets Pilate's permission to take the body and lays it in his own unused rock tomb, sealing it with a large stone while two women named Mary watch. The next day the chief priests and Pharisees remind Pilate that Jesus predicted he would rise, and ask for the tomb to be guarded against theft. Pilate grants a guard, and they seal the stone. These precautions set up the story of the empty tomb that follows.
entries.note: Romans expected those executed for treason to be left for scavengers, and even Jewish executions led to a criminals' grave, so a prominent man who asked for the body took a risk (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The Zondervan archaeology handbook answers that Josephus says the Romans let Jews follow their own burial law (Against Apion 2.73), and the crucified Jehohanan was buried in his family tomb. Burying someone in one's own family tomb was a special honor (Keener). The oldest tradition for the site, the Holy Sepulchre, lay outside the walls until Agrippa I extended them in the forties, while the Garden Tomb has no early evidence and was proposed only in 1883 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes and article on the tomb's location). The priests' visit to Pilate fell on the Sabbath, not a day for business with the governor (the cultural backgrounds notes). The sources differ over the guard: Keener thinks Roman soldiers put at the priests' disposal, since the guards later fear Pilate; the cultural backgrounds notes give that view and the view that Pilate let the priests post their own Levite guard; Wilkins thinks it was the Roman detachment already assigned to the temple authorities.

The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Matthew 28:1-15, Women at dawn and a bribed guard
entries.summary: At dawn after the Sabbath an angel rolls back the stone and tells two women that Jesus is risen. They meet him on the road, while the chief priests pay the guards to say the disciples stole the body.
entries.plain: At dawn after the Sabbath two women named Mary come to the tomb; an earthquake strikes, an angel rolls the stone away, and the guards freeze with fear. The angel tells the women that Jesus has risen and will meet his followers in Galilee, and on the way Jesus himself greets them. The chief priests bribe the guards to claim the disciples stole the body while they slept, a story Matthew says was still circulating in his day. Matthew is answering a charge that was being made against the first believers.
entries.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown, and the women set out as soon as there was light to see (Keener). The cultural backgrounds notes cite Josephus, the Mishnah and Roman law for the limited value given to a woman's testimony, and note that God's messengers entrust the news to women first. Guards who slept on duty faced severe penalties, among Romans even death, bribery was common, and Pilate was known to be open to it (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Tomb robbers in Judea took goods, not bodies (the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener and Wright both note that Matthew would hardly answer a charge that was not being made, and Keener adds that the authorities tried to explain the empty tomb, not to deny it. The theft story was still told nearly a century later (Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 108), and the Nazareth Decree, an inscription threatening death for disturbing tombs, shows how seriously the charge would be taken (Wilkins).

ideas.s: Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.

entries.title: Matthew 28:16-20, Make disciples of all nations
entries.summary: On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus claims all authority in heaven and on earth and sends the eleven to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them.
entries.plain: The eleven meet the risen Jesus on a mountain in Galilee, and they worship him, though some hesitate. He tells them he now holds every kind of authority across heaven and earth, and sends them to every nation to make followers, baptize them in the threefold name and teach them his commands. He promises to stay with them until the close of history. The scene recalls Daniel's vision of a figure given rule over all peoples.
entries.note: God had often revealed himself on mountains, above all to Moses (Keener). Some may have doubted because the dead were expected to rise together at the end, not the Messiah first (Keener). The claim to all authority echoes Daniel 7:13-14, in which a figure like a son of man is given rule over every people (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Only God was thought to be everywhere present, so the promise to be with them always speaks as God speaks (the cultural backgrounds notes). Wilkins notes that Jewish baptism was never performed in a person's name.

ideas.s: Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.

entries.title: Mark 1:1-13, John in the wilderness
entries.summary: John preaches and baptizes at the Jordan, dressed like Elijah. Jesus is baptized, hears the voice from heaven and is driven into the wilderness for forty days.
entries.plain: Mark opens with Isaiah's promise of a voice in the desert and a prophet who fits it. Crowds go out from Judea and Jerusalem to be baptized and confess their sins. Jesus comes from Galilee, is baptized, and is at once sent into the desert to be tested.
entries.note: Josephus also remembers John's baptism, and describes it as a washing for the purification of the body, the soul having first been purified by righteousness. Garland, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, notes that nearly 150 private immersion pools have been found in wealthy Jerusalem houses and that people immersed themselves, so John probably supervised as they went under. An inscription from Priene calls Augustus's birthday the beginning of good tidings for the world (the Zondervan archaeology handbook), and Garland reads Mark's opening word gospel as a challenge to imperial propaganda of good tidings and a new age of peace. The book names no author. Carson, Moo and Morris trace the name to Papias, who reports the elder as saying "Mark became Peter's interpreter", and take him to be almost certainly the John Mark of Acts. Carson, Moo and Morris judge Rome, the place early tradition names, the best choice; Garland finds the choice between Rome and Palestine hard to decide. Most scholars put Mark in the sixties; Garland dates it to AD 68 to 70, reading chapter 13 as written when a Roman legion was about to sack Jerusalem or just had; Carson, Moo and Morris favor the late fifties.

ideas.s: Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.
Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.

entries.title: Mark 1:14-20, Fishermen called
entries.summary: Jesus announces that God's kingdom is near, then calls two pairs of brothers from their nets on the Sea of Galilee.
entries.plain: Once John is in prison, Jesus starts announcing in Galilee that God's long-awaited rule is arriving and calls people to turn and trust it. Beside the lake he summons two pairs of brothers who fish for a living, and they walk away from their work and, in one case, from their father. Mark shows at the outset what following this teacher costs.
entries.note: Keener notes that many scholars think commercial fishermen, though not elite, were usually better off than the peasants who made up most of Galilee, and that hired men point to a family firm with ample income. These men were leaving something. Garland disagrees: owning a boat no more made Zebedee's family well off than owning oxen made a farmer rich; such fishermen leased their fishing rights and probably belonged to a cooperative that sold to wealthier middlemen. He describes the cast net and the trammel net, which could stretch five hundred feet and needed two boats.

ideas.s: Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
Fishing was a real business on the lake of Galilee: boats, costly nets, partnerships between families, work through the night and fish sold in the morning. Fishermen did better than most peasants.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

entries.title: Mark 1:21-45, A Sabbath in Capernaum and a leper
entries.summary: Jesus teaches in the synagogue, drives out a spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and, after sunset, the whole town. Then he touches and cleanses a leper.
entries.plain: Mark packs one Sabbath in Capernaum with teaching, an exorcism and healings, until the whole town gathers at a single house door. The listeners are struck that Jesus teaches on his own authority. Then he touches a leper, a man others kept away from, cleanses him and sends him to the priest for the required check, while telling him to keep quiet.
entries.note: Keener notes that many Capernaum homes were built around courtyards shared with other homes, with extended family living together, which helps explain how the whole town could gather at one door. He estimates Capernaum's population at about 1,500. Keener reads the spirit's claim to know who Jesus is as a possible attempt to ward him off. When Jesus touches the leper, the ESV Study Bible notes, Jesus does not become unclean; the leper becomes clean. Under the limestone synagogue visible at Capernaum, which is later, lies a building of rough basalt that probably marks the synagogue of Jesus' day; Garland gives it 4,838 square feet, the largest of its period. A house a hundred feet south of it, with first-century coins, lamps and fishhooks, may be Peter's, and an open area by its door had room for the town to gather (Garland; the cultural backgrounds article on houses). Garland puts the town at 1,000 to 1,500 people. A leper could attend synagogue behind a screen if he came in first and left last (Garland).

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.
The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

entries.title: Mark 2:13-22, Levi and the party
entries.summary: Jesus calls a tax collector from his booth and eats with tax collectors and sinners. He is questioned about eating with them and about not fasting.
entries.plain: Jesus calls Levi away from his tax booth by the lake, and soon he is at table with a crowd of tax collectors and sinners. Teachers of the law who are Pharisees ask why he eats with such people. Then he is asked why his disciples do not fast, and he answers with a wedding, a patch and wineskins.
entries.note: Keener notes that fasting went with mourning while weddings were for joy, so fasting at a wedding would insult the host. He adds that new wine still fermenting would burst old wineskins already stretched to their limit. Garland places Levi in the service of Herod Antipas, collecting tolls at the border with Philip's territory and perhaps taxes on fishing, and notes that the only fast the law commanded was the Day of Atonement.

ideas.s: Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.

entries.title: Mark 2:23-3:6, Grain and a withered hand on the Sabbath
entries.summary: Jesus defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, heals a man's hand in the synagogue, and the Pharisees start plotting with the Herodians.
entries.plain: Two Sabbath disputes come one after the other. First the disciples pick heads of grain and Jesus answers with David and the holy bread, ending with a saying about the Son of Man and the Sabbath. Then in the synagogue he heals a withered hand, and the Pharisees go out to plan his death with the Herodians.
entries.note: Keener notes that Ahimelek, not his son Abiathar, was chief priest at the time of the story Jesus cites, and that by the first century the title high priest covered anyone in the high-priestly families, as in Josephus; Mark names the era by the better-known son. Matthew and Luke leave out the name. In the synagogue Jesus does not even touch the man, and Keener notes that no one counted an order to stretch out a hand as work. Fields were marked out by stones, not fences, so walking through standing grain was normal (Garland). On the Herodians, Garland mentions a guess that the people used the name for the Essenes, whom Herod favored, while the Zondervan Bible Dictionary takes them as political supporters of Antipas.

Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.

entries.title: Mark 3:13-35, The Twelve, his family and Beelzebul
entries.summary: Jesus appoints twelve. His family thinks he is out of his mind, and teachers from Jerusalem say he drives out demons by Beelzebul.
entries.plain: Jesus chooses twelve men to stay close to him and to go out on his behalf. Back home, his own relatives think he has lost his mind, and teachers from Jerusalem claim he drives out demons by the power of their ruler. Jesus answers that Satan would never fight himself, and he redraws the lines of family around the people who do what God wants.
entries.note: Keener notes that Simon was one of the most popular Jewish names of the day, so a nickname like Peter, meaning rock, helped tell Simons apart. Zealot could mean simply a person known for zeal, though in the next generation it came to mean those who fought foreign rule; the cultural backgrounds chart of Jewish sects dates the Zealots' origin to Herod the Great's reign, and the Zondervan Bible Dictionary reads Cananaean as an Aramaic word for zealot used before it named a party. Keener ties the binding of the strong man to Isaiah 49:25 and sets it apart from magical binding. Iscariot may mean man of Kerioth, which would make Judas a Judean among Galileans (Garland). A later rabbinic tradition says Jesus was executed because he practiced sorcery, which Garland takes as independent evidence that he was known as a wonder worker; the Testament of Solomon names Beelzebul prince of the demons.

ideas.s: Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.

entries.title: Mark 4:1-34, Parables by the lake
entries.summary: From a boat Jesus tells the crowd the sower, the lamp, the growing seed and the mustard seed, and explains them in private.
entries.plain: Jesus teaches a large crowd from a boat, in parables about seed and soil. When he is alone with the Twelve and the others, they ask what the parables mean, and he says the secret of God's kingdom has been given to them. Mark adds that he explained everything privately to his own disciples.
entries.note: Keener notes that scholars do not agree which plant Jesus meant by the mustard seed; on the majority view it is a tiny seed that grows into a shrub of five to ten feet, where birds could perch. Garland reads the verb as to dwell or nest, echoing the great trees of Daniel 4 and Ezekiel 17 and 31, where the birds are the nations; it takes 725 to 760 black mustard seeds to make a gram. He adds that a voice carries better to a crowd from a little distance, which a boat offshore provides. The cultural backgrounds article on parables notes that the Hebrew mashal covered proverb, riddle and story, that Jesus told his parables mostly in story form, a type peculiar to Jewish teaching, and that Jewish parables often came with interpretations, so the explanation of the sower fits its setting.

entries.title: Mark 4:35-41, The storm on the lake
entries.summary: A storm swamps the boat while Jesus sleeps. He rebukes the wind and the sea, and the disciples ask who he is.
entries.plain: Crossing at evening, the disciples hit a violent storm and the boat starts to fill. Jesus is asleep on a cushion in the stern. They wake him, he orders the wind and sea to be still, and the calm frightens them more than the storm did.
entries.note: Keener describes a surviving Galilean fishing boat of the period, about 27 feet long and 7.5 feet wide, with places for four rowers (Garland gives 25.5 by 7.5 by 4.5 feet, carbon dated to between 120 BC and AD 40, with coins of AD 29 to 30 inside and room for a crew of five and ten passengers), and notes that rental contracts excused damage only from acts of God such as storms. Wright hears an echo of Jonah, asleep in a storm, and notes the contrast. Wright reads the calming of the storm as the parables acted out: God's kingdom at hand. The lake lies about 690 feet below sea level (the Zondervan Atlas) and wind funneled down the western valleys can raise waves over seven feet; the cushion was probably a ballast sandbag under the stern deck (Garland).

entries.title: Mark 5:1-20, Legion among the tombs
entries.summary: Across the lake, in Gentile country, Jesus frees a man possessed by many spirits. They enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea.
entries.plain: Jesus lands on the east shore and is met by a man who lives among the tombs and cannot be chained. The spirits in him beg Jesus by God not to torment them, give their name as Legion, and ask to be sent into the pigs. The herd runs into the lake, the townspeople ask Jesus to leave, and the healed man is sent home to tell what God has done.
entries.note: Keener notes that Gerasa lay a good deal further from the lake than Gadara, the town Matthew names, though it was the bigger and more famous of the two, that a region could be named for such a town, and that some suggest Gergesa, modern Kursi, which has a cliff and tombs nearby. Wright adds that even the scribes who copied Mark could not agree on the name. Keener suggests the townspeople may have taken Jesus for a dangerous magician, and Wright calls the man about as unclean as you could get. Garland puts a legion at about 5,400 foot soldiers and 120 horsemen, and notes that the Tenth Legion, which sacked Jerusalem and was then stationed there, bore the image of a wild boar on its standards, so readers after AD 70 may have heard the pigs driven into the sea against that background. The man shows the rabbis' signs of madness, roaming at night, sleeping in tombs, tearing his clothes, and in the Testament of Solomon a demon begs not to be condemned to water (Garland). Pompey had freed the Decapolis cities from Jewish rule, and the league had its own coinage, courts and army (the Zondervan Atlas).

Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Mark 5:21-43, A synagogue leader's daughter and a bleeding woman
entries.summary: On the way to heal Jairus' dying daughter, Jesus is touched by a woman who has bled for twelve years. Then he raises the girl.
entries.plain: Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, falls at Jesus' feet and begs him to come. In the crowd a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak and is healed, and Jesus stops to find her. News comes that the girl has died; Jesus goes in past the mourners, takes her hand and raises her.
entries.note: Keener notes that Jesus speaks to the girl in Aramaic, the mother tongue of most Galileans, and that at twelve she was near the usual minimum age for a girl's marriage; tomb inscriptions often mourned those who died too young to marry. He adds that the woman's condition had probably kept her from marriage or ended it. Keener notes that the woman had been brushing against people in the crowd all along. Garland lists the folk cures the Talmud records for a flow of blood and notes that only the wealthy could afford physicians. The Theodotus inscription from Jerusalem names a synagogue ruler whose father and grandfather held the same office (the Zondervan archaeology handbook).

Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Mark 6:14-29, Herod's banquet and John's death
entries.summary: Herod hears of Jesus and thinks John has risen. Mark then tells how Herod, at his birthday banquet, had John beheaded.
entries.plain: People guess Jesus is John raised, or Elijah, or a prophet. Herod is sure he is John, and Mark explains why: Herod had jailed John for condemning his marriage to Herodias. At a banquet Herodias' daughter dances, Herod swears to give her anything, and at her mother's urging she asks for John's head. Herod does not want to break his oath in front of his guests.
entries.note: Keener notes that beheading was considered the most merciful form of execution because it was quick, and that ancient readers of stories about rulers executing prisoners at banquets as a favor regarded the ruler as wicked. He puts Herodias' daughter between about 12 and 14. Machaerus stood five miles east of the Dead Sea, and archaeologists have found two large dining rooms suitable for a banquet and "a small one where the women would have eaten during the banquet", which fits the girl going out to ask her mother (Garland). Augustus had denied Antipas the title king, and he was later deposed after asking Caligula for it, so Mark's King Herod may be ironic (Garland; the Zondervan Bible Dictionary). The Zondervan Atlas doubts that a birthday banquet was held at Machaerus and prefers the palace at Tiberias. The cultural backgrounds article on Herod's successors adds that Antipas ruled from Sepphoris and later Tiberias until Caligula banished him in AD 39.

Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Mark 6:30-52, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
entries.summary: Jesus feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, then comes to his disciples walking on the lake at night.
entries.plain: Jesus and the disciples try to get away by boat, but the crowd gets there first. He sees them as sheep without a shepherd, teaches them, has them sit on the green grass, and feeds them all with plenty left over. That night the disciples struggle against the wind, and Jesus comes to them on the water and means to pass by them.
entries.note: Keener notes that a crowd of five thousand men was larger than most towns of the region, which marks Jesus as one of the most popular figures in Galilee. On the ghost the disciples think they see, he notes that some ancient people thought that anyone drowned and left unburied haunted the spot as a wandering soul. For the walk on the sea, Keener and the ESV Study Bible both point to Job 9:8 and 9:11, where God tramples the sea and passes by, and the ESV Study Bible notes that the Greek Old Testament of Job 9:8 uses the same words for walking on the sea as Mark 6:48. Two hundred denarii would buy about 2,400 thin loaves (Garland). Philip raised Bethsaida to a city and renamed it Julias, and the coins date the dedication to about AD 30, during Jesus' ministry; the mound of et-Tell now lies almost two miles from the lake, though the shoreline has shifted (Garland). The Zondervan Atlas places the feeding northeast of the lake, near Bethsaida, against the tradition at Tabgha.

ideas.s: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.

entries.title: Mark 7:1-23, Washed hands and the tradition of the elders
entries.summary: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem object that Jesus' disciples eat with unwashed hands. Jesus answers that what defiles comes from inside.
entries.plain: Mark stops to explain the washing customs for readers who do not know them. The visitors ask why the disciples ignore the tradition of the elders; Jesus answers with Isaiah and an example about dedicating money to God instead of supporting parents. Then he tells the crowd that nothing going into a person can make them unclean, and Mark draws the conclusion that all foods are clean.
entries.note: On Corban, Keener notes that property could be vowed to the temple and so made off limits to others, and that some used this to keep from others, including aged parents, what should have cared for them. Wright compares it to a tax accountant finding a loophole. The Letter of Aristeas, older than the first century, already has Jews washing their hands before prayer, and the Essenes immersed their whole bodies before eating (Garland). The Corban vow barred the parents from benefiting from the property while the son kept it (Garland).

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: Mark 7:24-37, A Greek woman and a deaf man
entries.summary: In the region of Tyre a Gentile mother asks Jesus to free her daughter, and answers his saying about dogs. In the Decapolis he heals a deaf man.
entries.plain: Near Tyre, in Gentile territory, a Greek mother begs Jesus to free her daughter from a demon. He answers with a saying about feeding Israel first, and she turns it back on him so deftly that he grants her request. On his way back through the Decapolis he heals a man who could neither hear nor speak clearly, using touch and an Aramaic word.
entries.note: Keener notes that this is the region where God once answered Elijah's prayer for a woman's child (1 Kings 17:9-24). Bailey reads the scene as Jesus deliberately reenacting the Elijah story for the education of his disciples. Josephus calls the people of Tyre bitter enemies of the Jews, and Tyre drew its food from Galilee (Acts 12:20), so the saying about bread lands in a setting of resentment (Garland). Sidon lies about twenty-five miles north of Tyre, and the roundabout route of 7:31 may have kept Jesus out of Antipas's reach (Garland). Suetonius tells of Vespasian healing with his spittle in Alexandria, a sign of the belief that a revered person's saliva could heal (Garland).

Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Mark 8:27-9:1, Peter's answer at Caesarea Philippi
entries.summary: Asked who he is, Peter says the Messiah. Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer, rebukes Peter, and calls followers to take up the cross.
entries.plain: In the villages around Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks what people say about him, then what the disciples say. Peter answers that he is the Messiah, and Jesus tells them to keep quiet. When Jesus starts teaching that he must suffer, be rejected and killed, and rise, Peter rebukes him, and Jesus rebukes Peter in front of the others.
entries.note: Wright notes that anyone growing up in Galilee then knew of holy men who hoped God would deliver Israel and ended up crucified instead. Openly challenging one's teacher, as Peter does in rebuking Jesus, was a serious breach of a disciple's protocol (the cultural backgrounds notes). The ESV Study Bible reads the call to take up the cross as freedom to follow the Messiah, not a martyr complex. Caesarea Philippi lay about 24 miles north of the lake, at the cave of Pan where the Jordan rises, and Herod the Great had built a marble temple to Augustus there; Philip made it his capital (Garland; the cultural backgrounds article on Herod's successors). First Maccabees assumes that no trustworthy prophet was active, so to be counted a prophet was a high claim (Garland). Garland also notes that Qumran and the philosopher Philodemus counted a teacher's harsh rebuke as proper discipline, and that Plutarch says each condemned criminal carries his own cross.

Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: Mark 9:2-13, The transfiguration
entries.summary: On a high mountain Jesus is changed before three disciples, Elijah and Moses appear, and a voice says to listen to him. Coming down, they ask about Elijah.
entries.plain: Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, and his clothes turn dazzling white. Elijah and Moses talk with him, a cloud covers them, and a voice calls him the beloved Son. On the way down the disciples ask why the teachers say Elijah must come first, and Jesus answers that Elijah has come, and been treated as people wished.
entries.note: Mark does not name the mountain: Wright and the ESV Study Bible think it was probably Mount Hermon, Heiser argues for Hermon at length, and both Wright and Heiser note that Mount Tabor, the traditional site, still has defenders. On the meaning, the ESV Study Bible calls the scene a glimpse into Jesus' divine nature, while Wright says it is not a revelation of his divinity, since that would make Elijah and Moses divine too, but a sign that he is the true prophet and Messiah. Keener and Wright both take the Elijah who has already come to be John. Garland adds two points against Tabor, a Roman camp on its summit and its modest height (about 1,843 feet against Hermon's 9,166), and the Zondervan Atlas rates the Hermon area strongest. A Targum on Exodus 24 has Nadab and Abihu struck down for seeing God's glory, which Garland reads behind Peter's offer of shelters.

entries.title: Mark 10:32-45, James and John ask for the best seats
entries.summary: On the road to Jerusalem Jesus predicts his death a third time. James and John ask to sit at his right and left, and he tells them the first must be slave of all.
entries.plain: On the road to Jerusalem Jesus lays out in detail the suffering and death waiting for him there, and his rising afterward. Right after that, James and John ask for the top places beside him. Jesus turns their request upside down: greatness among his followers means serving, and his own mission is to serve others and lay down his life so that many go free.
entries.note: Keener notes that the prophets used a cup as a picture of suffering, usually as God's judgment (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15-17), and that it points here to Jesus' death. Wright points out that the places at his right and left in 15:27 go to two crucified bandits. When Vitellius accepted the title of emperor in AD 68, he seated his generals on either side of his chair (Garland). Seneca wrote that a slave has no right to refuse, and 4 Maccabees treats the martyrs' deaths as atoning for the nation (Garland).

ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

entries.title: Mark 11:1-11, The ride into Jerusalem
entries.summary: Jesus sends for a colt no one has ridden and rides into Jerusalem over cloaks and branches while the crowd shouts Hosanna.
entries.plain: Near Bethphage and Bethany, Jesus sends two disciples for a colt, with the words that the Lord needs it. He rides toward the city while people spread their cloaks and cut branches, shouting blessings on the one who comes and on the coming kingdom of David. He goes into the temple, looks around, and goes back to Bethany for the night.
entries.note: Keener places Bethphage about three quarters of a mile east of the top of the Mount of Olives and Bethany about two miles east of Jerusalem, and notes that getting back to the village before dark mattered. Wright reads the climb from Jericho to the Mount of Olives as a long climb through the Judaean wilderness that was, for the pilgrims, the climb to the kingdom. Each detail, the colt no one had ridden, the cloaks, the branches and the shout about David's kingdom, belonged to the greeting of a king (Keener's notes). The Mishnah says no one else may ride a king's mount, men spread their garments under Jehu when he was proclaimed king (2 Kings 9:13), and Simon Maccabee entered Jerusalem with palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51) (Garland). Bethphage means house of early or unripe figs (Garland; Wilkins). Distances differ a little: the Zondervan Atlas puts Bethany about a mile and a half from Jerusalem. The cultural backgrounds map of Passion Week sets the entry on Sunday, the clearing of the temple on Monday, and the debates on Tuesday.

ideas.s: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

entries.title: Mark 11:12-25, The fig tree and the temple
entries.summary: Jesus curses a leafy fig tree with no fruit, overturns the tables in the temple, and the next morning the tree has withered.
entries.plain: Mark frames the temple scene with the story of a fig tree, so the reader takes the two together. Jesus curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit, then disrupts the trade in the temple courts, and the next morning the tree is dead. The temple leaders now want him dead too.
entries.note: Keener notes that near the Mount of Olives fig trees could be in leaf at Passover with only green early figs, and a tree with leaves but no early figs would stay fruitless that year; he reads the curse as an acted parable framing the protest in the temple. The ESV Study Bible notes that the fig tree often stands for Israel in the Old Testament. Garland and Wilkins put the market in the Royal Stoa, a hall of 162 columns on the south side of the courts, not across the whole outer court. Money changers set up three weeks before Passover for the half-shekel tax, paid in Tyrian shekels bearing the god Melkart and an eagle (Garland). The cultural backgrounds article on Herod's temple gives the courts' dimensions, about 1,590 feet on the west side, and notes that the Sanhedrin's hall and a ritual bath lay to the south. Josephus tells of Jesus son of Ananus, whom the city's leaders handed to the governor for crying woe on the temple (Garland).

entries.title: Mark 12:13-17, The coin with Caesar's face
entries.summary: Pharisees and Herodians ask whether it is right to pay tax to Caesar. Jesus asks for a coin and asks whose image is on it.
entries.plain: After flattering him, the questioners set a trap: pay the tax and lose the crowd, or refuse it and be reported to Rome. Jesus has them bring him a denarius and asks whose face and inscription it carries. They say Caesar's, and he tells them to give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's.
entries.note: Keener notes that this coin and the tax behind it had sparked a revolt about a quarter century earlier. Wright, who owns a coin of this type, notes that its inscriptions call Tiberius son of the divine Augustus and high priest, and says that if the Romans had set out to offend the Jews they could hardly have done better. Judea became a province in AD 6 and paid the poll tax on the basis of the census; the reverse of the denarius showed a seated woman, Livia or a priestess, standing for the Roman peace (Garland). The word for the tax is the Roman poll tax (the Zondervan Bible Dictionary).

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Mark 13:1-37, The temple's fall and the Son of Man
entries.summary: Leaving the temple, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he warns of what is coming and of the Son of Man on the clouds.
entries.plain: When a disciple admires the temple's great stones, Jesus predicts that it will be torn down completely. Asked when, he warns four of his disciples about impostors, wars, persecution and a crisis that will send people fleeing from Judea, and he speaks of the Son of Man's arrival in power. His last word is to keep watch, because nobody knows when it will happen.
entries.note: Keener notes that Josephus reports a number of false prophets in the decades before AD 70 who tried to imitate Moses or Joshua, and that the temple fell about forty years after Jesus spoke, the rough length often used for a biblical generation. Teachers normally lectured sitting, which is how Jesus gives this teaching. The cultural backgrounds article on Herod's temple dates the work from 20 to 19 BC, with adornment continuing until AD 63. Josephus, the article on the fall of Jerusalem notes, began the war as a rebel leader, changed sides and watched the siege from Titus's camp: the outer wall fell around May of AD 70 and the temple at the end of August. In the ruins archaeologists found the Burnt House, with rebel coins of 67 to 69 and none later, and a woman's arm bones (Garland; the cultural backgrounds article on houses). The temple mount walls rose about 165 feet (Garland). Garland notes that the participle of 13:14 is masculine, making the abomination a person, and that let the reader understand may be a word to the one reading Mark aloud.

The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

entries.title: Mark 14:1-11, Perfume at Bethany
entries.summary: Two days before Passover, at dinner in Bethany, a woman pours costly perfume on Jesus' head. He says she has anointed him for burial, and Judas goes to the chief priests.
entries.plain: The chief priests want Jesus dead but not during the feast. At Simon the leper's house a woman breaks a jar of pure nard over his head, and some at the table are angry at the waste. Jesus defends her, says she has prepared his body for burial, and promises her story will be told wherever the gospel goes. Judas then offers to hand him over.
entries.note: Keener notes that because lepers were unclean and contact with them was discouraged, Simon the leper may have been someone already healed. He notes that ancient writers used similar language about fame spreading through the world, but this woman's story really is told around the world. Guests could be given oil as a courtesy, kings were anointed on the head, and Jesus says she has anointed him for burial, so all three meanings sit in one act (Keener's notes). Garland estimates that 85,000 to 300,000 pilgrims came to a city that normally held 25,000 to 30,000, most of them sleeping in tents or in nearby towns. Alabaster flasks were five to nine inches high, nard came from India, and three hundred denarii was nearly a year's wage (Garland).

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.

entries.title: Mark 14:12-31, The Passover meal
entries.summary: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve, names a betrayer at the table, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and warns that all will scatter.
entries.plain: Two disciples follow a man carrying a water jar to a large upstairs room. At the meal Jesus says one who eats with him will betray him. He takes bread and a cup and speaks of his body and of his blood of the covenant. On the way to the Mount of Olives he quotes Zechariah, the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered, and tells Peter he will deny him three times.
entries.note: Keener notes that women usually carried water jars, which made the man easy to follow, and that a room big enough for all the disciples points to the wealthier upper city. On blood of the covenant he points to Exodus 24:8 and notes that the thought of drinking blood revolted Jewish people, so the words are not literal. Passover custom had people stay up late retelling God's acts of rescue, so when the disciples later fall asleep in Gethsemane (14:37-41), it is on the night they were meant to keep awake (Keener's notes). Garland cautions that the Passover rites known from the Mishnah developed after the temple fell and may not have been the custom in Jesus' day, so the hymn of 14:26 need not be the Hallel. The cockcrow may mean the Roman trumpet at the end of the third watch, though Garland prefers a real bird. The Synoptic Gospels make this a Passover meal on Nisan 15 while John 18:28 may put the death on Nisan 14; Carson, Moo and Morris name April 7, AD 30, and April 3, AD 33, as the likeliest dates.

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: Mark 14:32-52, Gethsemane and the arrest
entries.summary: At a place called Gethsemane Jesus prays in anguish while three disciples sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd from the chief priests, greets him with a kiss, and the disciples run.
entries.plain: After the meal Jesus takes his disciples to a place on the Mount of Olives called Gethsemane. He falls to the ground and asks his Father to take the cup from him, yet asks for the Father's will, while Peter, James and John keep falling asleep. Judas comes with a crowd carrying swords and clubs and marks Jesus out with a kiss. One of those standing by cuts off a servant's ear, Jesus asks why they come for him as for a bandit, and everyone flees, a young man leaving his linen cloth behind.
entries.note: Gethsemane means oil press, and Mark calls it only a place. Wilkins names the olive grove and the press cave as the two candidates; Garland reports Taylor's case for a cave beside the Church of All Nations that stood idle in spring, warm and dry on a chilly night. The sources differ on Abba. Keener's background commentary renders it Papa, a word of great intimacy that Jews did not use of God except in an occasional parable; Garland agrees that no individual is known to have addressed God this way before Jesus but says it does not mean Daddy, since Mark translates it with the ordinary word for father and disciples used it of an esteemed teacher. Keener takes the armed band as the temple guard; Wilkins thinks Roman soldiers assigned to the temple were among them. The sources also differ on the word Jesus uses at 14:48, robber or bandit: Keener calls it Josephus's standard term for revolutionaries, while Garland, citing another scholar, says Josephus used it for social bandits who preyed on the rich and never for a revolutionary against Rome. Jews generally abhorred nakedness (Keener).

ideas.s: Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

entries.title: Mark 14:53-72, At the high priest's house
entries.summary: The council tries Jesus at night. He says he is the Messiah and quotes the Son of Man coming with the clouds, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter denies him in the courtyard.
entries.plain: Mark sets two scenes side by side. Inside, false witnesses cannot agree, the high priest asks Jesus if he is the Messiah, Jesus says I am and speaks of the Son of Man at the right hand of power, and the council condemns him. Outside, a servant girl recognizes Peter, and he denies knowing Jesus three times before the rooster crows.
entries.note: Keener notes that Peter's curses and oath called on a deity as witness and avenger of any false oath, and that denying knowledge of a person insulted that person. Judeans, he notes on Matthew, thought Galileans did not pronounce their gutturals properly, and would tie Peter to his Galilean teacher. The Caiaphas ossuary, inscribed Joseph son of Caiaphas, held the bones of a man of about sixty, and Caiaphas kept office from AD 18 to 36 where Gratus had removed four high priests (Garland). The trial rules in Mishnah Sanhedrin were compiled around AD 220 and are idealized, so they say little about first-century procedure (Garland; the cultural backgrounds article on Jesus' trial, which adds that the hearing may only have framed a charge for Pilate). Under that later rule blasphemy required pronouncing the divine Name (m. Sanhedrin 7:5). A Talmud story mocks a Galilean whose word could mean ass, wine, wool or lamb, and the verb for Peter's curse has no object, so he may be cursing Jesus, as Pliny later made suspected Christians do (Garland).

Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.

entries.title: Mark 15:1-20, Before Pilate
entries.summary: The chief priests hand Jesus to Pilate as king of the Jews. Pilate releases Barabbas to the crowd, has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as a king.
entries.plain: The council hands Jesus over to Pilate, the Roman governor, and the question becomes political: is he a king? Jesus barely answers. Offered a choice of prisoner to free, the crowd, urged on by the chief priests, picks Barabbas, and Pilate gives in, has Jesus flogged and sends him off to be crucified. The soldiers then stage a mock coronation.
entries.note: Keener notes that most of Jesus' followers were Galileans, and a Judean crowd would be more easily swayed by the chief priests. Customs of releasing a prisoner existed in various places, and governors often kept their predecessors' customs though no law required it. The soldiers then repeat a king's greeting as a joke, purple, a crown, the cry Hail and kneeling (Keener's notes; Wright). An inscription found at Caesarea calls Pilate prefect, not procurator, and he owed his post to Sejanus, whose fall in AD 31 left him exposed to Jewish complaints in Rome (Garland; the Zondervan archaeology handbook). A papyrus of AD 85 has the prefect of Egypt tell a prisoner, I will give you to the people, and the Mishnah allows a Passover lamb to be slaughtered for one promised release from prison (Garland). The praetorium was probably Herod's palace, not the Antonia (Garland; the Zondervan Bible Dictionary).

Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.

entries.title: Mark 15:21-41, The cross
entries.summary: Jesus is crucified as king of the Jews between two bandits, mocked by passers-by, and dies with a loud cry. The temple curtain tears, and women watch from a distance.
entries.plain: A man from Cyrene is made to carry the cross, and Jesus is crucified under a notice naming his crime as being king of the Jews. Onlookers jeer, and in the afternoon he cries out with the opening of Psalm 22 and dies. A Roman centurion watching him die calls him God's Son, while women who had come with him from Galilee watch from a distance.
entries.note: Keener notes that Psalm 22 begins in abandonment and ends in God's vindication, and that Mark gives the cry in Aramaic, Eloi, where the psalm has Hebrew Eli. Gentiles called many figures, heroes and the emperor among them, sons of gods; Garland narrows this, since son of god was Augustus's title as the adopted son of the deified Caesar, "not a title applied to emperors in general"; Keener reads the centurion as seeing in Jesus the son of Israel's one God. Keener notes that the charge on the cross, King of the Jews, is the climax of Mark's preaching of the kingdom, and Wright notes that the bystanders think Jesus is still waiting for Elijah, when Elijah has already come. An ossuary inscribed Alexander son of Simon has been found in Jerusalem, and Golgotha was probably an abandoned quarry outside the Gennath Gate (Garland). The only crucified man's bones yet found are Jehohanan's, from Giv'at ha-Mivtar, crucified between AD 7 and 66 (Garland). The Mishnah makes the temple veil a handbreadth thick (Garland).

Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Mark 15:42-16:8, The tomb
entries.summary: Joseph of Arimathea buries Jesus before the Sabbath. When it is over, the women come with spices, find the stone rolled away, and hear that he has been raised.
entries.plain: With the Sabbath coming at sundown, Joseph, a council member, dares to ask Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen and lays it in a rock tomb. Two of the women see where. After the Sabbath three women bring spices to anoint him, wondering who will move the stone. A young man in white tells them Jesus has risen and is going ahead to Galilee, and they run from the tomb afraid and tell no one.
entries.note: The best manuscripts end at 16:8, and the sources disagree about why. Wright is convinced the original ending was lost, a torn last page or column; Bailey argues that 16:1-8 completes the same seven-part pattern as the burial account, so no lost final page is needed, and Garland calls theories of a lost ending unhelpful and reads the abrupt close as intended. The Garden Tomb was cut in the eighth or seventh century BC, so it cannot be the new tomb of 15:46 (Garland; the cultural backgrounds article on the tomb's location), and the Holy Sepulchre has a tradition reaching back before Constantine. Philo protests that the prefect Flaccus left executed Jews on their crosses, when on a festival the crucified were usually taken down and given to their kin (Garland). The cultural backgrounds map of Passion Week has the body in the tomb before six on Friday evening, when the Sabbath began.

ideas.s: The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.

entries.title: Luke 1:5-25, A priest's turn at the incense altar
entries.summary: An elderly village priest, picked by lot to offer incense in the sanctuary, learns from the angel Gabriel that his childless wife will have a son who will prepare Israel for God with an Elijah-like power.
entries.plain: Zechariah and Elizabeth are righteous, old and childless. While his division is on duty, the lot falls to Zechariah to burn incense inside the sanctuary as the people pray outside. Gabriel appears beside the altar, promises a son to be named John, and leaves Zechariah unable to speak when he asks for proof. Elizabeth conceives and says the Lord has taken away her disgrace.
entries.note: The incense was burned at the hours of the morning and evening sacrifice, which is why a crowd is praying outside (Keener and his notes). Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, adds that with so many priests the privilege may have come once in a lifetime, and that John's abstinence is probably a Nazirite vow, lifelong here. Whether Zechariah was deaf as well as mute is unclear: the ESV Study Bible thinks he probably was, since people make signs to him in 1:62, while Keener notes that the word can include deafness but need not. Luke names no author. Early tradition and the we passages of Acts point to Luke, the physician of Colossians 4:14, probably a Gentile (Carson, Moo and Morris; Strauss). Where Luke wrote is unknown. Some scholars put the Gospel in AD 75 to 85, after Jerusalem's fall; Carson, Moo and Morris favor the early sixties, since Acts leaves Paul in prison, and Strauss the late fifties or early sixties. Theophilus was probably a real patron of rank (Carson, Moo and Morris; Strauss; the Zondervan Bible dictionary), though his name, lover of God, has led some to read the book as addressed to every godly reader (Strauss).

ideas.s: Israel's ordinary priests were divided into twenty-four courses that took turns at the temple, a week at a time. Most lived in the country and came up to Jerusalem when their turn came round.

entries.title: Luke 1:26-56, A village girl, a greeting and a song of reversal
entries.summary: Gabriel greets Mary, a betrothed girl in Nazareth, with news that she will bear the son of David. She goes to Elizabeth in the hill country and sings of God bringing down rulers and lifting up the humble.
entries.plain: Gabriel visits Mary, a young woman of Nazareth promised in marriage to Joseph, a descendant of David, and announces a son who will rule David's kingdom without end. Mary asks how this can happen to a virgin, hears that God's Spirit and power will bring it about, and agrees. She then visits her relative Elizabeth, whose own unborn son stirs at her arrival, and Mary answers with a song about God overturning the powerful and raising up the poor.
entries.note: Nazareth was a lowly village beside Jerusalem's great building projects, and its size is disputed: Keener's background commentary estimates sixteen hundred to two thousand people, while his notes say many scholars think it had only a few hundred. It is never named in the Old Testament or in the Jewish writings of the day; the first inscription to mention it, found at Caesarea Maritima in 1962, puts the eighteenth priestly course in Nazareth (Strauss). The greeting is itself a surprise. Rank decided who greeted whom and with what words, and a young, unmarried village girl had virtually no standing (Keener and his notes); Strauss adds that a girl was usually betrothed between twelve and fourteen. The trip to the Judean hill country took three to five days, and with bandits on the roads Mary would not have gone alone (Keener). Her song closely resembles Hannah's in 1 Samuel 2, down to the word for the rulers brought down in 1:52 (Keener; Wright; the cultural backgrounds article on Mary's song), and many Jews expected the lowly to be raised and the proud brought low at the end (Keener's notes). Wright says the song is about God and about revolution.

A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.

entries.title: Luke 2:1-7, A census and a manger
entries.summary: Augustus orders a registration, and Joseph takes the pregnant Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the town of David. She gives birth there and lays the child in a manger, because there is no room for them in the lodging.
entries.plain: A decree from Caesar Augustus sends everyone to be registered in their own town, and Luke dates it by Quirinius, governor of Syria. Joseph, of David's family, goes up from Nazareth to Bethlehem with Mary. While they are there her time comes; she wraps her firstborn son in strips of cloth and lays him in a feeding trough, because there is no room for them in the katalyma, a word translated inn, lodging or guest room.
entries.note: Egyptian census records show people registering where they owned property, not where they were born, so Joseph probably still held property in Bethlehem (Keener and his notes). The date is disputed. Josephus describes Quirinius's census in Judea after Archelaus was removed; that census of AD 6 came after Herod's death, while Jesus was born in Herod's reign (the ESV Study Bible). Strauss lists four answers: inscriptions suggesting Quirinius governed Syria twice, first in 10 to 7 BC (the CSB Study Bible has 6 to 4 BC, and the ESV Study Bible says the idea of two terms lacks confirming evidence); an earlier command over the east; Quirinius finishing a predecessor's census; or the reading before Quirinius. Keener reads an earlier census under Herod; his notes report the views that Luke confused or deliberately joined the two. Strauss concludes the evidence cannot decide for or against Luke, and Carson, Moo and Morris that "the census does not help us date the birth of Jesus". Bailey argues from 2:6 that the birth came some time after the couple arrived. The katalyma was a guest room or informal shelter, not an inn, since Luke uses another word for the inn of 10:34 (Strauss).

entries.title: Luke 2:8-20, Shepherds hear of a savior
entries.summary: Angels announce to shepherds in the fields near Bethlehem the birth of a savior who is Christ the Lord, and the shepherds find the child lying in a manger as they were told.
entries.plain: Luke sends the first news of the birth to shepherds working through the night outside Bethlehem, not to anyone of rank. An angel tells the frightened men that a savior, the Messiah and Lord, has been born in David's town, and that they will know him by a newborn lying in a feeding trough. A crowd of heavenly beings joins in praise, and the shepherds go, find the family, and tell everyone what they were told.
entries.note: Flocks out at night point to a warmer season; Strauss puts it at about March to November, and Keener notes that Christians at Rome later fixed December 25 to replace a pagan festival held then. Wright reminds readers that Luke has just named Augustus, who claimed to have brought justice and peace to the world and was called savior and lord; now angels announce a savior, a Lord and peace for someone else. Strauss cites an inscription from Priene that calls Augustus savior and says "the birth date of our God has signaled the beginning of good news" for the world. Bailey reads the manger as a sign meant for shepherds in particular: a baby wrapped as peasants wrapped theirs and lying in a manger would be in a peasant home like their own, where they could expect a welcome rather than a closed door. How the shepherds were seen is disputed: the cultural backgrounds article Caesar and Christ calls them lowly and often despised, while Strauss agrees they were lower class but notes that the picture of dishonest shepherds comes from later rabbinic writings and that the Bible's portrait is almost always positive.

ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Luke 2:21-40, Two birds, Simeon and Anna
entries.summary: Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day. At the temple his parents make the offering the law allowed the poor, and two old people waiting for God's comfort, Simeon and the widow Anna, speak about the child.
entries.plain: On the eighth day the child is circumcised and named Jesus. When the days of purification are over, Mary and Joseph bring him to the temple and offer two birds, as the law required. Simeon, a righteous man on whom the Holy Spirit rests, takes the child in his arms and blesses God for letting him see the salvation promised for Israel and the nations. Anna, a prophetess and widow of great age who never leaves the temple, speaks about the child to everyone waiting for Jerusalem's redemption.
entries.note: Two doves or pigeons were the offering Leviticus 12:8 allowed to those who could not afford a lamb, so the family was poor or of modest means (Keener's notes; the ESV Study Bible). The meeting with Simeon would take place in the Court of Women (Keener). The consolation of Israel was the comfort God had promised in Isaiah (Isaiah 40:1; 49:13), his coming to rescue his people (Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Anna's name is the Hebrew Hannah (Keener). The forty days were seven before the circumcision and thirty-three after (Leviticus 12), and firstborn sons were redeemed for five shekels; since Luke never mentions the payment, some scholars think Jesus, like Samuel, was wholly given to God (Strauss). Anna's tribe, Asher, was a northern one, which shows that members of the northern tribes kept their identity through the exile (Strauss). The Greek leaves open whether she was eighty-four or had been a widow eighty-four years, and Strauss notes that the pious widow who stayed single for God was a familiar figure, from Judith to Antonia, the widow of Drusus, whom Josephus praises.

Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.

entries.title: Luke 2:41-52, A twelve-year-old among the teachers
entries.summary: On the family's yearly Passover pilgrimage the twelve-year-old Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem, and after three days his parents find him in the temple courts among the teachers.
entries.plain: Joseph and Mary make the yearly Passover trip to Jerusalem, and on the way home they realise their twelve-year-old is missing from the travelling party. They search for three days and finally discover him at the temple, seated with the teachers, hearing them out and putting questions, while his replies astonish the listeners. He tells his parents that he belonged in his Father's house, then returns to Nazareth and lives under their authority.
entries.note: The law required the pilgrimage (Deuteronomy 16:6), though Jews living far away could not come every year, and women were not always required to attend, so Mary's going with Joseph shows the family's piety (Keener; Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). A boy took on the law's obligations at about thirteen; the bar mitzvah ceremony itself came later (Keener; Strauss; the cultural backgrounds notes). Pilgrims traveled in caravans, often whole villages together, with neighbors watching the community's children, which is how his parents could assume he was elsewhere in the group (Keener and his notes; Strauss). The distance was about eighty miles by the route around Samaria, a little over three days on foot (Strauss; Keener). Some teachers held classes in the temple courts, and learning went by question and counter-question (Keener; Strauss). Ancient biographers liked stories of a child prodigy, and Josephus says the chief priests consulted him at about fourteen (Strauss; Keener). The obedience of 2:51 matters in a culture that counted honoring parents among the greatest commandments, and the last verse echoes the boy Samuel growing in favor with God and people (1 Samuel 2:26; Keener and his notes; Strauss).

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

entries.title: Luke 3:1-20, John's answers for toll men and soldiers
entries.summary: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius, John preaches repentance around the Jordan. He tells the crowds to share, tax collectors to take no more than is set, and soldiers not to extort, and Herod Antipas shuts him in prison.
entries.plain: Luke fixes the start of John's work against the names of the emperor, the governor, the local rulers and the high priests of the day. John calls people to be baptized as a sign of turning back to God, and gives practical answers: share spare clothing and food, toll collectors should take only what is due, and soldiers should stop squeezing people for money. He says someone stronger is coming who will baptize with Spirit and fire, and Herod Antipas jails him after John condemns his marriage to his brother's wife.
entries.note: How to count the fifteenth year of Tiberius is debated: from Augustus's death in AD 14 it gives AD 27 to 29, and from Tiberius's joint rule with Augustus in AD 11 or 12 it gives AD 25 to 27; Strauss and Carson, Moo and Morris think the later reckoning, about AD 28 or 29, most likely. Annas had been high priest until the governor deposed him in AD 15, but he kept the title and his influence, and Caiaphas, probably his son-in-law, held the office from AD 18 to 36 (Keener's notes). Keener thinks the soldiers were Syrian auxiliaries serving Rome; Wright thinks Herod's own troops more likely, and Strauss agrees: probably Jewish troops in Antipas's service, perhaps guarding the tax collectors. Strauss doubts that John modeled his rite on the immersion of converts, since the Talmudic evidence for it is late. Antipas had divorced the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV to marry Herodias. Luke ties the arrest to John's rebuke; Josephus says Herod feared "the great influence John had over the people might put it into his power and inclination to raise a rebellion"; Keener suggests Herod heard moral preaching as a political statement.
