ideas.s: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.

entries.title: Luke 4:1-13, The devil offers the kingdoms
entries.summary: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led through the wilderness for forty days, where the devil tests him with bread, with all the kingdoms of the world, and with a leap from the temple.
entries.plain: Fresh from his baptism, Jesus spends forty days without food in the wilderness under the Spirit's leading, and the devil tests him three times. He suggests turning a stone into bread, offers rule over every nation on the claim that it is his to give, and finally places Jesus on a high point of the temple and dares him to jump. Each time Jesus answers with a passage from Scripture, and the devil withdraws to wait for another chance.
entries.note: Forty days in the wilderness recall Israel's forty years in Deuteronomy 8:2, and every one of Jesus' answers comes from that part of Deuteronomy (Keener's notes). Some magicians claimed they could turn one material into another. The devil's claim to delegated authority over the world fits Jewish ideas of his rule over the wicked nations, but the authority to delegate belonged in the end to God (Keener's notes). Keener's background commentary adds that Luke and his first readers would have taken the devil as a literal, personal being. Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, notes that Luke's word for the world in 4:5 is the one often used of the Roman empire, which gives the offer a political edge, and that the Caesars made the same boast: Nero once said, "I have the power to take away kingdoms and to bestow them." The highest point of the temple is traditionally the Royal Portico at the southeast corner, above the Kidron Valley, whose dizzying height Josephus describes, and a later rabbinic tradition, perhaps not as old as the first century, says the Messiah will reveal himself standing on the temple roof (Strauss).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 4:1-2, 4:3, 4:4 and 4:6
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 4:1-13
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 4:5, 4:6 and 4:9

ideas.s: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.

entries.title: Luke 4:16-30, The year of the Lord's favor in Nazareth
entries.summary: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah's promise of good news for the poor and release for captives and says it is fulfilled today. When he points to Elijah and Elisha helping foreigners, the town tries to throw him off a cliff.
entries.plain: In the Nazareth synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus reads from Isaiah a passage about one anointed by the Spirit to bring good news to the poor, freedom to prisoners and sight to the blind, announcing a time of God's favor. He sits and tells the room that the passage is being fulfilled as they listen. Their warmth turns to rage when he reminds them that Elijah and Elisha were sent to foreigners rather than to Israel, and they try to throw him off a cliff, but he passes through the crowd and goes.
entries.note: Readers stood to read Scripture and sat to explain it (Keener and his notes). Isaiah 61 pictures the year of jubilee, the year of release in Leviticus 25, and the Dead Sea Scrolls read it that way (Keener). Bailey notes what Jesus leaves out, the line about binding up the brokenhearted and the closing day of vengeance of our God, and what he adds, a line from Isaiah 58:6. Why the crowd turned is debated. Keener points to the word today, since Nazareth saw no messianic age around it, and to the region's caution after the Romans destroyed nearby Sepphoris, which he dates to a revolt in AD 6; Josephus tells of Sepphoris burned in Varus' campaign after Herod's death. Bailey, with Jeremias, finds the rage in the missing vengeance on the nations, and reports Ibn al-Tayyib's view that it was envy of a carpenter's son; Wright puts it down to God being shown rescuing foreigners instead of Israel, and Strauss sides with him. A mob had no right to carry out an execution, least of all on the Sabbath (Keener). There is no obvious cliff just outside Nazareth, though the hills offer several plausible places (Strauss).

Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 4:18-19, 4:20, 4:21-22, 4:25-27 and 4:28-29

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.

entries.title: Luke 5:1-11, A catch that breaks the nets
entries.summary: Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, then tells the tired fishermen to let down their nets in deep water. The catch nearly sinks two boats, and Simon, James and John leave everything to follow him.
entries.plain: Jesus teaches the crowd at the lake from Simon's boat, then tells the tired fisherman, who has caught nothing all night, to head further out and try again. The haul is so large that the nets start to split and a second boat is needed, and both boats ride dangerously low. Simon drops to his knees and confesses that he is a sinner, and Jesus tells him that from now on he will gather people; Simon and his partners abandon everything to go with him.
entries.note: The shore worked like an amphitheater, and a cove near Capernaum could carry a voice to a large crowd, so speaking from a boat a little offshore made Jesus easier to hear (Keener and his notes). Keener notes that a fisherman might trust a rabbi on religion but had no need to in his own trade, which makes Simon's obedience stand out. Bailey reads the scene as Jesus asking tired fishermen for help before offering them anything: he needs their boat. Simon's cry recalls Isaiah's response to God's holiness at his call (Isaiah 6:5; Keener's notes). Leaving the business cost them a better than average living (Keener). Luke calls the water a lake, as Josephus does, where Matthew and Mark say sea, and a first-century fishing boat has been excavated near Kibbutz Ginosar on its shore (Strauss). The nets of 5:5 were probably long nets on floats for night fishing in deep water, not the round casting net of the shallows or the dragnet pulled between two boats. Partners is a business word, and fishermen often worked in cooperatives; Zebedee's hired men in Mark 1:20 point to a fairly successful business (Strauss).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 5:3, 5:4-5 and 5:11
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 5:3, 5:8 and 5:11
Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, ch. 11, The Call of Peter
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 5:1, 5:3, 5:5 and 5:7

ideas.s: To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
Fishing was a real business on the lake of Galilee: boats, costly nets, partnerships between families, work through the night and fish sold in the morning. Fishermen did better than most peasants.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: Luke 5:17-39, Through the roof, then a feast with toll men
entries.summary: Friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof and Jesus forgives his sins. Then Levi leaves his tax booth and gives a banquet for Jesus with other tax collectors, and Jesus is asked why his disciples do not fast.
entries.plain: With Pharisees and legal experts gathered from across the region, a group of friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof, and Jesus declares his sins forgiven, then heals him to show he has the authority to do so. Jesus then calls Levi away from his toll booth, and Levi throws a large dinner for his colleagues and other outsiders. Challenged about the company he keeps and why his followers feast instead of fasting, Jesus compares himself to a doctor who comes for the sick and to a bridegroom whose guests celebrate while he is present.
entries.note: Luke has the man let down through the tiles where Mark says they dug through the roof. Garland, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, explains Mark's picture: Capernaum's roofs of beams, reeds, palm branches and dried mud were re-laid every autumn, so digging through did no lasting harm. Strauss thinks Luke may be putting it in terms his Greek readers knew, though tile roofs were also in use in the land by then. Most people assumed that sin had to be forgiven before healing could come; the Talmud says a sick man "does not recover from his sickness until all his sins are forgiven him" (Garland). Whether the charge of blasphemy held is disputed. Keener notes that strictly it meant pronouncing God's name, and the Mishnah agrees; Strauss notes that blasphemy was elsewhere taken more widely as anything that dishonored God's name or authority, and Garland that only a priest could declare sins forgiven. A scrupulous Pharisee would not eat in a common Israelite's home, unsure whether the food was clean and tithed (Strauss). Pharisees often fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays, and fasting during a wedding was not allowed (Keener; Strauss).

NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 5:17 and 5:34-35

Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 5:19, 5:21, 5:30, 5:33 and 5:34

ideas.s: Most village families lived in one main room, with a lower end by the door where the animals spent the night, a flat roof of beams, branches and mud, and sometimes a guest room on the roof or built on at the end.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
Going without food, and often washing and oil, as a sign of mourning, penitence and longing. The law required one fast a year; the devout kept many more.

entries.title: Luke 6:20-36, Blessings, woes and lending with nothing back
entries.summary: Jesus blesses the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated, pronounces woes on the rich and the well fed, and tells his hearers to love enemies, turn the other cheek and lend without expecting anything back.
entries.plain: Jesus turns to his followers and pronounces God's blessing on the poor, the hungry, the grieving and the hated, promising them the kingdom and a reversal of their state. He matches each blessing with a warning to the wealthy, the well fed, the carefree and the popular. He then calls for love of enemies, for not hitting back, for giving freely and for lending without expecting repayment, because that is how God himself treats the thankless.
entries.note: The poor had become a name for the pious in some Jewish circles, and one Aramaic word may stand behind both Luke's poor and Matthew's poor in spirit (Keener and his notes); the ESV Study Bible reads Luke's poor as those poor in things who trust God. Many Jews expected a reversal of status at the end, the lowly raised and the exalted brought low (Keener and his notes). The backhanded blow on the right cheek was an insult to honor that could be taken to court, and the coat was the one thing a creditor could not legally seize (Exodus 22:26-27; Keener's notes). The usual rule was to harm enemies and help friends, as the Greek orator Lysias put it, and the Qumran scroll that tells its members to leave vengeance to God also tells them to detest the sons of darkness (Strauss). The Golden Rule was known in other forms, from Seneca to Hillel, who said, "What is hateful to you, do not do to anyone else" (Strauss). Because the law canceled debts in the seventh year, the rich were slow to lend as it came near (Deuteronomy 15:9; Strauss).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 6:20, 6:21, 6:29 and 6:34
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 6:17-26, 6:20, 6:22-23 and 6:34-35
ESV Study Bible, study note on Luke 6:20
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 6:31, 6:32 and 6:34-35 and sidebars Blessings and Woes and Love Your Enemies

ideas.s: Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.

entries.title: Luke 7:1-10, A centurion who built the synagogue
entries.summary: Jewish elders in Capernaum plead for a centurion whose valued slave is dying, because he loves their nation and built their synagogue. The centurion sends word that Jesus need not come under his roof, only give the order.
entries.plain: A centurion's slave, dear to him, is near death, and he sends Jewish elders to ask Jesus to come. They say he deserves it, since he loves their people and built their synagogue. As Jesus nears the house, friends bring another message: the centurion is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof, but as a man under authority who gives orders, he knows Jesus need only say the word. Jesus is amazed, says he has not found such faith in Israel, and the slave is well.
entries.note: A centurion led sixty to eighty men in practice (Keener and his notes), though Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, gives a century as about a hundred men. Whose soldier he was is disputed. Strauss says Roman troops were not stationed in Galilee until AD 44, so this man probably served Antipas in police or customs work, or was a retired Roman soldier; Garland describes Capernaum as a frontier town with a customs office and a detachment of soldiers under a centurion, and the Zondervan archaeology handbook calls it a garrison town with Roman soldiers. Keener puts the weight of Luke's version on worthiness: the elders say the man deserves it, and he says he does not. Strauss reads the scene through Roman patronage: the centurion is the town's patron, the elders act as his brokers, and by saying he is not worthy he makes himself Jesus' client; the Mishnah also says that "the dwelling places of Gentiles are unclean." Under the white limestone synagogue now standing at Capernaum lie the black basalt foundations of an earlier one, most likely the synagogue Jesus knew (Price and House; the Zondervan atlas; the cultural backgrounds article on the Capernaum synagogue).

ideas.s: Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: Luke 7:11-17, A widow's only son on the bier
entries.summary: At the gate of Nain Jesus meets a funeral for a widow's only son. He touches the bier, raises the young man and gives him back to his mother, and the crowd says a great prophet has arisen.
entries.plain: At the gate of the town of Nain, Jesus meets a funeral procession carrying out a widow's only son, with many townspeople walking alongside her. Moved by her loss, he tells her to stop crying, touches the stretcher, and tells the young man to rise; the dead man sits up and speaks, and Jesus returns him to his mother. The onlookers are awed and say that a great prophet has appeared and that God has stepped in for his people.
entries.note: The bereaved mother led the funeral procession out of town, with the townspeople behind her (Keener and his notes), and rabbinic writings said one should break off studying the law to join a small funeral procession but not a large one, so the size of this crowd shows the grief (Strauss). Keener writes, "Interrupting a funeral was a blatant breach of Jewish law and custom": touching the bier brought a day's uncleanness and touching the corpse a week's (Numbers 19). The bier was an open stretcher, not a closed coffin (Keener), and Wright notes that nobody but the official bearers would normally touch it. Elijah and Elisha had each raised a mother's son (1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 4:36), and the crowd's words echo the Old Testament language of God visiting his people (Keener and his notes). Wright puts Nain about five miles from Nazareth and Strauss about six, on the north slope of the hill of Moreh; Shunem, where Elisha raised a child, lies on the hill's south side (the Zondervan Bible dictionary). Wright sees Luke pointing ahead to another widow's only son carried out for burial at Jerusalem.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 7:11-17, 7:13, 7:14 and 7:15-17
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 7:13, 7:14 and 7:16
N. T. Wright, Luke for Everyone, comment on Luke 7:11-17
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 7:11-17, 7:11, 7:12 and 7:14
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, Nain

ideas.s: Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.

entries.title: Luke 7:36-50, A sinful woman at Simon's table
entries.summary: At a Pharisee's banquet a woman known as a sinner weeps over Jesus' feet, wipes them with her hair and anoints them. Jesus answers his host's silent objection with a story of two debtors.
entries.plain: A Pharisee named Simon has Jesus to dinner, and a woman known in the town for her sinful life comes in carrying a stone flask of scented oil. Crying at his feet, she dries them with her hair, kisses them and pours the oil on them, while Simon privately concludes that Jesus cannot be a real prophet. Jesus answers with a short story about two debtors whose debts are cancelled, points out the basic courtesies Simon left out, and declares the woman forgiven.
entries.note: Reclining shows that this was a banquet (Keener and his notes). Guests lay with their feet pointing away from the table, so she stands behind him. Uninvited people could come into some banquets but were expected to stay quiet and away from the couches (Keener). Married women covered their hair, and a woman with it loose in public was taken to be promiscuous (Keener and his notes). Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, suggests she meant to anoint his head, an honor for a guest (Psalm 23:5), but could not reach it as he reclined. Five hundred denarii was more than a year's wages (Keener's notes). Why Simon invited Jesus is read in different ways: Wright thinks he wanted a fair hearing for a possible prophet, Blomberg allows either honorable hospitality or an attempt to trap him, and Bailey pictures elders meaning to correct a young rabbi. The missing courtesies are also disputed. Bailey writes, "To omit the entire list would be a calculated and pointed insult"; Strauss answers that there is no evidence that a host was expected to provide water, a kiss or oil, so Simon was indifferent rather than insulting.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 7:36, 7:38, 7:41 and 7:44
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 7:36, 7:37, 7:38, 7:39 and 7:43-46
Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, ch. 18, The Woman in the House of Simon the Pharisee
N. T. Wright, Luke for Everyone, comment on Luke 7:36-50
Craig L. Blomberg, Interpreting the Parables, 6.3 The Two Debtors
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 7:38, 7:41 and 7:44-46

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.
A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.

entries.title: Luke 8:1-3, Women who paid the bills
entries.summary: As Jesus travels from town to town with the Twelve, women he has healed travel with them, among them Joanna, wife of Herod's household manager, and they support the group from their own means.
entries.plain: Luke pauses to describe the travelling company as Jesus moves from town to town announcing the kingdom. Alongside the Twelve are several women he had healed, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna, whose husband managed Herod's household, and Susanna. Luke says these and many other women supported the group from their own money.
entries.note: Women sometimes acted as patrons of religious teachers, though Keener says men outnumbered them more than ten to one because men held most of the money. For women to travel with the group would have looked scandalous, and men and women learning side by side as adults was unheard of (Keener). Bailey writes that even in the traditional Middle East of today he knows of nowhere such an arrangement would be possible, since women traveling with men must spend their nights with relatives, and he notes that the women were paying for the movement out of resources they controlled. The ESV Study Bible observes that a woman from Herod's household shows that some of the wealthy and powerful supported Jesus. Magdala lay on the western shore a few miles north of Tiberias, and the word for Chuza's post can mean a business manager, a guardian or even a governor, here probably the manager of Herod's estate (Strauss). Strauss agrees that wealthy patrons often supported traveling teachers in the Greco-Roman world; what was unusual was women traveling with a rabbi as his disciples.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 8:1-3
Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, ch. 14, Jesus and Women
ESV Study Bible, study note on Luke 8:3
CSB Study Bible, note on Luke 8:1-3
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 8:2 and 8:3

ideas.s: Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.

entries.title: Luke 9:51-62, A Samaritan refusal and three would-be followers
entries.summary: Setting out for Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village and rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire. On the road he tells three would-be followers what following him will cost.
entries.plain: Luke marks a turning point: Jesus now heads deliberately toward Jerusalem, and a Samaritan village turns him away for that reason. When James and John want to destroy the village with fire from the sky, Jesus rebukes them. Along the road three would-be followers hear how costly following him will be, with no home of his own, no delay even for a father's burial, and no turning back once the work has begun.
entries.note: James and John want to copy Elijah, who called down fire on the king's soldiers (2 Kings 1:10, 12; Keener and his notes). To the villagers Jesus was a man on his way to worship at the rival temple, and many pious Jews thought it scandalous to take Samaritan hospitality (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). Burying a father was a son's greatest duty; Wright calls Jesus' answer "This is, quite frankly, outrageous." What the man asked for is debated. Keener's notes give two readings: a polite request to wait until the father dies, perhaps for years, or the reburial of his bones a year after death. Keener's background commentary takes the second; Bailey calls the phrase a traditional idiom for staying at home until the parents die, and the CSB Study Bible also reads an excuse for a delay of possibly years. Strauss rejects both softer readings and thinks the father has died or is dying, so the answer is meant to be truly radical. Elijah let Elisha say goodbye to his parents (1 Kings 19:19-21); Jesus does not, and a plowman who looks back cuts a crooked furrow (Keener).

ideas.s: The people of the hill country between Judea and Galilee worshiped Israel's God on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans each claimed to be the true heirs of Israel, and centuries of hostility lay between them.
Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

entries.title: Luke 10:1-24, Seventy sent out, and Satan falling
entries.summary: Jesus sends seventy others, or seventy-two, ahead of him in pairs, with no purse, bag or sandals, to towns that will welcome or refuse them. They come back rejoicing that even the demons obey, and Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning.
entries.plain: Jesus sends out seventy messengers, or seventy-two in many manuscripts, in pairs ahead of him, travelling light and vulnerable. They are to accept hospitality where they find it, heal the sick and announce that God's kingdom is close, and towns that reject them will answer for it. When they return rejoicing over their power against demons, Jesus speaks of seeing Satan cast down from heaven, but tells them the greater cause for joy is that their names are recorded there.
entries.note: Messengers were usually sent in pairs (Keener and his notes), and the ESV Study Bible adds the law's demand for two witnesses. Withholding a greeting was offensive and the pious tried to greet first, so greeting no one on the way marks great urgency; the greeting peace was itself a blessing (Keener). Some Jewish teachers pictured Israel as sheep among the wolves of the nations (Keener and his notes). Exorcists usually needed incantations to make demons leave, so the disciples are amazed that the name alone works (Keener). Names written in heaven recall the book of the righteous known from Daniel 12:1, Jubilees and 1 Enoch (Keener). The Hebrew text of Genesis 10 lists seventy nations and the Greek Old Testament seventy-two, which may explain why manuscripts of Luke differ between seventy and seventy-two; Strauss thinks Luke wrote seventy-two and scribes later matched the Hebrew. The Testament of Levi says the coming priest will give his children authority to trample on wicked spirits, and the book of names in heaven draws on the citizen rolls that ancient cities and kingdoms kept (Strauss).

ideas.s: Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: Luke 10:25-37, The Samaritan on the Jericho road
entries.summary: A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life and then who his neighbor is. Jesus tells of a man left half dead on the road to Jericho, passed by a priest and a Levite and rescued by a Samaritan.
entries.plain: A legal expert tries to test Jesus and agrees that the law comes down to loving God and loving your neighbor, then asks where the boundary of neighbor lies. Jesus answers with a story about a traveller on the desert road from Jerusalem to Jericho who is robbed, beaten and left near death. A priest and then a Levite avoid him, but a Samaritan, one of a people Jews despised, cares for his wounds, brings him to an inn and covers the bill; Jesus asks who acted as a neighbor and tells the lawyer to live the same way.
entries.note: Neighbor usually meant a fellow Israelite, though Leviticus 19:34 extends the command to the foreigner living in the land (Keener); Sirach names among the nations he detests "the foolish people that live in Shechem," the Samaritans (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). The road drops more than three thousand feet over about seventeen miles of desert, with plenty of places for robbers (the CSB Study Bible). Bailey says the story "explodes in the faces of its listeners," because the third man is a hated outsider, not the Jewish layman a series of priest and Levite leads them to expect. Why the priest and Levite passed by is debated: Keener's notes and Bailey point to the impurity of touching what might be a corpse; the CSB Study Bible thinks fear of the robbers or not wanting the bother more likely; Strauss calls impurity a poor excuse for a priest going down, away from Jerusalem, and since many priests were aristocrats who kept apart from commoners, hearers may have expected snobbery. The Samaritan's promise to pay on his return was the usual wording for standing surety for a debt (Keener). Wright reads the parable as redrawing the boundary of the covenant people.

ideas.s: Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.

ideas.n: Priests on duty: the twenty-four courses
ideas.s: Israel's ordinary priests were divided into twenty-four courses that took turns at the temple, a week at a time. Most lived in the country and came up to Jerusalem when their turn came round.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

The people of the hill country between Judea and Galilee worshiped Israel's God on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans each claimed to be the true heirs of Israel, and centuries of hostility lay between them.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

entries.title: Luke 10:38-42, Mary at the teacher's feet
entries.summary: In Martha's house Mary sits at Jesus' feet listening while Martha works at serving. When Martha complains, Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.
entries.plain: Martha welcomes Jesus into her home. Her sister Mary sits at the Lord's feet and listens to his teaching, while Martha is pulled every way by the work of serving. Martha asks Jesus to tell Mary to help her; he answers that Martha is anxious about many things but only one is needed, and that Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken from her.
entries.note: Hosting a famous teacher was an honor, and preparing the food fell to the woman of the house (Keener and his notes). To sit at a teacher's feet was a disciple's posture (Acts 22:3), and disciples were training to become teachers, a role closed to women; women could hear the law in the synagogue but were not taught in the rabbis' schools (Keener and his notes). Wright says the real problem was that "Mary was behaving as if she were a man," crossing from the women's quarters into the room where the men sat, and that by the standards of the day "Only a shameless woman would behave in such a way." Bailey also reads Martha as upset that her sister has joined the men. The Mishnah tells a student to "sit amid the dust of their feet and drink in their words with thirst," speaking of the sages, and also says that teaching a daughter the law is like teaching her lechery; girls were taught only household skills (Strauss). Since a woman's honor rested on running her household well, Martha's complaint would have looked legitimate (Strauss).

A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Luke 11:1-13, Father, daily bread and a friend at midnight
entries.summary: Asked to teach his disciples to pray, Jesus gives a short prayer to the Father, then tells of a man who wakes a neighbor at midnight to borrow bread for a guest.
entries.plain: One of the disciples asks Jesus for a prayer of their own, the way John the Baptist had given one to his followers. Jesus gives a short prayer addressing God as Father, asking for his name to be honored and his kingdom to come, for bread each day, for forgiveness as they forgive others, and for protection in testing. He follows it with a story of a neighbor woken at midnight who gets up to lend bread because his friend will not stop asking, and promises that the Father will give the Spirit to those who ask.
entries.note: The prayer's opening echoes the Kaddish, which in its early form asked that God's great name be exalted and hallowed and that he cause his kingdom to reign (Keener's notes). Abba was not a child's word only, since adults also called their parents by it, but it was intimate, and Jews rarely if ever addressed God simply as my father or father (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). Sins and debts were one word in Aramaic (Keener). A refusal would shame the whole village, whose guest the traveler was (Keener and his notes; Bailey). The word in 11:8 often translated persistence is debated. Keener says it means shamelessness and may point either to the bold knocker or to the shame the sleeper and his village would suffer; Bailey takes it of the sleeper, who gets up to avoid shame; Blomberg, following Derrett, takes it of the asker's bold shamelessness and rejects Bailey's reading; the CSB Study Bible reads shameless boldness and persistence; Strauss sets out both readings without deciding. Most Jews thought the Spirit rested only on the holiest people, so the closing promise would have sounded like making them prophets (Keener).

ideas.s: Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

Most village families lived in one main room, with a lower end by the door where the animals spent the night, a flat roof of beams, branches and mud, and sometimes a guest room on the roof or built on at the end.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Luke 11:14-26, By Beelzebul, or by the finger of God?
entries.summary: When Jesus drives out a demon that kept a man from speaking, some say he does it by Beelzebul, the ruler of demons. He answers that a divided kingdom falls, and that if he drives out demons by the finger of God, God's kingdom has come.
entries.plain: After Jesus frees a man who could not speak from a demon, some accuse him of working by the power of Beelzebul, while others demand a heavenly sign as proof. Jesus replies that a kingdom at war with itself cannot stand, so Satan would not be expelling his own forces, and that if he acts by God's finger then God's rule has already arrived. He pictures a strong man's house raided by someone stronger, and warns that an evil spirit driven out can return with worse company if the house is left empty.
entries.note: Most pagan exorcists used incantations, and rabbis of the second century still accused Jesus and his followers of sorcery (Keener). Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, explains the name: Baal-Zebul probably means Baal the prince or Baal of the exalted house, which Israel mocked as Baal-Zebub, lord of the flies. Your sons means members of your own group, some of whom also cast out demons (Keener). The finger of God recalls Exodus 8:19, where Pharaoh's magicians, unable to copy Moses, admit that God is at work (Keener and his notes). Magicians tried to bind spirits into their service, but Keener's notes read the strong man as the devil and the plundering as God's promise in Isaiah 49:25 to rescue his people from the powerful one. Luke's strong man is a picture of war, two lords fighting over a castle, where Mark's is a house robbery (Strauss). Heiser observes that Luke 11:18 is the only verse in the Bible that names Satan and demons together. Wright reads the saying with Luke 10:18: Jesus claimed he had already met the prince of demons and beaten him, so his exorcisms showed the true battle being won.

entries.title: Luke 11:37-54, Woes at a Pharisee's table
entries.summary: At a Pharisee's meal Jesus does not wash before eating, and when his host is surprised he pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers: clean cups and greedy hearts, tithed herbs, the best seats, unmarked graves and the tombs of the prophets.
entries.plain: Invited to a Pharisee's meal, Jesus skips the ritual washing and his host is shocked. Jesus answers with a string of woes: the Pharisees scrub the outside of their dishes while their hearts are greedy, tithe garden herbs but ignore justice and love for God, crave honor in public, and spread uncleanness like hidden graves. When a legal expert protests, Jesus turns the same charge on the lawyers, accusing them of burdening others and of honoring the prophets their ancestors murdered, with the blood of all those prophets falling on the present generation.
entries.note: Washing the hands before meals was a Pharisaic custom, not an Old Testament practice (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). The schools of Shammai and Hillel argued over whether the inside or the outside of a cup should be cleaned first, and both Keener works say Jesus' words side with the Hillelites while turning the point to the heart. Whether garden herbs had to be tithed at all was debated, since tithes were on food. The Mishnah lists rue among the herbs exempt from tithing (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). Seats and greetings went by rank, and inferiors greeted superiors first (Keener's notes). Pharisees held that even a shadow over a grave made a person unclean, so tombs were whitewashed each spring to warn people off (Keener). Jerusalem was building monuments to the prophets, and in the Hebrew order of Scripture Abel is the first martyr and Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:20-22) the last (Keener and his notes). Keener's notes add that a man insulted in public could win back his honor only by humiliating the one who shamed him, which explains the plotting at the end.

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Luke 12:13-21, Bigger barns
entries.summary: A man asks Jesus to make his brother divide the inheritance. Jesus refuses, warns against greed, and tells of a rich farmer who plans bigger barns for his surplus and dies that night.
entries.plain: Someone in the crowd tells Jesus to order his brother to share the inheritance with him; Jesus asks who made him a judge or arbitrator over them, and warns that life does not consist in possessions. He tells of a rich man whose land yields so much that he plans to pull down his barns and build bigger ones, then tell himself to relax, eat, drink and be merry. God calls him a fool: that very night his life is demanded of him, and who will get what he has stored up?
entries.note: Archaeologists have found large grain silos on the farms of wealthy absentee landowners, as at Sepphoris, and such men belonged to a leisured class usually estimated at under one percent (Keener); Proverbs 11:26 warns against holding back grain while others go hungry (Keener's notes). Blomberg notes that in a world where seventy to eighty percent of people barely got by, a man with a surplus was expected to share it generously. Bailey points out that the man talks only to himself, in a village world where the leading men talked every matter over together at the gate, and sums up God's verdict: "You plan alone, build alone, indulge alone, and now you will die alone!" Eat, drink and be merry echoes Isaiah 22:13, and the Greco-Roman world heard it as a jab at the Epicureans (Keener's notes; Blomberg). Rabbis often settled disputes over the law of inheritance, and since the firstborn took a double portion, the man is probably a younger son demanding his legal share (Strauss). Sirach 11:18-19 tells of a man who says he will now feast on his goods, not knowing how soon he will leave them to others and die (Strauss).

ideas.s: A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

entries.title: Luke 12:35-48, Slaves waiting up for the master
entries.summary: Jesus tells his followers to be dressed for action with lamps lit, like slaves waiting for their master to come home from a wedding, and asks what a slave left in charge will do if the master is delayed.
entries.plain: Jesus tells his followers to stay dressed for work with their lamps lit, like household slaves awake for their master's return from a wedding, and says the master will reverse the roles and wait on the faithful ones himself. The Son of Man's arrival will be unannounced, like a burglar's. When Peter asks who the story is for, Jesus describes a steward left in charge, rewarded if he is found at his job, but punished hard if he abuses the other servants and drinks while his master is away.
entries.note: Tucked-up robes recall Israel ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11; Keener and his notes). Wedding celebrations could run late into the night, and well-to-do houses kept slave porters at the door (Keener and his notes). Apart from one Roman festival that briefly turned the social order upside down, slaves always served masters and never the reverse (Keener's notes); Keener says plainly that "masters' serving slaves was unheard-of." Here the night is counted in the Jewish three watches, not the Roman four (Keener). A steward was a high-level slave who handed out the household's rations, and such slaves could outrank free peasants in power and pay (Keener and his notes; Blomberg). Stories of a master away and those left behind tempted were common, and cutting a man in pieces was a punishment Luke's readers would find horrifying (Keener and his notes); commentators differ on whether it is meant literally here (Strauss). Lighter punishment for sins of ignorance is found in the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the Wisdom of Solomon warns that "the lowliest may be pardoned in mercy, but the mighty will be mightily tested" (Strauss).

ideas.s: Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

entries.title: Luke 13:1-9, Pilate's victims, the tower and the fig tree
entries.summary: People tell Jesus about Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices. He answers with a tower that fell in Siloam, a call to repent, and a fig tree given one more year.
entries.plain: People bring Jesus news of Galileans whom Pilate had killed during their sacrifices. Jesus rejects the idea that those victims, or the eighteen crushed by a collapsing tower at Siloam, were worse sinners than anyone else, and warns that his hearers face the same end unless they turn back to God. He adds a story about a fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years, which the owner wants removed and the gardener begs to tend for one more season.
entries.note: No other ancient source mentions the killing or the tower (Bailey; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), but it fits what Josephus tells of Pilate. Once "Pilate undertook to bring a current of water to Jerusalem, and did it with the sacred money," then sent soldiers in disguise to beat the crowd that protested. What perish means is debated: Wright hears a warning of Roman swords and of walls collapsing on the city's people in a coming siege; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles read final judgment and eternal loss. What the tower was is also disputed. Keener and Strauss suggest the city wall or Pilate's aqueduct, the Zondervan Bible dictionary the walls; the Zondervan archaeology handbook reports a round tower found near the pool of Siloam in 1913 and says "Scholars are almost universally convinced it was not a tower designed for defensive purposes": probably a dovecote raising pigeons for the temple. The worker asks for a fourth year to be sure, and since figs rarely needed manure, he does everything he can (Keener). Whom the tree stands for is debated: Bailey thinks of the nation's leaders, the ESV Study Bible and Strauss of Israel as a whole.

ideas.s: Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

ideas.n: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
ideas.s: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.
Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.

entries.title: Luke 13:10-21, A bent woman freed on the Sabbath; mustard and leaven
entries.summary: Teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman bent double for eighteen years. The synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus answers with an ox untied for water, then compares God's kingdom to a mustard seed and to leaven.
entries.plain: On a Sabbath in a synagogue, Jesus heals a woman who has been bent double for eighteen years by a spirit, and she straightens up and praises God. The synagogue leader scolds the crowd for seeking healing on the Sabbath, and Jesus answers that they all untie their animals to water them on that day, so a woman of Abraham's family held captive by Satan should certainly be released. His critics are shamed, the crowd is delighted, and he compares God's kingdom to a tiny seed that becomes a tree and to a little yeast that works through a huge batch of dough.
entries.note: The rule behind the ruler's objection is read two ways: Keener says Pharisaic rules officially forbade only healing by a physician, and debated whether even prayer for the sick was allowed on the Sabbath; Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, says the rabbis generally allowed medical help on the Sabbath only in an emergency or when life was in danger. Untying an animal to water it was among the few acts of tying and untying allowed on the Sabbath, so Jesus argues how much more for an Israelite woman bound by Satan (Keener). Controversy stories ended with the wise man's answer silencing his opponents, and the shamed side would normally look for a way to win back its honor (Keener and his notes). Wright reads the woman as a picture of Israel held in the satan's grip. How big the mustard grew is disputed: some scholars say eight to ten feet, others that the likeliest plant rarely passed five (the cultural backgrounds notes); Strauss says usually about four feet but sometimes ten or more. The three measures of flour, about sixty pounds (Strauss), would make bread for more than a hundred people (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.

entries.title: Luke 13:22-35, The narrow door, the feast, the fox and the hen
entries.summary: On the way to Jerusalem Jesus warns that many will find the door shut while people from east and west recline at the feast in God's kingdom. Warned that Herod wants to kill him, he calls Herod a fox and grieves over Jerusalem.
entries.plain: Asked whether only a few will be saved, Jesus turns the question back on his hearers and tells them to make every effort to get in before the door is shut, when claiming to have eaten with him will not help. He warns that people from every direction will feast with Abraham and the prophets while some who expected a place are left outside. When Pharisees warn him that Herod Antipas wants him dead, he calls Herod a fox and says he will keep going to Jerusalem, then laments over the city he wanted to shelter like a hen with her chicks.
entries.note: Most Jews held that almost all Israel would share in salvation (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1), though groups such as the Essenes believed they alone would be, and the later author of 4 Ezra warned that most would be lost (Keener and his notes). Who comes from the four directions is debated: Keener says the words could mean dispersed Jews coming home, but in Luke-Acts they point to Gentiles, and the cultural backgrounds notes say they presumably include Gentiles; Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, adds that Jewish hope often pictured the nations submitting to Israel, where here they share the banquet in full. Antipas, as tetrarch, could execute whom he chose and had already killed John; Keener and his notes take these Pharisees to be trying to help, while the CSB Study Bible doubts that they meant to protect him. A fox was worthless, treacherous or cunning, and foxes prey on hens (Keener and his notes). Jewish tradition spoke of a convert brought under the wings of God's presence, so Jesus takes a divine image for himself (Keener and his notes). The desolate house is the temple destroyed in AD 70 (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 13:22-24, 13:26-27, 13:29-30, 13:31, 13:32, 13:34 and 13:35

ideas.n: The banquet of the age to come
ideas.s: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.

ideas.n: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
ideas.s: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.

entries.title: Luke 14:1-14, Dropsy at a Pharisee's table, and guests who cannot repay
entries.summary: On a Sabbath at the house of a leading Pharisee, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, tells the guests not to grab the best places, and tells the host to invite people who cannot invite him back.
entries.plain: Jesus eats at the home of a leading Pharisee on the Sabbath while the guests watch him for a slip. He heals a man with severe swelling and asks which of them would not rescue a child or an ox from a well on that day. Noticing the guests jostling for the best places, he advises taking the lowest seat, and tells his host to invite people who can never return the favor, since God will reward him when the righteous are raised.
entries.note: It was an honor to host a famous teacher, and Jews thought it especially virtuous to invite one to a Sabbath meal (Keener and his notes). Dropsy, swelling from fluid, was a symptom of a more serious illness, and it is unclear whether the man was a guest, a plant or an onlooker (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). The Essenes would not rescue an animal on the Sabbath, but Pharisees and most others would, so Jesus argues from a rule his hosts already accepted (Keener and his notes); the Damascus Document lets a person be rescued from a pit only without a ladder or rope (Strauss). Seating by rank is well attested in Jewish Palestine, and Jesus' advice is Proverbs 25:6-7, already well known if not always followed (Keener and his notes). People of status invited those somewhat below them, such as clients, in return for honor, but never beggars or the destitute, and the crippled, lame and blind were barred from the Qumran community (Keener and his notes). Judaism taught that the righteous would be rewarded at the resurrection, and Proverbs 19:17 already says God repays kindness to the poor (Keener).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 14:1, 14:3-6, 14:7, 14:8-10, 14:12, 14:13 and 14:14

ideas.s: The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: Luke 14:15-24, The great banquet and the excuses
entries.summary: A guest blesses whoever will eat bread in God's kingdom. Jesus tells of a man whose invited guests all excuse themselves when the feast is ready, so he fills his house with the poor and with people from the roads.
entries.plain: A guest remarks how happy those will be who eat in God's kingdom, and Jesus answers with a story about a large dinner. When the meal is ready, the invited guests all send polite excuses about land, oxen and a new marriage. The furious host fills his house instead with the poor, the disabled and strangers from the roads outside town, and declares that none of the original guests will eat his food.
entries.note: Guests had accepted in advance and were called again when the meal was ready (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). No one bought land without seeing it or oxen without testing them (Keener and his notes). Bailey puts it plainly: "An implausible excuse is a deliberate public insult." Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, thinks Bailey's claim that the first man is lying "may be an exaggeration," since late rabbinic evidence speaks of land inspected after purchase, though the excuse is still an insult. Keener writes that "Bringing in beggars from off the street was unheard-of", and Qumran barred the lame, blind and deaf from the messianic banquet (Strauss). Compel reflects Middle Eastern courtesy, in which an outsider was expected to decline and the host to insist (Bailey; Blomberg); the ESV Study Bible prefers strongly urge. Whether the people from the roads and hedges stand for Gentiles is debated. Bailey, the ESV Study Bible and Wright say yes, since they come from beyond the town, and Strauss ties them to the mission to the Gentiles in Acts; Blomberg finds nothing in the picture to suggest anyone but the poorer people on the outskirts.

ideas.n: The banquet of the age to come
ideas.s: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

entries.title: Luke 15:1-10, A lost sheep and a lost coin
entries.summary: Pharisees and teachers grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them. He answers with a shepherd who searches for one lost sheep and a woman who sweeps the house for one lost coin.
entries.plain: Toll collectors and other outsiders gather to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and legal experts complain that he welcomes such people and shares meals with them. Jesus answers with two short stories: a shepherd who leaves his flock to hunt for one missing sheep and celebrates when he carries it back, and a woman who searches her house for one lost coin and calls her neighbors to rejoice when she finds it. Heaven, he says, celebrates the same way over one sinner who turns back to God.
entries.note: Intimate table fellowship meant acceptance, Pharisees also worried about untithed food, and grumbling recalls Israel murmuring in the wilderness (Keener and his notes). A hundred was an ordinary flock, and shepherds often watched their animals together, so this one could leave the ninety-nine with other herders (Keener and his notes). Each coin was worth about a day's wage (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Keener suggests the ten were her dowry; Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, calls that speculative, since the parable never mentions a marriage, and says her poverty alone makes the loss serious. Coins fell so often between the stones of poor homes' floors that archaeologists date houses by them (Keener and his notes). Did the first hearers despise shepherds? Keener says the Pharisees counted herding an unclean trade, and the cultural backgrounds notes say townspeople looked down on shepherds. Levine answers, "Such views are nonsense": the usual proofs are Philo, the Mishnah (Qiddushin 4.14) and a late midrash, none of them showing what is claimed, while Jewish tradition used the shepherd as a positive image.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 15:2, 15:3-7, 15:3-4, 15:5, 15:8 and 15:9-10
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 15:2, 15:4 and 15:8

CSB Study Bible, note on Luke 15:8-10

ideas.s: Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Luke 15:11-32, A father and two lost sons
entries.summary: A younger son takes his share of the estate early, wastes it in a far country, and comes home to a father who runs to meet him. The older brother refuses to join the feast.
entries.plain: A man's younger son asks for his share of the property, and the father divides it between his two sons. The younger son goes to a distant country and squanders it, and when famine comes he is sent to feed a Gentile's pigs and longs for their pods. He comes to his senses and heads home to ask to be taken on as a hired servant, but his father sees him far off, runs, embraces and kisses him, calls for the best robe, a ring and sandals, and kills the fattened calf for a feast. The older son, coming in from the field, hears the music, refuses to go in, and complains that he has slaved for years without being given even a young goat; the father comes out and pleads with him, and the story ends without his answer.
entries.note: Keener writes that to ask for one's share early amounted to saying, "Father, I wish you were already dead." Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, agrees; Levine disagrees, citing the Jewish legal scholar Bernard Jackson, who finds no support for that idea in Jewish sources. A father could assign his property before death but kept its use and income, so the son could not legally sell, yet he does (Keener and his notes). Bailey argues that a son who sold the family land faced a ceremony the later rabbinic sources call qetsatsah, and that the father runs to take on himself the shame the village had in store for his son; Levine answers that the ceremony is absent from the Mishnah, appears only in relatively late texts and leaves no trace in the parable. It was undignified for an older man to run (Keener and his notes; Bailey). The best robe was the father's own, the ring a family signet, and the sandals marked a son, not a slave (Keener and his notes). Wright reads the parable as Israel's own story: "This is the story of Israel, in particular of exile and restoration." Levine files Wright's reading under allegory.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 15:11-12, 15:13, 15:15, 15:16, 15:20, 15:21-22, 15:23, 15:25-28 and 15:29-30

ideas.s: A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

entries.title: Luke 16:1-13, The dishonest manager
entries.summary: A rich man's manager, about to be dismissed for wasting his master's property, calls in the master's debtors and cuts their bills. The master praises his shrewdness.
entries.plain: A wealthy owner learns that his estate manager has been squandering his goods and gives him notice. Too weak for manual labor and too proud to beg, the manager quickly reduces what each debtor owes so that they will take him in once he is out of work. The owner praises his cleverness, and Jesus draws lessons about using money to win friends, being faithful with small things, and the impossibility of serving both God and wealth.
entries.note: Who the debtors were is read differently: Bailey takes them to be renters paying a fixed quantity of the crop, while Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, thinks the size of the debts suggests wealthy merchants. The debtors make the changes in their own hand (the cultural backgrounds notes; Bailey). In hard times landowners sometimes wrote off part of a debt and were praised as benevolent, and Keener and his notes argue that the master cannot now undo the cuts without losing the honor he has just been given. What the manager cut is disputed. Wright argues that he removed hidden interest, since Jews got round the ban on lending at interest by lending in kind, so the master could not complain without exposing himself. Blomberg answers that the amounts "do not correspond to any known interest or commission rates of the day", the ESV Study Bible thinks the cuts too large for a commission, and Bailey rejects the interest theory because "it of necessity implicates the master in dishonest dealings." Bailey, Blomberg and Wright agree that the one who praises the manager is the master in the story.

ideas.s: Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.
A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Luke 16:19-31, The rich man and Lazarus
entries.summary: A rich man feasts every day while a beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate. Both die; Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side, and the rich man finds himself in torment in Hades.
entries.plain: Jesus tells of a wealthy man who lives in luxury while a sick beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate, hungry for scraps, with dogs licking his sores. After both die, Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side, while the rich man suffers in Hades and asks for relief and then for a warning to be sent to his five brothers. Abraham refuses both, saying the gulf between them cannot be crossed and that brothers who ignore the law and the prophets would not be convinced even by someone returned from the dead.
entries.note: The surprise is that Jesus names the beggar and not the rich man; Lazarus is the Greek form of Eleazar (Keener and his notes), meaning God helps (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). Blomberg writes, "Dogs were not pets in Jewish households"; these were unclean street scavengers, and their licking would have revolted the hearers (Keener and his notes). Jewish stories had angels carry the righteous away, and everyone, however poor, was owed a burial, so the silence about Lazarus's burial stands against the rich man's funeral, and the place at Abraham's side is the honored guest's place beside the host at a banquet (Keener and his notes; Blomberg). The story is close to a folk tale, Egyptian in origin and retold in Jewish circles, of a rich tax collector given a grand funeral and a poor scholar who reaches paradise (Blomberg). How far the details describe the afterlife is debated. Keener says some are standard Jewish tradition and some only serve the story; the ESV Study Bible holds that the story still seems to teach awareness at once after death; Blomberg suggests that Abraham's side may name a relationship with God more than a place.

ideas.s: Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Jews spoke of the dead going down to Hades, and of the righteous resting at Abraham's side or in paradise. The pictures were traditional, varied, and could be borrowed by a story.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.

entries.title: Luke 17:11-19, Ten lepers and the Samaritan who came back
entries.summary: On the border between Samaria and Galilee ten men with leprosy call to Jesus from a distance. He sends them to the priests, they are cleansed on the way, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank him.
entries.plain: Travelling along the border of Samaria and Galilee, Jesus is met by ten men with a skin disease who keep their distance and beg for help. He sends them to show themselves to the priests, and they are healed on the way. Only one turns back, loudly praising God and thanking Jesus at his feet, and Luke points out that this man is a Samaritan; Jesus asks about the other nine and tells the foreigner that his faith has saved him.
entries.note: The law put lepers in quarantine (Leviticus 13:45-46), so they were outcasts whom most people preferred to ignore, and many Jewish teachers went further than the Bible in blaming the disease on the leper's sin (Keener). The law also prescribed sacrifices when a leper was healed (Leviticus 14:1-32), so sending them to the priests keeps the law and gives the priests no offense (Keener). On their own terms Samaritans were devout, but Jews thought them irreligious and avoided close dealings; in this border region shared leprosy erased the usual divide (Keener and his notes). The route itself had a history. Josephus writes, "It was the custom of the Galileans, when they came to the holy city at the festivals, to take their journeys through the country of the Samaritans," and tells how men of Ginea, a village on that road, killed a great many of them, and how the governor Cumanus, bribed by the Samaritans, did nothing. Biblical leprosy was not Hansen's disease but a range of skin conditions (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). Naaman, the earlier foreigner cured of leprosy (2 Kings 5), is the one Jesus named at Nazareth (4:27; Strauss).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 17:11-12, 17:14 and 17:15-19
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, note on Luke 17:16

ideas.s: The people of the hill country between Judea and Galilee worshiped Israel's God on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans each claimed to be the true heirs of Israel, and centuries of hostility lay between them.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

entries.title: Luke 18:1-8, The widow and the judge
entries.summary: Jesus tells of a judge who neither feared God nor respected people and a widow who kept coming to him for justice until he gave in. How much more, he says, will God see justice done for his chosen ones.
entries.plain: Jesus tells this story to encourage persistence in prayer. A judge who has no regard for God or for people is pestered by a widow demanding a fair ruling against her opponent, and he finally gives in just to be rid of her. If even such a judge relents, Jesus argues, God will surely act quickly for his own people, though he closes by asking whether the Son of Man will find faith when he comes.
entries.note: The law required judges to be fair and forbade bribes (the cultural backgrounds notes), and the widow was its standard example of the oppressed (Exodus 22:22-24); she could not afford a bribe, and her opponent may have been trying to take her land for a debt (Keener). Men controlled the courts and usually only men pleaded cases, though women who did speak were thought courageous and usually won (the cultural backgrounds notes). Jesus argues from lesser to greater, how much more, a standard Jewish form (Keener and his notes). How helpless is the widow? The cultural backgrounds notes, the CSB Study Bible and Bailey make her almost powerless, with no bribe to give and no man to speak for her, and Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, agrees that widows were the most vulnerable members of society. Levine answers that the widows of the Bible, from Tamar and Ruth to Abigail and Judith, rarely fit that stereotype, and she reads the judge's fear literally: he is afraid she will give him a black eye, which is also how Wright renders 18:5. Strauss takes the phrase as a figure for wearing someone down, as one boxer wears down another.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 18:2, 18:3, 18:5 and 18:6-7
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 18:1-5 and 18:6-7
CSB Study Bible, note on Luke 18:2-3
