ideas.s: A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.

entries.title: Luke 18:9-14, Two men go up to the temple to pray
entries.summary: Jesus tells of a Pharisee who thanks God that he is not like other people and a tax collector who stands far off, beats his breast and asks for mercy. The tax collector goes home justified.
entries.plain: Jesus aims this story at people confident of their own goodness who hold others in contempt. A Pharisee prays in the temple, listing his fasting and tithing and thanking God that he is better than the toll collector nearby, while the toll collector keeps his distance, will not look up, strikes his chest and asks only for mercy. Jesus says it was the toll collector who went home right with God, because God lowers the proud and raises the humble.
entries.note: Bailey sets the scene at the daily atonement offering, when a lamb was sacrificed for the sins of Israel; the CSB Study Bible says only that the times around the morning and evening sacrifices were set for prayer. Thanking God for one's righteousness, instead of taking credit for it, counted as pious, so the first hearers would not have heard the Pharisee as a boaster (Keener and his notes), and Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, agrees that no first-century Jew would have equated Pharisees with hypocrisy. The most devout fasted on Mondays and Thursdays, and Pharisees tithed beyond what the law required (Keener and his notes; Bailey). Bailey points out that the tax collector's verb is not the usual word for mercy but one meaning to make an atonement. Keener adds that a prayer with no restitution would have struck many as invalid, so the ending would shock. Levine reads it differently: "The parable does not critique the Temple." In her reading the temple welcomes both men, and the Greek allows that both go home justified; Strauss notes, against her, that a tax collector's very presence in the temple was seen as defilement.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 18:10, 18:11, 18:12 and 18:13
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 18:9-10, 18:11, 18:12, 18:13 and 18:14

Amy-Jill Levine, Short Stories by Jesus, ch. 6, The Pharisee and the Tax Collector

ideas.s: Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Going without food, and often washing and oil, as a sign of mourning, penitence and longing. The law required one fast a year; the devout kept many more.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.

entries.title: Luke 18:18-30, A rich ruler and the needle's eye
entries.summary: A ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life; told to sell everything and follow, he goes away sad, and Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom.
entries.plain: A wealthy leader asks Jesus how to gain eternal life and says he has kept the commandments from his youth. Jesus tells him he lacks one thing, to sell all he owns, give to the poor and follow, and the man is deeply saddened. Jesus then uses the image of a camel squeezing through a needle to show what a struggle entry into the kingdom is for the wealthy, and when his hearers despair, he says God can do what people cannot and promises great reward to those who have given things up for the kingdom.
entries.note: People asked Jewish teachers how to gain eternal life, which meant the life of the world to come (Keener and his notes; Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). Judaism stressed charity, but Jewish teachers did not normally ask a prospective disciple to give away everything; a few radical Greek teachers made that demand of rich students, who usually went back to their wealth (Keener). Wealth was often taken as a sign of God's blessing, so the saying turns the social order over (Keener; Strauss). The camel through the needle's eye was a picture of the impossible: the largest animal in Judea and Galilee through the smallest opening, as teachers in Babylonia spoke of an elephant (the cultural backgrounds notes). The popular story of a small Jerusalem gate called the Needle's Eye, which a camel could pass only unloaded and kneeling, has no support: Strauss writes that "there is no archaeological or literary evidence that such a gate existed" in the first century, Keener that the gate people point to was built in medieval times, and there is no manuscript support for reading rope instead of camel (Strauss).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 18:18, 18:22-23, 18:24, 18:25-27 and 18:28-30 and on Mark 10:25
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 18:18, 18:25 and 18:29
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 18:18-30, 18:18, 18:21, 18:24 and 18:25

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
Giving to the needy was one of the three pillars of Jewish piety, with prayer and fasting. Greeks and Romans had nothing quite like it.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

entries.title: Luke 18:35-19:10, A blind beggar and Zacchaeus at Jericho
entries.summary: Near Jericho a blind beggar calls Jesus Son of David and receives his sight. In the town Jesus invites himself to the house of Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector, who promises to give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold.
entries.plain: Outside Jericho a blind beggar keeps calling Jesus Son of David and begging for mercy despite the crowd's attempts to quiet him, and Jesus restores his sight. In the town, Zacchaeus, a wealthy head toll collector too short to see, climbs a tree to watch, and Jesus singles him out and invites himself to his house, to the crowd's disgust. Zacchaeus promises to give half his wealth away and repay four times anyone he has defrauded, and Jesus declares that salvation has reached this household, since rescuing the lost is why he came.
entries.note: Son of David meant he took Jesus for the Messiah (Keener and his notes). Jericho was a border town between Judea and Antipas's Perea with a customs station (Keener and his notes). In Jesus' day there were two Jerichos, the abandoned mound of the Old Testament and the new city about a mile south, and some reconcile Mark's leaving Jericho with Luke's approaching it by placing the healing between them (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). People did not invite themselves to another's home, and respectable people did not ask hospitality of a sinner (Keener and his notes). A tax collector was thought to have forfeited his place as a son of Abraham, which gives 19:9 its edge (Strauss). Later rabbis thought it unwise to give away more than a fifth of one's goods, so half is radical, and fourfold repayment went beyond the law, which asked it only for stolen livestock (Exodus 22:1; Keener; Strauss). Bailey reads Jesus' choice of this house as taking the crowd's hostility onto himself, with the restitution following grace already given; Keener likewise says Zacchaeus repays in response to grace, not to earn it.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 18:35, 18:36-38, 19:1-2, 19:5 and 19:6-8
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 18:35, 18:38, 19:2, 19:4, 19:5, 19:7 and 19:8
Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, ch. 13, The Blind Man and Zacchaeus
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 19:2, 19:8 and 19:9 and sidebar Jericho

ideas.s: The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

entries.title: Luke 19:11-27, The nobleman who went to receive a kingdom
entries.summary: Because people think the kingdom is about to appear, Jesus tells of a nobleman who travels to a far country to be made king while citizens who hate him send a delegation after him, and of the servants who trade with his money.
entries.plain: Because his hearers think God's kingdom is about to appear immediately, Jesus tells of a nobleman who travels abroad to be made king. Before leaving he gives ten servants a sum of money each to invest, while his own people send messengers after him to reject his rule. On his return he rewards the servants who multiplied the money with authority over cities, takes the money from one who hid it out of fear, and has the opponents of his reign executed.
entries.note: Herod the Great and his son Archelaus both had to go to Rome to be granted their rule (Keener and his notes). Josephus tells the story of Archelaus: in Rome "the number of the ambassadors that were sent by the authority of the nation were fifty," asking that he not rule; Augustus made him ethnarch of half the kingdom, not king; and in his tenth year the leading men of Judea and Samaria had him accused before Caesar and banished. Wright and Blomberg both see Archelaus behind the parable. A mina was about a hundred days' wages, and rulers rewarded able servants with authority over cities (Keener and his notes). Keener writes that "Wrapping money in a perishable handkerchief was considered one of the most irresponsible ways" to keep it. Readings of the returning king differ. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles read the nobleman as Jesus going away and returning at the end of the age, and Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, agrees, taking the slaughter as the final judgment; Wright reads the vengeance as judgment falling on Jerusalem through Roman armies, and the CSB Study Bible also thinks AD 70 likely in the last verses.
sources: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 17.9.3, 17.11.1, 17.11.4 and 17.13.1-2, trans. William Whiston

ideas.s: Rome's king of Judea from 37 to 4 BC: an Idumean, a great builder, and a ruler who killed anyone he saw as a threat, his own family included.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.

entries.title: Luke 19:28-48, The king rides down to the city and weeps over it
entries.summary: Jesus rides a borrowed colt down the Mount of Olives while his disciples spread their cloaks and praise the king who comes. Seeing the city, he weeps over the siege to come, then drives the sellers out of the temple.
entries.plain: As he approaches Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, Jesus sends for an unridden colt, and his followers spread their cloaks and loudly praise God, hailing him as the coming king. When Pharisees demand he silence them, he says the very stones would shout if they did. Seeing the city, he weeps and foretells its siege and total destruction because it missed the moment of God's visit, then clears the temple of traders and teaches there daily while the leaders plot his death.
entries.note: Kings, like Roman soldiers, could commandeer animals (the cultural backgrounds notes), and Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, thinks that likelier than animals kept for travelers to hire; Keener adds that the owners might simply have seen it as hospitality to a famous teacher. Officials rode donkeys in civil, not military, processions, and cloaks on the road hailed a king, as in 2 Kings 9:13 (Keener and his notes). The cry comes from Psalm 118:26, part of the Hallel sung at Passover (Keener and his notes). Luke leaves out the palm branches, probably because Gentile readers would not know them as a nationalist symbol (Strauss). Josephus describes how Titus decided "they must build a wall round about the whole city", and when the city fell, "Caesar gave orders that they should now demolish the entire city and temple" (the ESV Study Bible draws the link). How far the city was leveled is read differently: Keener calls not one stone on another prophetic hyperbole, since the city was not leveled completely until after AD 135, while Strauss quotes Josephus that Titus leveled it so completely that visitors would have "no ground for believing that it had ever been inhabited."
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 19:30, 19:31, 19:35, 19:36, 19:38, 19:39, 19:46 and 19:47
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 19:30-34, 19:35, 19:38, 19:39-40, 19:41-42, 19:43, 19:44, 19:46 and 19:47
ESV Study Bible, study note on Luke 19:43-44
Josephus, The Wars of the Jews 5.12.1-3 and 7.1.1, trans. William Whiston
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 19:29, 19:30, 19:36, 19:40, 19:44 and 19:45

ideas.s: A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

ideas.n: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
ideas.s: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.

entries.title: Luke 20:9-19, The tenants who killed the heir
entries.summary: Jesus tells of a vineyard owner whose tenants beat his servants and kill his beloved son to take the inheritance. The leaders realize he has told it against them.
entries.plain: Jesus tells a story about a vineyard owner who leases his land to tenant farmers and travels abroad. Each servant he sends to collect his share is beaten and turned away, so finally he sends his own dear son, and the tenants kill him to take the property for themselves. Jesus asks what the owner will do, cites the psalm about a rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, and the religious leaders, realising the story is about them, want to arrest him.
entries.note: Absentee landlords were common, especially in Galilee, and tenants paid at harvest either a share, sometimes half, or a fixed amount (Keener and his notes; Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). Landowners always held the social and legal power, and a few reportedly kept hit squads for troublesome tenants; these tenants act as if the power were theirs (Keener). The parable builds on Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7), where the vineyard is Israel and the owner God, so hearers would catch its threat at once (Strauss), and they would think at once of Israel's killing of the prophets (Keener and his notes). Keener notes that tenants could seize an inheritance only under certain legal conditions, and that the owner could name someone else as heir. Psalm 118:22 came from the Hallel, fresh in everyone's mind at Passover, and the building in the psalm is the temple, so a new cornerstone threatened the builders of the old (Keener and his notes). Bailey reads the owner's choice to send his son, instead of coming with force, as a refusal to retaliate.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 20:9-18, 20:9, 20:10, 20:11-12, 20:14-15 and 20:17
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 20:9, 20:10, 20:11-12 and 20:17
Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, ch. 24, The Parable of the Great Banquet
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 20:9-19, 20:9, 20:10, 20:13, 20:15, 20:17 and 20:18

ideas.s: Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.

A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.

entries.title: Luke 20:20-26, Caesar's coin
entries.summary: Spies sent by the leaders ask Jesus whether it is right to pay tribute to Caesar, hoping to hand him over to the governor. He asks whose image is on a denarius.
entries.plain: The religious leaders send agents posing as honest inquirers to trap Jesus into saying something that could be reported to the Roman governor. After flattering him, they ask whether paying taxes to Caesar is permitted. Jesus sees the trick, has them produce a coin, asks whose face and name are on it, and tells them to give Caesar his due and God his; unable to trap him before the crowd, they fall silent.
entries.note: Roman governors had few staff and depended on local leaders to bring cases to them (the cultural backgrounds notes). The question had a history. Josephus tells how at the census Judas of Gamala urged the people to resist, and founded a fourth philosophy whose followers held that "God is to be their only Ruler and Lord." Keener calls it a disastrous tax revolt two decades earlier, so a no could get Jesus arrested and a yes could cost him his following. Judea's own copper coins carried no image of the emperor, but foreign silver bearing his image and claims to divinity circulated widely, and the rebels of AD 6 had protested its use (Keener). The question concerned the poll tax paid directly to Rome, not local tolls (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). The denarius of Tiberius carried his image and the words "Tiberius Caesar, Augustus, son of the divine Augustus," so the questioners themselves were carrying a coin with an idolatrous image and a claim to divinity (Strauss). Strauss notes that the answer was ambiguous enough for Rome's fiercest opponents to hear it as everything belongs to God, so nothing belongs to Caesar.

Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 20:19-21, 20:22 and 20:23-26
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 18.1.1 and 18.1.6, trans. William Whiston
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 20:20-26, 20:20, 20:22 and 20:24

ideas.s: Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Luke 20:27-40, The Sadducees and the woman with seven husbands
entries.summary: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask whose wife a woman married to seven brothers will be. Jesus answers that the risen do not marry and are like the angels, and argues from the burning bush.
entries.plain: The Sadducees, who deny any resurrection, test Jesus with a riddle built on the law requiring a man to marry his dead brother's childless widow: seven brothers wed the same woman in turn, so whose wife will she be? Jesus answers that marriage belongs to the present age, while those raised in the age to come no longer die or marry and are like angels. He argues from the burning bush, where God names himself the God of the patriarchs, that God is God of the living, and even some legal experts approve while no one risks another question.
entries.note: The case rests on levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-6), which protected widows in a world where women could not earn wages, and many men assumed that a woman widowed again and again was cursed (Keener and his notes). The story line borrows from Tobit, where a demon killed Sarah's first seven husbands (Keener and his notes), and rabbinic literature is full of such mocking questions from Sadducees and other opponents (Keener). Most Jews agreed that angels, being immortal, did not marry or have children (Keener and his notes). Against the Sadducees, Pharisees tried to prove the resurrection from the books of Moses, which is why the teachers of the law approve (Keener and his notes). Wright explains the Sadducees' position by their place in society: "They denied it because they were the conservatives." A hope of resurrection, he adds, was revolutionary, and the people in power had reason to fear it. The Sadducees probably came from priestly families that had backed the Hasmonean kings, accepted only the books of Moses as fully binding, and stressed free will against the Pharisees and Essenes (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 20:27, 20:28, 20:29-32, 20:33, 20:34-36 and 20:37-38
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 20:28, 20:29-31, 20:33, 20:36, 20:37 and 20:39
N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God, ch. 4, section 2, No Future Life, or None to Speak of: The Sadducees
N. T. Wright, Luke for Everyone, comment on Luke 20:27-40
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 20:28, 20:29, 20:36, 20:37 and 20:38 and sidebar The Sadducees

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Luke 20:45-21:4, Long robes and a widow's two coins
entries.summary: Jesus warns against teachers of the law who love long robes and the best seats and devour widows' houses. Then he watches a poor widow put two small coins into the temple treasury.
entries.plain: In front of the whole crowd, Jesus warns his followers about legal experts who parade in fine robes, crave public honor and the best places at gatherings, swallow up the property of widows and pray at length for appearance. They face the harsher judgment. Watching the offerings at the temple, he then contrasts the rich, who give from their surplus, with a poor widow who drops in two tiny coins and so gives everything she has.
entries.note: Teachers were greeted with titles of honor in the crowded marketplaces (Keener). The robes are described differently: Keener and Garland, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, give distinctive white linen robes like those of priests and temple officials, and Strauss long tasseled robes marking the teacher's office. Widows often had debts and no influential advocate, so the unscrupulous could take their property, often by legal means (the cultural backgrounds notes); Keener suggests either heavy tithes or legal rulings without the mercy the law required, and Strauss the exploiting of estates the teachers managed as appointed guardians, or the abuse of widows' hospitality. A later tradition places thirteen chests for gifts to the treasury in the Court of Women, where women could come (Keener; the ESV Study Bible cites the Mishnah), and Garland notes that a gift as small as hers could only go to the freewill offering. Each of her coins was worth 1/128 of a denarius (the cultural backgrounds notes). Readings of her gift differ: Keener thinks the temple's officials would probably waste it, so Jesus also laments the system, while the ESV and CSB Study Bibles simply hold up her giving.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Luke 20:45-21:4, 20:45-46, 20:47 and 21:1-4
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Luke 20:47, 21:1 and 21:2
ESV Study Bible, study note on Luke 21:1-4
CSB Study Bible, note on Luke 21:1-4
David E. Garland, Mark, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Mark 12:38, 12:41 and 12:42
Mark L. Strauss, Luke, in Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, ed. Clinton E. Arnold, on Luke 20:46, 20:47, 21:1, 21:2 and 21:3

ideas.s: Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

entries.title: Luke 21:5-38, The temple's stones and Jerusalem surrounded
entries.summary: When people admire the temple's stones, Jesus says not one will be left on another. He warns of false claimants, arrests in synagogues, Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and signs in the sky before the Son of Man comes.
entries.plain: When people admire the temple's fine stonework and gifts, Jesus predicts it will be torn down completely. He warns against false messiahs and lists coming wars, disasters and persecution, and tells his followers that when armies surround Jerusalem they must escape, because the city will be destroyed and its people scattered until the Gentiles' time runs out. He ends with cosmic signs and the arrival of the Son of Man, while Luke notes that Jesus spent his days teaching in the temple and his nights on the Mount of Olives.
entries.note: Josephus says the temple's front was covered in gold, and from a distance it looked "like a mountain covered with snow." Josephus counts ninety-seven thousand taken captive and over a million dead, many of them pilgrims shut in at the feast (Keener and his notes); Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, thinks the dead much exaggerated and the real toll perhaps a quarter to half a million. Eusebius records that the Christians of Judea, heeding this warning, fled to Pella in the Decapolis (Strauss), and Carson, Moo and Morris use that flight in dating Luke: it suggests the words of 21:21 were known before the siege. How much of the discourse concerns AD 70 and how much the end is debated. Keener and his notes say prophecy grouped events by topic, and Jesus answers two questions, the temple's fall and the end, and Strauss agrees; the CSB Study Bible reads most of it as the near destruction, with verses 25-28 about the second coming; Wright reads the coming of the Son of Man as the vindication of Daniel 7, fulfilled in the events of AD 70.

In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

ideas.n: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
ideas.s: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

entries.title: Luke 22:24-38, Benefactors, thrones, sifting and two swords
entries.summary: At the last supper the disciples argue over who is greatest. Jesus contrasts kings who are called benefactors with himself as one who serves, promises them thrones, warns Peter that Satan has asked to sift them, and speaks of swords.
entries.plain: At the last supper the disciples argue about who ranks highest, and Jesus contrasts foreign rulers, who dominate their subjects and take the title of benefactor, with his own way of greatness through service. He promises the Twelve a place at his table and a share in judging Israel's tribes. He warns Simon that Satan wants to test them all but that he has prayed for him, predicts his threefold denial, and tells them to arm themselves because Scripture says he will be classed with criminals; shown two swords, he cuts the conversation short.
entries.note: Inscriptions across the empire honored rulers and the powerful as benefactors for their gifts to the public (Keener and his notes), though, as Strauss notes in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, the title often "would conceal tyranny under extravagant expenditure." Jewish literature often pictured the kingdom as a banquet for Israel, and most Jews expected the twelve tribes to be restored (Keener and his notes). Satan's demand recalls Job 1-2, where the satan accuses Job before the heavenly court (Keener and his notes). Heiser notes that the Hebrew word means adversary or prosecutor, a legal role in God's council, and writes, "The satan in Job 1-2 is not a villain." The first you in 22:31 is plural, all of them sifted, and the second singular, for Peter (Strauss). The swords are debated. Keener and his notes read them as a brief symbolic act, so that Jesus could be charged as a rebel and counted with transgressors as Isaiah 53:12 says, two being enough for that; Wright hears it is enough as Jesus ending a conversation the disciples have misunderstood, and Strauss agrees, noting that Josephus says even the Essenes carried arms against thieves.

ideas.s: Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

entries.title: Luke 23:1-25, Before Pilate, before Antipas, and Barabbas
entries.summary: The council brings Jesus to Pilate charged with forbidding tribute and claiming to be a king. Pilate sends him to Herod Antipas, who mocks him, and in the end Pilate gives in to the crowd and releases Barabbas.
entries.plain: The whole council takes Jesus to Pilate and accuses him of misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar and calling himself the Messiah, a king. Pilate finds no basis for a charge, but on hearing that he is a Galilean sends him to Herod, who is in Jerusalem; Herod hopes to see a sign, gets no answer, and with his soldiers mocks Jesus, dresses him in a splendid robe and sends him back, and that day Herod and Pilate become friends. Pilate tells the leaders and the people that neither he nor Herod finds Jesus guilty and proposes to have him flogged and released, but they shout for Barabbas, a man jailed for rebellion and murder, and for Jesus to be crucified. Pilate gives them what they demand.
entries.note: Opposing tribute and claiming to be king were both treason, and a Galilean had led the tax revolt of AD 6 (Keener and his notes). The council could not carry out executions: Josephus tells how the high priest Ananus was deposed for having James, Jesus' brother, put to death between two governors (Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary). Antipas would be in Jerusalem for the feast, and Pilate could pass the case to him and be rid of it (Keener and his notes). Pilate and Antipas had clashed before, over Pilate's use of temple money for an aqueduct (Keener) and the golden shields he hung in Herod's palace (Strauss, from Philo). Wright writes, "Barabbas was not a common criminal": he was a rebel, and Strauss sets him beside the Sicarii, who stabbed opponents in festival crowds. Pilate first meant only a light beating as a warning, not the scourging that came before execution (Strauss). Pilate's own view is read in different ways: as seeing an impractical sage (the cultural backgrounds notes), as hearing a religious claim, not a political one (Keener), or, in Wright's view, as sharing Herod's dislike of the chief priests.

ideas.s: Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Luke 23:26-49, The road to the cross, paradise, and the ninth hour
entries.summary: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross, the women of Jerusalem mourn, and Jesus warns them of days to come. Crucified between two criminals, he promises one of them paradise and dies at the ninth hour.
entries.plain: On the way to the cross, Roman soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry it, and Jesus tells the women grieving for him to grieve instead for themselves and their children, because worse days are coming for Jerusalem. He is crucified between two criminals, prays for those killing him, and promises the one criminal who asks to be remembered that he will be with him in paradise that day. Darkness falls at midday, the temple curtain tears, and Jesus gives his spirit to his Father and dies, while the crowd leaves in grief and the women from Galilee look on.
entries.note: Cyrene, in North Africa, had a large Jewish community, Passover drew pilgrims from all over the Mediterranean, and Roman soldiers could press anyone into carrying for them (Keener). Pious women of Jerusalem often mourned those being led out to execution and gave them a drink to dull the pain, since public mourning was not allowed after death (Keener and his notes). The green and the dry wood are read in several ways. Keener lists three, the first being that Jesus is green wood, no rebel, so the real rebels will burn all the more; Wright says it in one line, "He was the green tree, they the dry." The cultural backgrounds notes and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles also hear in it the bloodshed to come, and Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, Rome's worse violence. A condemned man was expected to pray that his death would atone for his own sins; Jesus prays for his judges instead (Keener). The torn curtain may signal God leaving the temple, which Keener thinks more likely, or new access to God's presence; the cultural backgrounds notes allow both, and Strauss reads it as judgment and open access together.

ideas.s: Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

ideas.n: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
ideas.s: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.
Jews spoke of the dead going down to Hades, and of the righteous resting at Abraham's side or in paradise. The pictures were traditional, varied, and could be borrowed by a story.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

entries.title: Luke 24:13-35, A stranger on the Emmaus road
entries.summary: Two disciples walking home to Emmaus are joined by a stranger who explains the Scriptures to them. They press him to stay, and they recognize him when he breaks the bread.
entries.plain: On the day of the resurrection, two followers walking from Jerusalem to the village of Emmaus are joined by Jesus, whom they fail to recognise. They tell the stranger of their dashed hopes in Jesus and the report of an empty tomb, and he walks them through the Scriptures to show that suffering was the Messiah's path into glory. When he breaks bread at their table they suddenly know him, he disappears, and they rush back to Jerusalem with the news.
entries.note: Fellow Jews walking home from the feast would think nothing of a stranger joining them (Keener). The CSB Study Bible suggests that Cleopas may have been the husband of one of the women at the cross, and Wright suggests his companion was his wife Mary, while saying it cannot be certain. Many expected the Messiah to be a liberator who would redeem Israel (the cultural backgrounds notes). Making as if to go on was polite and could test a host's hospitality, and hospitality required insisting, especially near nightfall when the roads were dangerous (Keener and his notes). By giving thanks and breaking the bread the guest takes the part of the head of the household (Keener and his notes). Where Emmaus was is disputed. Keener and his notes say the site is no longer known; Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, names an Ammaous that Josephus puts thirty stadia out, which would make Luke's sixty a round trip, and el-Qubeibeh; the Zondervan atlas thinks Emmaus-Nicopolis about nineteen miles away the most probable, since one important manuscript reads 160 stadia; the Zondervan Bible dictionary counts at least half a dozen proposals, none confirmed.

ideas.s: Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

entries.title: Luke 24:36-53, Not a ghost; hands lifted in blessing
entries.summary: Jesus stands among the disciples, who think they are seeing a ghost. He shows his hands and feet and eats fish, opens the Scriptures to them, and leads them out to Bethany, where he lifts his hands and blesses them.
entries.plain: Jesus appears among the gathered disciples, who are terrified and take him for a ghost. He invites them to touch his body and eats fish in front of them to prove he is no phantom, then shows them how the whole of Scripture points to him and tells them to wait in Jerusalem for power from God. Leading them out to Bethany, he raises his hands to bless them and is taken up into heaven, and they go back to the city full of joy and spend their time praising God in the temple.
entries.note: The resurrection of all the dead had not yet happened, so the disciples think of a ghost (Keener and his notes). Many ancients pictured the dead as shades, and most Jewish traditions held that angels took no earthly food, so the touch and the meal show that he is neither (Keener and his notes). Heiser counts this as the one New Testament use of the word spirit for the disembodied spirit of a human being, a ghost. Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, notes that my hands and my feet is indirect evidence that Jesus was nailed rather than tied. Other Jewish writings also speak of the Scriptures in three parts (Keener and his notes). Priests lifted their hands to give the blessing of Numbers 6:24-27 (Keener and his notes), and Sirach 50:20 describes the high priest Simon II coming down after the temple service and lifting his hands "over the whole congregation of Israelites" to give the Lord's blessing (Strauss). Bethany was on the Mount of Olives, where Acts places the ascension (Strauss). Luke ends as he began, with people at prayer in the temple (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

entries.title: John 1:1-18, The Word made flesh
entries.summary: John begins before creation with the Word who was with God and was God, through whom everything was made, and who became flesh and lived among us.
entries.plain: John opens his Gospel the way Genesis opens, and places Jesus there as God's Word, present before creation, sharing God's own life, the one through whom everything came to be. This Word brings a light darkness cannot overcome, is turned away by many of his own people, and makes those who receive him God's children. Then John states his central claim: the Word took on human flesh and lived among people, who saw God's glory in him.
entries.note: The verb for the Word living among us means pitching a tent, a reminder of God's dwelling with Israel in the tabernacle (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Keener and Carson, Moo and Morris take 1:18 to call Jesus God, while some manuscripts read the only Son (the ESV Study Bible). The word often rendered only begotten means one of a kind: Heiser and the ESV Study Bible point out that Hebrews 11:17 calls Isaac Abraham's unique son although Ishmael was also his son. The Gospel is anonymous. Carson, Moo and Morris conclude that "it is highly probable that John the son of Zebedee wrote the fourth gospel," noting that a large majority of contemporary scholars reject that view. The church fathers place it at Ephesus. Carson, Moo and Morris tentatively suggest AD 80 to 85, and papyrus 52, a scrap of John 18 they date about AD 130 and Price and House no later than about 125, rules out second-century dates. Most scholars think the first readers included Jewish believers made unwelcome in their synagogues (the cultural backgrounds article on the Jews in John); Carson, Moo and Morris think of Diaspora Jews and proselytes the book meant to persuade.

ideas.s: Greek thinkers spoke of the logos, the reason that ordered the world, and Jewish teachers spoke of God's Word and Wisdom, through whom he made everything. John opens his Gospel with that language and then says the Word became flesh.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

entries.title: John 1:19-34, Not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the Prophet
entries.summary: Priests and Levites from Jerusalem ask John who he is. He denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet, calls himself the voice in the wilderness, and points to Jesus as the Lamb of God.
entries.plain: Leaders in Jerusalem send men to ask John the Baptist who he claims to be. He denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet, and describes himself as the voice from Isaiah preparing the way. When he sees Jesus he names him God's Lamb, who deals with the world's sin, and says he saw the Spirit come down and stay on him.
entries.note: The delegation's three questions name three separate expected figures: the Messiah, Elijah, whose return Malachi 4:5 promised, and the Prophet, the one like Moses of Deuteronomy 18:15-18 (Keener and his notes). By taking Isaiah 40:3 for himself John claims to herald a new exodus (Keener and his notes). Heiser notes that the commands in Isaiah 40:1-2 are plural, addressed to God's heavenly council, and that the voice of 40:3 answers them. A once-for-all immersion belonged to Gentiles converting to Judaism, so baptizing Jews treated them almost as Gentiles (Keener and his notes); Wright says John "treated Israel as a whole as if she were pagan." The Lamb of God is read in several ways: Keener hears the Passover lamb, blended with the Old Testament's sacrificial lambs and perhaps Isaiah 53:7; the ESV Study Bible sees Jesus fulfilling the Passover lamb and the other sacrifices; the CSB Study Bible allows that John may have meant a conquering lamb who brings judgment. This is the first time John uses the Jews for the Jerusalem leadership; most of his negative uses mean the Judean leaders (the cultural backgrounds article on the Jews in John).

ideas.s: Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.

Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him. In Jesus' day people asked whether a new preacher was the Prophet, and some expected the manna and the wonders of the exodus to return with him.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

entries.title: John 1:35-51, Come and see
entries.summary: Two of John's disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon, Philip brings Nathanael, and Jesus promises they will see heaven opened and angels going up and down on the Son of Man.
entries.plain: Two of John's disciples start following Jesus, and the news spreads person to person: Andrew brings his brother Simon, and Philip brings Nathanael. Each step adds a title for Jesus, from Messiah to Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus gives Simon a new name and promises Nathanael a sight like Jacob's dream, with heaven open and angels moving between it and the Son of Man.
entries.note: Teachers trained their own disciples, so sending them on to a greater teacher was rare and showed great humility (Keener and his notes). Asking where Jesus was staying was a polite, indirect way of asking to visit, and the tenth hour, about four in the afternoon, may have been too late to walk far home before dark, so a hospitable host would invite them for the night (Keener and his notes). Nathanael's scorn may reflect village rivalry or the idea that great people came from famous places (the cultural backgrounds notes); Keener's background commentary puts Nazareth at sixteen hundred to two thousand people, while his notes cite recent estimates below five hundred. The closing promise recalls Jacob's dream at Bethel, where angels went up and down a ladder between heaven and earth (Genesis 28:12-19): Jesus becomes the meeting place of heaven and earth (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). The site of Bethsaida, home of Philip, Andrew and Peter (1:44), is disputed: et-Tell is now commonly identified as Bethsaida, while excavations at el-Araj since 2016 have revived its claim (Price and House, in the Zondervan archaeology handbook).

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

Small farming and fishing villages, ringed by Greek cities, with two new royal towns that the Gospels never say Jesus entered. Most of Jesus' story happens in places of a few hundred to a few thousand people.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

entries.title: John 2:1-12, Water into wine at a village wedding
entries.summary: At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out. Jesus has the servants fill six stone purification jars with water, and the master of the feast tastes the best wine of the week.
entries.plain: Jesus, his mother and his disciples are guests at a wedding in Cana of Galilee when the wine runs out. His mother tells him, and he answers her with a distance that surprises readers, yet she tells the servants to do whatever he says. He has them fill six stone jars, kept for Jewish purification, with water and take some to the master of the feast, who finds it is fine wine and teases the bridegroom for saving the best until last. John calls it the first of Jesus' signs.
entries.note: Weddings lasted seven days; the host had to supply wine for the whole week, and running out was a lasting embarrassment (Keener and his notes). Guests helped pay for weddings with gifts, so Mary may be asking her son for one, Keener suggests; his notes read her words as a polite, indirect request. The cultural backgrounds notes say, "Jewish people preferred stone jars because they did not easily contract ritual impurity." Together these six held about as much as an immersion pool (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). What the empty wine means is read in different ways: the ESV and CSB Study Bibles see the barrenness of the religion of the day, and Wright sees God starting something new inside the old Jewish order. Most scholars now place Cana at Khirbet Qana, about nine miles north of Nazareth, where excavation has found Roman-period houses and a ritual immersion pool (the ESV Study Bible; the cultural backgrounds article on Cana; Price and House; the Zondervan atlas); the traditional site, Kefr Kenna, has the modern churches, and the Zondervan Bible dictionary leaves the question open.

ideas.s: A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

entries.title: John 2:13-25, Tables overturned at Passover
entries.summary: At Passover Jesus drives the animal sellers and money changers out of the temple courts. Asked for a sign, he tells them to destroy this temple and he will raise it in three days, and John explains that he meant his body.
entries.plain: At Passover Jesus drives the animal traders and money changers out of the temple courts and objects to his Father's house being turned into a marketplace. When the authorities demand a sign to justify this, he talks about the temple being destroyed and raised in three days. John explains that he meant his own body, which the disciples understood only after the resurrection.
entries.note: Pilgrims needed animals for the sacrifices and money changers to turn many currencies into the coinage the temple accepted (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). Josephus says Herod began rebuilding the temple "in the eighteenth year of his reign," and Keener dates the start to 20 or 19 BC, so the forty-sixth year falls in AD 27; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles give the alternative reading, built forty-six years ago, which refers to the sanctuary and points to AD 29 or 30. In Jesus and the Victory of God Wright notes, "It was the king who had ultimate authority over the Temple": a coming king was expected to rebuild and purify it (2 Samuel 7; Zechariah 6:12), so a temple action carried a royal claim. The other Gospels place a temple action at the end of Jesus' ministry; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles hold that there were two, while Wright leaves the question open and notes that an early action would explain why Jerusalem sent people to check on Jesus in Galilee. Carson, Moo and Morris point out that John's three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55) require a ministry of at least two years.

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: John 3:1-21, Born from above
entries.summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one sees God's kingdom without being born from above, of water and Spirit, and speaks of the Son of Man lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness.
entries.plain: Nicodemus, a respected Pharisee and council member, visits Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that entry into God's kingdom requires a new birth, from above and by the Spirit, and Nicodemus cannot follow. Jesus points to the bronze serpent Moses raised in the wilderness: the Son of Man too must be lifted up, so that those who trust him receive eternal life, because God loved the world enough to give his Son.
entries.note: Jewish sources know of a wealthy Naqdimon, or Nicodemus, in this period (Keener and his notes). The Greek word for again can also mean from above, a roundabout Jewish way of saying from God, and Wright reads both senses with the weight on from above (Keener and his notes; Wright). Jewish teachers said converts became like newborn children when they were immersed, much as a Roman adoptee left behind his old legal family, so a teacher of Israel should have caught the language of conversion (Keener and his notes). Wind and spirit are one word in both Hebrew and Greek, and Ezekiel 37 pictures God's Spirit as wind bringing Israel back to life (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible). The lifted serpent is the bronze snake of Numbers 21:6-9 (Keener and his notes). Born of water and Spirit is read three ways: as conversion language drawn from the immersion of converts, or water meaning the Spirit (Keener and his notes); as the cleansing water and new heart of Ezekiel 36:25-27, not baptism (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles); or as John's water baptism into the kingdom movement together with the Spirit (Wright).

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

entries.title: John 4:1-42, A Samaritan woman at Jacob's well
entries.summary: Tired at noon, Jesus sits on Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. They talk about living water, her husbands and the right mountain for worship, and her town comes out to meet him.
entries.plain: Traveling from Judea to Galilee through Samaria, Jesus sits by Jacob's well near Sychar at about noon while his disciples go to buy food. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water, and he asks her for a drink; she is astonished that a Jew would ask a Samaritan woman. He offers her living water, tells her about her five husbands and the man she now lives with, and when she raises the old question of Gerizim or Jerusalem, says a time is coming when the Father will be worshiped in spirit and truth. She speaks of the Messiah to come, Jesus says he is the one, and the townspeople she tells come out, ask him to stay and call him the Savior of the world.
entries.note: Jews could go around Samaria, but most commonly took the short route through it (the cultural backgrounds notes). Women usually drew water together, so a woman alone at noon, the hottest hour, suggests she was not welcome among them (the cultural backgrounds notes); Bailey adds that she may have been looking for travelers. Jewish tradition held a Samaritan woman to be unclean, so drinking from her vessel would defile (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Her five husbands are read differently: as widowhood or divorce, either seen as shameful (the cultural backgrounds notes); as a sign of her sexual history (Keener); as probably divorce, with Wright unsure whether she sinned more than she was sinned against; or as a statement that was technically true but meant to mislead (Bailey). Mount Gerizim stood in view, and she speaks of worship there in the past tense because a Jewish ruler had destroyed the Samaritan temple long before (Keener and his notes; Josephus). Samaritans awaited a prophet like Moses, the Taheb, not a son of David (Keener and his notes). The emperor claimed to be savior of the world (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: The people of the hill country between Judea and Galilee worshiped Israel's God on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans each claimed to be the true heirs of Israel, and centuries of hostility lay between them.

Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him. In Jesus' day people asked whether a new preacher was the Prophet, and some expected the manna and the wonders of the exodus to return with him.

entries.title: John 5:1-18, The pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath
entries.summary: At a pool with five porches, Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and tells him to pick up his mat. It is the Sabbath, and the dispute that follows turns on Jesus calling God his own Father.
entries.plain: At a festival in Jerusalem, Jesus goes to a pool near the Sheep Gate called Bethesda, with five porches where many sick people lie. He asks a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years whether he wants to be well; the man says no one helps him into the water when it is stirred. Jesus tells him to get up, take his mat and walk, and he does. Because it is the Sabbath, the Judeans object to his carrying the mat and then to Jesus, who answers that his Father is still working and so is he, which they hear as making himself equal with God.
entries.note: The pool had twin basins with five porches, four around the sides and one across the middle (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Healing shrines, above all those of Asclepius, usually had pools, and in later times this pool served pagans as a healing shrine; Price and House, in the Zondervan archaeology handbook, report a votive foot dedicated there by a Roman woman named Pompeia. Keener thinks popular religion probably already treated it as a place of healing, Wright says it was at one stage dedicated to Asclepius, and Keener's notes place the pagan shrine in later centuries. The verse about an angel stirring the water is missing from the earliest manuscripts, though the sick man's words show that people believed something like it (the ESV Study Bible; Keener; Wright). Everyone agreed that God went on working on the Sabbath to sustain the world, so claiming that right sounded like claiming to be equal with God (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris note that 5:2 says there is a pool, which some take as proof that John wrote before AD 70, but John often uses the present tense of the past.

ideas.s: The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.

entries.title: John 5:19-47, The Son sent by the Father, and his witnesses
entries.summary: Jesus answers the charge of making himself equal with God: the Son does what he sees the Father doing, gives life and judges, and has witnesses in John, in his works, in the Father and in the Scriptures.
entries.plain: Charged with claiming equality with God, Jesus explains how he relates to the Father: the Son acts only as he sees the Father act, and the Father has handed him the power to give life and to judge. He knows his word alone would not count as proof, so he lists other witnesses, John the Baptist, his works, the Father and the Scriptures. He ends by saying that Moses, whom his hearers trust, will be the one to accuse them.
entries.note: It was common wisdom that sons imitated their fathers (Keener), and Bailey describes Middle Eastern craftsmen who guard their trade secrets and show them only to their sons. Raising the dead and judging belonged to God alone, rehearsed daily in Jewish prayer (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). In Daniel 7:13-14 the Son of Man reigns on God's behalf, and to reign was also to judge (Keener). Jesus speaks as the Father's faithful agent, under the Jewish rule that a man's agent is as the man himself (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). Two or three witnesses were needed to prove a case (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15), and the ESV Study Bible sees a trial running through John in which, in the end, the world and not Jesus is on trial. The hand lamps of the Herodian period gave about as much light as a candle, so calling John a lamp is modest praise (Keener and his notes). Moses was thought of as Israel's intercessor; here he becomes their accuser (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: John 6:1-21, Bread in the wilderness and a walk on the sea
entries.summary: Near Passover Jesus feeds five thousand men from five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd hails him as the Prophet and wants to make him king, and that night he comes to his disciples walking on the sea.
entries.plain: Near Passover, Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men from a boy's small supply of barley bread and fish, with plenty left over. The people decide he is the prophet they have been waiting for and want to make him king by force, so he slips away into the hills. That night, as the disciples struggle across the lake against the wind, he comes to them walking on the water and tells them not to fear.
entries.note: Passover recalled God's rescue through Moses, so hopes of deliverance ran high, and a crowd at that season wanting to crown a prophet like Moses is no surprise (Keener and his notes); Wright says the crowd jumps from prophet to Messiah, that is, to king. First-century prophets who promised signs like those of Moses drew thousands, and Rome slaughtered their followers (the cultural backgrounds notes); Josephus tells of Theudas, who promised to part the Jordan and was beheaded. The barley loaves and the doubting servant echo Elisha's feeding in 2 Kings 4:42-44 (Keener and his notes). Only the men were counted, and Sepphoris, one of the two chief cities of Galilee, had a theater holding just three thousand (the cultural backgrounds notes). Leftovers showed a generous host (Keener and his notes). Moses, Joshua, Elijah and Elisha parted waters, but in the Old Testament "only God trod upon the water" (Keener; Job 9:8). It is I is literally I am; Keener sees a probable nuance of deity, and his notes say the setting supports it.

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him. In Jesus' day people asked whether a new preacher was the Prophet, and some expected the manna and the wonders of the exodus to return with him.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.

God gave his name to Moses at the burning bush as I AM, and in Isaiah he says I am he. To make God's name known was to show who he is, and when Jesus uses those words in certain settings, his hearers can take them as God's own name.

entries.title: John 6:22-71, The bread from heaven
entries.summary: In the synagogue at Capernaum the crowd asks for a sign like the manna. Jesus answers that he is the bread of life come down from heaven, and his hard words about eating his flesh drive many disciples away.
entries.plain: The crowd finds Jesus at Capernaum, and he tells them to work for the food that lasts to eternal life. They ask for a sign, reminding him that their ancestors ate manna in the wilderness; he answers that it was not Moses but his Father who gives the true bread from heaven, and that he himself is the bread of life. When he says that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life, the Judeans argue, and many of his disciples find the teaching too hard and leave. Jesus asks the Twelve whether they will go too, and Peter answers that he has the words of eternal life.
entries.note: Many Jews expected the manna to be restored in the world to come (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). The discourse works like a Jewish homily on Exodus 16:15 and Psalm 78:24, using the method do not read this, but that: not Moses, but God gave the bread (Keener and his notes). Wright puts it simply: "Moses was only God's agent." Manna and water were already used as symbols of wisdom and the law, and Wisdom invited people to eat of her (Sirach 24) (Keener and his notes). Strict Jews avoided Tiberias, which Josephus says was built over graves, so Antipas had to settle it with the lowest classes of the land (the cultural backgrounds notes; the Zondervan Bible dictionary). Remains of an earlier synagogue lie beneath the later one at Capernaum, probably the building where Jesus taught (the cultural backgrounds notes; Price and House). Greeks and Romans abhorred cannibalism (Keener and his notes). Eating flesh and drinking blood is read several ways: against the Passover lamb, with the blood read as wine since drinking blood was forbidden (Keener); against Wisdom's banquet (Keener's notes); or as trusting his atoning death (the ESV Study Bible).

The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

entries.title: John 7:1-36, Up to the Festival of Tabernacles
entries.summary: Jesus stays in Galilee while the Judeans look for a chance to kill him, then goes up to Tabernacles privately and teaches in the temple. The crowds argue over whether he is a deceiver or the Messiah, and the chief priests send guards to arrest him.
entries.plain: Jesus keeps to Galilee because the Judeans want to kill him, and his brothers, who do not believe in him, urge him to show himself at the Festival of Tabernacles. He says his time has not yet come, then goes up privately, and halfway through the feast begins teaching in the temple. People marvel that he knows so much without having studied; some call him a good man and others say he leads the people astray. He defends healing on the Sabbath by pointing to circumcision, the crowd argues over whether the Messiah's origins would be known, and the chief priests and Pharisees send officers to arrest him.
entries.note: Galilee under Antipas and Judea under the Roman prefect were separate jurisdictions, so a man in trouble in one could be safer in the other (Keener and his notes). Pious Galilean men were expected at the feast, and Keener notes that Josephus speaks of whole towns going. Teachers lectured in the temple's porticoes; Jesus had not studied with an advanced teacher, yet he taught without citing earlier authorities (Keener and his notes). Leading the people astray was a capital charge under Deuteronomy 13 (Keener and his notes). Circumcision on the eighth day overrode the Sabbath, so, arguing from lesser to greater, healing a whole person should too (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Some expected a hidden Messiah, a tradition known from later sources (Keener and his notes), and the ESV Study Bible says some rabbis taught that he would be unknown while others were sure of his birthplace. The chief priests could send Levite temple guards (Keener and his notes). The cultural backgrounds article on the Jews in John notes that here, as often, the word means the Judean leaders, which is how the NIV renders it in 7:1 and 7:11.

ideas.s: The autumn pilgrim feast, eight days long, when men lived in leafy shelters, priests poured water at the altar and torches lit the temple courts. It carried hopes of rain, of resurrection and of a coming king.

Small farming and fishing villages, ringed by Greek cities, with two new royal towns that the Gospels never say Jesus entered. Most of Jesus' story happens in places of a few hundred to a few thousand people.
The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.

entries.title: John 7:37-52, Rivers of living water on the last day
entries.summary: On the great last day of the feast Jesus cries out that the thirsty should come to him and drink. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Messiah, and the Pharisees scorn a prophet from Galilee.
entries.plain: On the final day of the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him, and John explains that the flowing water stands for the Spirit, who would be given later. The crowd splits over who he is, and some argue that the Messiah cannot come from Galilee. The temple police return empty-handed, amazed at how he speaks, and when Nicodemus asks for a proper hearing the Pharisees mock him too.
entries.note: On at least the first seven days, priests carried water in procession from the pool of Siloam and poured it at the base of the altar (Keener). The rite was first meant to bring rain, and Zechariah 14, read at the feast with Ezekiel 47, promised rivers of living water flowing from the temple (Keener); Wright adds that the feast's prayers were for rain and for the resurrection of the dead. Water usually stood for the law or wisdom in Jewish texts, but John follows Isaiah 44:3 and Ezekiel 36 in using it for the Spirit (Keener and his notes). Whose heart the rivers flow from is debated. With different punctuation the water flows from Jesus, as from the temple's foundation stone (Keener), and the cultural backgrounds article on Tabernacles and living water reads Jesus as the Spirit's source, hearing behind from his belly the image of Jerusalem and its temple as the earth's navel; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles and Wright read it as flowing from believers. The Pharisees' retort forgets that Jonah came from Gath Hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25) (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible).

entries.title: John 8:12-30, The light of the world by the treasury
entries.summary: Jesus calls himself the light of the world. Told that testimony about himself does not count, he answers with the law's rule of two witnesses: himself and the Father who sent him.
entries.plain: Teaching in the temple near the treasury, Jesus calls himself the world's light. The Pharisees say his testimony about himself proves nothing, and he answers that the Father who sent him is his second witness. No one arrests him because his time has not yet come, and he says that once they have lifted him up they will understand who he is.
entries.note: Torches lit up the city during Tabernacles, and the treasury lay beside the Court of Women where the lighting and the dancing took place; in the treasury can also mean near it (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Jewish literature gave the title light of the world to Israel, Jerusalem, the patriarchs, the Messiah, God, famous rabbis and the law, always for something of ultimate importance (Keener). The law required two or three witnesses, and Pharisaic tradition tightened the rule to make conviction harder; Jesus argues how much more the Father and the Son (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; Wright). A witness who could not be questioned in court could not count, so the question where his father is may be a legal jab (the cultural backgrounds notes). What the claim to be the light of the world carries is read differently: the lights of the feast (Keener and his notes); Isaiah's servant, the light to the nations, a claim to be Israel's Messiah that Wright says is not in itself a claim to be divine; or the light of God's presence promised in the Old Testament, the tabernacle lampstand included (the ESV Study Bible).
