entries.title: John 8:31-59, Abraham's children, and before Abraham, I am
entries.summary: Jesus tells Judeans who had believed him that the truth will make them free. They answer that they are Abraham's children and were never slaves, and the argument ends with Jesus saying before Abraham was, I am, and stones in their hands.
entries.plain: Jesus tells Jews who had come to believe him that the truth will make them free, and they take offense, since as Abraham's children they have never been anyone's slaves. The argument turns bitter on both sides over who their real father is, until Jesus claims to have existed before Abraham. His hearers take that as blasphemy and pick up stones, and he slips out of the temple.
entries.note: Jewish teachers granted that Israel had been under at least four kingdoms, Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome, yet held that angels and stars governed the other nations, while God alone governed Israel (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). To suggest that a man had one father by law and another by nature accused his mother of adultery, so the reply about not being born of immorality defends their descent (Keener and his notes); Wright thinks they were already sneering about Jesus' birth, while Keener says that is not clear in this debate. Jewish tradition made the devil the liar who deceived Eve and so brought death, the first murderer (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Samaritan was an insult, and Samaritans disputed the Jews' sole claim to Abraham (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Tradition said Abraham was shown the future kingdoms and the messianic age (Keener and his notes). Fifty was the minimum age for some kinds of public service (Keener). Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16), and the temple was still being built, so a mob could find things to throw (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 8:33, 8:41, 8:42-47, 8:48, 8:56, 8:57-58 and 8:59
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 8:33, 8:41, 8:44, 8:48, 8:56 and 8:59
ESV Study Bible, study note on John 8:44
N. T. Wright, John for Everyone, Part One, comment on John 8:37-47

ideas.s: Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

The people of the hill country between Judea and Galilee worshiped Israel's God on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans each claimed to be the true heirs of Israel, and centuries of hostility lay between them.

God gave his name to Moses at the burning bush as I AM, and in Isaiah he says I am he. To make God's name known was to show who he is, and when Jesus uses those words in certain settings, his hearers can take them as God's own name.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.

entries.title: John 9:1-41, A man born blind is put out
entries.summary: Jesus puts mud on a blind beggar's eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. Because it is the Sabbath the man is questioned, his parents are afraid, and when he defends Jesus he is thrown out.
entries.plain: The disciples assume a man's blindness from birth must be someone's fault, and Jesus rejects the idea. He heals the man with mud and sends him to wash at Siloam, but because it is the Sabbath the Pharisees open an inquiry, questioning the man and his frightened parents. The man grows bolder with each round and is expelled, and the story ends with him believing in Jesus while his questioners are shown to be the blind ones.
entries.note: Many held that suffering came from sin, even sin before birth or a parent's sin (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). Kneading, of dough and by analogy of clay, was among the thirty-nine kinds of labor banned on the Sabbath (Keener). Give glory to God was a solemn call to tell the truth (Joshua 7:19) (the cultural backgrounds notes; the CSB Study Bible). Which pool was Siloam is disputed. The cultural backgrounds article on the pool takes the Siloam of Jesus' day to be the upper pool, fed by Hezekiah's tunnel; Price and House call that a later Byzantine pool and identify the pool of John 9 with the great stepped pool found in 2004, built in the mid-first century BC and abandoned in AD 70. Carson, Moo and Morris note that many scholars read put out of the synagogue (9:22) as an anachronism from a ban on Christians agreed at Jamnia after AD 85, but that the thesis has been challenged at every point; the cultural backgrounds article on the Jews in John takes the expulsions as the experience of John's own readers.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 9:1, 9:2, 9:6, 9:7, 9:14-16, 9:18-21, 9:22-23, 9:24 and 9:32-33
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 9:1, 9:2, 9:6, 9:7, 9:8, 9:18, 9:21 and 9:24
CSB Study Bible, notes on John 9:2 and 9:24
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article The Pool of Siloam
J. Randall Price and H. Wayne House, Zondervan Handbook of Biblical Archaeology, ch. 12, John 9:7 The Pool of Siloam
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 5, John, Date
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article The Jews and Jewish Leaders in John's Gospel

ideas.s: The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.

A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.

The autumn pilgrim feast, eight days long, when men lived in leafy shelters, priests poured water at the altar and torches lit the temple courts. It carried hopes of rain, of resurrection and of a coming king.

entries.title: John 10:1-21, The good shepherd and the hired hand
entries.summary: Jesus contrasts the shepherd who enters by the gate, calls his sheep by name and lays down his life for them with thieves who climb in another way and a hired hand who runs from the wolf.
entries.plain: Jesus uses a picture every listener knew: a sheepfold, a shepherd whose voice the flock recognizes, and outsiders who sneak in to steal. He calls himself both the gate and the good shepherd, who gives up his life for the flock where a hired man would run, and speaks of other sheep to be brought into one flock. His hearers are split over him once again.
entries.note: Sheep were penned at night in the cool months behind a stone wall that might be topped with briers (Keener), and Bailey describes robbers who came in gangs with a ladder. Bailey, from the shepherding he knew, says sheep follow the shepherd's voice and not the tune, and that a few favorites have names; Keener's notes agree that sheep knew their shepherd's voice. In a wilderness enclosure the shepherd sleeps across the opening, and Bailey writes, "In such a scene the shepherd literally becomes the door"; Keener thinks Jesus simply moves between two images. Who the thieves and robbers are is disputed: Keener and his notes point to the leaders who had just expelled the blind man, while Bailey, following Chrysostom and Ibn al-Tayyib, thinks of messianic pretenders such as Judas the Galilean and Theudas. Bailey reads the hired hand as a coded reference to the high priestly establishment and the wolf as Rome; Keener takes the hired hands as religious leaders generally. The other sheep may be scattered Israel gathered again (Ezekiel 37; Micah 2:12) or Gentiles, which Bailey thinks the best reading (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible).
sources: Kenneth E. Bailey, The Good Shepherd, ch. 8, The Good Shepherd Amid Thieves and Wolves in John 10:1-18, commentary on 10:1, 10:2-4, 10:7-10, 10:8, 10:12-13 and 10:16
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 10:1-2, 10:3-4, 10:5, 10:6-9, 10:10-11, 10:12-13 and 10:16-18
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 10:1-18, 10:3-4, 10:12 and 10:16
CSB Study Bible, note on John 10:16

ideas.s: Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: John 10:22-42, In Solomon's Porch at the Festival of Dedication
entries.summary: In winter, at the Festival of Dedication, the Judeans press Jesus to say plainly whether he is the Messiah. He says he and the Father are one, they pick up stones, and he answers from Psalm 82.
entries.plain: It is the Festival of Dedication, in winter, and Jesus is walking in the temple in Solomon's Porch when the Judeans surround him and ask him to tell them plainly if he is the Messiah. He says his works testify for him, his sheep hear his voice and no one can snatch them from his Father's hand, and that he and the Father are one. They pick up stones, charging him with blasphemy because he, a man, makes himself God. He answers from their law, where God says to some, you are gods, and asks how they can charge the one the Father set apart and sent with blasphemy for saying he is God's Son; then he escapes and goes back beyond the Jordan, where many believe in him.
entries.note: Solomon's Porch was the colonnade along the eastern side of the outer court, a shelter in winter, and many believed its older stonework went back to Solomon (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible); Josephus says of the eastern cloister, "This was the work of king Solomon." Wright notes that the Maccabees became kings by freeing the temple, so at Dedication people thought about kings, and here Jesus speaks of the true shepherd. Being one with the Father echoes Israel's basic confession that God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4) (Keener). Stoning was the usual punishment for blasphemy, and the festival remembered liberation from Antiochus IV, a man who claimed to be divine (the cultural backgrounds notes). Jesus' answer is a standard Jewish how-much-more argument (Keener), and set apart may echo the setting apart of the temple at its rededication (Keener and his notes). Who the gods of Psalm 82 are is disputed: divine beings of God's council (Heiser), earthly rulers who thought themselves divine (Keener), Israel receiving the law at Sinai (Wright), or human judges (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Beyond the Jordan lay Perea, outside the reach of the Jerusalem leaders (Keener and his notes).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 10:22, 10:23, 10:31, 10:34-35, 10:36 and 10:40
ESV Study Bible, study notes on John 10:22, 10:23 and 10:34
CSB Study Bible, notes on John 10:22 and 10:34

N. T. Wright, John for Everyone, Part One, comments on John 10:19-30 and 10:31-42
Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm, ch. 31, Who Will Go for Us?, endnote 3

ideas.s: The eight-day winter feast of lights that remembered how Judas Maccabeus cleansed and rededicated the temple after Antiochus IV defiled it. It recalled liberation, and it called kings to mind.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Israel's Scriptures picture God presiding over an assembly of heavenly beings, the sons of God, and Psalm 82 calls its members gods. Who those gods are is one of the hardest questions behind John 10.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.

entries.title: John 11:1-44, Lazarus four days in the tomb
entries.summary: Jesus waits two days after hearing that his friend Lazarus is ill, reaches Bethany to find him four days buried, weeps with the mourners, and calls him out of the tomb still bound in his grave clothes.
entries.plain: Martha and Mary send word that their brother Lazarus is ill, but Jesus stays where he is two more days and then says they will go back to Judea, though the disciples remind him that people there had just tried to stone him. By the time he reaches Bethany, near Jerusalem, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days, and many have come from the city to comfort the sisters. Martha says she knows her brother will rise in the resurrection on the last day, and Jesus answers that he is the resurrection and the life. At the tomb he weeps, has the stone taken away despite Martha's warning about the smell, and calls Lazarus out, his hands and feet bound and his face wrapped in a cloth, and tells them to unbind him and let him go.
entries.note: Bethany was about a day's journey from where Jesus was, so Lazarus may have died before the messengers even reached him (Keener and his notes). Visiting and feeding the bereaved was a duty of piety, and the family spent the first week mourning at home (Keener and his notes). Greek and Roman philosophers prized calm in bereavement; Jesus grieves in the Jewish way, and mourning with the bereaved was counted a virtue (Keener and his notes). After four days decomposition was well under way; later Jewish sources held that the soul hovered near the body for three days and then left, and if that idea was current, no one expected even a miracle worker to bring Lazarus back (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). The dead were bound tightly in linen, so walking out at all underlines the miracle (Keener and his notes). Wright reads the raising as a signpost and only a signpost: nobody had to untie Jesus' grave clothes, and his own resurrection is of a different order. Bethany, now el-Azariyeh, named for Lazarus, lay under two miles from Jerusalem (the Zondervan Bible dictionary; the Zondervan atlas).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 11:6, 11:7-8, 11:17-19, 11:20, 11:28-37, 11:39 and 11:43-44
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 11:6, 11:19, 11:20, 11:24, 11:31, 11:35, 11:39 and 11:44
ESV Study Bible, study notes on John 11:17 and 11:24
N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God, ch. 9, Hope Refocused (1): Gospel Traditions Outside the Easter Narratives
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, Bethany
Carl G. Rasmussen, Zondervan Atlas of the Bible, The Life of Christ and Jerusalem

ideas.s: Small farming and fishing villages, ringed by Greek cities, with two new royal towns that the Gospels never say Jesus entered. Most of Jesus' story happens in places of a few hundred to a few thousand people.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: John 11:45-57, Caiaphas: one man for the nation
entries.summary: After the raising of Lazarus the chief priests and Pharisees call a council, afraid the Romans will take away their place and their nation. Caiaphas tells them it is better for one man to die for the people.
entries.plain: After Lazarus is raised, the council meets in alarm, afraid that a popular movement around Jesus will bring Roman reprisals on the temple and the nation. Caiaphas, the high priest, argues that one man's death is a better bargain than the ruin of everyone, and John reads his words as an unwitting prophecy. From that day the leaders plot to kill Jesus, and he withdraws while Passover crowds look for him.
entries.note: Wright points out that this is the "first and only time in all four gospels where the word 'Romans' is mentioned." Their place almost certainly means the temple (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), and Keener calls their fear legitimate and borne out by history: in AD 70 the Romans did take the temple and the nation. Caiaphas held the office from AD 18 to 36, longer than any other high priest of the century (Keener and his notes), and an ossuary inscribed Joseph son of Caiaphas, found in a family tomb south of Jerusalem in 1990, is taken by most archaeologists to be his (Price and House). Keener writes, "Sacrificing the few for the many makes good politics but bad religion," and notes that Jewish teachers said not to hand over a single Israelite to death even to save everyone; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles hear an echo of the Maccabean martyrs who died for the people (2 Maccabees 7:37-38). Greeks and Jews alike allowed that someone appointed as God's representative could prophesy without meaning to (Keener). Pilgrims came early because anyone defiled by a corpse needed seven days to become clean (Keener and his notes).
sources: N. T. Wright, John for Everyone, Part Two, comment on John 11:47-57
ESV Study Bible, study notes on John 11:48, 11:50-51 and 11:55
CSB Study Bible, notes on John 11:48, 11:49, 11:50-51 and 11:55
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 11:47-48, 11:49, 11:50-53 and 11:54-55
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 11:49, 11:50 and 11:55
J. Randall Price and H. Wayne House, Zondervan Handbook of Biblical Archaeology, ch. 12, John 18:24 The House of Caiaphas and The Ossuary of Caiaphas

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

entries.title: John 12:1-11, Mary's nard and loosened hair
entries.summary: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus' honor in Bethany, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on his feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects, and Jesus says she has kept it for the day of his burial.
entries.plain: At a dinner in Bethany shortly before Passover, Mary pours a very costly perfume on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects that the money could have gone to the poor, and John notes that he was a thief. Jesus defends her act as preparation for his burial, and the chief priests begin plotting against Lazarus as well.
entries.note: The pound was a Roman pound of nearly twelve ounces of spikenard imported from northern India, when a flask usually held about an ounce (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Hosts gave guests water for their feet and anointed only the head, and only servants normally handled feet, so pouring the perfume on his feet is doubly extravagant (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Keener says religious Jews resented married women who uncovered their hair before men; Mary was probably unmarried, which softens the act but might still raise pious eyebrows, and the cultural backgrounds notes say a single woman was not required to cover her hair. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles say Jewish women rarely unbound their hair in public, and Wright compares letting it down to a woman at a polite modern dinner party hitching her long skirt up to her thighs. What Jesus means by keeping it for his burial is read several ways: keep the rest of the perfume, keep the memory of the act, or she had saved it for this (the ESV Study Bible).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 12:1-2, 12:3, 12:4-5 and 12:6-7
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 12:2, 12:3, 12:6 and 12:7
ESV Study Bible, study notes on John 12:3 and 12:7
CSB Study Bible, note on John 12:3
N. T. Wright, John for Everyone, Part Two, comment on John 12:1-8

ideas.s: At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.

A good host set out water so arriving guests could wash the dust of the road off their feet. Doing the washing yourself was a slave's work, and a disciple was not expected to touch even his teacher's feet.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: John 12:12-19, Palm branches and a donkey's colt
entries.summary: The festival crowd goes out with palm branches, shouting Hosanna and hailing Jesus as King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey, as Zechariah had said Zion's king would come.
entries.plain: Festival crowds hear that Jesus is coming and go out with palm branches, hailing him as Israel's king with the shouts of a Passover psalm. Jesus rides in on a young donkey, which John links to Zechariah's picture of a king who comes in peace, though the disciples saw the link only later. Word of the raising of Lazarus keeps the crowds coming, and the Pharisees despair that everyone is following him.
entries.note: People already in Jerusalem usually went out to welcome arriving pilgrims (Keener). Palm branches had to be brought up from Jericho, were used at Tabernacles, and had been a national symbol since the Maccabees, waved to celebrate victories (Keener and his notes, citing 1 Maccabees 13:51 and 2 Maccabees 10:7). Wright hears the Festival of Dedication at Passover: when Judas Maccabaeus cleansed the temple, "his followers entered the city waving palm branches in celebration," and in Jesus and the Victory of God he calls the Maccabean echoes in the entry deliberate. Hosanna means save, and the shout comes from Psalm 118:25-26, part of the Hallel sung through the Passover season, so the words were fresh in everyone's mind (Keener and his notes). Military heroes rode horses or were drawn in chariots; a donkey, following Zechariah 9:9, marks a king who is not coming as a warrior-conqueror (Keener and his notes). The ESV Study Bible thinks most of the crowd took King of Israel in a political and military sense.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 12:12-13 and 12:14-16
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 12:13 and 12:15
N. T. Wright, John for Everyone, Part Two, comment on John 12:9-19
N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God, ch. 11, Jesus and Israel: The Meaning of Messiahship, endnote 40
ESV Study Bible, study notes on John 12:12-19 and 12:13

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.
The eight-day winter feast of lights that remembered how Judas Maccabeus cleansed and rededicated the temple after Antiochus IV defiled it. It recalled liberation, and it called kings to mind.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: John 12:20-50, Greeks at the feast, and the ruler of this world cast out
entries.summary: Some Greeks who came up to worship ask to see Jesus. He says his hour has come, that the ruler of this world will be driven out, and that when he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself; many leaders believe but stay silent.
entries.plain: When some Greeks ask to meet Jesus, he takes it as a sign that his hour has arrived. He speaks of a seed that must die to bear fruit, a voice from heaven answers his prayer, and he says that being lifted up will draw everyone to him, pointing to the way he will die. John closes the public ministry by noting that many did not believe, and that some leaders who did kept silent out of fear.
entries.note: The Greeks were probably Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God without converting, though Keener allows they could be Greek-speaking Jews of the East, and in Palestine and Syria the two peoples were notorious for disliking each other (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). Philip is one of the few disciples with a Greek name, and Bethsaida lay near the Greek cities of the Decapolis (Keener and his notes). Lifted up plays on exaltation and on hoisting a body onto a cross, and echoes the servant of Isaiah 52:13 (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Jewish texts recognized Satan's rule over the world, but the cultural backgrounds notes find no surviving Jewish use of this title for him. The word for glory can also mean honor or reputation, the goal of high society (Keener), and Keener reads the silent believers among the leaders as a sign that not all synagogue leaders of John's day were hostile. Whoever rejects Jesus rejects the one who sent him, since an agent or ambassador was received with the honor due his sender and was to speak the sender's message, not his own (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 12:20, 12:21-22, 12:28-30, 12:31, 12:32-33, 12:34, 12:39-41, 12:42, 12:43 and 12:48-49
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 12:20, 12:21, 12:31, 12:32, 12:34 and 12:50
CSB Study Bible, note on John 12:20
ESV Study Bible, study note on John 12:32

ideas.s: Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: John 13:1-30, Washing the disciples' feet, and the morsel for Judas
entries.summary: At supper before Passover Jesus takes off his outer clothes, ties a towel around himself and washes his disciples' feet. Then he hands Judas the dipped morsel, and Judas goes out into the night.
entries.plain: At supper before Passover, Jesus does a slave's job and washes his disciples' feet. Peter protests, and Jesus insists, then tells them to do the same for each other, since no servant ranks above his master. He announces that one of them will betray him, quietly marks out Judas by handing him a piece of bread, and Judas leaves into the night.
entries.note: Water for the feet was a host's courtesy on arrival, but the washing itself was servile, done by a servant or by very submissive wives or children (Keener and his notes); the ESV and CSB Study Bibles say the task was left to non-Jewish slaves. Disciples served their teachers, as Elisha served Elijah, but not even they were expected to handle the master's feet (Keener and his notes). The bath Peter has already had may be the purification before the feast (Keener and his notes), and Wright suggests the washing prepares them for something that would supersede the temple. Each diner lay on his left elbow slightly behind the man to his right, so the beloved disciple, at Jesus' right, could lean back against his chest, a place of honor (Keener and his notes; the cultural backgrounds article on the triclinium). For the host to dip a piece of bread and hand it to someone honored the receiver, so betrayal after it was heinous (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris argue that this disciple, first named here, was one of the Twelve, and most probably John the son of Zebedee.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 13:3-8, 13:9-11, 13:12-14, 13:16-17, 13:18, 13:20, 13:23, 13:24-27 and 13:28-30
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 13:5, 13:10, 13:14, 13:16, 13:18, 13:20, 13:23, 13:25, 13:26 and 13:29
ESV Study Bible, study note on John 13:1-17
CSB Study Bible, note on John 13:1-17
N. T. Wright, Jesus and the Victory of God, ch. 12, The Reasons for Jesus' Crucifixion, endnote 77
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article Triclinium
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 5, John, Author, Internal Evidence

ideas.s: A good host set out water so arriving guests could wash the dust of the road off their feet. Doing the washing yourself was a slave's work, and a disciple was not expected to touch even his teacher's feet.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

entries.title: John 14:1-31, Rooms in the Father's house, and another Advocate
entries.summary: Jesus tells his troubled disciples that he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house, that he is the way, and that the Father will send another Advocate, the Spirit of truth. He leaves them his peace.
entries.plain: Jesus tells the disciples not to let their hearts be troubled: in his Father's house are many rooms, he is going to prepare a place for them, and he will come back and take them to be with him. Thomas asks how they can know the way, and Jesus says he is the way, the truth and the life; Philip asks him to show them the Father, and Jesus says whoever has seen him has seen the Father. Whatever they ask in his name he will do, and he will ask the Father to give them another Advocate to be with them forever, the Spirit of truth, who will teach them and remind them of everything he has said. He leaves them his peace, not as the world gives, and says the ruler of this world is coming but has no hold on him.
entries.note: The Father's house is the temple (2:16), and the rooms probably echo the new temple of Ezekiel; the same word returns in 14:23 for God making his home with the believer (Keener and his notes). Keener takes the promised coming in 14:3 as Jesus' return after the resurrection to give the Spirit. In the Old Testament acting in God's name could mean acting as his representative, and Keener sets this far from pagan magic, which used names to manipulate spirits. The word for the Spirit can mean an advocate or defending attorney, and in Jewish pictures of the heavenly court Satan prosecutes while God, or the angel Michael, defends Israel (Keener); the cultural backgrounds notes say the term sometimes, though not always, carried a legal sense. The cultural backgrounds notes call the Roman peace "a hollow fiction in practice" wherever Rome was still at war or in danger of it. Wright reads the ruler of this world here on two levels, Caesar, whose soldiers will soon take Jesus, and the dark power behind Caesar; the ESV Study Bible sees Satan coming in the person of Judas and the arresting party.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 14:2, 14:3-4, 14:5, 14:8, 14:12-14, 14:16, 14:18-20 and 14:27
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 14:2, 14:5, 14:8, 14:13-14, 14:16, 14:18 and 14:27

ESV Study Bible, study note on John 14:30

ideas.s: Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

God gave his name to Moses at the burning bush as I AM, and in Isaiah he says I am he. To make God's name known was to show who he is, and when Jesus uses those words in certain settings, his hearers can take them as God's own name.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: John 15:1-17, The true vine, and friends rather than slaves
entries.summary: Jesus calls himself the true vine and his Father the vinegrower, who cuts off fruitless branches and prunes the fruitful. He calls his disciples friends, not slaves, because he has told them everything.
entries.plain: Jesus pictures himself as the true vine, his Father as the gardener and his disciples as branches that bear fruit only while joined to him. He commands them to love each other with the self-giving love he has shown, the kind that dies for friends. He calls them friends instead of slaves, because he has shared with them what the Father told him, and reminds them that the choice was his.
entries.note: Scripture pictured Israel as God's vineyard or vine (Isaiah 5:7; Psalm 80:8; Hosea 10:1), and calling himself the true vine sets Jesus against Israel's failure to bear fruit (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles); Wright takes it as a claim that Jesus himself is the true Israel. Prunes also means cleanses, one of John's plays on words (Keener). Vines were tied to posts and pruned through the year, and at the severest pruning the fruitless branches were cut out and, useless for building, burned; Ezekiel 15 says a barren vine is good only for the fire (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Greeks treasured dying for one's friends as the greatest act of friendship, while later rabbis did not give it special value, and ideal friends shared their secrets, as a servant would not (Keener and his notes). Scripture called Abraham God's friend, and God spoke with Moses face to face (Keener and his notes). Disciples usually attached themselves to a teacher, and the CSB Study Bible cites the saying, provide yourself with a teacher; the cultural backgrounds notes say the Gospels stress that Jesus chose his own core disciples.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 15:1, 15:2-3, 15:4-8, 15:12-13 and 15:14-15
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 15:1, 15:2, 15:6, 15:13, 15:15 and 15:16

CSB Study Bible, notes on John 15:1-17, 15:1, 15:6 and 15:16

ideas.s: The prophets and psalms pictured Israel as God's vine or vineyard, planted and tended by him and judged when it bore no fruit. A golden vine over the temple gate kept the picture in front of every worshiper.

ideas.n: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: John 15:18-16:15, Hated by the world and put out of the synagogue
entries.summary: Jesus warns that the world will hate his followers as it hated him, that they will be put out of the synagogues and even killed by people who think they are serving God, and that the Advocate will prove the world wrong.
entries.plain: Jesus warns the disciples that the world will hate and persecute them as it did him. They will be expelled from synagogues, and some who kill them will think they are serving God. He promises the Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who will testify about him, expose the world's error and lead the disciples into the truth, and he says his going away is for their good.
entries.note: In the Mediterranean world friendship normally meant taking on a friend's enemies, so the world that hates Jesus hates his friends (the cultural backgrounds notes). Jesus foresaw his followers being shunned, but John's repeated stress on expulsion probably spoke to his first readers, who without recognized Jewish status could lose their exemption from the imperial cult and face charges of disloyalty (Keener and his notes); Carson, Moo and Morris note that the theory dating such expulsions after a ban on Christians agreed at Jamnia after AD 85 has been challenged at every point. Who was expected to do the killing is disputed: the CSB Study Bible thinks Jewish persecution most likely; the cultural backgrounds notes say fatal persecution came especially from Gentiles; Keener says synagogue leaders in Asia handed believers to Rome rather than killing them. Keener says the Spirit, the believers' Advocate, becomes the world's prosecutor: Rome had no state prosecutors, so a case went forward only when someone with a stake in it brought the charge, and here the Spirit brings the world's case before God's court. Wright likewise pictures the Spirit as the advocate in a lawsuit who proves the world in the wrong.

ideas.s: A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: John 16:16-33, A woman in labor
entries.summary: Jesus tells the puzzled disciples that in a little while they will not see him and then will see him again, and that their grief will turn to joy like a mother's after childbirth. He warns that they will be scattered.
entries.plain: In a little while, Jesus says, they will no longer see him, and again a little while and they will see him, and the disciples ask one another what he means. They will weep while the world rejoices, he says, but their grief will turn to joy, as a woman in labor has pain but forgets it for joy that a child has been born into the world. They will see him again, no one will take their joy away, and they may ask the Father in his name. When they say that now they believe, he warns that they will be scattered and leave him alone, yet he is not alone, and he has overcome the world.
entries.note: Women often died in childbirth, and the prophets used birth pangs for suffering, often from judgment, and in some texts for the birth of a messianic era (Isaiah 66:7-10; Micah 5:1-4); early Judaism applied them to the last suffering before the resurrection of the dead (Keener). In Isaiah a little while (26:20) stands beside figurative childbirth (26:17-18) and the raising of the dead (26:19), and in Isaiah 66 Zion gives birth while her people see and rejoice (the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener pictures the tomb as the womb from which the resurrection comes, opening the new age, and Wright says that with Jesus' death and resurrection a new world is being born. Like many sages, Jesus spoke in proverbs and riddles (Keener and his notes). When their leader died or failed, God's people were scattered, as in Zechariah 13:7 and Ezekiel 34 (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 16:16-22, 16:25-28 and 16:31-32
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 16:16-18, 16:21, 16:22, 16:25 and 16:32
N. T. Wright, John for Everyone, Part Two, comment on John 16:12-22

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: John 17:1-26, The prayer: your name made known
entries.summary: Before his arrest Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays that the Father will glorify him, keep those given him in the Father's name and set them apart by the truth, and make all who believe one.
entries.plain: Jesus ends the supper by praying aloud. He asks the Father to glorify him, defines eternal life as knowing the one true God and the one he sent, and prays for the disciples he is leaving in the world, that they be protected and set apart by the truth. Finally he prays for believers still to come, that they will share the unity he has with the Father.
entries.note: Jewish sources often report a dying figure's last counsel to his children or followers, and Jewish literature had testaments of departing heroes, so final instructions before leaving fit the setting, whether or not John follows the form (Keener and his notes). Teachers sometimes called their disciples children, and disciples called their teachers father (Keener). Lifting the eyes to heaven was a common posture of prayer (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Revealing God's name meant revealing his character (Exodus 33:19; 34:5), and a daily prayer of many Jews asked that God's name be hallowed across the whole world (Keener and his notes); Heiser says the disciples could already read the name in their Scriptures, so Jesus was showing them who God was. Son of destruction is a Hebrew-style idiom, and the betrayer of Psalm 41:9 was not to triumph (Keener and his notes). Jewish tradition held that God set Israel apart by giving the law, a blessing still said over the Sabbath candles (Keener and his notes). Some Essenes withdrew to the wilderness; Jesus instead prays for his people's protection in the world (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible).

ESV Study Bible, study notes on John 17:1 and 17:15
CSB Study Bible, note on John 17:1

ideas.s: God gave his name to Moses at the burning bush as I AM, and in Isaiah he says I am he. To make God's name known was to show who he is, and when Jesus uses those words in certain settings, his hearers can take them as God's own name.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.

entries.title: John 18:1-27, Arrest across the Kidron, and Annas
entries.summary: Judas brings soldiers and temple police with torches to a garden across the Kidron. Jesus answers I am he, they fall back, and he is taken bound to Annas while Peter denies him three times by a charcoal fire.
entries.plain: Jesus crosses the Kidron valley to a garden, and Judas comes there with a detachment of soldiers and police from the chief priests and Pharisees, carrying lanterns, torches and weapons. When Jesus asks whom they want and says I am he, they draw back and fall to the ground; Peter cuts off the right ear of the high priest's slave Malchus, and Jesus tells him to put the sword away. They bind Jesus and take him first to Annas, father-in-law of Caiaphas. Another disciple known to the high priest gets Peter into the courtyard, where Peter warms himself at a charcoal fire and three times denies being a disciple; meanwhile Annas questions Jesus, who says he has always taught openly, an officer slaps him, and Annas sends him bound to Caiaphas as a rooster crows.
entries.note: The Kidron ran only in the rainy season, and the Passover moon was nearly full, so only a few needed torches (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Who made the arrest is debated. The cohort language fits Roman units, and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles speak of soldiers sent to prevent rioting, with the temple police making the arrest; Keener and his notes point out that the same terms were used of Jewish units, that Romans would not take a prisoner to Annas, whom Rome had deposed, and that Pilate seems unaware of the case. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15 and kept his power through his family (Keener and his notes); Josephus writes that "he had five sons who had all performed the office of a high priest to God." A disciple's denial shamed his teacher, which is why scholars think no Christian would have invented it (Keener and his notes). Where Caiaphas lived is disputed between a mansion under the Armenian monastery on Mount Zion and the site of St. Peter in Gallicantu (Price and House).

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

God gave his name to Moses at the burning bush as I AM, and in Isaiah he says I am he. To make God's name known was to show who he is, and when Jesus uses those words in certain settings, his hearers can take them as God's own name.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: John 18:28-40, Pilate's headquarters at dawn
entries.summary: At daybreak the leaders bring Jesus to the governor's headquarters but will not go in, so as to stay clean for Passover. Pilate questions him about being king of the Jews, finds no case, and offers to release him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.
entries.plain: The Jewish leaders bring Jesus to the Roman governor's residence at dawn but stay outside to avoid defilement before Passover. Pilate goes back and forth between them and Jesus, asks whether he is a king, and hears that his kingdom does not come from this world. Pilate finds no basis for a charge and offers to free him under a Passover custom, but the crowd chooses Barabbas instead.
entries.note: The governor came up from Caesarea to Herod's palace at the feasts to keep order (Keener and his notes); the ESV and CSB Study Bibles allow the Antonia fortress instead, and the Zondervan atlas thinks Herod's palace more probable. That they must stay clean to eat the Passover seems to put the meal on the following evening. The cultural backgrounds article on the Synoptic Passover meal and John's Passover lamb sets out both answers: some think Jesus kept the meal a night early, either since he would not live to the next evening or since his followers kept a sectarian calendar; others think John chose to tell Jesus' death as that of the Passover lamb, and it notes that in Jewish usage the whole festival could be called the Passover. Pilate would class a teacher who talked of truth with the harmless Cynic and Stoic sages who called themselves kings (Keener and his notes), and Bailey reads not from this world as the kingdom's origin, not its location. The word used of Barabbas can mean robber or revolutionary; the ESV Study Bible prefers robber, while Keener and his notes and the CSB Study Bible read revolutionary.

ideas.s: Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

entries.title: John 19:1-16, Flogged, mocked, and no friend of Caesar
entries.summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged, the soldiers crown him with thorns and hail him as king, and Pilate shows him to the crowd. Warned that releasing him makes Pilate no friend of Caesar, he sits on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement and hands him over.
entries.plain: Pilate has Jesus beaten and mocked as a king, then presents him to the crowd, hoping that will be enough. The priests demand crucifixion and say Jesus has claimed to be God's Son, which alarms Pilate further. When they warn that releasing him would make Pilate disloyal to Caesar, and declare Caesar their only king, Pilate gives way and hands him over.
entries.note: Whether this is the full scourging before execution is read differently: Keener calls it a lesser beating, since Pilate had not yet passed sentence, the ESV Study Bible the lightest Roman form, and the CSB Study Bible says it left Jesus too weak to carry the beam far. A faded red soldier's cloak could pass for purple, and Hail mimics the salute Ave, Caesar (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). Here is the man is heard in several ways: Keener reads a mock acclamation that presents a harmless fool, the ESV and CSB Study Bibles a cry of look at the poor fellow, the cultural backgrounds notes an echo of God presenting Saul in 1 Samuel 9:17, and Wright the true image of the true God. Jews prayed daily for the royal Messiah, and a prayer later used at Passover confesses no king but God, so the leaders' cry is bitter irony (Keener and his notes). Gabbatha was probably a platform on the east side of Herod's palace, since the pavement long taken as the Antonia's was not laid before AD 70 (the Zondervan Bible dictionary).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 19:1, 19:2, 19:3, 19:5, 19:7-9, 19:11, 19:12, 19:13, 19:14 and 19:15-16

A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.

ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.

entries.title: John 19:16-30, The cross, the notice in three languages, and his mother
entries.summary: Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha. Pilate's notice, King of the Jews, is written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek; soldiers cast lots for his seamless tunic; he gives his mother to the beloved disciple, takes the sour wine and says it is finished.
entries.plain: Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others. Pilate's notice names him king of the Jews in three languages, and Pilate refuses to alter it, while the soldiers gamble for his seamless tunic. From the cross Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple he loved, and he dies declaring his work complete.
entries.note: The condemned carried the crossbeam to the site, and Roman crucifixions, like Jewish stonings, took place outside the city (Keener and his notes); the cultural backgrounds notes say the soldiers would have led Jesus out through the Garden Gate, not along the route later tradition enshrined. Execution squads, typically four men, had a right to what the prisoner wore, and a seamless tunic was specially made and valuable (Keener and his notes). Keener notes that Josephus calls the high priest's robe seamless but thinks a priestly allusion probably reads too much into the text; the CSB Study Bible suggests Joseph's robe instead. Jesus' mother was probably a widow in her forties who depended on her eldest son (Keener and his notes). Sour wine was the cheap drink of soldiers and laborers, and hyssop was used at Passover (Exodus 12:22) (Keener and his notes). Where Golgotha was is disputed: the Church of the Holy Sepulchre has the stronger historical claim, with a tradition going back to the fourth century, while the Garden Tomb rests on a nineteenth-century identification (the Zondervan Bible dictionary; the Zondervan atlas).

ideas.s: Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.

entries.title: John 19:31-42, Legs unbroken and a hundred pounds of spices
entries.summary: Because the coming Sabbath is a high day, the leaders ask for the bodies to be taken down. The soldiers find Jesus already dead and pierce his side; Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him with a lavish weight of spices in a new tomb in a garden.
entries.plain: Because the Sabbath is about to begin, the leaders want the bodies taken down, and the soldiers break the legs of the other two men but find Jesus already dead. A spear thrust to his side brings out blood and water, and John insists the account rests on eyewitness testimony and fulfils Scripture. Two leading men who had followed Jesus quietly, Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, bury him with a lavish quantity of spices in a new tomb nearby.
entries.note: A crucified man could rest on a small seat and push himself up to breathe, so breaking the legs hastened death (Keener; the ESV Study Bible; the cultural backgrounds article on crucifixion). Romans often left bodies for the vultures, but in Judea they deferred to Deuteronomy 21:23 (Keener and his notes); as Wright and Bird write, "many victims of crucifixion did indeed receive a proper burial," and Josephus says the Jews "took down those that were condemned and crucified, and buried them before the going down of the sun." The unbroken bones fit Psalm 34:20 and the rule that no bone of the Passover lamb be broken (Exodus 12:46) (Keener and his notes). When Jesus died is disputed: Keener and his notes read John as placing the death while the Passover lambs were being slaughtered, a day earlier than the other Gospels, and suggest a calendar difference or a symbolic point, and the article on the Synoptic Passover meal and John's Passover lamb reads John's timing as showing Jesus as the lamb; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles read Preparation as the day before the Sabbath of Passover week, so that all four Gospels agree.

ideas.s: Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.

entries.title: John 20:1-18, The empty tomb and the gardener
entries.summary: Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, who see the linen cloths lying in the empty tomb. Weeping outside, she takes the risen Jesus for the gardener until he says her name, and he sends her to tell the others.
entries.plain: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb open before dawn and runs to tell Peter and the beloved disciple, who race there and find the grave clothes left behind. The beloved disciple sees and believes. Mary, weeping by the tomb, meets Jesus without recognizing him until he speaks her name, and he sends her to tell the others that he is going up to his Father, which makes her the first to announce the risen Lord.
entries.note: Tomb entrances were often closed with a disk-shaped stone set in a groove, which took several people to move (Keener and his notes). Robbers would not have unwrapped a body or left its cloths in order (Keener; the ESV Study Bible). What the cloths show is disputed: the CSB Study Bible says the body passed through the wrappings, the ESV Study Bible says nothing in the text suggests it and that Jesus most likely unwrapped them, and Keener says the rolled face cloth could mean neatness or that the body rose straight out of the wrappings. The CSB Study Bible notes that two witnesses made the evidence admissible under Jewish law (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). Men often thought women undependable witnesses, and both Jewish and Roman law gave their word limited value, so sending a woman to testify runs against the culture (Keener and his notes); Wright adds that critics later scoffed at the story for that very reason. Gardeners were at the bottom of the social scale (Keener and his notes), and Wright, recalling Pilate's here is the man, calls Jesus "the new Adam, the gardener," in a garden on the first day of new creation.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 20:1, 20:2-3, 20:6-7, 20:11-18, 20:15, 20:16 and 20:17-18
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 20:1, 20:2, 20:3, 20:5, 20:15, 20:16 and 20:17

CSB Study Bible, notes on John 20:7, 20:8-9 and 20:18
N. T. Wright, John for Everyone, Part Two, comment on John 20:11-18
N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God, ch. 13, General Issues in the Easter Stories

ideas.s: Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.

Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: John 20:19-31, Locked doors, and my Lord and my God
entries.summary: On the evening of the first day Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors, shows his hands and side, sends them as the Father sent him and breathes the Spirit on them. A week later Thomas sees the wounds and confesses him as Lord and God.
entries.plain: On Easter evening Jesus appears to his frightened disciples behind locked doors, greets them with peace and shows his wounds. He sends them out as the Father sent him and breathes the Spirit on them. Thomas, absent that night, refuses to believe without proof; a week later he sees Jesus and calls him Lord and God, and John says he has written so readers will believe and have life.
entries.note: The disciples would still be in Jerusalem, in the first heavy week of mourning and with the festival still going on (Keener and his notes). Peace be with you was the standard Jewish greeting, shalom (Keener and his notes), and Bailey reads the double greeting as reconciliation offered to men who had run away, before they are sent out. A commissioned agent acted with his sender's authority as far as he faithfully represented him (Keener and his notes). Breathing on them recalls God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) (Keener and his notes). Domitian, emperor when John probably wrote, reportedly wanted to be called Lord God, while readers of the Greek Old Testament knew my God and my Lord as a divine title (Psalm 35:23) (the cultural backgrounds notes); Wright hears Thomas's words as a direct challenge to the rising imperial cult. Carson, Moo and Morris argue from the syntax of 20:31 that the verse answers who the Messiah, the Son of God, is, namely Jesus, a question that Jews and proselytes who expected a Messiah would ask, and so read the Gospel as written to persuade them.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 20:19, 20:20, 20:21, 20:22, 20:24-25 and 20:27-28
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 20:19, 20:20, 20:21, 20:22, 20:25 and 20:28
Kenneth E. Bailey, The Good Shepherd, ch. 7, The Disciples as Good Shepherds in Matthew 18:10-14
N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God, ch. 17, New Day, New Tasks: John
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 5, John, Purpose

ideas.s: Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: John 21:1-14, Breakfast on the beach
entries.summary: Back in Galilee, seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore tells them to cast to the right side, the net fills with 153 large fish, and Jesus gives them bread and fish by a charcoal fire.
entries.plain: Back in Galilee, seven disciples fish all night on the lake and catch nothing. A stranger on the shore at dawn tells them where to cast, the net fills, and the beloved disciple realizes it is Jesus; Peter leaps into the water to reach him. Jesus has a fire going and feeds them bread and fish, his third appearance to the disciples since rising.
entries.note: Commercial fishing mattered to the lake's economy; Galileans fished at night, sometimes with torches, so the catch could be sold fresh in the morning, using dragnets weighted along the wide edge (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Naked could mean without the outer garment, which men took off for hard work, and pious Jews avoided public nakedness (Keener and his notes). Nets were woven from flax or hemp rope, and that this one did not tear under such a load is part of the wonder (the cultural backgrounds notes). Proposals for 153 abound, from a triangular number to Jerome's unsupported claim of 153 kinds of fish, but Keener and his notes think the disciples simply counted the catch, and the ESV Study Bible says fishermen routinely counted fish before selling them. The host passed out the bread (Keener). Some scholars once held chapter 21 a later addition because it seems an anticlimax after 20:30-31, but the Iliad also ends with an anticlimactic book, and more scholars now treat the chapter as part of the Gospel (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 21:1-14, 21:1-3, 21:5-6, 21:7, 21:11 and 21:12-14
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 21:1-25, 21:3, 21:6, 21:7 and 21:11
ESV Study Bible, study notes on John 21:3 and 21:11
CSB Study Bible, note on John 21:3

ideas.s: Fishing was a real business on the lake of Galilee: boats, costly nets, partnerships between families, work through the night and fish sold in the morning. Fishermen did better than most peasants.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

entries.title: John 21:15-25, Feed my sheep, and stretch out your hands
entries.summary: Three times Jesus asks Peter whether he loves him and three times tells him to tend his sheep. He foretells Peter's death and answers his question about the beloved disciple, whose testimony closes the book.
entries.plain: Three times Jesus asks Peter whether he loves him, three times he gives him the work of caring for his flock, and the third asking hurts Peter. Jesus then hints at the kind of death Peter will die and calls him to follow. When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus tells him that is not his concern, and the Gospel closes by naming this disciple as its witness and writer.
entries.note: The two Greek verbs for love were used interchangeably in John's time, including by John (Keener and his notes); the ESV Study Bible says most modern commentators agree, though many older ones saw a difference. Stretching out the hands could mean prayer, or having one's hands tied before execution (the cultural backgrounds notes), and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles take it as crucifixion. How Peter died is told differently: the cultural backgrounds notes cite early tradition that Nero had him crucified upside down about AD 64, Keener a strong tradition that he was crucified in Rome under Nero, the CSB Study Bible a tradition that Peter chose that way to die, and the ESV Study Bible calls the later accounts overlaid with legend. Carson, Moo and Morris draw dating clues from this chapter: 21:19 implies that Peter had already died when it was written, and the rumor of 21:23 points to a date late rather than early. The chapter also names the beloved disciple as the one who wrote these things (21:24), the basis for treating him as the Gospel's main author (Carson, Moo and Morris; the Zondervan Bible dictionary).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on John 21:15-17 and 21:18-19
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on John 21:15-17, 21:18, 21:19, 21:24 and 21:25
