J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, Beloved Disciple

ideas.s: Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.

entries.title: Acts 1:1-11, The kingdom question and the cloud
entries.summary: Luke's second volume opens with the risen Jesus speaking about God's kingdom for forty days. Asked whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he promises the Spirit, sends the apostles as witnesses to the end of the earth, and is taken up in a cloud.
entries.plain: Luke picks up where his Gospel left off: the risen Jesus spends weeks with his followers, teaching about God's reign and telling them to wait in Jerusalem for the Spirit. Their question about Israel's restoration gets a redirected answer, with the timing left to God and a mission handed to them that runs outward from Jerusalem to every nation. Then he is taken from their sight in a cloud, with a promise that he will return. For a first reader this sets the agenda of the whole book: the hope of Israel goes forward through Spirit-filled witnesses.
entries.note: Neither book names its author. Carson, Moo and Morris accept the early church's unanimous ascription to Luke, the physician who traveled with Paul, citing the we passages and a tradition that "runs against form in singling out a nonapostle as the author"; many critics since the late 1700s doubt it, chiefly because the Paul of Acts seems to them unlike the Paul of the letters. Most scholars date Acts to 80-95; Carson, Moo and Morris argue for about 62, since the book ends before Paul's trial. On reliability, Haenchen and Conzelmann treat the speeches as Luke's own compositions, while Ramsay, Hengel and Hemer find his details confirmed by other sources (Carson, Moo and Morris). Theophilus was probably a patron who paid for publication (Carson, Moo and Morris; Keener). The disciples' question was natural, since the prophets' promises of the Spirit sit within Israel's restoration (Keener and his notes). Greek ascension stories told of spirits becoming gods at death; the likelier model is Elijah's bodily ascension, with Elisha receiving his spirit as the disciples will receive the Spirit (the cultural backgrounds article Ascensions). The cloud evokes Daniel 7:13-14 and God's glory (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible).
sources: D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 6, Acts, sections Author (The Traditional Case; The Case Against the Tradition; Conclusion), Date, Genre, Addressees, and Purpose, Acts in Recent Study and The Contribution of Acts (Ancient Historical Standards; The Speeches of Acts)
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 1:1, 1:6 and 1:9, and article Ascensions
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 1:1-5, 1:6 and 1:9-11
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 1:9

ideas.s: Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

entries.title: Acts 1:12-26, The Twelve made whole by lot
entries.summary: Back in Jerusalem the apostles pray in an upstairs room with the women and Jesus' family. Peter says Judas's place must be filled, and the lot falls on Matthias.
entries.plain: Back in the city the apostles, the women and Jesus' own family gather to pray while they wait. Peter argues that Judas's betrayal and death leave a gap the Scriptures foresaw, and that someone who had walked with them from the start must fill it. Two candidates are named, the group prays, and lots choose Matthias. Restoring the number twelve matters because it pictures a renewed Israel ready for what comes next.
entries.note: A Sabbath day's walk was a measure of distance, about two thousand cubits, not a sign that it was the Sabbath (Keener and his notes); the ESV Study Bible says the limit came from later tradition rather than an explicit Old Testament law. Twelve leaders stood for a renewed Israel, and the Dead Sea Scrolls community also had twelve (Keener and his notes). Ancient readers expected the wicked, especially apostates, to die painfully (Keener and his notes). Akeldama lies on the south slope of the Hinnom valley, among burial caves that the Ritmeyers argue held Jerusalem's elite (Price and House). Lots were marked stones or potsherds shaken in a container until one fell out (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). Gentiles chose many officials by lot, and Jews did too (1 Chronicles 24:5); because Scripture allowed it, they did not count it divination (Keener and his notes). The sources differ on whether it is a model: the CSB Study Bible ties the method to the time before the Spirit was given, the ESV Study Bible says it does not mean believers should cast lots today, and Wright says Luke does not seem to think the choice arbitrary.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 1:12, 1:13, 1:15-26, 1:18-19 and 1:23-26
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 1:12, 1:13, 1:18-19, 1:22 and 1:26
ESV Study Bible, study notes on Acts 1:12 and 1:26
CSB Study Bible, note on Acts 1:24-26
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part One, comment on Acts 1:15-26
J. Randall Price and H. Wayne House, Zondervan Handbook of Biblical Archaeology, Acts 1:19 Akeldama, The Field of Blood

ideas.s: The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.
Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.

entries.title: Acts 2:1-13, Pentecost and the nations
entries.summary: On the day of Pentecost wind and fire come on the gathered believers, and Jewish pilgrims from every nation hear them speaking in their own languages.
entries.plain: At the harvest festival of Pentecost the gathered believers experience something like rushing wind and fire, and they begin speaking in languages they never learned. Jewish worshipers from across the known world, in the city for the feast, are stunned to hear these Galileans praising God in their own home tongues. Some are puzzled and ask for an explanation, while others laugh it off as drunkenness. For Luke's readers the scene answers the scattering of the nations: God is gathering people of every language again.
entries.note: The most sensible setting for a crowd of thousands is the temple courts (Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Wind could recall the Spirit raising the dead in Ezekiel 37, and fire both God's glory on the tabernacle and his coming judgment (Keener and his notes); Heiser reads wind and fire as the imagery of a divine council commissioning. Keener finds the supposed Greek parallels to tongues weak and says Luke presents real languages with an Old Testament prophetic background; the CSB Study Bible lists three readings and prefers languages the hearers recognized, and Wright notes that everyone's second language was Greek, yet that day nobody needed it. Heiser points out that the words for the divided tongues and for the crowd's confusion are the words the Greek Old Testament uses at Deuteronomy 32:8 and Genesis 11:7, and Keener suggests Luke has updated the names of Genesis 10. Whether those staying in Jerusalem were pilgrims or settled residents is debated (the cultural backgrounds notes); the ESV Study Bible says both. Philo wrote of divine intoxication, and Greeks believed in frenzied inspiration, so the mockers' charge had a ready model (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 2:1, 2:2, 2:3, 2:4, 2:5-13, 2:9-11 and 2:12-13
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 2:2-3, 2:5 and 2:13
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 2:5
CSB Study Bible, note on Acts 2:4
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part One, comment on Acts 2:5-13
Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm, ch. 34, Infiltration

ideas.s: The harvest feast fifty days after Passover, one of the three festivals that brought Jewish pilgrims to Jerusalem from across the world. Some Jews also tied it to the covenant at Sinai.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.

Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.

entries.title: Acts 2:14-41, Peter's sermon: the Spirit poured out
entries.summary: Peter explains the scene from Joel: God has poured out his Spirit, the crucified Jesus is raised and exalted as Lord and Messiah, and three thousand are baptized in his name.
entries.plain: Peter stands with the eleven and says these men are not drunk, since it is only nine in the morning; this is what Joel foretold, that in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on all people and they would prophesy. Jesus of Nazareth, whom they put to death, God raised from the dead, as David foresaw, for David died and his tomb is still among them. Exalted to God's right hand, Jesus has poured out the Spirit, and God has made him both Lord and Messiah. Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what to do; Peter tells them to repent and be baptized in Jesus' name for the forgiveness of sins, and about three thousand are baptized that day.
entries.note: Many Jews, especially the elite, believed prophets no longer existed in their day, and Peter's added line, and they will prophesy, is not in Joel (Keener and his notes). The sermon unpacks the final line of the Joel quotation, about rescue for all who call on the Lord's name, and shows that the Lord's name is Jesus (Keener and his notes); Keener cites Kenneth Bailey's reading of the speech as a chiasm. Joining Psalm 16 and Psalm 110 by their shared right hand is the Jewish technique of linking texts through a common word, called gezerah shavah (Keener and his notes). Tombs of David and of Huldah were known in Jerusalem (Keener and his notes). Baptism as a once-for-all rite of conversion was associated with Gentiles becoming Jews, so calling Jews to be baptized asked for a public and costly step (Keener). The temple mount had many immersion pools, so three thousand could be immersed in a few hours, a large number when Josephus counts only six thousand Pharisees in all Judea (Keener and his notes). Ancient historians summarized speeches, and Luke condenses this one (Keener and his notes).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 2:17, 2:18, 2:21, 2:29, 2:34-35, 2:38, 2:40 and 2:41
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 2:16-18, 2:20-21, 2:22-40, 2:29-31, 2:33-35, 2:36, 2:37-38, 2:40 and 2:41

ideas.s: Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.

entries.title: Acts 2:42-47, The common life
entries.summary: The first believers devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers, share their possessions, and meet daily in the temple courts and in their homes.
entries.plain: Luke pauses to show what the new community looked like day to day. They stayed close to the apostles' instruction, shared meals and prayer, and sold goods so that nobody went without. They kept worshiping in the temple while eating together in homes, and outsiders thought well of them as their numbers kept growing. The picture is of Israel's hopes for a people of God being lived out in a small group in Jerusalem.
entries.note: Most special groups ate together, but Greek associations typically met once a month; a daily shared meal is unusual in antiquity and most resembles family life (Keener and his notes). The CSB Study Bible thinks the breaking of bread included both fellowship meals and the Lord's Supper. Keener notes public prayer at the morning and evening offerings, and that temples made good public gathering places. Luke's wording echoes ancient descriptions of ideal communities (Keener and his notes). Wright likens the believers to a family firm with three generations sharing one purse, and notes that they sold extra property, part of an ancestral inheritance, while keeping the houses they met in. The ESV Study Bible insists the sharing was voluntary and no abolition of property, while Keener warns against reading it as a mistake and calls it valuing people above possessions. The CSB Study Bible says the earliest evangelism seems to have happened through gatherings in the temple and in houses.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 2:44-45 and 2:46
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 2:42, 2:43-45 and 2:46-47
CSB Study Bible, notes on Acts 2:42 and 2:47
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 2:44
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part One, comment on Acts 2:42-47

ideas.s: Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.

The first believers in Jerusalem shared their possessions and sold property to meet each other's needs. Ancient writers used the same words for ideal communities, and only a few groups, such as the Essenes, tried it.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.

entries.title: Acts 3:1-26, The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
entries.summary: At the afternoon hour of prayer Peter heals a man lame from birth who begged at the temple gate, then tells the gathering crowd that Jesus is the prophet Moses promised.
entries.plain: Going to the temple for afternoon prayer, Peter and John meet a man who has never walked and who begs at one of the gates. Peter has no money to give, but he heals him by the authority of Jesus, and the man goes into the courts leaping and praising God. When a crowd gathers, Peter insists the power is God's, not theirs, and says the God of Israel's ancestors has vindicated the Jesus they rejected. He urges them to turn back so that renewal can come, presenting Jesus as the promised prophet Moses spoke of.
entries.note: Three in the afternoon was the hour of the evening offering (Keener and his notes). Keener identifies the Beautiful Gate with the Nicanor Gate on the east, of costly bronze above fifteen steps, beyond which women and the maimed could not go; the cultural backgrounds notes call this a suggestion, since the name is not attested elsewhere, and Price and House also weigh the eastern gate and the southern Double Gate, where the impure, such as the lame, would wait. Josephus describes "one gate that was without the [inward court of the] holy house, which was of Corinthian brass" and outshone the gates plated with silver and gold. Because Judaism tied piety to generosity, the temple was a good place to beg, and the disabled had few other means (Keener and his notes). Ancient miracle workers usually prayed or invoked spirits, but Peter speaks like an Old Testament prophet declaring God's word, and he disclaims the holy man's piety that Jewish tradition sometimes credited for miracles (Keener and his notes). Christians seem to have been the first to proclaim a suffering Messiah (Keener and his notes). Qumran and Samaritan sources expected a prophet like Moses (Keener and his notes).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 3:1, 3:2, 3:3, 3:12, 3:18, 3:20 and 3:22-23
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 3:1, 3:2-3, 3:4-10, 3:12, 3:18, 3:19 and 3:22-23
Josephus, The Wars of the Jews 5.5.3, trans. William Whiston
J. Randall Price and H. Wayne House, Zondervan Handbook of Biblical Archaeology, Acts 3:2 The Beautiful Gate

ideas.s: Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
Giving to the needy was one of the three pillars of Jewish piety, with prayer and fasting. Greeks and Romans had nothing quite like it.

Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him. In Jesus' day people asked whether a new preacher was the Prophet, and some expected the manna and the wonders of the exodus to return with him.

entries.title: Acts 4:1-31, Before the temple rulers
entries.summary: The temple authorities arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus. Before the council the unschooled fishermen speak boldly, are warned and released, and pray with the believers in the words of Psalm 2.
entries.plain: The temple leadership, Sadducees prominent among them, arrest Peter and John because they are announcing resurrection through Jesus. Questioned by the high priestly families the next day, Peter credits the healing to Jesus, the rejected stone now made the cornerstone, and says rescue comes through him alone. The council, unsettled by the boldness of men with no formal training and by the healed man standing in front of them, can only threaten and release them. The believers respond by praying with a royal psalm, and God answers with a fresh filling of the Spirit and the room shaken.
entries.note: The captain of the temple, the sagan, led the Levite temple police and ranked next to the high priest (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Night trials were illegal, so the hearing waited for morning (Keener; the CSB Study Bible). Most Judeans and Galileans believed in the resurrection, and the Sadducees rejected it but tolerated the Pharisees (the cultural backgrounds notes); the apostles said the first case had already happened, which threatened the Sadducees (Keener and his notes). Wright writes that "resurrection always was a radical, dangerous doctrine," because it promises God will put the world right. Unschooled means without the rhetorical training of the elite, and disciples were expected to reflect their teachers (Keener and his notes). The elite's public honor was at stake, and they did not tolerate challenges from people of lower status (the cultural backgrounds notes). The apostles' answer about obeying God recalls Socrates and the prophets (Keener). Psalm 2 was read messianically (Keener and his notes), and the shaking of the place recalls Isaiah 6:4 (the cultural backgrounds notes).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 4:1, 4:2, 4:13, 4:17, 4:21, 4:25-26 and 4:31
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 4:1, 4:2, 4:3, 4:13, 4:19-22 and 4:25-28
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 4:1
CSB Study Bible, note on Acts 4:1-3
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part One, comment on Acts 4:1-12

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Acts 4:32-5:11, Barnabas, Ananias and Sapphira
entries.summary: The believers share everything, and Barnabas sells a field for the common fund. Ananias and Sapphira sell land too but lie about the price, and both fall dead.
entries.plain: The believers act as one family, and those with land or houses sell them so the apostles can meet every need. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, is held up as a model of that generosity. Ananias and Sapphira sell property as well but pretend to give the full amount while keeping some back, and Peter treats this as lying to God's Spirit, since nobody forced them to give. Both die, one after the other, and fear grips the whole community and everyone who hears.
entries.note: Nicknames were common, Cyprus had many Jews, and although Levites held no land under Old Testament law, they commonly did by this time (Keener and his notes). Setting a good example beside a bad one was a recommended technique of ancient writing (Keener and his notes). Kept back is the word the Greek Old Testament uses at Joshua 7:1 for Achan, who kept back what was devoted to God (Keener and his notes). Keener notes that Qumran barred a member who lied about his property from the common meal for a year and cut his food by a quarter, while here God himself judges. Ananias and Sapphira wanted the honor of the gift without its cost (the cultural backgrounds notes). Jewish literature presented Satan as tempter, deceiver and accuser (the cultural backgrounds notes). Burial came the same day, and here the church acts as the family (Keener and his notes). Judean women went to market and elsewhere freely, though married women covered their hair (the cultural backgrounds notes).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 4:36, 4:37, 5:1, 5:2, 5:3, 5:6 and 5:7
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 4:36, 4:37, 5:1-11, 5:1-4 and 5:6

ideas.s: The first believers in Jerusalem shared their possessions and sold property to meet each other's needs. Ancient writers used the same words for ideal communities, and only a few groups, such as the Essenes, tried it.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Acts 5:12-42, Peter's shadow, the prison and Gamaliel
entries.summary: Crowds bring the sick for Peter's shadow to fall on them. The apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, and brought before the council, where Gamaliel compares the movement to the failed causes of Theudas and Judas the Galilean.
entries.plain: Healings multiply, and people lay the sick along the streets hoping even the passing shadow of Peter will reach them. The high priest's party locks the apostles up, but they are freed in the night and found teaching in the temple again the next morning. Before the council they insist that God must be obeyed above any human authority, and the furious leaders want them dead. Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee, points to earlier movements that collapsed and counsels caution, so the apostles are beaten, warned, and sent away glad to suffer for Jesus.
entries.note: Many thought a shadow carried something of its owner, and power passed by contact was a pagan magical idea, so the crowd may have mixed in superstition (Keener and his notes). Miraculous prison escapes appear in Greek stories about Dionysus (Keener), and Heiser lists this angel among those who open doors. The council could not legally execute without the governor (the cultural backgrounds notes). Gamaliel I was the most prominent Pharisee of his day, of the school of Hillel (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible); Wright calls him Saul's teacher. Josephus says that under the governor Fadus "a certain magician, whose name was Theudas" led a crowd to the Jordan, promising to divide the river. That puts Theudas about AD 44, after this speech: Keener allows that Luke or Josephus is mistaken or that a better-known name was supplied, the ESV and CSB Study Bibles suggest an earlier Theudas, Wright thinks Gamaliel got the order wrong, and the cultural backgrounds notes say the undisputed point is that Gamaliel compares Jesus to revolutionaries. Flogging, up to thirty-nine lashes, was meant to shame (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 5:15, 5:18, 5:33, 5:34, 5:36-37 and 5:40
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 5:14-16, 5:18, 5:19, 5:34-35 and 5:36
CSB Study Bible, note on Acts 5:35-36
ESV Study Bible, study notes on Acts 5:34, 5:36 and 5:40
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 20.5.1, trans. William Whiston
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part One, comment on Acts 5:27-42
Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm, ch. 23, Giant Problems

ideas.s: Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

entries.title: Acts 6:1-7, The Hellenists' widows and the Seven
entries.summary: Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The Twelve have the community choose seven men, and lay hands on them.
entries.plain: As the community grows, Greek-speaking Jewish believers complain that their widows are missing out when food is shared each day. The Twelve decline to leave their teaching and prayer to run the tables and ask the believers to pick seven trusted, Spirit-filled men instead. All seven chosen have Greek names, Stephen and Philip among them, and the apostles pray over them and lay hands on them to commission them. The dispute settled, the message keeps spreading, even among many priests.
entries.note: Each local synagogue cared for its own poor widows, but Jews from abroad who had settled in Jerusalem had an unusually high share of widows, because many moved to the land late in life to die and be buried there (Keener and his notes); Wright reports the same suggestion. Wright adds that widows were normally supported by blood relatives, and joining the movement could cut those ties, so the new family took on the old family's duty. Keener mentions a later rabbinic tradition that the righteous who died abroad would have to roll underground back to the land for the resurrection. Distributors of charity later became an office in Palestinian Judaism (Keener). All seven have Greek names, so they seem to come from the offended group, a striking choice when fewer than 40 percent of Jews even in Rome had Greek names (Keener and his notes). Moses delegating in Exodus 18 is a precedent, and groups of seven judges were common (the cultural backgrounds notes). Many of the priests would have been poorer priests, not Sadducees (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 6:1, 6:2-4, 6:5 and 6:7
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 6:1, 6:3-4, 6:5 and 6:7
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part One, comment on Acts 6:1-7

ideas.s: Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.
Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.

Hands laid on a person to bless, to heal, or to set someone apart for a task, the way Moses laid hands on Joshua. In the early church it went with prayer, the gift of the Spirit and sending people out.

entries.title: Acts 6:8-7:53, Stephen's charge and speech
entries.summary: Men from the Diaspora synagogues accuse Stephen of speaking against the temple and the law. He answers with Israel's story, from Abraham to the temple, and turns the charge back on his judges.
entries.plain: Stephen, one of the Seven, works wonders and out-argues Diaspora Jews from a synagogue of former slaves and others from abroad. They find witnesses to accuse him before the council of attacking the temple and the law of Moses. His defense retells Israel's history, showing God at work far from the land, a people who kept rejecting the leaders God sent, and a God whom no building made by people can contain. He ends by turning the charge around and accusing his judges of resisting the Spirit and killing the Righteous One, just as their ancestors treated the prophets.
entries.note: Archaeology attests a Jerusalem synagogue founded by a freedman named Vettenos, though whether it is this one is debated (the cultural backgrounds article Synagogue of the Freedmen; Keener); Price and House think the Theodotus inscription, from a synagogue with a hostel for visitors from abroad, may be it. Luke's word means freed slaves of Roman citizens, who became citizens on release; Jews Pompey enslaved were bought free by Rome's Jews, and their descendants kept the status, so Saul was probably one of the Cilicians in this synagogue and his family may have gained citizenship this way (the article). Defendants answered the charges laid against them, and Stephen argues from the law itself, then turns the charge on his accusers, as defense speeches often did (the cultural backgrounds article Answered Charges and Parallel Figures in Acts 7; Keener). Some teachers held that God revealed himself directly only in the land, and Stephen stresses God's appearing in Mesopotamia, Egypt and Sinai (Keener and his notes). Apart from the angel at the bush, the Old Testament does not say the law came through angels; Keener says tradition added them, while Heiser traces the idea to the Greek text of Deuteronomy 33:2.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, articles Synagogue of the Freedmen and Answered Charges and Parallel Figures in Acts 7
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 6:9-10, 6:11, 7:2-4, 7:51-53 and 7:53
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 6:11, 7:2, 7:51 and 7:53
Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm, ch. 21, God's Law, God's Council
J. Randall Price and H. Wayne House, Zondervan Handbook of Biblical Archaeology, Mark 5:35 Ruler of the Synagogue (Theodotus Inscription)

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Acts 7:54-8:3, The stoning of Stephen
entries.summary: Stephen sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, and his hearers drag him out and stone him while a young man named Saul looks after their coats. Persecution scatters the church.
entries.plain: Stephen's hearers are enraged, but he looks up and says he sees Jesus standing beside God in glory. They drown him out, drive him outside the city and stone him, and the witnesses leave their outer clothes with a young man called Saul. Stephen dies praying that his killers be forgiven, much as Jesus did. His death sets off a persecution that scatters the believers beyond Jerusalem, with Saul leading the hunt from house to house.
entries.note: Judges stood to give a verdict, so the standing Son of Man vindicates Stephen as his accusers condemn him, and in Daniel 7 the Son of Man vindicates the righteous against their oppressors (Keener and his notes). Stephen's last words echo Jesus' prayers on the cross (Keener and his notes). A condemned man was supposed to confess his sins and pray that his death would atone for them; Stephen confesses his accusers' sin instead (Keener and his notes). The law stripped the condemned, but here the witnesses strip themselves, which Keener and his notes read as Luke quietly marking who is really on trial. Young man most likely means a man in his twenties (Keener and his notes). Public mourning for a condemned criminal was forbidden, so the loud mourning honors Stephen in defiance of the court; dying unburied was the greatest dishonor, and risking one's life to bury the dead was counted heroic (Keener and his notes). Only the most severe persecutions took women as well as men (Keener and his notes). Wright pictures Saul guarding the coats of men who believed they were cleansing the city.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 7:56, 7:58, 7:59, 7:60, 8:2 and 8:3
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 7:54-55, 7:56, 7:57-58, 7:59, 7:60, 8:2 and 8:3
N. T. Wright, Paul: A Biography, ch. 1, Zeal

ideas.s: Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

The law of Moses named stoning as the penalty for blasphemy, but under Rome Jewish courts could not execute without the governor. In practice stoning was what angry crowds did, in Jewish and Gentile towns alike.

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Acts 8:4-25, Samaria and Simon the magician
entries.summary: Philip preaches the Messiah in Samaria, and even the famous magician Simon is baptized. When Peter and John lay hands on the Samaritans and they receive the Spirit, Simon offers money for the power.
entries.plain: The scattered believers carry the message with them, and Philip announces the Messiah in Samaria, where healings and exorcisms draw large crowds. Simon, a magician the Samaritans had long revered as a divine power, is baptized too. When Peter and John come from Jerusalem and the Samaritans receive the Spirit through their prayer, Simon tries to buy the ability to give it. Peter rebukes him sharply, since God's gift has no price, and tells him to repent.
entries.note: The city may be Neapolis, on the site of Shechem, since Sebaste's people were Greeks (Keener and his notes); the ESV Study Bible prefers Sebaste, the old city of Samaria. Samaritans were already circumcised, so becoming Jews would have meant denying their own people (Keener and his notes). People called magic whatever was done in secret for the practitioner's own good, and above all any spiritual power that fit a rival belief; some Jewish teachers thought some magic fake and some real and dangerous (the cultural backgrounds article Magic in the New Testament). Arnold reads Philip's signs as a power encounter that outshone Simon's, one of four episodes of magic in Acts, three of which Luke ties to Satan. A second-century writer claims Simon presented himself as the male form of the deity with his consort Helena (Keener), a tradition the cultural backgrounds notes call not necessarily dependable; Arnold reports the later legend in the Acts of Peter of Simon flying over Rome and falling at Peter's prayer. The cultural backgrounds notes say, "Treating the Spirit like a magic charm was an insult to the Spirit," and simony takes its name from Simon (Wright).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 8:5, 8:10, 8:12, 8:18 and 8:20, and article Magic in the New Testament
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 8:5, 8:10-11, 8:12, 8:18-24 and 8:25
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 8:5
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part One, comment on Acts 8:4-25
Clinton E. Arnold, Powers of Darkness, ch. 1, Magic and Divination, sections Simon the Magician: Acts 8 and Summary

ideas.s: The people of the hill country between Judea and Galilee worshiped Israel's God on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans each claimed to be the true heirs of Israel, and centuries of hostility lay between them.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

Hands laid on a person to bless, to heal, or to set someone apart for a task, the way Moses laid hands on Joshua. In the early church it went with prayer, the gift of the Spirit and sending people out.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

entries.title: Acts 8:26-40, The Ethiopian official
entries.summary: On the desert road to Gaza, Philip meets a eunuch who serves the queen of the Ethiopians, reading Isaiah in his chariot on the way home from worship in Jerusalem, and baptizes him.
entries.plain: Directed by an angel, Philip goes to a desert road toward Gaza and meets a eunuch who manages the royal treasury of the Ethiopian queen. The official, going home after worshiping in Jerusalem, is reading the Isaiah passage about the suffering servant and wants to know who it describes. Philip starts there and explains Jesus, and when they reach water the man asks for baptism and receives it. Philip is then taken away by the Spirit, and the official goes home full of joy, carrying the message south into Africa.
entries.note: Ethiopia meant all of Africa south of Egypt, and the kingdom meant is Meroë in Nubia, not Axum in today's Ethiopia; Rome, unable to conquer it, made a treaty, and most of Rome's trade with Africa farther south passed through it, so its treasurer handled great wealth (the cultural backgrounds article The African Empire of Meroë; Keener). The CSB Study Bible says Candace "was not the queen's name but a title"; the article adds that Greeks applied it to the ruling queen mother, while Africans probably used it more widely, and names Nawidemak as one queen who reigned then, while the Zondervan Bible dictionary thinks this one probably Amantitere, about AD 25-41. Only the wealthy owned a chariot or a personal scroll of Isaiah (Keener and his notes). Men who served queens were often eunuchs, and Deuteronomy 23:1 barred them from the assembly (the cultural backgrounds notes), yet Isaiah 56:3-5 promised them a place among God's people (Keener). Whether he was a eunuch in the literal sense is open: the Greek Old Testament sometimes uses the word for any court official (Keener), though the cultural backgrounds notes argue that the repeated use points to a true eunuch.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article The African Empire of Meroë, and notes on Acts 8:27, 8:28, 8:30 and 8:36
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 8:26, 8:27, 8:28 and 8:29-30
CSB Study Bible, note on Acts 8:26-29
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Candace

ideas.s: Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.

entries.title: Acts 9:1-31, Saul on the Damascus road
entries.summary: Carrying the high priest's letters to the synagogues of Damascus, Saul is stopped by a light and a voice. Blinded, healed and baptized, the persecutor begins to proclaim Jesus and has to escape over the city wall.
entries.plain: Saul, determined to stamp out the followers of the Way, gets authority from the high priest to arrest them in the Damascus synagogues. On the road he is struck down by a blinding light and hears the risen Jesus ask why Saul is persecuting him. A disciple named Ananias, sent in a vision, restores his sight, and Saul is baptized and starts announcing Jesus as Son of God, until a plot forces his escape over the wall in a basket. In Jerusalem Barnabas speaks up for him, and the churches across the land enjoy a season of peace and growth.
entries.note: Social superiors wrote letters to introduce or authorize the bearer (the cultural backgrounds notes), and Josephus confirms that agents could act on the council's orders (Keener). Damascus had tens of thousands of Jews in many synagogues (Keener and his notes), and it was the hub of caravan routes into Mesopotamia, Anatolia, Persia and Arabia, so a movement rooted there would spread fast (the cultural backgrounds article Roman Damascus). A mile-long colonnaded street there may be the Straight Street of verse 11 (the article). A light, a fall and a doubled name are features of Old Testament calls (Keener and his notes); Carson, Moo and Morris add that the companions saw the light and heard a sound but neither saw Jesus nor understood. Arabia in Galatians 1:17 is the Nabatean kingdom, whose king Aretas IV was behind the watch on the gates (2 Corinthians 11:32) (the article; Carson, Moo and Morris; the Zondervan Bible dictionary). Tarsus was Cilicia's largest city, a free city and a university town that Strabo ranked above Athens for philosophy (the cultural backgrounds article Tarsus); whether Paul grew up there or in Jerusalem is debated, and Carson, Moo and Morris favor Jerusalem.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 9:2, 9:3 and 9:4, and articles Roman Damascus and Tarsus
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 9:1-2 and 9:3-4

D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 7, Paul, sections Born in Tarsus of Cilicia (Acts 22:3), Brought up in this city (Acts 22:3), As I came near Damascus (Acts 22:6) and From Paul's First Missionary Journey to His Death
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Damascus

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.
Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.

entries.title: Acts 9:32-43, Lydda and Joppa
entries.summary: Peter heals a paralyzed man at Lydda and, at Joppa, raises Tabitha, a disciple known for her charity, while the widows she clothed stand weeping. He stays on with a tanner.
entries.plain: At Lydda Peter finds Aeneas, paralyzed and bedridden for eight years, and tells him Jesus Christ heals him; he gets up, and people in Lydda and Sharon turn to the Lord. In Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, Dorcas in Greek, known for her good works and her gifts to the poor, falls sick and dies; they wash her body, lay it in an upstairs room and send for Peter. The widows stand weeping and show him the tunics and other clothing she had made; Peter sends them all out, kneels and prays, tells Tabitha to get up, and presents her alive to the believers and the widows. Many in Joppa believe, and Peter stays a long time there with a tanner named Simon.
entries.note: Joppa was the only significant Jewish port (Keener and his notes). Tabitha in Aramaic and Dorcas in Greek both mean gazelle; many women of means were benefactors, and Jewish women were devoted to charity (Keener and his notes). Women prepared women's bodies for burial, and burial before sunset made the trip of about eleven miles urgent (Keener and his notes). Sending everyone out and presenting her alive recall Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 4) (Keener and his notes). Tanners handled carcasses and lived outside town near water; strict pietists avoided them as unclean, though many were more bothered by the smell, and later rabbis let a tanner's wife divorce him (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 9:32, 9:36, 9:37, 9:38, 9:40, 9:41 and 9:43
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 9:32-36, 9:36, 9:37-38, 9:40, 9:41-42 and 9:43
ESV Study Bible, study notes on Acts 9:36 and 9:43

ideas.s: A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

entries.title: Acts 10:1-23, Cornelius and Peter's vision
entries.summary: A God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea is told in a vision to send for Peter. At noon on a Joppa rooftop Peter sees a sheet full of unclean animals and hears a voice tell him to eat.
entries.plain: Cornelius, a Roman officer stationed at Caesarea, prays to Israel's God and gives to the poor, and an angel tells him to send for Peter in Joppa. Around midday the next day Peter, praying on a rooftop, sees a vision of a sheet full of animals the law forbids and is told to kill and eat. He refuses, as a lifelong keeper of the food laws, and is told not to treat as unclean what God has cleansed. As he puzzles over it, Cornelius's men arrive, and the Spirit tells Peter to go with them.
entries.note: Caesarea was the governor's seat, with five auxiliary cohorts and a cavalry unit; auxiliaries were mostly local Syrian recruits, not Roman citizens, and the city's Syrian and Jewish residents often clashed (the cultural backgrounds article Caesarea and Its Soldiers). A centurion commanded about eighty men and a cohort up to six hundred; a cohort kept the name of the place it was first raised, so the Italian Regiment was probably largely Syrian, though Cornelius's Roman name suggests he was a citizen (the article; Keener). The sources differ on pay: Keener says a centurion earned fifteen times a soldier's pay, the ESV Study Bible as much as five times. Soldiers were officially forbidden to marry, so household may mean servants (Keener and his notes). Keener dates the scene before AD 41, when Agrippa I had his own troops in Caesarea; the Zondervan Bible dictionary doubts the Italian cohort was stationed there then and notes the suggestion that Cornelius was retired. Wright notes that the first Roman Luke introduces overturns the picture of army officers as Rome's demigods. Lodging Gentiles overnight broke strict piety, and a tanner's house was already suspect to strict pietists (Keener and his notes).
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article Caesarea and Its Soldiers, and notes on Acts 10:2, 10:3, 10:14 and 10:23
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 10:1, 10:2, 10:3, 10:14-16 and 10:23a
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 10:1
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part One, comment on Acts 10:1-16
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Italian Regiment

ideas.s: Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

entries.title: Acts 10:24-11:18, Peter in Cornelius's house
entries.summary: Peter enters a Gentile home, preaches Jesus, and sees the Spirit fall on the uncircumcised listeners. In Jerusalem he is criticized for eating with Gentiles, and his account silences the critics.
entries.plain: Peter enters Cornelius's house, refuses the officer's bow, and explains that God has taught him to call no person unclean. He tells the story of Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection and of Jesus as appointed judge of all. Before he finishes, the Spirit comes on the Gentile listeners as it had on the Jewish believers, so Peter has them baptized. When Jerusalem believers object that he ate with uncircumcised people, his account persuades them that God has opened the way of life to Gentiles too.
entries.note: Falling at someone's feet was the homage paid to gods and rulers; Greco-Roman paganism believed in semidivine men, and even Gentiles expected mortals to refuse divine honors (Keener and his notes). Devout Jews would not enter idolaters' homes, and Gentile food and wine counted as unclean, which made Romans think Jews antisocial (Keener and his notes); the ESV Study Bible says against the law reflects later strict tradition, not an Old Testament command. God's impartiality was a common Jewish theme, and Lord of all a Jewish title for God (Keener and his notes). Doing good is the language of benefaction, what rulers and gods were praised for (Keener). Most Jewish teachers thought the Spirit came only on the most pious or belonged to the age to come, so Gentiles receiving it showed that God accepted them uncircumcised (Keener and his notes). The complaint in Jerusalem is about eating with Gentiles (Keener and his notes). Many Jews believed decent Gentiles who kept the laws given to Noah could be saved, but no one had thought of Gentiles saved on the same terms as Jews (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.

entries.title: Acts 11:19-30, Antioch, and the name Christian
entries.summary: Scattered believers bring the message to Gentiles in Antioch, where the disciples are first called Christians. When a prophet foretells famine, the church sends relief to the elders in Judea.
entries.plain: Believers driven out after Stephen's death travel north and west, mostly speaking to fellow Jews, but some begin telling Greeks in Antioch about Jesus, and many respond. Barnabas is sent to look into it, rejoices, and brings Saul from Tarsus to help teach for a year, and Antioch is where outsiders first call the disciples Christians. When the prophet Agabus foretells a widespread famine, the Antioch believers collect what each can give. Barnabas and Saul carry the gift to the elders in Judea.
entries.note: Antioch on the Orontes was the third city of the empire, with perhaps half a million people, seat of the governor of Syria, with many God-fearers (Keener and his notes). Its Jews held civic privileges from Seleucid times (the Zondervan atlas), and the Greeks here are Gentiles, unlike the Hellenists of chapter 6 (the cultural backgrounds notes). The name Christian was formed like the names of political parties, Caesarians, Herodians, Pompeians, and was given by outsiders (Keener and his notes); in Antioch's Greek Christ meant Messiah, so Wright hears the believers labeled the king's people, and the name later became a legal charge, as 1 Peter 4:16 shows (the cultural backgrounds notes). A series of famines struck under Claudius, and Josephus says "queen Helena sent some of her servants to Alexandria with money to buy a great quantity of corn" for Judea. Keener, his notes, the ESV and CSB Study Bibles and Carson, Moo and Morris date the Judean famine and this visit to the mid 40s, while Wright argues for the early 50s. Carson, Moo and Morris take this to be the visit of Galatians 2:1; many scholars equate that visit with the council of Acts 15 instead.

ideas.s: Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
Giving to the needy was one of the three pillars of Jewish piety, with prayer and fasting. Greeks and Romans had nothing quite like it.

Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.

entries.title: Acts 12:1-25, Herod Agrippa, the prison and the king struck down
entries.summary: King Herod Agrippa kills James and jails Peter at Passover, but an angel leads Peter out. Later, in Caesarea, the king accepts the crowd's cry that he speaks with a god's voice and is struck down.
entries.plain: King Herod Agrippa executes the apostle James and, seeing it wins him favor, jails Peter during the Passover season, planning a public trial. On the eve of it an angel frees Peter from chains and guards, and he goes to the house where believers are praying, though at first they do not believe the servant girl who hears him at the door. Later, at Caesarea, Herod lets a crowd hail him as divine and is struck down for taking God's glory. Luke sets the persecutor's fall against the steady spread of the word.
entries.note: As king, Agrippa held the power of life and death, and beheading was the more merciful death (Keener and his notes). Four squads of four soldiers covered the four watches of the night (Keener; the ESV Study Bible), and Romans punished a guard with the penalty due to the prisoner who escaped (Keener and his notes). Tyre and Sidon depended on grain from Agrippa's lands (Keener and his notes). Josephus tells how, at shows for Caesar, Agrippa's silver robe shone in the morning sun and "presently his flatterers cried out, one from one place, and another from another, [though not for his good,] that he was a god"; he did not rebuke them, was seized with pain in his belly, and said, "I, whom you call a god, am commanded presently to depart this life." Under Rome even Caesar expected others to refuse such flattery (Keener and his notes), and death from worms was counted fit for tyrants (the cultural backgrounds notes). Agrippa died in 44, before the famine visit, so Luke places his death here by theme rather than date (Carson, Moo and Morris).

ideas.n: Agrippa I and the later Herods
ideas.s: Herod the Great's grandson Agrippa I was made king of all Judea by Claudius and ruled from AD 41 to 44, courting his Jewish subjects. His son Agrippa II later ruled smaller territories and heard Paul's defense.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: Acts 13:1-12, Sent from Antioch: the proconsul and the magician
entries.summary: The church at Antioch fasts, prays and sends out Barnabas and Saul. On Cyprus the Roman proconsul believes after Paul confronts the Jewish magician in his entourage.
entries.plain: Antioch's church is led by a varied group of prophets and teachers, including Barnabas, Saul, an African called Simeon and a man raised alongside Herod Antipas. During worship and fasting the Spirit marks out Barnabas and Saul for a mission, and the church commissions them. On Cyprus the Roman governor Sergius Paulus wants to hear them, but a Jewish sorcerer in his household tries to block it. Paul, as Luke now calls him, pronounces temporary blindness on the man, and the governor comes to faith, struck by the teaching.
entries.note: Since the Spirit was known above all as the Spirit of prophecy, the Spirit speaking probably means a prophet spoke (Keener). From Seleucia, Antioch's port, they crossed about eighty miles to Salamis and took the island's main road to Paphos, the governor's seat (Wright; the Zondervan atlas; the cultural backgrounds notes). Proconsul is the right title: Cyprus was a senatorial province from 22 BC, and inscriptions answered scholars who once doubted Luke here (Price and House). Sergius Paulus was proconsul about AD 45-46; whether he belongs to the family known from Pisidian Antioch is uncertain (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), and Price and House call the link speculative, though Wright treats Antioch as the family's home. Jewish magicians were reputed among the best in the empire (Keener and his notes), and Arnold, noting that officials often consulted astrologers and diviners, guesses that Elymas had a say in the proconsul's government. Roman citizens had three names, and Paul is a Roman cognomen that sounded like his Jewish name (Keener and his notes); Wright adds that the Greek Saulos described an effeminate walk, "not a word that would help people to forget the messenger".

ideas.s: Going without food, and often washing and oil, as a sign of mourning, penitence and longing. The law required one fast a year; the devout kept many more.

Hands laid on a person to bless, to heal, or to set someone apart for a task, the way Moses laid hands on Joshua. In the early church it went with prayer, the gift of the Spirit and sending people out.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

entries.title: Acts 13:13-52, The synagogue at Pisidian Antioch
entries.summary: Invited to speak after the synagogue readings in a Roman colony, Paul tells Israel's story from the exodus to Jesus. Gentiles welcome the message, and the city's leading men and women drive the apostles out.
entries.plain: The team sails to the mainland, where John Mark leaves them, and reaches Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony with a synagogue. Invited to speak after the scripture readings, Paul traces Israel's story through David to Jesus, whom God raised as the psalms and prophets said he would. The next week a huge crowd turns out, some synagogue members turn hostile, and Paul and Barnabas announce they will take the message to Gentiles, who welcome it gladly. Opponents stir up influential women and city leaders, and the pair are expelled and move on to Iconium.
entries.note: The road from Perga ran more than a hundred miles uphill along the Via Sebaste, at least a week's walk (the cultural backgrounds notes). Pisidian Antioch, strictly in Phrygia, was the administrative center of southern Galatia (the Zondervan atlas), a Roman colony of about five thousand colonists whose most conspicuous temple honored the emperor, and the god of the region was Men (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). Rulers of the synagogue invited visiting teachers to speak after the readings from the Law and the Prophets (Keener and his notes). Linking Isaiah 55:3 and Psalm 16:10 through the shared word holy is the Jewish technique Peter used at Pentecost (Keener and his notes), and Wright notes that Isaiah 55 follows the Servant and opens with an invitation to everyone who is thirsty. The reaction in verse 45 is often translated jealousy; Wright reads it as zeal for God and his law, the zeal Paul confessed of himself (Galatians 1:14). Shaking off the dust was done on returning from pagan land, so the gesture treats the opponents as pagans (Keener and his notes), and Jesus had told his messengers to do it (Luke 10:11; Wright).

ideas.s: Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.

entries.title: Acts 14:1-20, Iconium and Lystra: taken for Zeus and Hermes
entries.summary: After a plot in Iconium, Paul heals a lame man at Lystra and the crowd hails him and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus. When they refuse the sacrifice, the crowd is turned against them and Paul is stoned.
entries.plain: In Iconium the message divides the town, and a plot to stone them sends Paul and Barnabas on to Lystra. There Paul heals a man unable to walk since birth, and the locals, speaking their own language, decide the gods Zeus and Hermes have come in human disguise. The priest from the nearby temple of Zeus arrives to sacrifice, and the two men, horrified, insist they are mortals and point the crowd to the living Creator who sends rain and harvest. Opponents from earlier cities then turn the crowd, Paul is stoned and left for dead, yet he gets up and goes back into town.
entries.note: In Lystra the landowning citizens spoke Latin, while the crowd spoke Lycaonian, which is why the apostles grasp late what is happening (Keener and his notes). A local legend told how Zeus and Hermes once visited the region in disguise and only an old couple, Baucis and Philemon, took them in (Keener and his notes); Wright notes that Ovid tells the story, and inscriptions and a temple near Lystra honor the two gods together (Price and House). Hermes was the messenger who spoke for Zeus, which Arnold takes as the reason Paul, the main speaker, became Hermes. A sacrifice was a rite, a party and a shared meal at once, which helps explain why the crowd was hard to stop (Wright). The speech calls the gods worthless things, a common Jewish term, not demons (Arnold), and needs no Bible, speaking of the God who sends rain and harvest (Keener and his notes). Stoning went beyond the law and was mob action (Keener and his notes); though Lystra was a Roman colony, the Zondervan atlas remarks, justice there bent to local prejudice. Wright notes that a crowd's stones could stun without killing, as here.

ideas.s: Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

The law of Moses named stoning as the penalty for blasphemy, but under Rome Jewish courts could not execute without the governor. In practice stoning was what angry crowds did, in Jewish and Gentile towns alike.

entries.title: Acts 14:21-28, Elders appointed, and home to Antioch
entries.summary: Paul and Barnabas retrace their route, warning that the kingdom comes through hardships and appointing elders in each church, then report to Antioch that God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
entries.plain: After making many disciples in Derbe, Paul and Barnabas retrace their route through the cities where they had been attacked. They encourage the new believers to hold on, warning that hardship is part of the road into God's kingdom, and they appoint elders in each church with prayer and fasting. Then they travel back through the south coast and sail home to Antioch. There they tell the church everything God has done, above all that Gentiles have been given a way into faith.
entries.note: Many Jews expected a time of suffering before the kingdom, the birth pangs of the Messiah (Keener and his notes). From Derbe the short way home ran through the Cilician Gates and Tarsus, but they went back through the cities that had just driven them out, on a journey of some 1,200 miles (the Zondervan atlas). Elders had governed towns and villages in the Old Testament and in much of the Mediterranean, and most synagogues had several elders acting as a council (Keener and his notes); the ESV Study Bible says Paul's churches followed that pattern. Fasting went with prayer in seeking God (the cultural backgrounds notes). Pamphylians and Pisidians were reputed skilled in augury, reading omens from the flight of birds (Keener). Wright holds that the Galatians of Paul's letter are these southern churches and that the long stay in Antioch is when Peter and the men from James came (Galatians 2:11-12); Carson, Moo and Morris also date Galatians before the council of Acts 15, though many scholars instead equate Galatians 2 with that council.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.

Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.
Going without food, and often washing and oil, as a sign of mourning, penitence and longing. The law required one fast a year; the devout kept many more.

entries.title: Acts 15:1-21, The council in Jerusalem
entries.summary: Teachers from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem; Peter and James argue that God has accepted Gentiles as they are, and James proposes a few rules for them to keep.
entries.plain: Teachers from Judea tell the Antioch believers that Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved, and the sharp dispute is taken up to Jerusalem for the apostles and elders to settle. Peter reminds them that God gave Gentiles the Spirit without circumcision and purified them through faith, so no heavier load should be imposed. James adds a reading of Amos about God rebuilding David's house so the nations can seek him. He proposes that Gentile believers be spared circumcision but asked to avoid a short list of practices tied to idol worship and blood, things that synagogue communities everywhere would notice.
entries.note: Many Jews thought righteous Gentiles could be saved by keeping the laws given to Noah, while others demanded conversion, and even the lenient did not count an uncircumcised Gentile part of Israel (Keener and his notes). The Greek Old Testament read Edom in Amos 9:12 as Adam, humankind (Keener and his notes), and Wright notes that the passage follows Amos 9:7, which sets Israel among the nations. What the four rules were for is disputed. The cultural backgrounds notes and Keener read them as the rules Jewish tradition applied to righteous Gentiles, later called the Noahide laws; the ESV Study Bible reads them as making fellowship with law-keeping Jewish believers possible, with the ban on sexual immorality permanent; the CSB Study Bible and Wright think they targeted pagan temple rites, which Wright takes to include drinking blood and ritual prostitution. Wright sums up the outcome as "no needful circumcision on the one hand and no needless offence on the other." On verse 21, Keener and Wright read it as avoiding offense to the many who hear Moses read in every city; the CSB Study Bible also offers that synagogue reading had already made Moses known to Gentiles.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 15:1, 15:5, 15:15-16, 15:17-18, 15:19-20 and 15:21
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 15:1, 15:5, 15:17, 15:20 and 15:21
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 15:19-21
