N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Acts 15:12-21

ideas.s: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

entries.title: Acts 15:22-35, The letter to the Gentile churches
entries.summary: The council sends Judas and Silas with Paul and Barnabas to carry a letter to the Gentile believers of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. It is read to the church at Antioch, who rejoice at its encouragement.
entries.plain: The Jerusalem leaders and the whole church send Judas Barsabbas and Silas back with Paul and Barnabas, carrying a written decision. The letter distances Jerusalem from the agitators, says the Spirit and the gathering agree on a light requirement, and lists the few practices Gentile believers should avoid. Read aloud in Antioch, it brings great relief and encouragement. Judas and Silas, both prophets, stay to strengthen the believers before returning home.
entries.note: The greeting and the closing Farewell are the standard forms of Greco-Roman letters, and the address marks a circular letter to be copied and carried round its regions (Keener and his notes). Officials and councils sent respected representatives with their decrees, and the messengers would be trusted as speaking for the council (Keener and his notes); Wright adds that Judas and Silas let Antioch know Paul had not written the letter himself. The formula it seemed good belongs to council resolutions and imperial decrees, and because the Spirit was linked with prophecy, readers would hear a claim that God led the decision (Keener and his notes). Delivering the letter meant reading it aloud, since most people could not read well (the cultural backgrounds notes). Verse 34, that Silas stayed on, is missing from the earliest manuscripts; Wright thinks scribes added it to explain how Silas was in Antioch in verse 40. Wright also notes that Paul never cites the decree, even in 1 Corinthians 8-10, and suggests he did not want to look like Jerusalem's deputy; others solve the puzzle by dating the council later.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 15:23, 15:24-27, 15:28 and 15:29
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 15:23-29, 15:28, 15:30 and 15:33
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Acts 15:22-35

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

entries.title: Acts 16:11-15, Lydia at the place of prayer
entries.summary: In Philippi, a Roman colony, Paul finds women gathered by the river on the Sabbath. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, believes, is baptized with her household and insists that the missionaries stay at her house.
entries.plain: Crossing from Asia into Europe, Paul's group reaches Philippi, a major Roman colony and a leading city of its part of Macedonia. Finding no synagogue, they go out to the river on the Sabbath, where women meet to pray. One of them, Lydia, a merchant of expensive purple fabric from Thyatira who already worships Israel's God, responds to Paul's message. She and her household are baptized, and she presses the missionaries to stay in her home.
entries.note: Philippi was a Roman colony, so its citizens were citizens of Rome (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The notes date the colony to 42 BC, while the Zondervan Bible dictionary says Octavian made it one after Actium in 31 BC, settling Antony's partisans there; the notes and Keener also place it at the eastern end of the Via Egnatia, which the Zondervan atlas runs on to Byzantium. The ESV Study Bible thinks the women may have been God-fearers rather than Jews, and Wright counts Lydia one. Thyatira was known for its dyers' guilds (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); the notes treat purple as a luxury, while the atlas says Thyatira's dye came from the madder plant, cheaper than shellfish purple. Lydia's standing is unclear: Keener says her name and trade may mark her as a freedwoman; the cultural backgrounds notes say heading a household could mean she was widowed, divorced or a prosperous freedwoman; the CSB Study Bible says Lydia may only mean a woman from Lydia. With no synagogue to work from, her house became the mission's base (Wright), and taking the missionaries in made her their patron (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

entries.title: Acts 16:16-24, The slave girl with a Python spirit
entries.summary: A slave girl who earns her owners money by fortune-telling follows Paul, crying out about the Most High God. Paul drives the spirit out, and her owners drag him and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed.
entries.plain: In Philippi a slave girl possessed by a fortune-telling spirit earns money for her owners, and for days she follows Paul's party shouting that they serve the highest God and announce salvation. Exasperated, Paul orders the spirit out by Jesus' authority, and it leaves. Her owners, their income gone, haul Paul and Silas before the city authorities, accusing them as Jews who promote customs unlawful for Romans. The crowd joins in, and the magistrates have the two beaten and locked in the inner cell with their feet fastened.
entries.note: The Python spirit tied the girl to Apollo's oracle at Delphi, whose priestess was believed to have a god in her belly and was nicknamed a belly-talker for the deep second voice some writers credited to a daimon (Arnold); Wright notes that some diviners were frauds and some seemed truly possessed. Exorcists often used the names of higher spirits to drive out lower ones; Paul instead speaks with Jesus' delegated authority (Keener and his notes). On the girl's cry, the cultural backgrounds notes say Most High was a title Gentiles also gave Zeus, and Wright adds that salvation to a Philippian meant health, prosperity or rescue; Keener notes that magical texts treated the supreme God, identified with the Jewish God, as the most powerful. The owners turn a loss of income into a charge of teaching un-Roman customs: Romans complained that Jews made converts, and anti-Judaism was fashionable (Keener and his notes), though practicing a different religion was not itself illegal (the CSB Study Bible). The magistrates were the duoviri, the colony's two chief officials, whose lictors carried rods, and unless the accused were citizens they were normally beaten before trial (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Greeks and Romans sought the future from oracles, omens and seers, above all from Apollo's priestess at Delphi. A girl with a Python spirit was linked to that famous oracle.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.
Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: Acts 16:25-40, The jailer and the Roman citizens
entries.summary: At midnight an earthquake opens the prison. The jailer, about to kill himself, believes with his household; next day Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens beaten without trial, and the magistrates come to apologize.
entries.plain: About midnight, as Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns with the prisoners listening, an earthquake shakes the prison, the doors open and everyone's chains come loose. The jailer wakes, sees the doors open and draws his sword to kill himself, but Paul shouts that they are all still there; trembling, he asks what he must do to be saved, and they tell him to believe in the Lord Jesus, he and his household. He washes their wounds, he and all his household are baptized at once, and he brings them into his house and sets food before them, rejoicing. In the morning the magistrates send word to let them go, but Paul refuses to leave quietly: they beat Roman citizens in public without a trial, so let them come and escort them out themselves; the magistrates, alarmed, come and apologize, lead them out and ask them to leave the city, and after visiting Lydia's house they go.
entries.note: Romans thought suicide a noble way out when facing execution, and guards whose prisoners escaped could be made to serve their sentences (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). Wright reads the jailer's question about being saved as first a plea for rescue from that crisis, since saved commonly meant rescued or healed. Binding or beating an untried citizen broke the Julian law, and the magistrates could lose office (Keener and his notes); Wright recalls Cicero's prosecution of Verres, the governor of Sicily who had flogged and crucified a man crying out that he was a Roman citizen. Why Paul waited to speak is read two ways: Keener sees a strategy that put the magistrates in the wrong; the cultural backgrounds notes suggest Paul and Silas may not have expected the illegality to be taken seriously. On the household's baptism, the ESV Study Bible notes that Christians disagree whether infants were included, and Keener warns that the jailer's possible young children cannot settle the question. The building shown at Philippi as Paul's prison was a religious complex, not a prison (Price and House).

ideas.s: Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Acts 17:1-9, Another king in Thessalonica
entries.summary: Paul argues from the Scriptures in the synagogue at Thessalonica that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Some believe; opponents raise a mob, drag Jason before the city officials and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king.
entries.plain: In Thessalonica Paul spends three Sabbaths in the synagogue arguing from Scripture that the Messiah was meant to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is that Messiah. Some Jews and many God-fearing Greeks, including prominent women, are convinced. Jealous opponents hire troublemakers, raid Jason's house where the missionaries stayed, and drag Jason before the city rulers, charging that these agitators defy Caesar by naming a rival king. The officials make Jason post bond and release him.
entries.note: Thessalonica, some sixty-eight miles from Philippi along the Via Egnatia (the Zondervan atlas), was a free city with some self-rule, the seat of Macedonia's governor and not a Roman colony (Keener and his notes; Wright). Accusers had to bring the accused to court themselves (Keener and his notes). The city's officials were politarchs, a title critics once called Luke's mistake because no Greek author uses it; an inscription from an arch in Thessalonica opens with it, and many inscriptions now attest it, mostly in Macedonia (the Zondervan Bible dictionary; Keener and his notes). The city's devotion to the emperor showed in its imperial temple and coins, and speaking of another king was treason (Keener and his notes); Wright adds that northern Greece had seen Rome's civil wars fought out, so a rival king was no idle fear, and the CSB Study Bible notes the same charge against Jesus in Luke 23:2. As host, Jason was held responsible for his guests and had to post bond, a light penalty (Keener and his notes). Wright links Paul's sympathy in 1 Thessalonians 2:14 for what the church suffered from its neighbors to this ordeal.

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Some Greek cities, such as Thessalonica and Ephesus, kept a measure of self-rule under Rome, with their own officials and a citizen assembly. A riot could cost a city those privileges.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

entries.title: Acts 17:16-21, Athens: idols, the marketplace and the philosophers
entries.summary: Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed at a city full of idols. He argues in the synagogue and the marketplace, and Epicurean and Stoic philosophers take him for a preacher of foreign gods and bring him to the Areopagus.
entries.plain: Waiting in Athens for his coworkers, Paul is deeply troubled by the idols filling the city. He debates in the synagogue and daily in the public square with anyone he meets, including Epicurean and Stoic thinkers. Some dismiss him as a scrap-collector of ideas, while others think he is introducing new deities, since he speaks of Jesus and resurrection. Curious, as Athenians proverbially were about anything novel, they bring him before the Areopagus to explain himself.
entries.note: City streets were often lined with statues, and Athens was famous for the Hermae, pillars topped with heads of Hermes (Keener and his notes). Sages without schools of their own worked the marketplace (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Stoics, the dominant school, held that reason structured the universe and fate ruled it, so one should master one's own attitude; Epicureans, followed only by the upper classes, held the gods far off and uninvolved and made the goal of life freedom from pain and disturbance (the cultural backgrounds article Ancient Philosophies; Wright). The word for babbler meant a seed-picker, a bird pecking at grain (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Keener and his notes). Because Anastasis, resurrection, was also a woman's name, the critics seem to have heard Jesus and Anastasis as a new pair of gods (Keener and his notes; Wright). The charge of proclaiming foreign gods recalled the trial of Socrates (Keener and his notes; Wright), and Wright hears a veiled threat in their asking to know the new teaching. Athens was proverbial for its curiosity (Keener and his notes), though Wright notes that new was a sneer in a world where old was best.

ideas.s: The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: Acts 17:22-34, Paul before the Areopagus
entries.summary: Before the Areopagus, Paul starts from an altar to an unknown god and from the Athenians' own poets, speaks of the one Creator who made every nation from one man, and ends with a coming judgment and a man raised from the dead. Some mock; a few believe.
entries.plain: Before the Areopagus Paul takes an altar dedicated to an unknown god as his starting point and offers to name the God they honor without knowing. He describes the Creator who needs no temple or offerings, who made all peoples from one ancestor and arranged their times and places so they might look for him, and he borrows lines from Greek poets to say that humans come from God. Since that is so, God cannot be pictured in metal or stone, and he now calls all people to turn, because a day of judgment is set and the judge has been raised from death. The mention of resurrection draws ridicule from some, interest from others, and faith from a few, including Dionysius of the council and a woman called Damaris.
entries.note: Athenian tradition said that in an old plague, on the advice of Epimenides, altars were raised to unknown gods (Keener and his notes), though the CSB Study Bible notes that no such inscription has been found. Wright reads the altar against the Academic school's doubt that anyone could know the gods, so Paul frames the speech with ignorance. Heiser reads verses 26-27 as alluding to "the situation with the nations produced by God's judgment at Babel." Arnold notes that Paul does not call the Athenian gods demons, perhaps because the hearers lacked the Jewish background to follow it. Greeks could not conceive of bodily resurrection (Keener and his notes), and in Aeschylus, Apollo says there is none once blood is spilled (Wright). What the hearing was is disputed: Wright writes, "The Areopagus was a court. Paul was on trial," and calls natural-theology readings a misunderstanding; the CSB Study Bible calls verses 24-29 a basic natural theology; the cultural backgrounds notes and the Zondervan Bible dictionary say the council vetted public teachers, a view Keener also reports. The Zondervan atlas puts the council in the Royal Colonnade in the Agora; the dictionary keeps it on the hill.

ideas.s: The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.

Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: Acts 18:1-11, Tentmakers in Corinth
entries.summary: In Corinth Paul lodges and works with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome who share his trade. When the synagogue turns against him he moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, and the synagogue leader Crispus believes with his household.
entries.plain: Paul moves on to Corinth and joins Aquila and Priscilla, Jewish refugees recently expelled from Rome under Claudius, who make tents as he does. He works with them during the week and argues in the synagogue on the Sabbath, then devotes himself fully to preaching once Silas and Timothy arrive. When synagogue opposition hardens, he moves his teaching to the house of a God-fearer next door, and the synagogue ruler Crispus believes with his household. Encouraged by a night vision promising protection, Paul stays eighteen months.
entries.note: Corinth, destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, was refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BC, and Latin was the language of civic business (the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright and Bird). Claudius expelled the Jews of Rome, probably in AD 49, after trouble over one Chrestus, usually taken as debate about Jesus as the Christ (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible); Wright adds that Chrestus and Christus sounded almost alike, and that the edict lapsed when Claudius died in AD 54, which is why Priscilla and Aquila are back in Rome in Romans 16:3. Guild banquets used sacrificial food, which shut out observant Jews and made them glad of Jewish partners (Keener). The word for tentmaker often meant a leatherworker (the cultural backgrounds notes; the CSB Study Bible), while Carson, Moo and Morris tie it to the goat-hair cloth of Paul's home region. People of status despised manual labor (Keener and his notes), but Jewish teachers commonly kept a trade (Wright). The inscribed synagogue lintel found at Corinth dates from the second to fifth centuries, so it shows a later synagogue, not Paul's (Price and House).

ideas.s: Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
Craftsmen of one trade lived and worked in the same streets and banded together in guilds, which set standards, defended their interests and met for meals in honor of a patron god.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.

entries.title: Acts 18:12-17, Gallio's judgment seat
entries.summary: Jewish leaders bring Paul before Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, accusing him of teaching a worship contrary to the law. Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about words, names and their own law and drives them from the judgment seat.
entries.plain: When Gallio governs Achaia, Jewish leaders in Corinth bring Paul to the governor's court, charging him with promoting worship that breaks the law. Gallio cuts the case off before Paul speaks, saying he will rule on crimes but not on arguments about words, names and Jewish law. He has them cleared from the court. The crowd then beats Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, right there, and Gallio ignores it, leaving the believers free to keep meeting in the city.
entries.note: Gallio, brother of the Stoic Seneca, is named as proconsul in a letter of Claudius found at Delphi, which places him in office about AD 51-52 and makes this hearing one of the firm points for dating Paul's travels (Price and House; Keener and his notes; Wright and Bird). Keener, his notes and Carson, Moo and Morris put his arrival on July 1, 51, the CSB Study Bible early in the year, and the Zondervan Bible dictionary allows 51-52 or 52-53. The ESV Study Bible, Wright and Price and House say the judgment seat was excavated in the marketplace, though Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes place it differently. Edicts left internal Jewish affairs to Jewish courts, so Gallio treats Paul's faith as a form of Judaism (Keener and his notes), giving Christians the Jews' standing (Wright; the ESV Study Bible). Since Julius Caesar, Jews had been excused from worshiping Rome's gods, and "they agreed to pray for the emperor but not to pray to him" (Wright). Who beat Sosthenes is debated, Gentiles hostile to Jews or the Jewish community itself (Keener and his notes); he may be the Sosthenes of 1 Corinthians 1:1 (the dictionary).

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Acts 18:18-28, A vow at Cenchreae and Apollos of Alexandria
entries.summary: Paul has his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow and sails for Syria by way of Ephesus. In Ephesus Priscilla and Aquila teach the eloquent Alexandrian Apollos more accurately, and the believers write ahead to Achaia to welcome him.
entries.plain: Paul sails east with Priscilla and Aquila, cutting his hair at the port of Cenchreae because of a vow, stops briefly at Ephesus, and then travels on to Judea, Antioch and the churches inland. While he is away, Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria with a deep grasp of Scripture, arrives in Ephesus teaching about Jesus but knowing only John's baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and fill out his understanding. With letters of recommendation he goes on to Achaia, where he argues publicly and powerfully that Jesus is the Messiah.
entries.note: Jews shaved the head at the end of a vow, normally in Jerusalem, but Diaspora practice may have been looser (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Cenchreae, Corinth's port on the Aegean, had temples of Isis, Artemis, Aphrodite, Asclepius and Poseidon, and some priests of Isis shaved their heads (Keener; the ESV Study Bible); its church later had Phoebe as deacon (Romans 16:1; Wright). Who made the vow is debated: the CSB Study Bible says the Greek seems to point to Aquila, though it is uncertain, while Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes, the ESV Study Bible and Wright take it as Paul; Wright suggests he let his hair grow from the night he was told to stay in Corinth and cut it on leaving. Alexandria may have been a third Jewish, and its Jews were mostly shut out of the city's citizenship (Keener and his notes). Letters of recommendation were standard and could be carried by the person recommended (Keener and his notes), and one from Priscilla and Aquila would carry weight in Corinth (the ESV Study Bible). Corinth prized public speaking, so being refuted in public was a humiliation (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.

entries.title: Acts 19:8-20, The lecture hall and the burned books
entries.summary: In Ephesus Paul teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years, and even cloths that touched him bring healing. When the sons of Sceva try to use Jesus' name as a spell, the spirit overpowers them, and believers burn their magic books in public.
entries.plain: After three months of synagogue debate in Ephesus, Paul moves his daily teaching to a rented lecture hall belonging to Tyrannus and keeps at it for two years, so the message reaches the whole province. Unusual healings follow, even through cloths that had touched him. When seven sons of a priest named Sceva try using Jesus' name as a formula against a demon, the possessed man overpowers them. Shaken, many believers confess their magical practices and burn costly scrolls of spells in public.
entries.note: Philosophers lectured in rented halls, and public life in Ephesus ended around noon, so Paul may have used the hall in the midday hours; some manuscripts add the hours eleven to four (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). The handkerchiefs and aprons were probably sweat rags and work aprons; the ESV Study Bible insists they were not magical objects, while Keener notes that magicians often healed by such means. Ephesus was a center of magic: amulets bore the Ephesian letters, six magical names, and Arnold tells of an Ephesian wrestler at Olympia who lost three bouts once the referee found one on his ankle; Keener writes that "rolls of these formulas are called Ephesia grammata, or Ephesian writings." Sceva, a Latin name, probably claimed the high priestly title for himself, since no high priest bore that name (Keener and his notes; Wright). Spells were believed to work only while secret, so divulging them destroyed their power (Keener and his notes). Arnold reads those who burned their books as people who had already believed, tempted back to old ways. Fifty thousand drachmas came to about fifty thousand days' wages (Keener; the ESV Study Bible).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 19:8-9, 19:11-12, 19:13-20, 19:13, 19:14, 19:18 and 19:19-20

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

entries.title: Acts 19:23-41, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians
entries.summary: Demetrius the silversmith rouses the craftsmen who make shrines of Artemis, warning that Paul's teaching threatens their trade and the goddess's honor. The city rushes into the theater chanting for two hours, until the city clerk calms them with a warning about Rome.
entries.plain: Demetrius, a silversmith who makes miniature shrines of Artemis, gathers his fellow craftsmen and warns that Paul's claim that handmade gods are no gods threatens both their livelihood and the honor of the great goddess. The crowd erupts in chants for Artemis, seizes two of Paul's companions and floods the theater, while friends, among them some of the city's leading men, keep Paul away. A Jewish spokesman is shouted down for hours. Finally the town clerk calms them, insisting the men have committed no crime, that the courts are open, and that Rome could treat this unlawful gathering as a riot.
entries.note: The silversmiths' shops apparently lined the street from the theater to the harbor, and most souvenir shrines were terra cotta, so silver ones were costly (Keener and his notes). Of Paul's nearly three years in Ephesus, Arnold notes, Luke tells mainly of this clash with Artemis's worshipers. The theater, where the citizen assembly met, held some 20,000 to 25,000 (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). The Asiarchs are disputed: Keener and the ESV Study Bible make them leading men who presided over the cult of Rome and the emperor, while Price and House report the case that they were civic officials, few of them named with any priestly office; nearly three hundred inscriptions and coins have answered the old charge that Luke's title was anachronistic. The city clerk was the top official and the link to Rome; temple robbery counted among the worst crimes, and pagans often charged Jews with it, so his clearing Paul joins Gallio's ruling as an official finding of innocence (Keener and his notes; Wright). Carson's Quick Introduction notes that Rome made desecrating any temple a capital offense.

ideas.s: The great goddess of Ephesus, whose temple was one of the seven wonders of the world and a bank as well. Her cult was the city's pride and the living of its craftsmen.
Craftsmen of one trade lived and worked in the same streets and banded together in guilds, which set standards, defended their interests and met for meals in honor of a patron god.
Some Greek cities, such as Thessalonica and Ephesus, kept a measure of self-rule under Rome, with their own officials and a citizen assembly. A riot could cost a city those privileges.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.

entries.title: Acts 20:1-12, The collection party and Eutychus at Troas
entries.summary: Paul leaves Ephesus for Macedonia and Greece, then sets out for Jerusalem with delegates from the churches. At Troas the believers meet on the first day of the week, and a young man who falls from a window is taken up alive.
entries.plain: After the Ephesus riot Paul travels through Macedonia to Greece, then a plot changes his route home, and a group of men from several churches travels with him. At Troas the believers gather on the Sunday to share bread, and Paul talks with them late into the night in a crowded upper room lit by many lamps. A young man named Eutychus dozes off in a window and falls three stories. Paul goes down, embraces him and says he is alive, and the meeting continues until morning.
entries.note: Luke mentions the collection for Jerusalem only at 24:17, but Paul's letters show this journey was about it (Keener and his notes; Wright). Respected delegates carried each Jewish community's temple tax to Jerusalem, and Paul's companions from several churches follow that pattern (Keener and his notes); Wright adds that a large party gave safety with a sum of money and witnesses that it arrived. Most religious associations met monthly, while the Christians appear to have made Sunday their main meeting day, probably in honor of the resurrection (Keener). Sunday was a working day, so they met early, late or both (Keener; Wright); whether this meeting began on Saturday or Sunday evening depends on whether days ran from sundown, as Jews reckoned them, or from midnight, as Romans did (Keener). The heat or smell of so many lamps may have made Eutychus drowsy (Keener and his notes). His name, meaning Lucky, was a common slave's name, and he may have worked all day (Wright; Keener). Paul's embrace recalls Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34-35), and Wright notes that Luke does not say whether the boy had died or was stunned.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 20:1-2, 20:3, 20:4, 20:7, 20:8, 20:9 and 20:10
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 20:2, 20:3, 20:4, 20:7, 20:8 and 20:10
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Acts 20:1-12

ideas.s: Paul gathered money from his mostly Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, much as Jews everywhere sent the temple tax to the holy city.
The day early Christians kept for Jesus, most likely Sunday, the weekday of the resurrection. In the cities of Asia one day a month was already given to honoring the emperor.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

entries.title: Acts 20:17-38, Farewell to the Ephesian elders
entries.summary: Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus. He reminds them how he lived among them, warns of wolves who will attack the flock, charges them as overseers to shepherd God's church, and leaves them in tears.
entries.plain: Hurrying toward Jerusalem, Paul stops at Miletus and sends for the leaders of the Ephesian church. He recalls his years among them, his humble service and open teaching, and says the Spirit is leading him toward suffering in Jerusalem, though finishing his task matters more to him than his life. He charges them to guard and shepherd the flock God bought, warning that false teachers will come from outside and from among them, and points to his own manual work and a saying of Jesus about the blessing of giving. They kneel to pray together and part in tears, believing they will never see him again.
entries.note: Paul is hurrying to present the collection at Pentecost, when Jerusalem would be full (Keener and his notes); Wright adds that he may have bypassed Ephesus because it would be easier to get in than out, with enemies there and money in hand. The elders are also called overseers, and the ESV Study Bible and Wright take the terms as one office held by each elder, though within a generation overseer came to mean something like a bishop (Wright). Overseer was a Greek administrative title also found in the Greek Old Testament and the Dead Sea Scrolls, and leaders were often called shepherds, as in Ezekiel 34 (Keener and his notes), though Wright notes that Paul's letters never use the sheep and shepherd image. Because many sages were charlatans, honest ones had to deny greed, and the upper class and most philosophers despised manual work (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). The saying Paul credits to Jesus about giving and receiving appears in no Gospel; Wright's nearest parallel is Sirach 4:31. Repeated kisses showed the affection given to family or a dear teacher (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 20:17, 20:18-35, 20:28, 20:29-30, 20:33, 20:34-35 and 20:36-38
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 20:16, 20:18-35, 20:28, 20:33 and 20:37
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 20:17
CSB Study Bible, note on Acts 20:33-35
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part Two, comments on Acts 20:13-27 and 20:28-38

ideas.s: Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

entries.title: Acts 21:17-26, James, the rumors and the vow
entries.summary: In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome Paul but warn him that thousands of believers zealous for the law have heard he teaches Jews abroad to abandon Moses. They ask him to pay for four men completing a vow and to purify himself with them in the temple.
entries.plain: Arriving in Jerusalem, Paul tells James and the elders how God has worked among the Gentiles, and they praise God. They then warn him that thousands of law-observant Jewish believers have heard he tells Diaspora Jews to abandon circumcision and Moses. To show the rumor is false, they ask him to join four men completing a vow, go through purification with them and cover the cost of their offerings, while confirming that the earlier ruling for Gentile believers stands. Paul agrees and goes to the temple to arrange it.
entries.note: Welcoming the delegation meant lodging uncircumcised Gentile believers in Jewish homes (Keener and his notes), and Wright notes that Mnason's was the last friendly roof Paul would stay under. Agrippa I's reign had fanned Judean nationalism (the cultural backgrounds notes), and sicarii were murdering aristocrats suspected of collaboration (Keener), so a movement thought to mix with Gentiles faced pressure; Wright says zeal for the law took in the temple, the land and the hope of liberation from Rome. The rumor blurred a distinction Paul kept: Gentile converts needed no circumcision, but that never meant Jews should drop their customs (Wright). A Nazirite abstained from wine and grapes, avoided the dead and did not cut his hair, and at the end shaved and offered sacrifice in the temple (the ESV Study Bible, citing the Mishnah, Nazir 6.3). Whether Paul was himself under a vow is disputed: Keener thinks he may have been paying for an earlier vow of his own, and Wright and the Zondervan atlas read him as under a vow, while the cultural backgrounds notes say Luke does not say so.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 21:16, 21:20, 21:24 and 21:27
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 21:17, 21:20-22 and 21:23-26
ESV Study Bible, study note on Acts 21:23
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Acts 21:15-26
Carl G. Rasmussen, Zondervan Atlas of the Bible, The Journeys of Paul, Paul's Third Missionary Journey

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

entries.title: Acts 21:27-40, Riot in the temple, rescue by the tribune
entries.summary: Jews from Asia see Paul in the temple and cry that he has brought Greeks into the holy place. The city riots, and the Roman tribune's soldiers pull him from the crowd, chain him, and nearly mistake him for the Egyptian rebel.
entries.plain: Near the end of the purification period, Jews from Asia spot Paul in the temple and raise an outcry, accusing him of opposing Israel, the law and the temple and of bringing a Gentile, Trophimus, inside. The city erupts, Paul is dragged out and the gates shut, and only the arrival of the Roman commander and his troops stops the beating. Bound and carried up the steps away from the mob, Paul addresses the officer in Greek, who had taken him for an Egyptian rebel leader. Paul identifies himself as a citizen of Tarsus and gets permission to speak to the crowd in their own language.
entries.note: A barrier separated the outer court from the inner courts, with warnings in Greek and Latin that no foreigner might pass; Josephus describes pillars "declaring the law of purity, some in Greek, and some in Roman letters," one complete inscription and a fragment have been found, and Rome let the Jewish authorities execute even Roman citizens for this offense (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible; Price and House). A cohort held the Antonia fortress at the temple's north side, whose stairs led straight down into the outer court (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Josephus tells of an Egyptian false prophet who "got together thirty thousand men" and led them to the Mount of Olives, though his Antiquities counts four hundred killed and two hundred taken (the Zondervan Bible dictionary); Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes find Luke's four thousand more realistic. Keener and Wright take the tribune's surprise to be at Paul's educated Greek, while the cultural backgrounds notes allow that he expected a rebel to prefer Aramaic, the language Wright thinks Paul then used with the crowd.

J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Egyptian, the

ideas.s: Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: Acts 22:22-29, A Roman citizen under the lash
entries.summary: When Paul speaks of his mission to the Gentiles, the crowd erupts again. The tribune orders him examined by flogging, until Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen.
entries.plain: The crowd hears Paul out until he says God sent him to the Gentiles, then it explodes, demanding his death and tossing garments and dust in fury. The commander takes him into the fortress and orders him questioned under the whip to find out what lies behind the uproar. As they tie him down, Paul asks the officer nearby whether Roman law permits scourging a citizen who has not been tried. The commander, who bought his own citizenship, learns that Paul was born a citizen and is alarmed at having bound him.
entries.note: It was legal to scourge slaves or aliens to extract a confession, and the flagellum, leather thongs set with metal or bone, could kill (Keener and his notes); Wright notes that this flogging was for interrogation, not punishment. The Porcian and Julian laws exempted citizens from beating without trial (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Citizenship was very rare in the East outside the colonies, and a claim had to be honored before it could be checked (the cultural backgrounds notes); Wright says a citizen could prove it with "a little double-faced tablet, made of bronze most likely, known as a ‘diploma’" and that false claims were severely punished. How Paul's family gained citizenship is unknown: as freed slaves of a Roman (the cultural backgrounds notes and their article Synagogue of the Freedmen), by special service or a grant from a well-to-do Roman (Keener), through an ancestor's service, perhaps making tents for the army (the CSB Study Bible), or by means no one can now tell (Wright and Bird). Wright and the Zondervan Bible dictionary note that some Jews of Tarsus were citizens a century before Paul.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 16:37, 22:21, 22:24, 22:25, 22:26-27 and 22:28, and article Synagogue of the Freedmen

CSB Study Bible, notes on Acts 22:25 and 22:26-28

N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Acts 22:23-30
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Tarsus

ideas.s: In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: Acts 22:30-23:11, Paul before the council
entries.summary: The tribune brings Paul before the chief priests and the council. Struck on the high priest's order, Paul calls him a whitewashed wall, then declares himself a Pharisee on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council splits.
entries.plain: To learn the real accusation, the Roman commander has the Jewish council convene and brings Paul before it. When the high priest orders him struck, Paul calls him a whitewashed wall, then apologizes on learning who he is, citing the law against cursing a ruler. Seeing Pharisees and Sadducees in the room, he declares himself a Pharisee on trial for the hope of resurrection, and the council splits so violently that soldiers have to pull him out. That night the Lord tells Paul he will bear witness in Rome as he has in Jerusalem.
entries.note: Ananias was high priest from AD 47 to about 58 or 59, a Roman vassal known for greed (Keener and his notes); he had been sent to Rome in 52 on charges of cruelty and acquitted through Agrippa II (the Zondervan Bible dictionary). Josephus says that his servants "took away the tithes that belonged to the priests by violence," and when the revolt broke out in 66 he was hunted down and killed (Keener and his notes; the dictionary, citing Josephus, War 2.17.9). Whether Paul truly did not recognize the high priest or spoke with irony is debated (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Wright takes the apology as genuine, since Ananias wore nothing marking his office. The Pharisees held to the future resurrection and the Sadducees denied it; Keener and the ESV Study Bible say the Sadducees also rejected the developed teaching on angels and spirits, while Wright reads angel and spirit here as Pharisaic ways of speaking of the dead awaiting resurrection (compare Acts 12:15), so the Pharisees grant that Paul may have met Jesus' spirit without granting that he was raised.

ESV Study Bible, study notes on Acts 23:3 and 23:8
CSB Study Bible, note on Acts 23:1-3

J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Ananias (3)
N. T. Wright, Acts for Everyone, Part Two, comment on Acts 23:1-11

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Acts 23:12-35, The oath, the nephew and the night march
entries.summary: More than forty men bind themselves by an oath not to eat until they have killed Paul. His nephew learns of the ambush, and the tribune sends Paul under heavy escort by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter explaining the case.
entries.plain: More than forty men take an oath to fast from food and drink until Paul is dead, planning an ambush when he is brought back for further questioning. Paul's nephew hears of it and warns him, and the commander quietly sends Paul off by night under a large guard of infantry, cavalry and spearmen. A letter goes with him to the governor Felix, presenting Paul as a Roman citizen accused only over disputes about Jewish law. Felix receives him in Caesarea and holds him in Herod's palace until his accusers come.
entries.note: The plotters put themselves under a curse; revolutionaries took such vows, and Jewish law let a man who broke such an oath bring an atonement offering (Keener and his notes). Collaborators were the revolutionaries' chief targets, which put the nephew in danger (the cultural backgrounds notes). Antipatris, thirty to forty miles off, marked the northwest limit of Judea (Wright; the Zondervan Bible dictionary), so the foot soldiers could turn back there and leave the cavalry to ride on (Wright). There was no public post, so the letter went with the soldiers; it is a formal referral in which Lysias paints himself well (Keener and his notes), and Wright notes it reverses the order of events, hiding that Lysias had chained Paul and nearly flogged him. Wright thinks Felix asked Paul's province hoping to pass the case on, as Pilate did with Herod, but Cilicia too answered to Syria. Felix was a freedman whose brother Pallas had the emperor's favor (Keener and his notes). His rank is disputed: Keener says Felix was not an equestrian, while Wright and Bird list him among the equestrian governors.

ideas.s: Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Acts 24:1-27, The hearing before Felix
entries.summary: The high priest's orator Tertullus charges Paul before Felix with stirring up riots and trying to profane the temple. Paul answers point by point; Felix puts off a decision and keeps him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.
entries.plain: Within the week the high priest arrives at Caesarea with elders and a hired advocate, Tertullus, who flatters Felix and accuses Paul of stirring unrest worldwide, leading the Nazarene sect and trying to defile the temple. Paul denies causing any disturbance, says nothing can be proven, and admits only that he worships Israel's God as one who belongs to the Way and shares their hope of a resurrection. Felix postpones judgment, keeps Paul in loose custody and later listens with his wife Drusilla until Paul's talk of justice and judgment frightens him. Hoping for a bribe, he leaves Paul in custody for two years and passes him on to his successor Festus.
entries.note: The accuser spoke first, opening with praise of the judge; Tertullus's praise was false, since revolutionaries multiplied under Felix (Keener and his notes), and Wright notes that his word for stirring up strife is the one Luke uses of Barabbas. Verse 7 is a late addition missing from good manuscripts (Wright). Paul's alms and offerings in verse 17 are Luke's only mention of the collection for Jerusalem (Wright). Drusilla, youngest daughter of Agrippa I, had married the king of Emesa at about sixteen (the Zondervan Bible dictionary); Josephus says Felix used a Cypriot Jew posing as a magician to win her and that she "was prevailed upon to transgress the laws of her forefathers, and to marry Felix." Tacitus said Felix "wielded the power of a king with the mind of a slave" (quoted in the dictionary). Josephus says Felix "had certainly been brought to punishment" at Rome but for his brother Pallas. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles tie his removal to a quarrel between Jews and Gentiles in Caesarea and date it to AD 59 or 60; Carson, Moo and Morris call 59 the growing consensus, and Wright prefers 58.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Acts 23:33-24:9, 24:2-3, 24:5-6, 24:10, 24:23-24, 24:26 and 24:27

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

ideas.n: Agrippa I and the later Herods
ideas.s: Herod the Great's grandson Agrippa I was made king of all Judea by Claudius and ruled from AD 41 to 44, courting his Jewish subjects. His son Agrippa II later ruled smaller territories and heard Paul's defense.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: Acts 25:1-12, Festus and the appeal to Caesar
entries.summary: The new governor Festus hears the case again at Caesarea. When he asks whether Paul will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and after conferring with his council Festus grants it.
entries.plain: The new governor Festus visits Jerusalem soon after arriving, and the priestly leaders ask him to bring Paul there, secretly planning to ambush him. Festus has the case heard in Caesarea instead, where the accusers make serious charges they cannot prove and Paul denies any offense against Jewish law, the temple or the emperor. When Festus, seeking Jewish favor, proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul insists his case belongs in the emperor's court and appeals to Caesar. After consulting his advisers, Festus grants the appeal.
entries.note: Josephus writes that "Festus succeeded Felix as procurator, and made it his business to correct those that made disturbances in the country," and Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes rate him more just than Felix; Wright, in his biography, is harsher, calling him uninterested in justice. Moving the case to Jerusalem needed Paul's consent (Wright) and would have favored the nationalists and invited an ambush (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Paul's denial of any offense against Caesar suggests the accusers had added political charges (Wright). Keener writes that "Roman citizens had the right to appeal to Caesar's tribunal," though appealing before a verdict was unusual; Wright stresses that the appeal was not against a sentence but asked for the whole case to go to the highest court, and that few citizens dared trouble the emperor so. A governor could confer with his council of advisers (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Whether Festus had to grant the appeal is debated, the CSB Study Bible notes; Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say refusing it would have been politically awkward and that sending Paul on spared Festus a hard decision.

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Acts 25:13-26:32, Agrippa and Bernice hear Paul
entries.summary: King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice visit Festus, who asks them to hear Paul so that he will have something to write to the emperor. Paul tells his story; Festus calls him mad, Agrippa turns the question aside, and all agree he could have been set free had he not appealed to Caesar.
entries.plain: King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice visit Festus, who explains that Paul's accusers argue about their religion and a dead man Paul says is alive, and asks for help writing up the case for the emperor. At a formal hearing Paul tells his story, from strict Pharisee and persecutor to his encounter with the risen Jesus near Damascus and his commission to the Gentiles, and says he stands trial for Israel's hope, a Messiah who suffers and is first to rise from death. Festus calls him mad, Agrippa deflects Paul's direct appeal, and Paul answers that he wishes all of them shared his faith, without his chains. Afterward the officials agree Paul has done nothing worthy of death, and Agrippa remarks that he could have gone free had he not appealed to the emperor.
entries.note: Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I, ruled small, mostly Gentile territories; Claudius gave him oversight of the temple and the right to appoint high priests (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Bernice, his sister, had married their uncle Herod of Chalcis and later Polemo of Cilicia (Wright; the Zondervan Bible dictionary). Some ancient writers accused the two of incest, which Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes call slander; the CSB Study Bible speaks of her checkered marital history, while the cultural backgrounds notes say she appears favorably in Josephus, and the dictionary recalls her confronting the governor Florus at the risk of her life in 66. A dossier had to go to Rome with the prisoner (Keener and his notes), and Wright reads this hearing as an informal interview to help Festus write it. Agrippa's reply is read as sarcasm, a jest or near persuasion (the CSB Study Bible), a witty escape (the cultural backgrounds notes), or a serious answer (Keener). Once Paul had appealed, freeing him risked the emperor's anger (Wright). Luke sets these hearings beside Jesus' hearings before Pilate and Herod Antipas (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener).

ideas.n: Agrippa I and the later Herods
ideas.s: Herod the Great's grandson Agrippa I was made king of all Judea by Claudius and ruled from AD 41 to 44, courting his Jewish subjects. His son Agrippa II later ruled smaller territories and heard Paul's defense.

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: Acts 27:1-26, Sailing late in the season
entries.summary: Paul sails for Rome in the custody of a centurion named Julius, changing to an Alexandrian grain ship at Myra. With the Fast already past, the owner presses on against Paul's warning, and a northeaster drives the ship helpless for days until an angel promises Paul that all aboard will live.
entries.plain: Paul and other prisoners are put in the charge of a centurion, Julius, who treats Paul kindly and transfers them to a grain ship from Alexandria headed for Italy. Progress is slow, and by the time they reach Crete the safe sailing season has passed, so Paul warns of disaster, but the officer follows the captain and owner instead. A fierce wind off the island drives them out to sea, and after days of storm and jettisoned cargo, with no sun or stars visible, they give up hope. Paul then reports that an angel has promised he will stand before Caesar and that everyone aboard will survive, though they will be wrecked on an island.
entries.note: Myra was a regular port of call for the grain ships (the Zondervan atlas). The cultural backgrounds notes and Keener make Alexandrian grain ships some 180 feet long, while the Zondervan Bible dictionary gives 140 feet for an exceptional one and puts most merchant ships far smaller. The Fast was the Day of Atonement; sailing was risky from mid-September and closed from about November into March (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Wright puts the Day of Atonement on October 5 in AD 59, and Carson, Moo and Morris report an argument that the Fast's timing points to that year, an argument weakened if safe sailing ended on September 14, as Vegetius says. The CSB Study Bible says Paul's warning may have come from revelation or a seasoned traveler's judgment, and Wright notes Paul had already been shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:25). The wind's name joins Greek for east wind and Latin for north wind, a sailors' word for a northeaster (the dictionary). The Syrtis, shoals off Libya, had wrecked whole fleets (Keener and his notes). Wright sees the voyage as Luke's parallel to the trial and death of Jesus.

ideas.s: Outside winter, ships were the quickest and cheapest way to travel, but they were built for cargo, not passengers, and from mid-September the sea grew dangerous. The great grain ships of Alexandria fed Rome.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
Greeks and Romans sought the future from oracles, omens and seers, above all from Apollo's priestess at Delphi. A girl with a Python spirit was linked to that famous oracle.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

ideas.n: The Day of Atonement and the mercy seat
ideas.s: Once a year the high priest went into the holy of holies with sacrificial blood, for his own sins and then the nation's. It was the one fast the law commanded, and the mercy seat on the ark was the place the blood was brought.

entries.title: Acts 27:27-44, Shipwreck off Malta
entries.summary: On the fourteenth night the sailors sense land, drop anchors from the stern and try to slip away in the ship's boat. Paul urges everyone to eat and gives thanks over bread, and when the ship breaks up the centurion stops the soldiers from killing the prisoners; all 276 reach the shore.
entries.plain: Two weeks into the storm the sailors sense land, drop anchors behind and try to escape in the lifeboat, but Paul warns that everyone must stay aboard, and the soldiers cut the boat loose. Before dawn Paul urges all 276 people to eat, gives thanks for bread where all can see, and their spirits lift, then dump the grain to lighten the ship. At daylight they run aground on a sandbar and the stern is smashed by the waves. The soldiers want to kill the prisoners to stop escapes, but the centurion protects Paul, and everyone reaches shore by swimming or clinging to wreckage.
entries.note: A ship blown southwest from Cauda would take about two weeks to reach Malta, and the ancient Adriatic Sea reached that far south (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Anchors were normally dropped from the bow; dropping them from the stern kept the ship from swinging round (Keener and his notes), and archaeologists have found lines of anchors laid and cut one after another before a wreck (Wright). Paul's thanks and breaking of bread follow the Jewish custom of the head of a household at a meal (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). Large ships often carried several hundred people, and Josephus writes that the ship on which he was wrecked in the Adriatic carried "about six hundred in number." The traditional site, St Paul's Bay on Malta, fits the details (Keener and his notes). Guards answered for their prisoners: the CSB Study Bible says a soldier whose prisoner escaped suffered the prisoner's punishment, the cultural backgrounds notes say shipwreck would normally absolve them but they took no chances, and Keener says they were less liable if prisoners died at sea than if they escaped.

Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

entries.title: Acts 28:1-10, Malta: the viper and the goddess Justice
entries.summary: The islanders of Malta welcome the shipwrecked with a fire. When a viper fastens on Paul's hand they decide that Justice will not let a murderer live; when he takes no harm they call him a god. Publius, the island's chief man, takes them in, and Paul heals his father and many others.
entries.plain: The survivors find they are on Malta, and the islanders welcome them warmly with a fire against the rain and cold. When a snake bites Paul as he adds wood, the locals conclude that divine justice is punishing a murderer the sea failed to drown, then decide he must be a god when he suffers no harm. Publius, the island's leading official, hosts them, and Paul heals his father of fever and dysentery. Other sick islanders come and are healed, and when the party leaves, the people load them with honors and supplies.
entries.note: The word for the islanders meant people who did not speak Greek, without contempt here; most Maltese spoke Punic (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible), and Malta was a prosperous Roman municipium whose fine houses Cicero praised (the Zondervan Bible dictionary). Hospitality to strangers was a valued virtue, owed above all to the shipwrecked (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Justice, Dike, was a personified goddess, and stories told of people who escaped the sea only to die another way as the gods' curse caught up with them (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). The CSB Study Bible notes that there are no poisonous snakes on Malta today. Those who survived snakebite were thought holy men, sometimes divine, a reversal ancient readers would find comic (Keener and his notes); Wright sets it against Lystra, where the crowd went from god to stoning. Publius's title, first man, appears on Maltese inscriptions, probably for the island's governor (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). The honors and supplies follow the Mediterranean rule of reciprocity (the cultural backgrounds notes), and Wright notes that some take the honors as a tactful word for payment.

ideas.s: Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

Outside winter, ships were the quickest and cheapest way to travel, but they were built for cargo, not passengers, and from mid-September the sea grew dangerous. The great grain ships of Alexandria fed Rome.
Greeks split humanity into Greeks and barbarians, people whose speech sounded like babble. Jews split it into Israel and the nations. Paul uses both maps.

entries.title: Acts 28:11-16, The Twin Brothers and the road to Rome
entries.summary: After three months they sail in an Alexandrian ship with the Twin Brothers as its figurehead, land at Puteoli and walk the Appian Way toward Rome, where believers come out to meet Paul. In Rome he is allowed to live on his own with a soldier guarding him.
entries.plain: After the winter they sail on another Alexandrian ship, one whose figurehead honors the twin sons of Zeus, Castor and Pollux, and land at Puteoli on the Italian coast. Believers there host them for a week. As they travel the road toward Rome, believers from the city walk out to meet them at two stopping points, and Paul thanks God and is encouraged. In Rome he is allowed to live in his own lodging, guarded by a single soldier.
entries.note: The Twin Brothers were Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, sons of Zeus whom sailors called on as protectors in storms, and ships were named for their patron deity, whose image served as the figurehead (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). At Rhegium the ship waited for a south wind to carry it through the strait (the Zondervan Bible dictionary). Puteoli, near Naples, was a chief port of the Alexandrian grain fleet with an old Jewish community (Keener and his notes); Rome's official port was Ostia, but passengers from the east often landed at Puteoli, some 140 miles south, and went on by road (Wright; the Zondervan atlas). Delegations from a city normally went out to meet and welcome an important visitor; the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns lay roughly forty and thirty miles from Rome on the Appian Way (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Living on his own with one soldier showed that Paul was treated as a person of rank who posed no danger, and his guard was likely drawn from the Praetorian Guard (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible).

A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.

entries.title: Acts 28:17-31, Two years in rented quarters
entries.summary: Paul calls the Jewish leaders of Rome, explains why he is in chains, and spends a day arguing from Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and some are not; for two whole years he lives at his own expense, welcoming everyone and preaching the kingdom without hindrance.
entries.plain: Soon after arriving, Paul invites Rome's Jewish leaders and explains that he is in chains for Israel's hope, not for any offense against his people, and that he appealed to Caesar only because he was forced to. They say no word about him has reached them but want to hear more about a movement opposed everywhere. On a set day he spends hours making the case from Moses and the prophetic books about Jesus and God's kingdom; some are persuaded and some refuse, and he applies Isaiah's words about hearing without understanding and says God's rescue is now going to the Gentiles. The book closes with Paul living two years in rented rooms, welcoming visitors and teaching openly with nothing to stop him.
entries.note: Rome's Jewish community was made up of many autonomous synagogues with no single leader (Keener and his notes), and Wright thinks Paul called their leaders first to head off trouble like that behind Claudius's expulsion. Paul's ship had come early in the sailing season, perhaps before any letters could arrive; if his accusers gave up, the case would eventually be thrown out (the cultural backgrounds notes). What came next is uncertain. Keener says that if no accusers came Paul would normally be released after two years; Carson, Moo and Morris think he was almost surely released, since tradition puts his death under Nero in 64 or 65 and the Pastoral Letters need further travels; the CSB Study Bible says he may have been executed after the two years. Why Acts ends here is read several ways: Carson, Moo and Morris argue that Luke wrote about AD 62, before the outcome; Wright thinks Luke wrote it as evidence for Paul's coming trial, a view Carson, Moo and Morris call unlikely; the CSB Study Bible points to Luke's aim of showing the gospel reach Rome; and Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes observe that many ancient works ended abruptly.

The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
