Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: Romans 1:1-7, A slave of the Messiah writes to Rome
entries.summary: Paul opens with his name and titles, a short summary of the good news about God's Son, and a greeting of grace and peace to believers in Rome he has never met.
entries.plain: Paul opens the letter by naming himself and his commission to a church he has never met. In a few lines he sums up his message: it is about God's Son, Israel's promised king from David's line, shown to be Son of God by rising from the dead. In the emperor's own city, where Caesar was hailed as a son of the gods, this was a weighty way to begin.
entries.note: No one seriously doubts that Paul wrote Romans. Carson, Moo and Morris place it at Corinth near the end of his third journey, about AD 57 (the Zondervan dictionary says the winter of 56-57). Why he sent so long an argument to a church he had never visited is debated: support for a mission to Spain, a summing up after the fights in Galatia and Corinth, a rehearsal for Jerusalem, or healing a split between Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome. Carson, Moo and Morris think several purposes meet, and they reject the view that chapter 16 was a separate letter, for which there is no textual evidence. Rome held close to a million people and perhaps 40,000 to 50,000 Jews, and Greek was the language of its Jewish community and of this letter (the cultural backgrounds article Rome). A slave of someone powerful had status: "the emperor's slaves were some of the highest-ranking people in the empire" (Keener). Gentiles called the emperor a son of the gods (Keener and his notes), and Wright hears in verses 3-4 a counter-claim to Caesar drawn above all from Israel's psalms and prophets.

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: Romans 1:8-17, Longing to see Rome
entries.summary: Paul thanks God that the Roman believers' faith is spoken of everywhere, explains why he has not yet come, and states his theme: the good news is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew and Greek.
entries.plain: Paul thanks God for the Roman believers, whose trust in Christ is talked about widely, and explains that he has long wanted to visit them but has been blocked. He feels a debt to every kind of person, educated or not. Then he states the theme of the whole letter: the good news is God's saving power for everyone who trusts it, Jews first and Gentiles too.
entries.note: Who first brought the gospel to Rome is not known. The ESV, CSB and cultural backgrounds notes point to Roman Jews who were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and so do Carson, Moo and Morris, who reject the later tradition that Peter founded the church; Wright finds no first-century evidence for it, though the cultural backgrounds article Rome calls a later visit by Peter very probable. Rome's Jews met in many synagogues with separate leaders, which apparently helped the message spread (the article). Claudius expelled them, probably in AD 49. Keener thinks the church was then wholly Gentile until Claudius died; the article doubts that every Jew left, and Carson, Moo and Morris think the edict soon lapsed but left Gentiles in charge and returning Jewish believers a minority. Wright pictures the first readers across the Tiber: "it was in a crowded room in someone's house in the low-lying poorer district." Keener and his notes take verses 16-17 as the letter's thesis statement, and Wright sums up the clash: "Caesar claimed to rule the world; God's gospel claimed that Jesus did."

For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.

entries.title: Romans 1:18-32, Images of the immortal God
entries.summary: Paul describes God's anger against people who knew him from creation yet traded his glory for images of humans and animals, and the disorder that followed.
entries.plain: Paul begins his case by describing God's anger at a human race that could see God's power in creation yet refused to honor him. People swapped the worship of God for statues of humans and animals, and Paul traces how that one exchange led to disordered desires and broken relationships. Three times he says God handed them over to what they wanted, and he closes with a long catalogue of vices.
entries.note: Paul's argument resembles one in the Wisdom of Solomon, and Stoics argued that God's nature was evident in creation, an argument Diaspora Jews used to win pagans to the one God (Keener). Greeks and Romans gave their chief gods human form and mocked Egyptians for gods shaped like animals; to Jews idolatry was among the worst sins and a mark of Gentiles (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Yet Paul's wording borrows what Scripture said about Israel's own idolatry (Psalm 106:20; Jeremiah 2:11), which sets up the turn to his Jewish hearers in chapter 2 (Keener and his notes). For verses 26-27 the cultural backgrounds article Homosexual Activity in Antiquity, with Keener, gives the setting: among Greeks, male same-sex relations most often involved adolescent boys, and seldom to the exclusion of women; elite Romans had taken up the practice; some Greek and especially Roman moralists called it against nature; Greek-speaking Jews joined that charge to the argument from creation; and Jewish sources treated it as a Gentile sin. The article reads Paul as starting from sins his Jewish hearers already counted Gentile, then moving to a list that takes in everyone. Such vice lists were common (Keener).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 1:18-23, 1:19-22, 1:23, 1:24-32, 1:26-27 and 1:28-32
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, note on Romans 1:23, and article Homosexual Activity in Antiquity

ideas.s: The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
Greeks split humanity into Greeks and barbarians, people whose speech sounded like babble. Jews split it into Israel and the nations. Paul uses both maps.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

entries.title: Romans 2:17-29, You who boast in the law
entries.summary: Paul turns on an imagined Jewish teacher who boasts in the law yet steals, commits adultery and robs temples, so that God's name is blasphemed among the nations, and says true circumcision is of the heart.
entries.plain: Paul speaks to an imagined Jewish teacher who is proud of the law and sure he can instruct others, and asks whether he lives by what he teaches. Citing Scripture, he says such failure brings God's name into disrepute among the nations. Circumcision is worth something to one who keeps the law, but Paul argues that what makes someone truly a Jew is an inner change worked by the Spirit, not a mark on the body.
entries.note: Paul is using diatribe, a teaching style with an imaginary opponent and pointed questions; the opponent was a worst case, not typical Jewish behavior (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Temple robbery is read three ways. Keener calls it one of the most impious crimes and notes that pagans sometimes suspected Jews of it (Acts 19:37). The ESV Study Bible says "Robbing temples was a common crime in the ancient world," and that for a Jew it would add self-defilement to theft. Wright says Jews were often accused of it because, not believing in idols, they treated pagan temples as trivial. Rome remembered a real scandal. Josephus tells how four Jewish swindlers persuaded Fulvia, a noblewoman who had become a convert, to send purple and gold to the temple in Jerusalem and kept it, and how Tiberius banished the Jews of Rome: "Thus were these Jews banished out of the city by the wickedness of four men." The cultural backgrounds notes and Keener connect verse 24 with that memory. Circumcision of the heart goes back to Moses and the prophets (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4), and the cultural backgrounds notes suggest a wordplay, since praise sounds like the Hebrew name Judah.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 2:1-29, 2:17-24, 2:21-23, 2:24 and 2:29
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 2:17-24, 2:21-23, 2:24 and 2:25-29
ESV Study Bible, study note on Romans 2:22
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: Romans, Part One, comment on Romans 2:17-24
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 18.3.5, trans. William Whiston

ideas.s: Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

entries.title: Romans 3:21-31, Redemption and the mercy seat
entries.summary: Paul announces that God's righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus for all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike, through a redemption and an atoning death he links to the mercy seat.
entries.plain: Paul reaches the turning point of his argument: God has now shown his justice in a new way, apart from the law yet in line with what the Scriptures said, through faith in Jesus. Every person has failed, Jew and Gentile alike, and every person is put right freely by God's grace through Jesus, whose death Paul describes in the language of atoning sacrifice. Because there is only one God, he is God of Gentiles as much as of Jews, and no one has grounds to boast.
entries.note: Redemption meant freeing a slave, usually at a price; God had redeemed Israel at the cost of the Passover lamb (Keener and his notes), and Wright reads the cross as the new exodus. The word in verse 25 points to the mercy seat on the ark, consecrated each year with sacrificial blood (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), and Wright makes Jesus the place where, and the means by which, God meets his people and forgives. God passing over earlier sins echoes Exodus 12:13 (Keener and his notes). The basic confession of Judaism was that God is one, and Paul concludes that he must be the God of Gentiles too (Keener). What Paul's Jewish contemporaries thought about works and boasting is disputed. Carson, Moo and Morris set out E. P. Sanders's view that Jews believed they were saved by belonging to the covenant people, with obedience keeping them in it rather than earning entry. They call it a needed corrective to caricatures of Judaism, but doubt that it rules out more legalistic Jews, and hold that the Reformers' reading of justification by faith remains the most natural.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 3:24, 3:25, 3:26 and 3:29-30
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 3:24 and 3:25
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: Romans, Part One, comment on Romans 3:25-26
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 8, Romans, Romans in Recent Study

ideas.s: Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

ideas.n: The Day of Atonement and the mercy seat
ideas.s: Once a year the high priest went into the holy of holies with sacrificial blood, for his own sins and then the nation's. It was the one fast the law commanded, and the mercy seat on the ark was the place the blood was brought.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

entries.title: Romans 4:1-25, Abraham, father of the uncircumcised too
entries.summary: Paul argues from Genesis 15:6 that Abraham was counted righteous by trusting God before he was circumcised, so he is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not.
entries.plain: Paul turns to Abraham, the father every Jewish reader claimed, and points out from Genesis that God counted him righteous because he trusted God. That happened years before Abraham was circumcised, so circumcision confirmed something he already had, and he can be father to uncircumcised believers as well as circumcised ones. The promise rested on trust, and Abraham trusted a God who brings the dead to life.
entries.note: Jewish tradition spoke often of our father Abraham and treated him as the model of faith, the model Pharisee and the model convert, a Gentile before his circumcision who destroyed idols; some traditions said his merit sustained Israel in later generations (Keener). Genesis 15:6 was a favorite text, often read as Abraham's faithfulness, one of his works, and the verb for counted or credited was a bookkeeping term from business documents (Keener). Keener counts over thirteen years between Genesis 15:6 and Abraham's circumcision and notes that some Jewish interpreters made it twenty-nine. Many Jews allowed that exceptional Gentiles who kept the laws given to Noah could be saved, but required male Gentiles to be circumcised to join God's people, so making uncircumcised Gentiles full heirs of Abraham would make Jewish ears recoil (Keener and his notes). The Hebrew word translated land can equally mean earth, and Jewish interpreters taught that Abraham's offspring would receive the entire coming world as their inheritance (Keener). Wright frames the chapter around one question: what kind of family have believers been adopted into?
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 4:1-22, 4:1, 4:2, 4:3, 4:10, 4:11-12 and 4:13
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, note on Romans 4:11
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: Romans, Part One, comment on Romans 4:1-8

ideas.s: Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.

entries.title: Romans 5:1-21, Peace with God, and Adam
entries.summary: Justified by faith, believers have peace with God and are reconciled to him by the death of his Son. As sin and death came through Adam, grace and life come through Christ.
entries.plain: Paul says that those justified by faith have peace with God through Jesus, and boast in hope and even in sufferings. Christ died for the ungodly, though one would hardly die even for a good person, and enemies have been reconciled to God through his Son's death. Then Paul sets the one man Adam, through whom sin and death entered the world and spread to all, beside the one man Jesus Christ, through whom grace reigns much more.
entries.note: Peace usually meant a relationship without hostility, made by treaty or imposed by a conqueror, as in the Roman Empire (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Wright's biography of Paul notes that the Caesars presented their rule as a golden age of justice, salvation and peace won by their power, and that Paul used the same words to mean something quite different. Greeks praised giving one's life for a friend, but outside war it was rare (Keener and his notes), and they did not speak of a god taking the first step to reconcile offending mortals (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Jewish writers said Adam brought sin and death into the world but that each descendant chose to follow him (4 Ezra 7:118; 2 Baruch 54:15, 19), and Keener sees Paul's how much more as a standard Jewish and Greco-Roman argument from lesser to greater. The cultural backgrounds article Adam in Jewish Tradition adds that Jewish tradition did not normally speak of inheriting Adam's guilt, though it agreed that everyone had sinned, and suggests why Paul starts from Adam: Jews could appeal to descent from Abraham, but Jew and Gentile alike descend from the sinner Adam.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 5:1, 5:7, 5:10, 5:12 and 5:17, and article Adam in Jewish Tradition
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 5:1, 5:6-9, 5:10-11, 5:12-21, 5:12-14 and 5:16-21
N. T. Wright, Paul: A Biography, ch. 12, Corinth II

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

The Old Testament says little about Adam outside Genesis, but by Paul's day Jewish writers spoke often of his lost glory and of the sin and death he brought into the world. Each person, they added, became his own Adam.

entries.title: Romans 6:1-23, Slaves of a new master
entries.summary: Baptized into Christ's death, believers are dead to sin. Once slaves of sin, they have been set free to become slaves of God, whose gift is eternal life.
entries.plain: Paul answers an objection: if grace covers sin, why not keep sinning? He replies that baptism joined believers to Christ's death, so their old life has ended and sin no longer has the right to rule them. Drawing on the everyday reality of slavery, he says they have changed masters, from sin, which pays out death, to God, who gives eternal life as a gift.
entries.note: For Jews, baptism was the act by which a Gentile converted, the final removal of Gentile impurity that made him a new person in Jewish law, and in Jewish legal theory a Gentile slave who escaped a Jewish owner and converted by baptism was free of that owner (Keener). The old self can be translated old humanity, the humanity of Adam (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Owners often freed slaves, who kept obligations to them, but death ended every obligation (the cultural backgrounds notes). The word for instruments could mean weapons, as of soldiers reporting for duty (Keener). Some scholars see sacral manumission behind the chapter, a slave freed by becoming the property of a god and his temple; Keener finds the philosophers' talk of slavery to false ideas and pleasure clearer, and notes that Jewish teachers said Israel became God's slaves when freed from Egypt. Slaves often received wages, called a peculium, which they could use and sometimes spend on buying their freedom, so wages were normally a good thing, which makes Paul's wages of sin all the more striking (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 6:1-5, 6:6-7, 6:12-13, 6:14-21 and 6:23
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 6:6, 6:7 and 6:23

ideas.s: Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.

The Old Testament says little about Adam outside Genesis, but by Paul's day Jewish writers spoke often of his lost glory and of the sin and death he brought into the world. Each person, they added, became his own Adam.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: Romans 7:1-25, Bound while the husband lives
entries.summary: A wife is bound to her husband only while he lives, and believers have died to the law to belong to Christ. Then Paul describes a divided self that knows the good and cannot do it.
entries.plain: Paul uses marriage law to make a point: a wife is free to remarry once her husband dies, and believers have likewise died to the law through Christ and now belong to him. He insists the law itself is holy and good, but sin used it as a foothold and brought death. He then speaks in the first person of a self that wants the good and does the opposite, ending in a cry of despair and then thanks to God; who this speaker is remains debated.
entries.note: Under biblical law both death and divorce ended a marriage, and Paul uses the one that fits his picture (Keener); some Jewish traditions pictured God's people married to the law (the cultural backgrounds notes). The ESV Study Bible takes the law in verse 1 to be the law of Moses, known to Jews and to Gentiles familiar with the Old Testament. Greek interpreters read laws by their principle, while Palestinian Jews attended to exact wording, down to letters and spellings (Keener). Jewish teachers said study of the law overcame the evil impulse, philosophers spoke of reason at war with the passions, and many Diaspora Jews held that a mind informed by the law could master the passions (Keener; the cultural backgrounds article Flesh and Spirit). The article notes that Paul does not share this confidence: the mind too can be ruled by the flesh (verses 23 and 25). Keener says the cry of verse 24 was a familiar way of voicing despair. Who the I is remains debated: Keener reads it as Paul's own past under the law seen in hindsight, while Wright notes that a first-person I speaking for something more general was common in the ancient world.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 7:2-4, 7:6, 7:7-13, 7:9, 7:10-11, 7:15-22 and 7:24
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, note on Romans 7:2, and article Flesh and Spirit
ESV Study Bible, study note on Romans 7:1-3
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: Romans, Part One, comment on Romans 7:7-12

ideas.s: A Jewish husband ended a marriage, or a betrothal, by handing his wife a written certificate before witnesses that left her free to marry again, and the teachers argued over the grounds. In Greek and Roman law either partner could end a marriage by leaving.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

entries.title: Romans 8:12-17, Not slaves but adopted heirs
entries.summary: Those led by God's Spirit are God's children. They have received the Spirit of adoption, not of slavery, and cry Abba, Father, as heirs of God with Christ.
entries.plain: Paul tells believers they no longer owe the flesh anything, because the Spirit now leads them and makes them God's children. The Spirit they received brings adoption, not a slave's fear, and through him they address God as Abba, Father. Adopted children inherit, so they will share Christ's inheritance as they share his suffering.
entries.note: Flesh in the Old Testament meant mortal, breathing creatures, and the Dead Sea Scrolls add moral weakness without treating the body as evil, while Platonists pictured a pure soul tied to a mortal body (the cultural backgrounds article Flesh and Spirit). The article reads Paul's flesh and Spirit as two kinds of people, not two parts of a person: those depending on God's Spirit and humanity left to itself. Roman adoption could take place at any age; it cancelled previous debts and relationships and made the son his new father's heir, and as a legal act it needed witnesses, the role Paul gives the Spirit (Keener and his notes). Ancient sources often contrast a householder's children, his heirs, with his slaves (the cultural backgrounds notes). Abba was a respectful but intimate way to address a father; it does not appear in Jewish prayers and was apparently learned from Jesus (Mark 14:36), according to the cultural backgrounds notes, and the ESV Study Bible also traces Paul's use to Jesus. Keener hears the exodus as well: God led Israel through the wilderness and called Israel his son (Exodus 4:22).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 8:14, 8:15 and 8:16
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 8:14-17, 8:15 and 8:16, and article Flesh and Spirit
ESV Study Bible, study note on Romans 8:15

ideas.s: A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

entries.title: Romans 8:18-30, Groaning and firstfruits
entries.summary: Creation groans as in labor, waiting to be freed from decay, and believers who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan too as they wait for their adoption and the redemption of their bodies.
entries.plain: Paul sets present suffering against the glory still to come and says the two do not compare. He pictures all creation as frustrated and in bondage to decay, groaning like a woman in labor as it waits to be freed, and believers groan with it while they wait for their bodies to be redeemed. In the meantime the Spirit prays for them, and God is working all things toward good for the people who love him.
entries.note: Greek tradition saw the world declining from a golden age, Stoics expected everything to come apart until only the primeval fire remained, and most people of the time believed decay and Fate ruled (Keener). Israel's groaning in Egypt hastened God's redemption (Exodus 2:23), and some Jewish traditions called the time just before the end birth pangs (Keener). Firstfruits were the actual beginning of the harvest (Leviticus 23:10), not simply a promise of it (Keener and his notes). Israel was redeemed from Egypt but entered the land nearly forty years later, and Keener reads Paul's present age as that time in between. The ESV Study Bible notes that adoption is already a legal fact in verse 15 and still awaited in verse 23.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 8:20, 8:22 and 8:23-25
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, note on Romans 8:23
ESV Study Bible, study note on Romans 8:23

ideas.s: Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

entries.title: Romans 8:31-39, Angels, rulers and powers
entries.summary: With God on the believers' side, Paul asks who could oppose them, then names hardships and powers, from the sword to angels, rulers, height and depth, and none of them can cut believers off from God's love in Christ.
entries.plain: Paul asks who can bring a charge against God's chosen when God is the one who justifies and Christ intercedes for them. He lists trouble, hardship, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger and sword, and quotes a psalm about being killed all day long like sheep for the slaughter. He ends sure that neither death nor life, angels nor rulers, things present nor things to come, powers, height, depth or anything else in creation can separate them from God's love in Christ Jesus.
entries.note: Keener notes Jewish texts in which God clears Israel at the final judgment the way the Day of Atonement cleared his people every year. Lists of hardships showed that a wise man had passed his tests, and the sword was the usual way Roman citizens were executed (Keener and his notes). By the second century rabbis applied Psalm 44:22 to martyrs; some Roman believers had recently come back after the expulsion of AD 49, and from AD 64 Nero killed hundreds of Christians in the city (the cultural backgrounds notes). The rulers and powers named with angels are probably the spiritual rulers of the nations (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; Heiser), though the ESV Study Bible says only angelic and demonic authorities. Arnold reads the angels here as rebellious angels in league with Satan, as Paul uses the word in 2 Corinthians 12:7. Height and depth may be astrological terms for powers that ruled through the stars, or simply everything from heaven to Hades (Keener and his notes). Arnold takes the first view: in astronomical texts the words named the highest and lowest points a star reached, and he reads them as the astral spirits believed to control human destiny.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 8:33-34, 8:35-36, 8:38 and 8:39
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 8:35, 8:36, 8:38 and 8:39
ESV Study Bible, study note on Romans 8:38-39
Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm, ch. 37, This Means War
Clinton E. Arnold, Powers of Darkness, ch. 8, A New Kingdom and Identity for Believers, Secure and Protected

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Romans 9:1-5, Israel's privileges
entries.summary: Paul grieves for his own people and lists what belongs to Israel: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs and the Messiah.
entries.plain: Paul turns to the hard question of why most of his own people have not believed, and begins with grief so deep he would accept being cut off himself if it helped them. He lists Israel's privileges, from adoption as God's son and the covenants to the law, the temple worship, the promises, the patriarchs and the Messiah himself. Whether the words of praise at the end of verse 5 call the Messiah God is read both ways.
entries.note: Paul's wish to be cut off for his people recalls Moses, who offered himself for Israel (Exodus 32:32), as Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes point out. The blessings Paul gave believers in chapter 8, adoption and glory among them, belonged to Israel in the Old Testament, and Jewish people celebrated them (Keener and his notes). In Greek the list rhymes, its nouns ending in a repeated pattern of sounds that would appeal to the hearers (the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener reads the plural covenants as God's covenants with the patriarchs or his many renewals of the covenant. Jewish doxologies praised only the one God; the cultural backgrounds notes say many scholars argue that Paul here praises Jesus as God, and Keener reads it that way.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 9:1-3 and 9:4-5
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 9:3, 9:4 and 9:5

ideas.s: A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Romans 10:1-21, How beautiful are the feet
entries.summary: Paul prays for Israel, whose zeal for God lacks knowledge, and argues from Scripture that the word of faith is near, that whoever calls on the Lord will be saved, and that heralds must be sent.
entries.plain: Paul prays for Israel's salvation and grants their zeal for God, though he says it is not guided by true understanding. Drawing on Deuteronomy, he argues that God's word is close at hand, needing only confession and trust, and that rescue is open to anyone, Jew or Gentile, who calls on the Lord. He then traces a chain: people cannot call without believing or believe without hearing, and they cannot hear unless messengers are sent.
entries.note: Jewish literature of the period often praised zeal for the law, even to the point of violent resistance against those who tried to suppress it (Keener). Paul reads Deuteronomy 30:12-14 in good Jewish fashion: no one needs to climb Sinai again to bring down the law or go down into the sea again to be redeemed (Keener). The verb for sent is the verb behind the word apostle, and Isaiah 52:7 announced good news that still needed heralds to carry it (Keener). Wright's glossary traces the word gospel to Isaiah's herald and also to the announcements of the emperor's birthday and accession. Psalm 19:4, which Paul quotes about the message going out to the ends of the world, speaks in context of creation's witness, and word about Christ had already begun to reach most Jewish centers (Keener).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 10:1-2, 10:6-7, 10:15 and 10:18
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: Romans, Part One, Glossary, entry good news, gospel

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.
Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.

entries.title: Romans 11:11-24, The olive tree
entries.summary: Israel's stumbling has brought salvation to the Gentiles. Paul pictures Gentile believers as wild olive shoots grafted into Israel's tree and warns them not to boast over the natural branches.
entries.plain: Paul insists Israel's stumble is not a final fall: through it the good news has reached the Gentiles, and their gain is meant to stir Israel to jealousy. He uses the picture of an olive tree, with Gentile believers as wild shoots grafted in among the native branches. They have no reason to look down on the branches that were broken off, since they live from Israel's root and God can just as easily graft the original branches back in.
entries.note: Ancient speakers counted self-praise acceptable only to stir others to imitate the good, which is how Paul speaks of magnifying his ministry (Keener and his notes). The first of the dough offered to God (Numbers 15:20-21) made the whole batch holy, and mixed metaphors were common (Keener and his notes). Gentiles had joined Israel before, Rahab and Ruth among them, but as a small minority; now Gentile believers apparently outnumbered Jewish ones in the Roman church (Keener and his notes). The cultural backgrounds notes add that later Gentile Christians did boast that they had replaced Israel, and Wright reads the passage as a warning that Gentile believers must not suppose they had replaced the Jews in God's plan. Writing when many Jews had recently been allowed back to Rome, in a city where many people distrusted and sneered at them, Wright thinks a mostly Gentile church could easily have picked up the anti-Judaism around it. Carson, Moo and Morris likewise picture Jewish believers coming back as a minority, perhaps looked down on by the now dominant Gentile wing, and note that these verses are addressed to Gentiles.

ideas.s: Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

Olive trees lived for centuries, and growers grafted shoots from one tree into another. Scripture called God's people an olive tree, and Jewish writers pictured Israel as a tree whose roots were the patriarchs.
Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.

entries.title: Romans 11:25-36, The full number of the nations
entries.summary: Paul reveals a mystery: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved. He ends in praise of God's wisdom.
entries.plain: Paul tells Gentile believers a mystery so they will not think too highly of themselves: Israel's hardening is partial and lasts until the full number of Gentiles comes in, and so Israel as a whole will be rescued, though who that Israel is remains disputed. For now Israel opposes the gospel, yet God still loves them for the patriarchs' sake and never takes back his gifts. Paul ends in a hymn of praise to God's wisdom, which no one can trace.
entries.note: Many Jews expected Israel's repentance to bring the end, and Keener and his notes read Paul to say that God had delayed it to make room for the promised witness to the Gentiles. It was common for Jewish teachers to promise salvation to every Israelite and then name the exceptions; the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 10:1) leaves out only notorious sinners, so the phrase meant Israel as a whole (Keener and his notes). Heiser reads the full number of the Gentiles as the reversal of Babel, where the nations were disinherited (Deuteronomy 32:8-9). Who all Israel is remains disputed. Keener says ethnic Israel as a whole will return in the end time, and rejects both the view that Israel and the church are wholly separate and the view that the church replaces Israel; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles also take Israel here as the Jewish people; Heiser reads Gentiles from the disinherited nations as brought into Israel, God's family. Stoics thought all things would be resolved back into God, but Paul's closing words mean, as Jews meant them, that God directs history (Keener).

ideas.s: Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.

entries.title: Romans 12:1-21, A living sacrifice
entries.summary: Paul urges believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, to see themselves as members of one body, and to love without pretense: honoring one another, welcoming strangers, weeping with those who weep and repaying evil with good.
entries.plain: Paul now turns from argument to how believers should live, asking them to give their whole selves to God as an offering and to let their thinking be remade instead of shaped by the present age. Each has a different gift within one body. He then sketches genuine love in practice: honoring one another, sharing with those in need, welcoming strangers, sharing in others' joys and sorrows, and meeting an enemy's hunger with food instead of revenge.
entries.note: Judaism and some philosophical schools often used sacrifice figuratively; Paul's word for worship or service evokes the work of priests in the temple, and a living sacrifice strains the picture on purpose (Keener). This world is literally this age (Keener and his notes). Philosophers used the picture of a body to defend each class's place in the state, and Keener suggests Paul may be the first to give every member of a religious community a function. Soldiers swore never to prefer anyone above Caesar in honor (Keener). Hospitality meant free lodging for travelers, who carried letters from people their hosts trusted, and Jewish travelers counted on fellow Jews (Keener and his notes); the ESV Study Bible adds that most early Christians could not afford lodging houses. The public joined Jewish funeral processions, though philosophers warned against weeping too much (Keener). Humility was a Jewish virtue but not a Greek one, except for the lowly (Keener). The coals of fire are debated: Keener and his notes allow that Paul may mean judgment on an enemy who will not repent, while both name the preferred goal as turning an enemy into a friend, which some Greek and Jewish sages also valued.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 12:1, 12:2, 12:3-5, 12:9-10, 12:11-13, 12:15, 12:16, 12:20 and 12:21

ideas.s: Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Romans 13:1-7, The sword and the tax
entries.summary: Paul tells believers to be subject to the governing authorities, whom God has put in place. The ruler bears the sword, and they should pay taxes and give honor where it is owed.
entries.plain: Paul tells believers in the capital to submit to the ruling authorities, on the ground that all authority comes from God. Rulers exist to restrain wrongdoing and reward good conduct, and they carry the sword for that purpose. So believers should pay their taxes and give each official the respect and honor that is due.
entries.note: Loyalty to the state was a standard topic of moral writers, though they meant a general principle, not submission to evil (Keener and his notes). Rome's Jews had been expelled less than a decade before, minorities worked to avoid scandal, and Jews and Christians stressed their good citizenship against charges of subversion (Keener and his notes). Nero had not yet persecuted anyone (Keener and his notes). The sword stood for the right to execute, and Keener writes that "Swords were carried in front of Roman officials" to show it. The empire levied a property tax and a head tax, with local taxes and customs on top, and the money paid for roads, armies and temples to the emperor; the cultural backgrounds notes observe that "Paul does not ask Christians to pay only for what they approve of." Wright notes that rulers put in place by God would be news to emperors who claimed to be divine. What being subject means is read two ways: Keener says submission in Judaism meant not resisting, not always obeying, while the ESV Study Bible says it generally means obeying, except where obeying the state would mean disobeying God.

ideas.s: Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Romans 14:1-23, Vegetables, holy days and wine
entries.summary: Some believers eat only vegetables and keep certain days; others eat anything and treat every day alike. Paul tells both not to judge one another, since all will stand before God's judgment seat, and not to wreck another's faith over food.
entries.plain: Paul addresses a split in the Roman church over food and holy days: some eat anything and treat all days alike, while others, whom he calls weak, eat only vegetables and keep special days. He tells both groups to stop judging and despising each other, since each serves the Lord and each will answer to God. He himself is convinced no food is impure by nature, but he says love means giving up meat or wine before causing a fellow believer to fall.
entries.note: Romans mocked three Jewish customs above all, circumcision, food laws and holy days, and Jews did not expect Gentiles to keep their food laws, though they did expect converts to (the cultural backgrounds article Pure and Unclean Foods). Jews avoided unclean meat, not meat as such; where kosher meat could not be had they might live on vegetables, as Daniel did (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), and Josephus says priests held prisoner in Rome "supported themselves with figs and nuts." Many Jews had died rather than eat pork, which Greeks thought delicious (Keener), and Wright adds that "pork was the cheapest and most readily available meat in that world." Gentile meat might have been offered to idols, and Gentile wine poured out to the gods (Keener and his notes). Who the weak and the strong were is debated: Keener and his notes, and Carson, Moo and Morris, see mainly Jewish and Gentile believers, while Wright and Bird warn that Paul, a Jew, counted himself strong. The days are read as the Sabbath (the ESV Study Bible), the Jewish festivals (Wright) or fast days (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.
The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.

entries.title: Romans 15:14-24, To Spain by way of Rome
entries.summary: Paul describes his priestly work of offering the Gentiles to God, from Jerusalem round to Illyricum, and his plan to visit Rome on his way to Spain and be helped on his journey there.
entries.plain: Paul explains why he has written so boldly: God has given him a priestly task, serving the good news so that the Gentiles become an offering God accepts. He has preached in a great arc from Jerusalem to Illyricum, aiming at places where Christ was unknown. With that work done, he plans to visit Rome on his way to Spain and hopes the Roman church will help send him on.
entries.note: Many Jews expected the nations one day to bring tribute to Jerusalem (Isaiah 60:11-14), and here the Gentiles themselves are the offering (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). There is little evidence of Jewish settlement there before the third century, so Paul could not begin in synagogues (Keener and his notes). A traveler bound for Spain went on from Rome to Tarraco, some 900 miles (the cultural backgrounds notes). To be helped on his journey meant having his costs covered; a direct request could cost honor, so Paul only implies it (Keener and his notes), and Carson, Moo and Morris count winning that support as a major reason for the letter, though not the only one. Why Spain is read two ways. Wright notes that "Tarragona boasted a large temple to Caesar," where Paul would long to announce Jesus as Lord. Heiser writes, "In Paul's day, Spain was where Tarshish was," the westernmost nation in the Table of Nations, so that reaching it would complete the reversal of Babel. Whether Paul ever got there is uncertain; the CSB Study Bible says scholars are divided.

Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Romans 15:25-33, The gift for Jerusalem
entries.summary: Before coming west Paul must take a gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor among the believers in Jerusalem. He asks for prayer that he will be kept safe and the gift accepted.
entries.plain: Before coming west, Paul must first take a gift to Jerusalem, money collected by the churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the needy believers there. He sees it as a debt: the Gentiles have shared in Israel's spiritual blessings and should share their material goods in return. He asks the Romans to pray that he will be kept safe from opponents in Judea and that the Jerusalem believers will accept the gift.
entries.note: Every year Jewish men throughout the world paid the half-shekel temple tax, and trusted messengers carried it to Jerusalem; this offering would show the same solidarity between Jewish and Gentile believers (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Augustus had ordered that the Jews' "sacred money be not touched, but be sent to Jerusalem" (Josephus). In some circles, Qumran above all, the poor served as a name for Judea's devout (Keener). Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say some Jerusalem believers may have seen the gift as the first of the nations' promised tribute, and the notes add that refusing a gift declared enmity, so a refusal would be rare; Wright thinks some Jewish believers may still have found Gentile money tainted. Sealing the fruit recalls the seal on commercial goods that guaranteed their contents (Keener). Wright's biography sums up the plan: "Phoebe, then, will travel west with the letter," while Paul goes east with the money. In the second century the Roman church was known for sending funds to needy churches and freeing Christian slaves from the mines (Keener).

ideas.s: Paul gathered money from his mostly Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, much as Jews everywhere sent the temple tax to the holy city.
Every year free adult Jewish men across the empire paid two drachmas toward the temple in Jerusalem. After AD 70 Rome went on collecting the same sum for a pagan temple.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

entries.title: Romans 16:1-2, Phoebe of Cenchreae
entries.summary: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant or deacon of the church at Cenchreae and a patron of many, Paul included, and asks the Romans to welcome her and help her in whatever she needs.
entries.plain: Paul introduces Phoebe, who serves the church at Cenchreae, and asks the Romans to receive her as fellow believers should and give her any help she needs. His reason is that she has been a patron to many people, Paul among them. She very probably carried the letter to Rome.
entries.note: Since the only mail service was the imperial couriers' for the government, Paul had to send his letter with a traveler (Keener). People of higher status wrote letters of recommendation for those somewhat below them, and the bearer could be asked to explain the document, which made Phoebe's qualifications matter (the cultural backgrounds notes). Wright's biography says she read the letter aloud in the Roman congregations and probably expounded it; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles say only that she probably carried it. The word for her help was applied especially to patrons; the patron of a religious association was usually well-to-do, let the group meet in his or her home and held some authority, and some women patrons are known (Keener). Wright notes that "the emperor himself claimed to be the state's supreme benefactor." Her title, diakonos, is read as servant or as deacon: Wright takes it as deacon, probably a junior office; the ESV Study Bible says the meaning is debated; Keener compares the synagogue officer in charge of the building and adds that the word usually means a minister of God's word.

ideas.s: A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.

entries.title: Romans 16:3-16, Greet the church in their house
entries.summary: Paul greets more than two dozen believers in Rome by name, from Prisca and Aquila and the church in their house to the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, and tells them to greet one another with a holy kiss.
entries.plain: Paul sends greetings to more than two dozen people by name, starting with Prisca and Aquila, who once risked their lives for him and host a church in their home. Many on the list are women, and Andronicus and Junia are described in a phrase that may mean they were prominent apostles or that the apostles held them in high regard. The list shows a network of households and gatherings across the city, and Paul asks them all to exchange a holy kiss.
entries.note: Priscilla and Aquila, expelled under Claudius (Acts 18:2), had come back after his death in AD 54 ended the edict (Keener and his notes), and the cultural backgrounds article Rome says even the leaders of the old disputes could return; Carson, Moo and Morris suggest many of those greeted were exiles Paul had met on his travels. Synagogues and associations often met in homes, most people in Rome lived in apartments, and Rome allowed Jews no assembly larger than the local synagogue, a limit that could keep the house churches apart (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The household of Narcissus probably means the slaves and freedmen of Claudius's powerful freedman, and Aristobulus may be Herod the Great's grandson, who lived in Rome (Keener and his notes). Nearly 40 percent of those named are women (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Junia is read two ways. Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes and Wright take her as a woman and an apostle; the ESV Study Bible agrees she was a woman but reads well known to the apostles, and the CSB Study Bible allows either.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

entries.title: Romans 16:17-27, Tertius, Gaius and Erastus
entries.summary: Paul warns against those who cause divisions, promises that God will soon crush Satan under the believers' feet, and passes on greetings from Corinth, including his scribe Tertius, his host Gaius and Erastus the city treasurer.
entries.plain: Paul adds a sharp warning about people who stir up division and lead the unsuspecting astray with smooth words, and promises that God will soon crush Satan under the believers' feet. Then come greetings from his companions in Corinth: Timothy, Tertius the scribe who wrote the letter down, Gaius who hosts the church, and Erastus the city treasurer. The letter ends in praise to the one wise God.
entries.note: Crushing Satan under their feet echoes Genesis 3:15; Jewish sources often saw the serpent as Satan or his tool, and Paul applies the promise to believers (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; Heiser). Most letter writers dictated to scribes, often slaves, and scribes rarely added greetings of their own, which makes Tertius a fellow believer (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). A Latin inscription in the pavement near the Corinthian theater says that Erastus laid it at his own expense in return for his aedileship, an elected post over streets, markets and public buildings (the ESV Study Bible; the cultural backgrounds notes and article The Erastus Inscription). Whether he is Paul's Erastus is debated. Price and House favor it, since the name is rare and the only first-century instance yet found, and inscriptions from Asia Minor show Paul's title, oikonomos, used for such a post. The cultural backgrounds notes think he probably is, their article only that he may be. The Zondervan dictionary notes that such stewards were generally slaves or freedmen: "That he was the Erastus of Romans is possible, but not probable." The closing doxology stands in different places in the manuscripts; Carson, Moo and Morris think Paul wrote it.

Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 1:1-9, Grace to the church in Corinth
entries.summary: Paul and Sosthenes greet the church of God in Corinth and thank God that its members have been made rich in every kind of speech and knowledge as they wait for the Lord to be revealed.
entries.plain: Paul writes with Sosthenes to the believers in Corinth, reminding them that God has set them apart and joined them to every church that calls on Jesus. He thanks God that they are rich in eloquence and knowledge and lack no spiritual gift while they wait for Christ's return. He assures them God will keep them firm to the end, because God is faithful.
entries.note: Few question that Paul wrote it (Carson, Moo and Morris). Corinth sat on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, with a port on each sea (Carson, Moo and Morris; the Zondervan atlas). Rome destroyed the old city in 146 BC; Julius Caesar refounded it as a colony in 44 BC (the CSB Study Bible; the atlas), and it became capital of Achaia, in 27 BC (the CSB Study Bible) or 29 BC (Carson, Moo and Morris). The settlers included freedmen from Rome and retired soldiers, and with no landed nobility "there arose an aristocracy of wealth" (Carson, Moo and Morris). Paul wrote from Ephesus, answering reports from Chloe's people and a letter the church sent with its delegates. Carson, Moo and Morris date it early in 55, or a year earlier; the cultural backgrounds notes say 55, Wright and Bird around 53, the ESV Study Bible 53 to 55 and the CSB Study Bible 56. Bailey reads the address to all who call on the Lord in every place as making this a letter for the whole church; many scholars read it as occasional, and some as several letters joined, a view Carson, Moo and Morris reject.

Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 1:10-17, I belong to Paul, I belong to Apollos
entries.summary: Told by Chloe's people that the church is splitting into camps behind Paul, Apollos, Cephas and Christ, Paul appeals for unity and asks whether Christ has been divided.
entries.plain: Paul urges the believers to agree with one another and to let there be no divisions among them. Chloe's people have told him of quarrels: one says I belong to Paul, another to Apollos, another to Cephas, another to Christ. Paul asks whether Christ is divided or whether Paul was crucified for them, and is glad he baptized only a few of them, since Christ sent him to preach the good news, not with clever words that would empty the cross of its power.
entries.note: Chloe's people were probably agents of a businesswoman, slaves or freed persons of her household traveling between Corinth and Ephesus (Keener and his notes). The phrase I am of could be a slogan of political partisans, and students of rival teachers sometimes fought (the cultural backgrounds notes). Churches met in homes, and the size of homes split believers into several house churches, where divisions could grow (Keener). What the camps were is read several ways. Keener and his notes think only the Paul and Apollos parties were real; Carson, Moo and Morris think Peter probably worked in Corinth too, though "There is no evidence that these or other leaders had fostered a party spirit"; the ESV Study Bible suggests factions formed by who had baptized whom; Wright's biography sees a dispute over speaking style. Bailey reads the names as masks for ethnic groups in a Roman colony: "In Corinth the Romans were inevitably at the top of the pecking order", with Greeks second and Jews last. Carson, Moo and Morris add that the church was both divided against itself and, as Fee stresses, largely set against Paul.

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 1:18-2:5, The foolishness of the cross
entries.summary: Paul sets the message of a crucified Messiah, folly to Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews, against the wisdom and eloquence Corinth admired, and reminds the believers that few of them were wise, powerful or well born.
entries.plain: Paul admits that a crucified Messiah sounds like nonsense to those headed for ruin, yet to those being saved it is God's power. Jews want miraculous signs and Greeks want clever wisdom, but God chose what the world counts weak and foolish, and few of the Corinthians themselves were educated, influential or well born. Paul reminds them that he first came with no polished rhetoric, only weakness and fear, so that their trust would rest on God's power instead of human skill.
entries.note: The cross was reserved for slaves and rebel provincials, the opposite of the benefactors hailed as saviors (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Jews counted anyone hanged on a stake accursed (Deuteronomy 21:23). In Corinth even most of the wealthy descended from freed persons (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), and Wright and Bird report a newer consensus that the church was socially mixed. A visiting orator gave a showcase speech, critics mocked weak delivery, and audiences ridiculed a speaker who trembled (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Why Paul came in weakness and fear is read three ways. The cultural backgrounds article Rhetoric and Paul's Letters thinks his speaking fell short of Apollos's and of educated expectations, perhaps through humility or a Judean accent, though his letters show real rhetorical skill; Wright thinks Paul writes polished rhetoric here on purpose; Carson, Moo and Morris point to the beatings he had just escaped in Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. Following Winter, they read chapters 1-4 against the Sophists, orators admired more for skill than for ideas, and they trace the Corinthians' wisdom to their pagan past rather than to Hellenistic Jewish wisdom speculation, the more common theory today.

ideas.s: Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 2:6-16, The rulers of this age
entries.summary: Paul speaks of a hidden wisdom of God, planned before time began, which the rulers of this age failed to grasp, or they would never have put Jesus to death.
entries.plain: Paul says he does teach wisdom to the mature, but it belongs neither to the present age nor to its rulers, who are passing away. It is God's hidden plan, prepared before time, which those rulers failed to grasp, or they would never have put Jesus to death. Who these rulers are, human or spiritual, is debated. God has made this wisdom known by his Spirit, and the person who has the Spirit shares the mind of Christ.
entries.note: Mature was a philosophers' word for those advanced in wisdom (Keener and his notes). Jewish writers set the present corrupted age against an everlasting age still to come (the cultural backgrounds notes). Who the rulers of this age are is disputed. Keener notes that many scholars take them as angelic powers, but thinks earthly rulers fit the context better, the powerful people of 1:26-28; the cultural backgrounds notes speak of human power that passes away. Heiser points out that the Greek translation of Daniel calls both the prince of Persia and Michael archon, and argues that Paul means the spiritual rulers of the nations. Arnold agrees: Paul calls Satan archon elsewhere, and the verb for coming to nothing is the one he uses for the powers in 15:24, never for the doom of unbelieving people. He thinks the powers worked through Pilate and the priests, and that Paul's point is that "not even the angelic powers could understand the secret wisdom of God." Bailey reads the phrase against a Roman colony that worshiped Caesar. Most Jewish teachers did not think the Spirit active in their own day, so knowing God's mind by the Spirit was a radical claim (Keener).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 1 Corinthians 2:6, 2:7, 2:8 and 2:10-13

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 3:1-23, Milk, builders and God's temple
entries.summary: Paul calls the Corinthians infants still on milk, says he and Apollos are only servants, warns builders that fire will test their work, and reminds the church that it is God's temple and that all things are theirs.
entries.plain: Paul tells the Corinthians that their rivalry, with some claiming Paul as their leader and others Apollos, shows they are still infants in the faith. He and Apollos are only workers in God's field, one planting and the other watering, and it is God who makes things grow. Christ is the only foundation, and a coming day of fire will test what each builder has put on it. The church is God's temple where his Spirit lives, so no one should boast about human leaders, since everything already belongs to them.
entries.note: Writers often compared beginners to babies who needed milk, and teachers expected students to start with the basics and then move on, so the image insulted people who thought themselves mature (Keener and his notes). A master builder directed a building project, and builders were not paid for shoddy work (Keener and his notes). Bailey notes that much of Roman Corinth was new building on the scorched ground of the city Rome burned in 146 BC, in a city famous for its bronze, whose metalworkers knew what survives fire. The Dead Sea Scrolls also pictured God's people as a temple, and almost everyone believed the gods avenged any violation of their temples (Keener and his notes); Wright's biography of Paul stresses that no first-century Jew used temple language as a mere illustration. Stoic and Cynic philosophers claimed that all things were theirs, since they were friends of the gods who owned everything, and the most extreme took it to mean they could use anything they liked (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 1 Corinthians 3:1-2, 3:10-11, 3:12-15 and 3:16-17, and introduction to 3:21-23

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 4:6-13, Apostles on display
entries.summary: With biting irony Paul sets the Corinthians, already full, rich and reigning, beside the apostles, put on show last of all like men condemned to die, hungry, ragged, homeless and treated as the world's scum.
entries.plain: Paul tells the Corinthians not to be puffed up for one leader against another, since everything they have was given to them. Already they are full, already rich, already reigning without the apostles. God, he says, has exhibited the apostles last of all, like men sentenced to death, a spectacle to the world, to angels and to people. They are fools, weak and dishonored; they go hungry and thirsty, are poorly clothed, beaten and homeless, work with their own hands, bless when cursed, and are treated as the scum of the world.
entries.note: Philosophers claimed to be the only true kings and the only truly rich, and Paul concedes the claim with irony (Keener and his notes); Wright and Bird note that rich and reigning were Stoic catchwords going back to Diogenes, who settled in Corinth. Carson, Moo and Morris add an over-realized hope: the Corinthians thought the blessings of the age to come were already theirs in full, which explains Paul's outburst here. Paul's hunger, poor clothes and homelessness fit the stock picture of the wandering Cynic, and lists of hardships proved a sage's integrity (Keener and his notes). Most sages charged fees, had a patron or begged, and people of status thought manual labor demeaning (Keener and his notes). The picture of 4:9 is read two ways. Wright and Bailey see captives dragged at the end of a Roman triumph, while Keener, his notes and the CSB Study Bible prefer the arena, where the last show of the day was kept for the most wretched condemned criminal. The ESV Study Bible gives both, and the Zondervan dictionary joins them: the captives at the end of a triumph were the ones condemned to fight beasts.

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

Rome celebrated a great victory with a triumph, a parade of the general, his army and the spoils, with chained captives at the end who were killed or sold. Cities also staged shows in which condemned criminals fought or were thrown to beasts.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 4:14-21, Ten thousand guardians, one father
entries.summary: Paul writes as the Corinthians' father in the gospel, sends Timothy to remind them of his ways, and asks whether they want him to come with a rod or with love.
entries.plain: Paul says he writes not to shame them but to warn them as his dear children. They may have countless guardians in Christ, but not many fathers, for he became their father through the gospel, so he urges them to imitate him. He is sending Timothy, his faithful son in the Lord, to remind them of his ways, and he will come soon to test the power, not the talk, of those who are arrogant. Shall he come with a rod, or in love and a gentle spirit?
entries.note: Moralists said they admonished people only because they cared for them, often in a parent's terms, and fathers were responsible for their sons' education (Keener). The guardian was a slave who escorted boys to and from school, and Keener notes that by calling himself their father Paul demotes the other teachers, since slave attendants were nothing like fathers; Wright pictures the guardians as household baby-sitters and the other teachers in Corinth as being like them. Disciples could call a teacher father and be called his children, and students imitated their teachers; Keener calls imitation one of the most common ideas in Greek literature. Fathers used the rod, and Roman political rhetoric made the proper father stern; Corinthians shaped by Roman values liked gentle fathers but knew that a father put duty first (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris trace what followed: Timothy found the situation beyond him, and Paul's warning came true in a painful visit (2 Corinthians 2:1).
