ideas.s: A trusted household slave walked a boy to school and back, watched his manners and kept him out of trouble until he came of age. He was neither the teacher nor anything like the father.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 5:1-13, A man and his father's wife
entries.summary: A church member is living with his stepmother and the church is proud of itself. Paul tells them to hand the man over to Satan, clear out the old leaven as a household does before Passover, and not eat with a so-called brother who lives that way.
entries.plain: Paul has heard that a man in the church is living with his stepmother, a union even pagans condemned, and that the church is proud of itself instead of grieving. He tells them to gather with his authority and hand the man over to Satan, with his final rescue as the hoped for result; what that handing over means is debated. Using the Passover custom of clearing out old yeast, he says a little sin spreads through the whole community, and they must not share meals with a believer who lives this way, while judging outsiders is God's business.
entries.note: Relations with a stepmother counted as incest, abhorred everywhere in the Roman world, and since men often took much younger second wives, a stepmother might be near the son's age (Keener and his notes). Keener says Roman law punished incest with banishment to an island, while the CSB Study Bible says that for a son and stepmother it "was a capital crime in a Roman colony, calling for death or banishment." The man may have been a high-status member whose connections mattered to the church's standing (the cultural backgrounds notes). Handing over to Satan is read two ways. Keener compares pagan curse tablets that devoted a person to the gods of the underworld. Heiser reads it as putting the man back outside the holy ground of the church into Satan's domain, and Arnold, following Fee, agrees, doubting any literal delivery to Satan and stressing that the aim is restoration. Passover bread was unleavened (Keener and his notes), and Wright adds that leaven used as a picture almost always meant a corrupting influence. Carson, Moo and Morris suggest that the earlier letter of verse 9 answered a question about church discipline, and some read it in the widest sense.

ideas.n: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
ideas.s: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 6:1-11, Lawsuits before unbelievers
entries.summary: Paul is appalled that believers take one another to court before pagan judges, reminds them that God's people will judge the world and even angels, and asks why they would not rather be wronged.
entries.plain: Paul is shocked that believers are suing one another before pagan judges. Since God's people are destined to sit in judgment over the world and even over angels, they ought to be able to settle everyday disputes among themselves; better to be wronged than to go to court at all. He reminds them that wrongdoers will not inherit God's kingdom, and that some of them once lived that way but have been washed and made right through Jesus.
entries.note: Keener writes, "Like modern North American society, Roman society was extremely litigious." Judges came from the elite and favored their own, and social inferiors could not sue their betters (Keener and his notes); Wright and Bird take the cost of going to law to mean rich members suing poorer ones. Minority communities were expected to settle their own affairs, since public suits fed prejudice against them (Keener and his notes). A Roman decree for the Jews of Sardis, preserved by Josephus, says they had "a place of their own, wherein they determined their suits and controversies with one another." Wright notes that Corinth prided itself on its Roman legal status, and Bailey recalls Paul's own hearing before Gallio; the judgment seat at Corinth was excavated in 1935-37 (Price and House). Keener says Jewish traditions had the righteous judge the nations and so the angels believed to rule them, and Heiser reads verse 3 as believers displacing the divine beings set over the nations. What case lies behind the passage is disputed: Keener and Bailey suggest it grew out of the incest case of chapter 5, while the ESV Study Bible and the cultural backgrounds notes think of ordinary property disputes.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 1 Corinthians 6:1-11, and on 6:1, 6:2, 6:3 and 6:6

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 6:12-20, The body and the prostitute
entries.summary: Answering slogans such as everything is permissible and food is for the stomach, Paul argues that the body belongs to the Lord, will be raised, and must not be joined to a prostitute, for believers were bought at a price.
entries.plain: Paul quotes slogans some Corinthians were using, such as the claim that everything is allowed and that food and the stomach are made for each other. He answers that freedom must not become a new master and that the body belongs to the Lord, who will raise it as he raised Jesus. Since their bodies are united to Christ and are a temple of the Spirit, they must run from sexual sin, for God bought them at a high price.
entries.note: Food for the stomach was a Greek way of arguing that the body was made for sex, and since Greeks thought one was done with the body at death, what one did with it seemed not to matter (Keener and his notes); Carson, Moo and Morris trace that low view of the body to neoplatonism. The cultural backgrounds article Prostitution and Sexual Immorality notes that a few philosophers allowed prostitutes so long as one was not ruled by the habit, while many said intercourse was only for having children; that Greek men often married around thirty; and that most prostitutes were slaves, many raised from abandoned babies, often working as tavern barmaids. Corinth's reputation is disputed. The cultural backgrounds notes speak of a long reputation, and Wright says prostitution was often linked to temples "but was much wider as well, especially in a port city like Corinth." Carson, Moo and Morris warn against reading the old city's notoriety into the Roman colony, though a great port was unlikely to be known for virtue. Bought refers to redemption from slavery; Keener suggests a play on the price of freeing a slave prostitute.

ideas.n: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
ideas.s: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 7:1-16, Married couples and unbelieving spouses
entries.summary: Replying to the Corinthians' letter, Paul tells married couples not to deprive each other, advises the unmarried and widows, repeats the Lord's word against divorce, and says a believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not bound.
entries.plain: Paul turns to questions the Corinthians raised in a letter, beginning with the claim that a man does well to abstain from sex. He answers that married couples should not deny each other except briefly by agreement for prayer, and that the unmarried may stay single but should marry before desire consumes them. Passing on the Lord's teaching, he forbids divorce between believers, tells those married to willing unbelievers to stay, and says a believer whose unbelieving spouse leaves is no longer bound.
entries.note: Now about marks Paul's replies to the Corinthians' letter, and many scholars take the line about not touching a woman as theirs (Keener and his notes); Bailey, weighing the Syriac and Arabic versions, reads it as their question about the ascetic life, and Carson, Moo and Morris see the church split between the promiscuous and those who thought celibacy best. Most people valued marriage; only a few sages, mostly Cynics, and two small Jewish groups, the Essenes and the Therapeutae, rejected it, and later rabbis read Genesis 1:28 as a command to marry by twenty (the cultural backgrounds article Celibacy in Antiquity). Many Gentiles expected only the wife to be faithful, so the word that each has authority over the other's body runs both ways (the cultural backgrounds notes); Wright calls it a striking statement of mutual equality. Arnold reads verse 5 as Satan using long abstinence to tempt a partner to unfaithfulness. In Judean practice only the husband could normally divorce, while in Greek and Roman marriage either party could end it simply by leaving, and divorce was widespread in Corinth (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Nearly everyone in the ancient world thought people should marry and have children. A few, from Cynic philosophers to some Essenes, refused marriage for a higher calling, and some in Corinth thought holiness meant giving up sex even within marriage.

A Jewish husband ended a marriage, or a betrothal, by handing his wife a written certificate before witnesses that left her free to marry again, and the teachers argued over the grounds. In Greek and Roman law either partner could end a marriage by leaving.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 7:17-24, Circumcised or not, slave or free
entries.summary: Paul tells each believer to live the life the Lord assigned when he was called: the circumcised should not undo it, the uncircumcised should not seek it, and a slave should not be troubled, though he should take his freedom if he can.
entries.plain: Paul gives a rule for all his churches: believers should stay in the life they had when God's call reached them. Circumcision and its absence make no difference; what counts is obeying God. A slave should not let his status trouble him, though he should take freedom if he can, because in the Lord a slave is free and a free person belongs to Christ, and all of them were bought at a price.
entries.note: Stoics urged people to accept their lot, but identified the God who directed it with Fate (Keener and his notes). Greeks exercised naked and mocked circumcision, and some Jews had an operation to pull the foreskin forward; Josephus says that the Hellenizers who built a gymnasium in Jerusalem "hid the circumcision of their genitals, that even when they were naked they might appear to be Greeks." Urban household slaves could suffer hardship but some wielded real power, and slaves who earned money could buy their freedom; the ESV Study Bible stresses that Roman slavery differed from slavery in North America (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). A freed slave stayed part of the former owner's household and owed him honor (Keener and his notes). Corinth had many Roman citizens, and a slave freed by a citizen usually gained citizenship as well (the cultural backgrounds notes). Price and House read bought at a price against manumission: the verb was common in deeds of sale, and an inscription at Delphi records Apollo buying a slave woman, Nicaea, for freedom at a stated price.

ideas.s: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 7:25-40, The present distress
entries.summary: Because of the present distress and the shortness of the time, Paul advises the unmarried to stay as they are, though marrying is no sin, and tells a widow she is free to remarry, only in the Lord.
entries.plain: On the unmarried, Paul says he has no direct teaching from Jesus and offers his own judgment: because of the present crisis, people should stay as they are, though marrying is no sin. Time is short and this world in its current shape is fading, so he wants them free of the distractions marriage brings. A widow may remarry anyone she chooses, provided he is a believer.
entries.note: Wright links the present distress to a severe grain shortage across the Greek world in the years after Paul left Corinth, most likely in AD 51, which shook colonists' trust that Rome would keep them fed; Keener and his notes point to the Jewish expectation of great suffering just before the end, when marrying and having children only made things harder. Virgin usually meant a woman, the only one expected to avoid sex before marriage outside Judaism (Keener). Cynics avoided marriage as a distraction, with Hipparchia, wife of Crates, the only recorded exception (Keener and his notes). Parents, especially fathers, arranged marriages; Jewish men often married around twenty, Greek men around thirty to women about twelve years younger, and breaking a betrothal was an official act (Keener and his notes). Whether 7:36-38 speaks to the fathers of virgins or to their fiancés is debated, and Keener finds no evidence in this period for the spiritual engagements of later Christianity. Free, in talk of divorce and widowhood, always meant free to remarry; widows, unlike virgins, had much say in whom they married, and Augustus had used taxation to push younger Roman widows toward a second marriage (Keener and his notes).
sources: N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: 1 Corinthians, comments on 1 Corinthians 7:25-31 and 7:32-40
Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 1 Corinthians 7:25, 7:26, 7:32-35, 7:36-38 and 7:39
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 1 Corinthians 7:26, 7:32-34, 7:36-38 and 7:39

ideas.s: Nearly everyone in the ancient world thought people should marry and have children. A few, from Cynic philosophers to some Essenes, refused marriage for a higher calling, and some in Corinth thought holiness meant giving up sex even within marriage.
A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 8:1-13, Knowledge, idols and the weak
entries.summary: Answering those who know that an idol is nothing, Paul agrees there is one God and one Lord but warns that their freedom to eat sacrificial food, even in an idol's temple, can destroy a weaker believer.
entries.plain: Paul responds to Corinthians who argued that, since idols are nothing, eating meat offered to them is harmless. He agrees there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, but says knowledge can puff people up while love builds others up. Some believers still feel the pull of the gods they once served, and if they see a confident believer dining in an idol's temple they may be drawn back and ruined, so Paul would give up meat entirely before causing that.
entries.note: Corinth was full of gods; the most honored were Poseidon, Aphrodite and the emperor (the cultural backgrounds notes), and Arnold adds Apollo, Asclepius, Demeter, Isis, Sarapis and the Great Mother. Sacrifice did double duty, since most of the animal was eaten, and even ordinary banquets opened with a libation, so most Gentile meals were consecrated to some god (the cultural backgrounds article Sacrificed Food). Wright notes that Roman citizens in Corinth "had a special right to share in meals connected with imperial festivals," so staying away would be noticed. Paul names both the Father and Jesus in Judaism's confession of one God and one Lord (Keener and his notes). Whether the gods of verse 5 are real is debated. Heiser writes, "These gods and lords are considered real by Paul"; the ESV Study Bible says idols represent no real gods; Arnold takes a middle line, no gods in their own right but demons behind the images (10:20), and real to those who worshiped them. The weak are read as the socially powerless (Keener), as weaker consciences (the cultural backgrounds notes), or as former idol-worshipers (Wright's biography; Carson, Moo and Morris; Arnold, who thinks some had gone back to the temples).

ideas.s: Most meat in a Greek city had passed through a sacrifice at a temple. Eating it at the temple's table, buying it in the market or meeting it at a friend's dinner raised the question of whether a believer was sharing in the worship of the god.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 9:1-27, Free, unpaid and in training
entries.summary: Paul defends his right as an apostle to be supported and explains why he has never used it, makes himself a slave to all to win more, and pictures his discipline as an athlete's training for a wreath that will not wither.
entries.plain: Paul defends his rights as an apostle: like soldiers, farmers and temple priests, he and Barnabas could expect support from those they serve, and could travel with a wife who believed, as other apostles did. He has deliberately refused that support so that nothing gets in the way of the gospel. He adapts himself to Jews and Gentiles alike to win as many as he can, and like an athlete in training for a wreath he keeps his body under strict control so that he is not disqualified.
entries.note: Philosophers lived on a wealthy patron, on fees, on begging, or, least respectable of all, on manual work, and aristocrats despised manual labor (Keener and his notes). If wealthy believers supported Paul he could be seen as their client, expected to please them (Keener and his notes). Bailey sets the two worlds side by side: rabbis had to keep a trade, while among Greeks "Intellectuals were expected to be financially independent." Carson, Moo and Morris add that the church as a whole was unhappy with Paul's leadership, which partly explains why he defends his apostleship here. Most wandering sages could not marry, but most apostles by this time were married (the cultural backgrounds notes). Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, next to the Olympics the most popular, and Paul's stay overlapped at least one (the cultural backgrounds article Athletic Imagery; Keener; the ESV Study Bible); athletes and spectators lodged in tents (Bailey). The article gives the victor's wreath as pine or withered celery, while the Zondervan dictionary names laurel, olive or pine. Boxers' leather gloves left the fingers bare, and shadowboxing was no preparation for a real bout (the article; Keener).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introductions to 1 Corinthians 9:1-14 and 9:15-27, and on 9:6, 9:11-12, 9:19-23, 9:24-25 and 9:26-27

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Craftsmen of one trade lived and worked in the same streets and banded together in guilds, which set standards, defended their interests and met for meals in honor of a patron god.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 10:1-22, Israel in the desert and the table of demons
entries.summary: Paul warns that Israel too had its baptism and its spiritual food in the wilderness, yet fell into idolatry and immorality and was struck down, and tells the Corinthians that they cannot share both the Lord's table and the table of demons.
entries.plain: Paul warns the Corinthians from Israel's history: the wilderness generation had their own baptism in the sea and their own spiritual food and drink, with Christ present among them, yet most died because of idolatry, immorality and grumbling. Those stories stand as warnings, so believers must run from idolatry. Sharing the Lord's cup and bread joins them to Christ, and since pagan sacrifices go to demons, they cannot share the Lord's meal and the demons' meal at once.
entries.note: Jewish people awaited a new exodus in the Messiah's time, and some traditions had the well follow Israel through the wilderness (Keener and his notes). Verse 8 recalls Baal Peor (Numbers 25); Josephus retells it, the young men "supposing there were many gods, and resolving that they would sacrifice to them according to the laws of that country which ordained them, they both were delighted with their strange food." Carson, Moo and Morris think some Corinthians treated baptism and the Lord's Supper as almost magical guarantees of life (10:1-5). Eating together made a bond, and sacrificial meat was tied to the god it was offered to (the cultural backgrounds notes). The Greek Old Testament calls false gods demons (Deuteronomy 32:17; Psalm 96:5), as most early Jewish and Christian sources do (Keener and his notes; Arnold). Heiser writes, "For Paul the pagan gods were demons", and Arnold notes that Paul uses the word four times in two verses and treats demons as the real recipients of the sacrifice, so a temple meal was fellowship with them.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 1 Corinthians 10:1-2, 10:3-4, 10:7, 10:16-17 and 10:19-20

ideas.s: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

Most meat in a Greek city had passed through a sacrifice at a temple. Eating it at the temple's table, buying it in the market or meeting it at a friend's dinner raised the question of whether a believer was sharing in the worship of the god.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 10:23-11:1, Dinner at an unbeliever's house
entries.summary: Paul tells believers to eat whatever is sold in the meat market and whatever an unbelieving host serves without asking questions, unless someone points out that it was offered in sacrifice.
entries.plain: Paul gives practical rules on sacrificial meat. Believers may buy anything in the market and eat what an unbelieving host serves without asking where it came from, since the whole earth belongs to the Lord. If someone points out that the food was offered to a god, they should decline for that person's sake. The aim in all of it is God's glory and the good of others, and Paul asks them to follow his example as he follows Christ's.
entries.note: Leftover sacrificial meat went to the meat market in Corinth's agora, unlabeled among other meat; Jews in big cities usually had their own markets, and most people could not afford meat, so Paul is speaking to the well-to-do (Keener and his notes). Jewish tradition used Psalm 24:1 for thanking God at meals (Keener and his notes). People invited friends and subordinate clients to banquets, and refusing insulted the host and made an enemy (the cultural backgrounds notes). A pagan friend would take eating openly sacrificial food as accepting the sacrifice (the cultural backgrounds notes). The CSB Study Bible notes that the word used here was the pagan term for meat devoted to a god. Arnold, following Fee, separates the two cases: a meal in a temple was idolatry, but meat once sacrificed and eaten at home was a matter of the weaker believer's conscience, not of idolatry. Bailey suggests that a new believer might fear that meat offered to a god he no longer served, Asclepius in his example, would make him sick. Philosophers often held up their own lives as models for their pupils (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Most meat in a Greek city had passed through a sacrifice at a temple. Eating it at the temple's table, buying it in the market or meeting it at a friend's dinner raised the question of whether a believer was sharing in the worship of the god.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 11:2-16, Heads covered and uncovered
entries.summary: Paul tells men who pray or prophesy to keep their heads uncovered and women who do so to cover theirs, arguing from headship, creation, the angels, nature and the custom of the churches.
entries.plain: Paul addresses how men and women should present themselves when they pray or prophesy in worship: men with heads uncovered, women with heads covered. He argues from headship, from the order of creation, from the presence of angels, from what nature teaches about hair and from the practice of the other churches. What the covering was, and what headship and the angels mean here, are all debated.
entries.note: Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy. Women did not lead prayers in most synagogues, though Israel honored women prophets (Keener and his notes); Bailey stresses that men and women are doing the same things, so the issue is distinction between them. Romans covered their heads for worship and Greeks uncovered, but neither custom divided men from women; covering a woman's hair was mainly about modesty, especially for wives (the cultural backgrounds article Head Coverings in Antiquity). The article adds that many scholars think upper-class women, with costly hairstyles, were less inclined to cover, and Keener reads the passage as a clash of class; Bailey and Wright point to what bare heads said to outsiders; Carson, Moo and Morris see competing opinions in the church. Whether the covering is a garment or long hair (verse 15) is debated; the Zondervan dictionary favors something like a shawl. Head could mean authority, source or prominent part (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The angels are read as the Watchers of Genesis 6 (Heiser, and one of Keener's options), as angels present at worship (the ESV Study Bible), or as the angels believers will judge.

ideas.s: In much of the eastern Mediterranean a respectable woman covered her hair in public, while fashionable rich women showed theirs off. Romans covered their heads to worship and Greeks did not, so in Corinth a covered or bare head sent several signals at once.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 11:17-34, The Lord's Supper in a rich man's house
entries.summary: Paul rebukes the church because at the Lord's Supper some go hungry while others eat their fill and get drunk, retells the tradition of the Last Supper, and tells them to wait for one another.
entries.plain: Paul rebukes the church because its shared meal has become a scene of division, with some eating their fill and even getting drunk while poorer members go hungry. He repeats the tradition of Jesus' last meal with his followers, the bread and cup that proclaim his death until he returns. Eating carelessly, without recognizing the body, brings judgment, so they must wait for one another and satisfy their hunger at home.
entries.note: At Corinthian banquets rank decided the couch and the quality of food and wine, and slighted guests complained (the cultural backgrounds article Banquets in Corinth). Churches met in the larger homes of the wealthy few, where a dining room held nine to twelve on couches and an atrium perhaps forty (the article); Keener explains that patrons often seated their own class in the dining room and served the others in the atrium with poorer food and wine. With no landed nobility, Corinth had an aristocracy of wealth, and the poor were despised or ignored (Carson, Moo and Morris). The cultural backgrounds notes give two readings: laborers and slaves came late from work, or hosts and elite guests ate their own better food apart. Bailey takes the first: "The idle rich had arrived early and eaten all the available fare", and Wright and Bird agree. The Corinthians seem to have treated the supper as a Greek festive banquet rather than as a Passover, an intimate family meal that celebrated redemption (Keener and his notes; the article). The Passover bread was the bread of affliction, and Passover looked ahead to a future redemption (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 12:1-31, Mute idols and one body
entries.summary: Paul reminds the Corinthians that as pagans they were led astray to mute idols, describes the many gifts of the one Spirit, and pictures the church as one body whose weaker and less honored members are indispensable.
entries.plain: Paul reminds the former pagans in Corinth that they once followed lifeless idols, and that confessing Jesus as Lord is itself the Spirit's work. The Spirit hands out many different gifts, but all come from the same God and serve the common good. Paul pictures the church as one body made up of Jews and Greeks, slaves and free, where every member is needed and the parts that seem weaker or less honored deserve special care.
entries.note: Idols could not speak, and Paul may also have in mind the Greek oracles, where possessed people prophesied in ecstasy (Keener and his notes). Gentiles in Corinth could seek healing at shrines, above all that of Asclepius (the cultural backgrounds notes); Arnold notes that Asclepius, often hailed as savior, was among the most popular gods, that Epidaurus, one of his great centers, lay near Corinth, and that the sick slept in his precincts hoping for a healing vision. Outside the church there are no ancient parallels to healings as regular events in a congregation, nor to tongues (Keener and his notes). Greek and Roman writers compared the state and the universe to a body, usually to support hierarchy: Keener tells how the aristocrat Menenius Agrippa talked rebelling plebeians round by saying they were like the stomach, less noticed but necessary. Wright notes that Roman orators used the body politic to show that different jobs carried different status, and the cultural backgrounds notes suggest that Paul's honor language may subvert that use. Carson, Moo and Morris think being spiritual meant status to the Corinthians. Numbered lists, first, second, third, usually signaled rank (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introductions to 1 Corinthians 12:1-3, 12:4-11 and 12:12-26, and on 12:27-28
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 1 Corinthians 12:2, 12:9, 12:10, 12:12, 12:23 and 12:28
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: 1 Corinthians, comment on 1 Corinthians 12:21-26
Clinton E. Arnold, Powers of Darkness, ch. 2, Asclepius: God of Healing
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 9, 1 and 2 Corinthians, The Character of Paul's Opponents in 1 and 2 Corinthians

ideas.s: The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
Greeks and Romans sought the future from oracles, omens and seers, above all from Apollo's priestess at Delphi. A girl with a Python spirit was linked to that famous oracle.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 13:1-13, Noisy bronze and a dim mirror
entries.summary: Paul says that tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even martyrdom are nothing without love, describes what love is, and sets today's partial knowledge, like a dim reflection in a mirror, against seeing face to face.
entries.plain: In the middle of his teaching on spiritual gifts, Paul says that tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even self-sacrifice count for nothing without love. He describes love by what it does and refuses to do: it is patient and kind, free of envy and pride, and does not keep score of wrongs. Gifts like prophecy and knowledge are partial and will end, like a dim reflection in a mirror, but faith, hope and love last, and love outranks them all.
entries.note: Orators sometimes praised a virtue at length in exalted prose, and Paul's praise of love answers the Corinthians' boasting point by point (Keener and his notes). Most Jews assumed angels understood human languages, since angels were set over the nations (Keener). Cymbals were used in pagan and Jewish worship, but Keener takes the point to be that, though loud, they communicate nothing; he adds that Corinth was famous for its bronze, and bronze vases were often used to amplify voices in outdoor theaters. Josephus describes a gate of Herod's temple "which was of Corinthian brass, and greatly excelled those that were only covered over with silver and gold." Moving mountains was a figure of speech for the impossible, and giving one's body to be burned probably recalls the Jewish martyrs (Keener). A Roman boy came of age at about sixteen, when he put off his childhood toga for the white toga of a man (the cultural backgrounds notes). Mirrors were usually bronze and gave a far less clear image than direct sight (Keener and his notes). Keener notes that love as the supreme virtue was unusual in antiquity.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 1 Corinthians 13:1-3, and on 13:1, 13:2-3, 13:8-13 and 16:14
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 1 Corinthians 13:1-13, 13:11 and 13:12
Josephus, The Wars of the Jews 5.5.3, trans. William Whiston

ideas.s: Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
A trusted household slave walked a boy to school and back, watched his manners and kept him out of trouble until he came of age. He was neither the teacher nor anything like the father.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 14:26-40, Order when the church meets
entries.summary: Paul regulates a meeting where everyone brings a hymn, a teaching, a revelation or a tongue: speakers take turns, prophets weigh one another's words, women are to be silent and ask at home, and everything is to be done decently and in order.
entries.plain: Paul brings order to a gathering where many members contribute a song, teaching, revelation or tongue, insisting that everything must build the church up. Tongues speakers take turns and need an interpreter, prophets speak two or three at a time while others weigh their words, and a speaker gives way when someone else receives a revelation, because God is a God of peace. He tells women to keep silent and ask their husbands at home, a command whose scope is much debated, and ends by calling for decency and good order in all of it.
entries.note: The house churches probably held at most about fifty people (Keener and his notes). Order mattered in lectures and assemblies; among the Essenes one needed permission to speak (Keener and his notes). Many Greeks linked inspiration with the frenzy of possession and thought it could not be controlled, while Paul treats it as something a prophet can govern (the cultural backgrounds article Prophecy in Antiquity; Keener). Verses 34-35 are read in several ways. Keener notes that "Informed listeners customarily asked questions during lectures", that unlearned questions were thought rude, and that women had far less training, so he reads Paul as stopping disruptive questions while giving wives private instruction. Bailey reads the verb as chatting: women with little Greek talking among themselves during worship. Keener also reports the view that Paul quotes a Corinthian position and answers it in verse 36; the cultural backgrounds notes say the verses may be a digression on another matter of order. Fee argues that the verses were added later; Carson, Moo and Morris reply that some manuscripts move them after verse 40 but "not one omits it".

ideas.s: For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 15:1-11, What I received
entries.summary: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the good news he handed on to them as he had received it: that Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and last of all to Paul.
entries.plain: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the core message he passed on to them, a tradition he had himself received. It runs like this: Christ died for sins as the Scriptures foretold, was buried, rose on the third day, and appeared to Peter, the Twelve, a crowd of over five hundred, James and the apostles. Paul adds himself as the last witness, unworthy because he had persecuted the church, yet made what he is by God's grace.
entries.note: Received and handed on were the words for passing on a tradition: the Mishnah tractate Abot opens with Moses receiving the Torah at Sinai and handing it on to Joshua, and Jewish teachers expected students to memorize what they learned (Bailey; Keener and his notes). Keener thinks the tradition may be quoted word for word in verses 3-5 or 3-7, Bailey, citing Wright, dates it within two or three years of Easter, and Carson, Moo and Morris call this the earliest written list of witnesses to the resurrection. Jewish law required burial even for executed criminals, and since resurrection meant a new body, the mention of burial presupposes an empty tomb (Keener and his notes). Many people believed in ghosts, so a claim to have seen Jesus' spirit would not have been controversial; it was the claim to have seen him bodily that stood out, and the dying and rising gods of fertility myth are poor parallels (the cultural backgrounds article Resurrection). Appealing to witnesses still alive invited readers to check (Keener and his notes). One untimely born usually meant a miscarried fetus, and Paul is probably running himself down (Keener).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 1 Corinthians 15:3, 15:4, 15:6 and 15:8
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 1 Corinthians 15:3, 15:4 and 15:6, and article Resurrection

D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 9, 1 and 2 Corinthians, The Contribution of 1 and 2 Corinthians

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 15:12-34, If the dead are not raised
entries.summary: Against some who say there is no resurrection of the dead, Paul argues that then Christ was not raised either, calls Christ the firstfruits, and asks why anyone is baptized for the dead or why he fights wild beasts if the dead are not raised.
entries.plain: Some in Corinth deny that the dead will rise, and Paul shows what follows: Christ was not raised either, their faith is empty and they remain in their sins. But Christ has been raised as the firstfruits of a coming harvest, undoing the death that came through Adam, and he will reign until every hostile power and finally death itself is defeated. Paul points to the puzzling practice of baptism for the dead and to his own daily risks as pointless if the dead stay dead, and warns them against bad company.
entries.note: Resurrection meant that the dead would be given new bodies, a hope most Judeans held (Daniel 12:2), while Greeks thought at most the soul survived (Keener; the cultural backgrounds article Resurrection). What the Corinthian deniers believed is read two ways. Wright, Keener and the article set them against a pagan world that denied bodily resurrection; Carson, Moo and Morris think they denied neither a future resurrection nor Jesus' rising, but believed "they have already been raised" in spirit and would end as they were, minus the body. Firstfruits, gathered at the start of harvest, guaranteed the rest (Keener and his notes). Arnold reads every rule, authority and power of verse 24 as hostile spirits, to be stripped of power rather than annihilated, with death the last enemy. Being baptized for the dead is a puzzle with many guesses: the Zondervan dictionary and the CSB Study Bible find a believer baptized for someone who died unbaptized the most natural, the dictionary adding that the Marcionites later did this; others suggest washing the dead. The ESV Study Bible calls it uncertain, and Keener and his notes say it is not clear that Paul approved; the dictionary doubts it.

ideas.s: Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

The Old Testament says little about Adam outside Genesis, but by Paul's day Jewish writers spoke often of his lost glory and of the sin and death he brought into the world. Each person, they added, became his own Adam.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

Rome celebrated a great victory with a triumph, a parade of the general, his army and the spoils, with chained captives at the end who were killed or sold. Cities also staged shows in which condemned criminals fought or were thrown to beasts.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 15:35-58, Seeds, stars and the last trumpet
entries.summary: Asked what kind of body the dead will have, Paul answers with the seed that dies and rises as a plant and with the differing glories of sun, moon and stars, sets the first Adam beside the last, and ends with the trumpet and death swallowed up.
entries.plain: Paul takes up the question of what kind of body the raised dead will have. A seed must die before it grows into a plant, and God gives each thing the body he chooses, just as sun, moon and stars each have their own splendor. The present body is mortal and the resurrection body will be imperishable and given by the Spirit, as the first Adam was made a living being and Christ, the last Adam, gives life. At the final trumpet the dead will rise and the living be transformed, and death will be defeated for good.
entries.note: Jewish teachers listed questions like this as the standard objections to resurrection, such as bodies lost at sea or burned; later rabbis answered with an indestructible bone in the neck, Paul with the analogy of the seed, which later rabbis also used (Keener and his notes). Many Jewish teachers expected the body to rise exactly as it had died and then be healed (Keener; the cultural backgrounds article Resurrection). Most people thought the stars were made of fire; Gentiles took them as divine and Jews as angels, and many Jews compared the resurrection body to the stars (Daniel 12:2-3; the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Heiser notes the Greco-Roman belief that the dead had bodies of aether, the stuff of the stars, and argues that Paul draws on Daniel 12 instead. Philo set the heavenly man of Genesis 1 above the earthly man of Genesis 2, and Paul reverses the order (Keener and his notes; the cultural backgrounds article Adam in Jewish Tradition). Flesh and blood was a common phrase for mortals (Keener). The trumpet gathered people for assembly or war, and a daily Jewish prayer looked for a trumpet gathering God's people at the end (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 1 Corinthians 15:35-38, 15:39-41, 15:42-43, 15:46-49, 15:50 and 15:52

ideas.s: Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

The Old Testament says little about Adam outside Genesis, but by Paul's day Jewish writers spoke often of his lost glory and of the sin and death he brought into the world. Each person, they added, became his own Adam.
The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: 1 Corinthians 16:1-24, The collection and final greetings
entries.summary: Paul arranges a weekly setting aside of money for the believers in Jerusalem, plans his travels, commends Timothy, Apollos and the household of Stephanas, and closes with greetings, a line in his own hand and the Aramaic prayer Marana tha.
entries.plain: On the first day of each week each should set something aside, as he has prospered, for the collection for the saints, and when Paul comes, people the Corinthians approve will carry their gift to Jerusalem with letters. He will come after passing through Macedonia and may spend the winter with them, but will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a wide door has opened. He commends Timothy, says Apollos will come later, and urges them to submit to the household of Stephanas, whose visit with Fortunatus and Achaicus refreshed him. Aquila and Prisca greet them with the church in their house; Paul writes the greeting in his own hand, adds Marana tha, Our Lord, come, and sends his love.
entries.note: Diaspora Jews chose respected members to carry the annual temple tax to Jerusalem (Keener and his notes); without banks, Wright notes, money had to be carried in person. Carson, Moo and Morris say the gift was for believers in Jerusalem suffering famine and persecution, and that Paul meant to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, probably in AD 55, before changing his plans (2 Corinthians 1:15-16). Other associations usually charged dues, but believers' gifts were voluntary (the cultural backgrounds notes). The first day may show believers meeting on Sunday, as the ESV Study Bible says, while the cultural backgrounds notes say explicit evidence for Sunday meetings comes from the second century. Supplied what was lacking is read two ways: a gift the delegates brought (Carson, Moo and Morris) or, as most interpreters take it according to the Zondervan dictionary, their company making up for the absent church. Stephanas's party probably carried this letter home (Keener and his notes). Maranatha may mean our Lord has come or our Lord, come; most prefer the second, and either way the Aramaic shows Jesus confessed as Lord in the land of Israel (the dictionary; Keener).

ideas.s: Paul gathered money from his mostly Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, much as Jews everywhere sent the temple tax to the holy city.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.

Outside winter, ships were the quickest and cheapest way to travel, but they were built for cargo, not passengers, and from mid-September the sea grew dangerous. The great grain ships of Alexandria fed Rome.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 1:1-11, The God of all comfort and the sentence of death
entries.summary: Paul opens by blessing the God of all comfort and tells the Corinthians that in Asia he was so crushed that he felt he had received the sentence of death, so that he learned to rely on the God who raises the dead.
entries.plain: Paul and Timothy write to the believers in Corinth and across Achaia, opening with praise to God, who comforts Paul in every trouble so that he can comfort others. He tells them of a crisis in Asia so severe that he expected to die, which taught him to trust the God who brings the dead back to life. He asks for their prayers, so that many will thank God when he is rescued.
entries.note: Paul wrote from Macedonia after Titus brought news from Corinth, between a painful second visit and a promised third (the CSB Study Bible; Wright and Bird). Carson, Moo and Morris date it within a year or so of 1 Corinthians, which they put early in 55, and allow every date to move a year earlier; the CSB Study Bible says about AD 56. Corinth was a Roman colony refounded in 44 BC, settled mostly by freedmen (the cultural backgrounds article Corinth). Whether the letter is one or several joined together is debated. Keener puts the burden of proof on those who divide it, and Wright and Bird answer a five-letter theory from the manuscripts. Carson, Moo and Morris weigh four views of chapters 10-13: the severe letter, part of one letter written at one time, a later fifth letter (the commonest view today), or news that reached Paul before he finished; they find the last "marginally stronger than the third". Asia was the province whose capital was Ephesus; Keener thinks of chronic opposition climaxing in the riot of Acts 19, while the ESV Study Bible and Carson, Moo and Morris say the details are unknown.

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 1:12-2:4, Changed plans, the seal and the down payment
entries.summary: Accused of fickleness for changing his travel plans, Paul answers that his word is reliable because all God's promises are Yes in Christ, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a down payment, and explains that he stayed away to spare them.
entries.plain: Paul's conscience tells him he has behaved toward them with sincerity, and he hopes they will be proud of him as he is of them. He had planned to visit them twice, on the way to Macedonia and back, and denies that changing the plan means he says yes and no at once, for all God's promises find their Yes in Christ, and it is God who establishes them with Paul in Christ, has anointed them, put his seal on them and given the Spirit in their hearts as a down payment. Calling God as his witness, Paul says he did not come again in order to spare them, and wrote to them instead out of much anguish and many tears.
entries.note: Carson, Moo and Morris reconstruct the background. Timothy found Corinth beyond him, Paul hurried there, and the visit was painful: at least one opponent insulted him, and he left resolved not to return at once, which opened him to the charge of fickleness. Ancient sources condemned fickleness, especially in leaders, who had to give good reasons for changing announced plans (the cultural backgrounds notes). Hospitality was a key virtue and hosting a prominent guest an honor, so Paul's failure to come could look like an insult (Keener and his notes). The benefit of 1:15 is the word for grace: "Paul is their benefactor, not their client", yet he seeks honor only for God (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Friendly letters often protested a friend's failure to visit, and a writer might explain that he stayed away for the reader's own good (the cultural backgrounds notes). Titus carried the tearful letter, which demanded that the ringleader be punished; Keener and Carson, Moo and Morris think it lost, while some think it survives as chapters 10-13, which Carson, Moo and Morris reject, noting among other things that those chapters lack that demand.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 2 Corinthians 1:12-22, and on 2 Corinthians 1:15, 1:16 and 2:1-4
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 2 Corinthians 1:12-22, 1:15, 1:17, 1:23 and 2:4
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 9, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Occasion (Historical Reconstruction; The Integrity of 1 and 2 Corinthians)

ideas.s: Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 2:5-13, Forgive the offender; no rest at Troas
entries.summary: The man who caused the grief has been punished enough by the majority, so Paul urges the church to forgive him lest Satan outwit them, then tells how he left an open door at Troas because Titus had not come.
entries.plain: Whoever caused grief has grieved the whole church and not Paul alone, and the punishment by the majority is enough, so they should now forgive and comfort him and reaffirm their love, lest he be overwhelmed by sorrow. Paul has forgiven too, so that they are not outwitted by Satan, whose schemes they know. When he came to Troas to preach and found a door opened in the Lord, he had no rest because he did not find his brother Titus there, so he said goodbye and went on to Macedonia.
entries.note: Keener takes the majority as a name for the whole believing community, a usage also found at Qumran. Most ancient legal settings, including discipline in synagogues and at Qumran, set a period of punishment such as exclusion before restoration, while Pharisaic Judaism stressed receiving back the repentant (Keener and his notes). Who the offender was is disputed (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris hold that he was not the incestuous man of 1 Corinthians 5: these passages hint at no sexual sin, and "The offense was against Paul", the question being whether the church would stand with him. One of Judaism's basic convictions about Satan was that he deceived and came in disguises (Keener and his notes). Troas is Alexandria Troas, the port for Macedonia (Keener), though Carson, Moo and Morris note that the name could mean the region around it. Communication moved no faster than travel, so Paul could not know how Titus or his letter had been received, and he feared for him on the road (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Carson, Moo and Morris think he had a fallback plan to meet Titus in Macedonia.

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

ideas.n: Roads, robbers and the dangers of travel
ideas.s: Travel by land was slow and risky. Robbers worked the lonely roads, rivers had to be forded, and news moved no faster than the people who carried it.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 2:14-17, Led in God's triumph
entries.summary: Paul thanks God, who leads him in triumphal procession and spreads the fragrance of Christ through him, a smell of death to some and of life to others, and denies that he peddles God's word for profit.
entries.plain: Paul thanks God, who leads him along in a victory procession, the picture of a Roman triumph, and uses him to spread the knowledge of Christ like a scent. To some that scent means death and to others life, and Paul asks who is fit for such work. Unlike many, he does not sell God's message for gain but speaks honestly, as one sent by God.
entries.note: Keener sets the image against the Roman triumph, for which the senate decreed public thanksgivings, and incense was burned at triumphs as at sacrifices (Keener and his notes). The Zondervan dictionary adds that only the senate could grant a triumph, only for victory over foreigners, and that there is no clear evidence for the older reading of a general leading his own troops. What part Paul plays is read differently. Keener sees believers as Christ's captives, with Paul the prisoner of war who himself offers the thanks. The ESV Study Bible says most interpreters see God as victor and Paul as captured but now joyfully following, and reports a view in which God leads Paul like a prisoner into suffering; the dictionary, since captives were normally led to death, thinks Paul may allude to his sufferings. Professional speakers had long been accused of adulterating truth for gain, like dishonest merchants (Keener and his notes). Keener and his notes read 2:14-7:4 as a long digression, and Carson, Moo and Morris agree against those who make it a separate letter: 7:5 sounds like Paul resuming a theme.

ideas.s: Rome celebrated a great victory with a triumph, a parade of the general, his army and the spoils, with chained captives at the end who were killed or sold. Cities also staged shows in which condemned criminals fought or were thrown to beasts.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 3:1-18, Letters of recommendation and Moses' veil
entries.summary: Paul needs no letters of recommendation, since the Corinthians are his letter, written by the Spirit on hearts; he sets the fading glory on Moses' veiled face against the greater glory of the new covenant.
entries.plain: Paul asks whether he needs letters of reference like some teachers carry, and says the believers themselves are his letter, written by God's Spirit on human hearts instead of on stone. God has made him a servant of a new covenant that gives life through the Spirit, where the written code brought death. He compares the glory on Moses' face, which Moses veiled, with the far greater and lasting glory of the Spirit's work, and says that whoever turns to the Lord has the veil lifted and is changed into his likeness.
entries.note: Jewish travelers often carried letters so that householders would trust them with lodging, and Keener notes that "such recommendations naturally carried more weight than the person's own claims." Wright, citing the Didache, explains that churches used such letters to check that people claiming to be servants of Jesus were genuine. The rivals in Corinth carried letters of their own (the CSB Study Bible; Wright and Bird), and Carson, Moo and Morris think they called themselves apostles in the general sense of agents commissioned by others. Commending oneself was acceptable only for good reason, such as self-defense (Keener and his notes). Keener notes that many saw Moses as a divine man and suggests the rivals appealed to him. Who the rivals were is debated: Wright and Bird think Greek-speaking Jewish Christians shaped by rhetoric, the CSB Study Bible Judaizers, and Keener a dispute about models of ministry and status. Carson, Moo and Morris combine them: Jews with Sophist values, "a new kind of Judaizing" more concerned with prestige than with circumcision; they add that in the first century to Judaize meant a Gentile living like a Jew.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

Jeremiah and Ezekiel promised a day when God would write his law on hearts instead of stone and put his own Spirit within his people. Some Jews of Paul's day believed the promise belonged to their own group.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 4:1-6, The god of this age
entries.summary: Paul renounces cunning and tampering with God's word; if his gospel is veiled, it is veiled to the perishing, whose minds the god of this age has blinded, while God has made his light shine in believers' hearts.
entries.plain: Paul says he does not give up, because God has given him this ministry, and he refuses trickery or distorting God's word, preferring to set out the truth openly. If anyone cannot see the good news, it is because the god of this age keeps unbelievers blind to it; who that god is is debated. Paul preaches Jesus as Lord, not himself, because the God who first called light out of darkness has shone in believers' hearts to show them his glory in Christ's face.
entries.note: Philosophers accused professional speakers of adulterating the truth like dishonest merchants (Keener and his notes). The cultural backgrounds notes say no Jewish source gives Satan the title god of this age, though Jewish writers did describe the Gentiles as ruled by Satan or by hostile angels, and Keener writes that most Jewish teachers held the nations to be ruled by spiritual powers under Satan's command. Who the god of this age is, is debated. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles take it as Satan, and Wright writes of the satan; Arnold agrees, setting the title beside John's prince of this world and calling Satan's authority real but not absolute. Heiser writes, "Nearly all scholars identify this figure as Satan," but points out that the name does not occur in the context and that the phrase may refer to God himself, who in the Greek version of Isaiah 6:9-10 blinds the eyes of those who do not believe. Christ as God's image fills the place Jewish tradition gave to Wisdom, a mirror of God's glory (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26) (Keener and his notes). God spoke light out of darkness in Genesis 1:3 (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

Greek thinkers spoke of the logos, the reason that ordered the world, and Jewish teachers spoke of God's Word and Wisdom, through whom he made everything. John opens his Gospel with that language and then says the Word became flesh.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 4:7-18, Treasure in clay jars
entries.summary: Paul carries God's treasure in a clay jar, hard pressed but not crushed, carrying Jesus' dying in his body so that Jesus' life may show, while the outer self wastes away and the inner self is renewed day by day.
entries.plain: Paul says the treasure of the gospel is held in fragile clay pots like him, so it is plain that the power comes from God. He lists his hardships in pairs, pressed hard yet never defeated, and says he carries Jesus' death in his body so that Jesus' life will show too. Because God raised Jesus and will raise them, he keeps going, knowing that the outer self is wearing out while the inner self is renewed daily, and that brief troubles are producing lasting glory.
entries.note: Clay jars, unlike bronze ones, were cheap and thrown away when broken or made ritually impure, "an odd container for a rich treasure" (Keener); Corinth produced such fragile pottery, notably ceramic lamps (the cultural backgrounds notes). The ESV Study Bible calls jars of clay a common ancient metaphor for human weakness (Psalm 31:12), and Wright puts Paul's point in one line: "the messenger must be dispensable." Some Greek writers described the body as the soul's container, but Paul contrasts human frailty with God, not body with soul (Keener and his notes). Stoic philosophers listed their sufferings to show their contentment, while Jews pointed to the prophets and martyrs as models of endurance (Keener and his notes). Orators often hammered a point home with a series of contrasts, as in 4:8-9 (the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener notes that the word for carrying around was used of pallbearers. Many Platonists thought the body weighed down the soul, and Paul may play on the Hebrew word that means both weight and glory (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 2 Corinthians 4:7, 4:8-9, 4:10-12, 4:16 and 4:17-18
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 2 Corinthians 4:7, 4:8-12 and 4:17
ESV Study Bible, study note on 2 Corinthians 4:7
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: 2 Corinthians, comment on 2 Corinthians 4:7-12

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 5:1-10, The tent and the judgment seat
entries.summary: Paul sets the earthly tent of the body against a building from God, longs to be clothed rather than found naked, names the Spirit as a down payment, and says that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
entries.plain: Paul compares the present body to a tent that will be taken down and the resurrection body to a permanent building from God. Groaning in this tent, he longs to be clothed with the new body instead of being left naked, so that life takes over what dies, and God has given the Spirit as a pledge of it. He would prefer to leave the body and live with the Lord, but either way his goal is to please him, since everyone will stand before Christ's judgment seat to answer for their life.
entries.note: Greek authors likened the body to a vessel, a dwelling or a tent, and frequently to a tomb, and some thought death a release; Paul's hope is not death but a resurrection body, a thought unintelligible to Greeks (Keener and his notes). The ESV Study Bible suggests the tent picture suited a tentmaker in Corinth, where tents were likely sold to sailors or used to house visitors to the Isthmian Games, and the Zondervan atlas also pictures Paul making tents for visitors to the games; Wright stresses that the hope is not to give up having a body. The ESV Study Bible reads nakedness as the state between death and resurrection. The judgment seat, the bema, was the raised tribunal from which the governor gave his decisions; Corinth's survives in the forum, and the Corinthians knew Paul had stood before it under Gallio (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible; Keener). Keener and his notes add that Paul's main image is the biblical day of judgment. What that judgment decides is read differently: the CSB Study Bible says rewards, not destination, while the ESV Study Bible thinks both rewards and evidence of who is saved are in view.
