ideas.s: Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 5:11-6:13, New creation, Christ's ambassadors and a list of hardships
entries.summary: Because one died for all, anyone in Christ is a new creation; Paul, God's ambassador, appeals to the Corinthians to be reconciled to God and commends his ministry with a long list of hardships and paradoxes.
entries.plain: Paul explains what drives him: Christ's love, shown when one died for all, so that the living now live for him. Anyone joined to Christ belongs to a new creation, and God, who has made peace between the world and himself through Christ, has made Paul his ambassador to urge people to be reconciled. Paul backs his appeal with a long list of hardships and paradoxes, poor yet enriching many, owning nothing yet having everything, and asks the Corinthians to open their hearts to him as he has to them.
entries.note: Early texts such as Jubilees and the Dead Sea Scrolls use the language of new creation mainly for the coming world, as in Isaiah 65:16-18, while later rabbis used it of someone who made a proselyte (Keener and his notes). The ESV Study Bible ties it to Isaiah 43 and 65-66 and to Israel's final restoration. Greek speakers often spoke on concord, urging reconciliation and unity (Keener and his notes). An ambassador was usually the emperor's legate in the East, and how an envoy was treated honored or shamed his sender (Keener and his notes). "Philosophers often listed their hardships, sometimes in triads," Keener writes, to prove the sincerity of their message, and the cultural backgrounds notes count nine hardships and eight virtues in 6:4-10, followed by sets of contrasts, a pattern worthy of any orator. Soldiers carried a spear or sword in the right hand and a shield in the left (Keener and his notes). Cynic and Stoic philosophers claimed to own the world while owning nothing (Keener and his notes). Wright and Bird see the hardship lists of 4:7-15 and 6:3-10 preparing for the boasting of chapter 11, a sign of the letter's underlying unity.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 2 Corinthians 5:16-17, 5:18-19, introduction to 5:20-6:10, and on 5:20, 6:4-5, 6:7 and 6:10
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 2 Corinthians 5:17, 5:20, 6:4-10 and 6:7
ESV Study Bible, study note on 2 Corinthians 5:17
N. T. Wright and Michael F. Bird, The New Testament in Its World, ch. 21, 1 and 2 Corinthians, The argument of 2 Corinthians

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

An ambassador spoke for one state to another, in Paul's day usually as the emperor's legate in the East. The way an envoy was received honored or insulted the one who sent him, and communities chose respected envoys to carry their gifts.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

ideas.n: Manual work and the leisured class
ideas.s: The well-to-do despised people who worked with their hands. A respectable teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees or even on begging, so an apostle who made tents for his keep looked low class.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1, Unequal yoke, Belial and the temple of God
entries.summary: Paul tells the Corinthians not to be yoked with unbelievers, for light has no fellowship with darkness nor Christ with Belial, and calls them the temple of the living God, who must come out and be separate.
entries.plain: Paul warns the Corinthians against close partnerships with unbelievers, asking what light and darkness, or Christ and Belial, could share. He tells them they are God's temple, and strings together promises from the prophets: God will live among them, they must separate from what is unclean, and he will be their Father. On the strength of those promises he urges them to purify themselves completely out of reverence for God.
entries.note: The yoke comes from Deuteronomy 22:10, two kinds of animals plowing under one yoke (Keener). Jewish sources set the righteous against the wicked and light against darkness, as in the War Scroll (the cultural backgrounds notes). Belial or Beliar was a Jewish name for Satan, pervasive in the Scrolls, from a Hebrew word meaning worthlessness (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles); Heiser calls him in Second Temple texts the one who "is the leader of the powers of darkness," and Arnold notes that this is the only evil spirit Paul names. Whether the passage belongs here is debated. Carson, Moo and Morris report that most scholars now call it an insertion, citing its rare words, its break in the flow from 6:13 to 7:2 and its Scroll-like contrasts, and some call it non-Pauline; they answer that Paul's outbursts often use rare words and that Beliar was too common in Jewish writing for Paul not to know it. Keener suggests earlier sermon material. Who the unbelievers are is also read differently: pagans and idol worship (Carson, Moo and Morris; Fee, through them), or the false apostles (the CSB Study Bible; Arnold).

ideas.s: The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 7:2-16, Titus arrives and the letter that hurt
entries.summary: In Macedonia Paul is comforted by Titus's arrival and his news that the Corinthians grieved over Paul's harsh letter in a way that led to repentance, and that they received Titus with fear and trembling.
entries.plain: Paul asks the Corinthians to make room for him in their affections and insists he has wronged no one. He describes arriving in Macedonia worn out by conflict and fear, until God cheered him with Titus's arrival and the news that the church missed him and was sorry. His severe letter had hurt them, but he no longer regrets it, because their grief led to real repentance, and Titus came back full of affection for them.
entries.note: Writers ending a digression often picked up where they had left off, and speakers softened their tone after harsh images (the cultural backgrounds notes). Greeks considered willingness to die with a friend the greatest expression of friendship, and letters between friends stressed affection and frank speech (Keener and his notes). Teachers of speaking and letter writing warned that open rebuke should be kept for extreme cases and mixed with praise, and moral teachers likened harsh words to a doctor's painful cure (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris note that Paul had second thoughts after sending the severe letter, and that chapters 1-9 read like bruised relations recently eased, with a sigh of relief that the worst was over. Titus received hospitality, as local synagogue communities housed Jewish travelers (Keener and his notes), and he was a Gentile whom Paul had refused to have circumcised (Galatians 2:3; the Zondervan dictionary). Receiving Titus with such respect meant treating him as Paul's own representative (Keener and his notes). Boasting about one's friends, unlike praising oneself, was always thought acceptable (Keener and his notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 2 Corinthians 7:2-3, 7:5-7, 7:8-9, 7:13, 7:14 and 7:15-16
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 2 Corinthians 7:2, 7:3, 7:4, 7:8-9, 7:13 and 7:14
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 9, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Occasion, Historical Reconstruction
J. D. Douglas and Merrill C. Tenney, Zondervan Illustrated Bible Dictionary, entry Titus

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

ideas.n: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 8:1-15, The Macedonians' giving and the manna
entries.summary: Paul holds up the generosity of the poor Macedonian churches, appeals to Christ who became poor, and asks the Corinthians to finish their gift so that there may be equality, as there was with the manna in the wilderness.
entries.plain: Paul urges the Corinthians to complete their gift for the Jerusalem believers, holding up the Macedonian churches, who gave generously out of hardship and poverty. He says he is not issuing an order but testing the reality of their love, and points to Jesus, who gave up his riches to make them rich. They started the collection a year earlier and should finish it in proportion to what they have; the aim is a fair balance, as with the manna in the wilderness, when no one had too much or too little.
entries.note: Speakers used old city rivalries, such as Macedonia's and Corinth's, to spur their hearers (Keener and his notes). Philippi was prosperous, but its wealth had not reached the poor, and persecution may have deepened the believers' hardship (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; Carson, Moo and Morris). Inscriptions praised benefactors who gave as much as they could and beyond (the cultural backgrounds notes). The word for sharing was used in business documents for a partnership, and giving according to one's means was the biblical rule (Deuteronomy 15:14), which the Macedonians went beyond (Keener and his notes). Because cities sometimes forced wealthy donors to fund public works, appeals stressed that giving was voluntary (Keener and his notes). Friendship meant equality and sharing all things (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); the ESV Study Bible prefers fairness to equality. Other Diaspora Jewish writers used the manna of Exodus 16:18 to urge equality (the cultural backgrounds notes; the CSB Study Bible). The need in Jerusalem was famine (the cultural backgrounds notes) and, Carson, Moo and Morris add, persecution; they think Paul feared the intruders' demands for support were draining the fund. Wright calls the collection a benchmark that Jewish and Gentile believers belong together.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 2 Corinthians 8:1-9, and on 8:1, 8:2, 8:4-5, 8:8 and 8:13

ideas.s: Paul gathered money from his mostly Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, much as Jews everywhere sent the temple tax to the holy city.
Giving to the needy was one of the three pillars of Jewish piety, with prayer and fasting. Greeks and Romans had nothing quite like it.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

ideas.n: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 8:16-9:15, Envoys for the collection and the cheerful giver
entries.summary: Paul commends Titus and two brothers appointed by the churches to carry the gift, takes care that no one can fault him in handling it, and urges the Corinthians to have their promised gift ready, since God loves a cheerful giver.
entries.plain: Paul sends Titus and two other trusted believers, chosen by the churches, to collect the gift, taking care that no one can accuse him of mishandling such a large sum. He wants the Corinthians' promised contribution ready before he arrives with Macedonians, so that his boasting about them is not exposed as empty. Generous sowing brings a generous harvest, God delights in those who give gladly, and their gift will lead many to thank God.
entries.note: Verses 8:16-18 work as a letter of recommendation for Titus and his companion (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), and the CSB Study Bible and the Zondervan dictionary take Titus as the carrier of this letter. Jewish men everywhere paid a half-shekel tax to the temple each year, and Diaspora communities sent respected people to carry it to Jerusalem (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Wright adds that pilgrims traveled in sizable groups, since a known shipment of money invited robbery. Josephus says the Jews of Babylonia stored it in Nehardea and Nisibis: "they made use of these cities as a treasury, whence, at a proper time, they were transmitted to Jerusalem." By boasting of Corinth to the Macedonians Paul staked his own honor on the gift (Keener and his notes). God loves a cheerful giver adapts a line that the Greek translation added to Proverbs 22:8 (Keener and his notes). The Corinthians did give in the end (Romans 15:26). Some scholars treat chapters 8 and 9 as separate letters; the cultural backgrounds notes and Carson, Moo and Morris answer that the thought runs on, and that the brothers of 9:3 assume chapter 8's introduction.

ideas.s: Paul gathered money from his mostly Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, much as Jews everywhere sent the temple tax to the holy city.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.

An ambassador spoke for one state to another, in Paul's day usually as the emperor's legate in the East. The way an envoy was received honored or insulted the one who sent him, and communities chose respected envoys to carry their gifts.
Every year free adult Jewish men across the empire paid two drachmas toward the temple in Jerusalem. After AD 70 Rome went on collecting the same sum for a pagan temple.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 10:1-18, Weighty letters, a weak presence and the siege of the mind
entries.summary: Answering the charge that he is bold in letters but weak in person, Paul describes a war that takes every thought captive and refuses to compare himself with rivals who measure themselves by themselves.
entries.plain: Paul answers critics who say he is forceful in his letters but weak and unimpressive in person. He says his warfare is not fought with human weapons; God's power tears down fortresses of argument and brings every thought into obedience to Christ. He refuses to measure himself against rivals who commend themselves and promises that his actions in person will match his letters, boasting only within the field God gave him, which includes Corinth.
entries.note: Greek culture did not usually count meekness a virtue (Keener), and Carson, Moo and Morris suggest that 10:1 may answer a fresh charge, that Paul was too meek to be a true apostle. Greek sages at times pictured their fight with false ideas as warfare, and the word for arguments was a technical term for rhetorical or philosophical reasoning (Keener and his notes). Invaders besieged strongholds, and Rome had destroyed Corinth in 146 BC before rebuilding it as a colony (the cultural backgrounds notes). Arnold reads the strongholds as the wall of hostility Paul's opponents had built and as their false teaching. Greeks expected a respectable speaker to be forceful, with the right accent, gestures and grooming (the cultural backgrounds notes), and Keener writes, "Paul was a better writer than public speaker." Comparison was a standard rhetorical technique, but comparing oneself with oneself was foolish (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris note that the regions beyond you of 10:16 do not require that Paul wrote from Ephesus. Jeremiah 9:23-24 stands behind boasting in the Lord (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 11:1-15, The betrothed virgin, the free gospel and the angel of light
entries.summary: Jealous as a father who has promised his daughter to one husband, Paul fears the Corinthians will be led astray as Eve was; he defends preaching to them free of charge and calls his rivals false apostles disguised as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
entries.plain: Paul asks the Corinthians to put up with some foolishness: he has pledged them to Christ like a bride and fears they are being seduced away, as the serpent deceived Eve. He defends his choice to preach to them without pay, accepting help from Macedonia instead, and says he will keep doing so to deny his rivals any claim to equality. He calls those rivals false apostles in disguise, which is no surprise, since Satan himself poses as an angel of light.
entries.note: Fathers normally arranged their daughters' marriages and were responsible for their virginity until the wedding (Deuteronomy 22:15-21), and the Bible pictures God as Israel's husband (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Keener notes that other commentators see Paul as the best man rather than the father; the CSB Study Bible makes Paul the father, the church the daughter and Christ the groom. Paul casts his rivals as men who corrupt a betrothed virgin, a crime punished by banishment under Roman law and by death under Old Testament law (Keener and his notes). Jewish tradition often identified the Eden serpent with Satan (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24), and one tradition, hard to date, has Satan deceive Eve by appearing as a good angel (Keener and his notes). Arnold calls the rivals polished orators who styled themselves apostles, apparently claimed authority from Jerusalem, and publicly scorned Paul, and he writes that "Paul regarded Satan as the master of masquerade and deceit." In this culture "a rejection of someone's gift was also a rejection of friendship" (the cultural backgrounds notes), and the Philippians probably supported Paul in Corinth (Keener).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 2 Corinthians 11:1-15, and on 11:2, 11:3, 11:5-6 and 11:9

ESV Study Bible, study note on 2 Corinthians 11:2
CSB Study Bible, note on 2 Corinthians 11:2-3

ideas.s: A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

ideas.n: Manual work and the leisured class
ideas.s: The well-to-do despised people who worked with their hands. A respectable teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees or even on begging, so an apostle who made tents for his keep looked low class.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 11:16-33, The fool's boast and the basket over the wall
entries.summary: Forced to boast like a fool, Paul matches his rivals' Jewish credentials and then lists sufferings instead of achievements: lashes, rods, stoning, shipwreck, the dangers of the road, hunger and cold, and a night escape down the wall of Damascus.
entries.plain: Paul plays the fool and boasts as his rivals do, matching their claims to be Hebrews, Israelites and Abraham's descendants. Then he turns boasting on its head by listing sufferings instead of achievements: floggings by Jewish authorities, beatings with rods, a stoning, shipwrecks, dangers on every road, hunger, cold and constant worry for the churches. He ends with a humiliating escape from Damascus, lowered down the wall in a basket while an official of King Aretas guarded the city to catch him.
entries.note: Audiences resented boasting except for good reasons, such as self-defense or necessity, and aristocrats boasted of heritage and achievements, not sufferings (the cultural backgrounds article Ancient Boasting; Keener). The article reads Paul as playing the fool and parodying the self-promotion his culture prized. Under Jewish law a synagogue court sentenced lesser offenses to 39 lashes (Deuteronomy 25:2-3), and an offender could escape by renouncing his community, which Paul would not do (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The Mishnah describes the method, as the Zondervan dictionary reports: "Thirteen strokes were administered on the chest and thirteen on each shoulder." The Porcian law forbade scourging a Roman citizen, but officials sometimes beat citizens with rods anyway (the dictionary; Keener and his notes). Josephus tells of a wreck after which passengers "swam for our lives all the night." Whether Aretas IV controlled Damascus is debated: Keener thinks he may have, the dictionary takes the ethnarch as the city's governor under him, and the cultural backgrounds notes say he may only have led the Nabatean community. Rome honored the first soldier up an enemy wall with a wall crown, and Wright reads the escape as a parody of it (the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright).

ideas.s: Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

ideas.n: Roads, robbers and the dangers of travel
ideas.s: Travel by land was slow and risky. Robbers worked the lonely roads, rivers had to be forded, and news moved no faster than the people who carried it.

Outside winter, ships were the quickest and cheapest way to travel, but they were built for cargo, not passengers, and from mid-September the sea grew dangerous. The great grain ships of Alexandria fed Rome.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 12:1-10, Caught up to the third heaven; the thorn
entries.summary: Paul tells of a man caught up to the third heaven and into paradise who heard things no one may utter, then of the thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, which God would not remove because his power is made perfect in weakness.
entries.plain: Pushed further into boasting, Paul tells of someone he knows, joined to Christ, who was taken up fourteen years earlier to the third heaven, into paradise, and heard things no one may repeat. To keep him from pride, he was given a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan. He asked three times for it to be removed, but the Lord told him that grace was enough and that power reaches its full strength in weakness, so Paul is content with weakness, because it is then that he is strong.
entries.note: Telling the story in the third person was a way to avoid boasting, and the cultural backgrounds article on the third heaven thinks Paul means himself (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Some Jewish mystics sought visions of God's throne by fasting and meditation, but Paul is caught up without seeking it (the article). Jewish sources counted three, seven or more heavens; Paul's third heaven, where he places paradise, probably means the highest, where God is (the article). The Zondervan dictionary notes that later Jews divided the heavens into seven, and that paradise, a Persian word for a park, meant Eden in the Greek Old Testament before it came to mean the place of final bliss. Carson, Moo and Morris suggest the rivals faulted Paul for saying little about visions. Wright compares the thorn to the slave who whispered to a triumphing general that he too was mortal. What the thorn was is disputed. Keener suggests persecution or the rival teachers; the ESV Study Bible and the dictionary say most commentators prefer a physical condition, and Arnold thinks it an illness caused by an evil angel, arguing that Paul would not pray to be spared opposition.

ideas.s: Jewish visionaries told of being caught up through the heavens to see God's throne and paradise, and writers numbered the heavens differently. Paul's third heaven speaks that language, though he refuses to make it his credential.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 12:11-18, Not a burden: parents save for their children
entries.summary: Paul says the Corinthians forced him to play the fool; the signs of an apostle were done among them, and his only fault was not to burden them, since parents save up for their children, not children for their parents.
entries.plain: Paul says the Corinthians forced him into this foolish boasting, when they should have been the ones speaking up for him, since he is in no way behind the so-called super-apostles and did the signs of an apostle among them. His only offense, he says with irony, was refusing to be a financial burden, and he will refuse again on his third visit, because parents provide for children, not the reverse. He denies that he or Titus exploited them through anyone he sent.
entries.note: Many ancient writers held that self-praise was inoffensive only when one was compelled to it, and philosophers usually counted public speakers nobodies (Keener and his notes). Appealing to what the hearers had seen for themselves, as the orator Isocrates did, softened a boast (Keener and his notes), and the signs and wonders recall God's acts in Egypt (the cultural backgrounds notes). The well-to-do in the church wanted Paul to stop working and accept their support, to become their client, and his forgive me this wrong is irony (Keener and his notes). Calling himself their parent reverses the question of who depends on whom, since "Patrons viewed both their clients and their children as dependent members of their households" (the cultural backgrounds notes); Keener adds that Roman parents supported the children they acknowledged and helped young couples get established. People defending themselves sometimes demanded that their hearers show what wrong they had done (1 Samuel 12:3-5), and Paul's rivals may have questioned the integrity of the collection for Jerusalem as well as his refusal of support (Keener and his notes). Wright notes that Paul took nothing from Corinth while accepting help from Macedonia.

ideas.s: Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

ideas.n: Manual work and the leisured class
ideas.s: The well-to-do despised people who worked with their hands. A respectable teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees or even on begging, so an apostle who made tents for his keep looked low class.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.
Paul gathered money from his mostly Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, much as Jews everywhere sent the temple tax to the holy city.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 12:19-13:14, Two or three witnesses
entries.summary: Paul warns that on his third visit every charge will be established by two or three witnesses and that he will not spare the unrepentant, then closes with a call to restoration, the holy kiss and a threefold blessing.
entries.plain: Paul says all this has been for their strengthening, not his own defense, and fears he will find quarreling and immorality when he visits. On this third visit charges will be settled on the word of two or three witnesses, and he warns that he will not go easy on the unrepentant, for Christ, though crucified in weakness, now lives by God's power. He urges them to examine themselves, to mend their ways and live in peace, and closes with greetings and a threefold blessing that names Christ's grace, God's love and the Spirit's fellowship.
entries.note: Moralists attacked strife and envy, so the Corinthians' behavior failed even by their own culture's ethics (Keener and his notes). Moses' law required at least two witnesses for a charge (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Keener reads Paul as treating his visit as a courtroom battle; the cultural backgrounds notes say he will prosecute the unrepentant before God, and the CSB Study Bible expects the congregation to carry out discipline. Josephus gives the rule: "let not a single witness be credited, but three, or two at the least." Corinthian culture evaluated speakers, and Paul turns the test back on them (the cultural backgrounds notes). Wright does not think chapters 10-13 are the painful letter of chapter 2. Carson, Moo and Morris note that this threatened third visit fits neither the mood nor the plans of chapters 1-9, the main support for treating 10-13 as later. The visit did take place, and Paul wrote Romans from Corinth with no anxiety about it, which gives some hope that the letters worked, at least for a time; forty years later Clement of Rome wrote to the same church about its divisions.

ideas.s: Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: Galatians 1:1-10, A letter with no thanksgiving, and a curse
entries.summary: Paul opens by insisting that his commission came from God and not from people, skips the thanksgiving his letters usually give, and pronounces a curse on anyone, even an angel, who preaches a different gospel.
entries.plain: Paul opens by insisting that his apostleship came from God the Father and Jesus Christ, not from any human source, and greets the Galatian churches in the name of the Christ who gave himself to free us from this evil age. Where his letters usually give thanks, he expresses shock that they are so quickly abandoning the gospel for a counterfeit that is no gospel. He twice calls down a curse on anyone, even an angel or Paul himself, who preaches something different, and asks whether he is trying to win human approval or God's.
entries.note: No one seriously doubts that Paul wrote Galatians (Carson, Moo and Morris). Leaving out the usual thanksgiving marks it as a letter of blame, a convention "found only among the harshest of ancient letters" (Keener and his notes). Who the Galatians were is debated, and the answer moves the date. Galatia could mean the Celtic north around Ancyra, which Acts never mentions, or the whole Roman province, taking in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Keener). Wright and Bird, the ESV Study Bible and Carson, Moo and Morris favor the south, and the Zondervan dictionary calls that the majority view, while Carson, Moo and Morris say many recent scholars hold the north. On dating, the ESV Study Bible and Carson, Moo and Morris put the letter about AD 48, before the Jerusalem council it never mentions; the dictionary answers that the Galatians already knew the decrees and dates it about 52, and Keener thinks the council probably already past, a view the cultural backgrounds notes also report. The rival teachers were almost certainly Jewish Christians from outside, and verse 10 answers the charge that Paul sought human approval (Carson, Moo and Morris).

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
God's covenant set blessings for keeping it against curses for breaking it, and Deuteronomy spelled both out. Curses were also a familiar part of ancient religion, magic and everyday life.

entries.title: Galatians 1:11-24, Saul the zealot, Arabia, and fifteen days with Cephas
entries.summary: Paul insists that his gospel came by revelation and not from human teachers, and tells of his zeal as a persecutor, his call, his time in Arabia and Damascus, and a short first visit to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas.
entries.plain: Paul insists that his gospel was not taught to him by anyone but came through a revelation of Jesus Christ. He recalls his past as a violent persecutor of the church and a rising star in Judaism, fiercely devoted to his ancestral traditions, until God revealed his Son to him and sent him to the Gentiles. He went to Arabia and Damascus without consulting anyone, made only a brief visit to Jerusalem three years later to meet Peter and see James, and remained unknown by sight to the Judean churches.
entries.note: Speeches and letters often included a narrative of past events to establish the speaker's character, and anything that sounded like boasting offended unless one was defending oneself (Keener and his notes). A disciple who passed on his teachers' tradition was their subordinate, and Paul claims he was not a disciple of Jesus' disciples (Keener and his notes). The highest training in Scripture was in Jerusalem, and the traditions of the fathers were the teaching prized by Pharisees (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Arabia meant the Nabatean kingdom of Aretas IV, not the peninsula (Keener and his notes; Carson, Moo and Morris). Why Paul went is read two ways. Wright argues that, like the zealous Elijah, he went to Sinai: "Sinai was where Elijah had gone when it all went horribly wrong." Carson, Moo and Morris think "it is unlikely that this was simply a period of retreat", since Aretas's later hunt for him (2 Corinthians 11:32) suggests he had been preaching, and the Zondervan dictionary also places ministry there. Ancient reckoning usually counted part of a year as a whole, so three years may mean two or less (Keener and his notes; Carson, Moo and Morris).

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

entries.title: Galatians 2:1-10, Titus, the pillars and the right hand of fellowship
entries.summary: Fourteen years later Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and the uncircumcised Titus; Titus is not made to be circumcised, and the leaders reputed to be pillars give Paul the right hand of fellowship, asking only that he remember the poor.
entries.plain: Fourteen years later Paul went to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, prompted by a revelation, and privately laid out his gospel before the leaders. Titus, a Gentile, was not made to be circumcised, despite pressure from people Paul calls false brothers. The leaders added nothing to Paul's message, and James, Peter and John, the men regarded as pillars, shook hands on a division of the work, asking only that Paul and Barnabas keep remembering the poor.
entries.note: Which visit this is, is debated. A majority, Keener among them, take 2:1-10 as the Jerusalem council of Acts 15, and the Zondervan dictionary agrees, explaining the differences as a private meeting beside Luke's public sessions; others match it to the famine visit of Acts 11:28-30, as the ESV Study Bible, Wright and Bird, and Carson, Moo and Morris do, the last finding it "much simpler to accept both accounts" as two visits. The dates move with it: Keener puts the conversion around AD 31, while Carson, Moo and Morris, counting years inclusively, allow 32 to 35, leaning to the later years. Many Jews believed non-idolatrous Gentiles would be saved, but "almost no one believed that they were adopted into the covenant on equal terms" until circumcised (Keener and his notes). Wright explains why circumcision became the test: a man was either circumcised or not. Some still think Paul did circumcise Titus, as he later did Timothy (Acts 16:3); Wright and the dictionary think he did not, the dictionary noting that Timothy's mother was Jewish while Titus, a Gentile, was the test case. Influential people were called pillars, and taking the right hand sealed an agreement (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Paul gathered money from his mostly Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, much as Jews everywhere sent the temple tax to the holy city.

entries.title: Galatians 2:11-21, Peter leaves the table at Antioch
entries.summary: At Antioch Peter, who had been eating with Gentile believers, draws back when people come from James, and Paul rebukes him in front of everyone, arguing that Jews and Gentiles alike are put right with God through Christ and faith, not by doing what the law requires.
entries.plain: At Antioch Peter had been sharing meals with Gentile believers, but when men from James arrived he pulled back out of fear of the circumcision party, and other Jewish believers, Barnabas included, followed him. Paul confronted him publicly for living like a Gentile while pressing Gentiles to live like Jews. He goes on to argue that a person is put right with God through Christ and faith, not by doing what the law prescribes, and that if the law could make people righteous, Christ's death would have been pointless. It is unclear where his words to Peter end.
entries.note: Jews in Judea and Galilee who cared about their standing avoided eating with Gentiles, and rising nationalism in Judea pressed moderates such as Peter and probably James (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). When this happened is disputed: the Zondervan dictionary places it after the council, which had left open how Jewish believers should keep the law, while Carson, Moo and Morris think it more likely before. Who sent the visitors, and what they wanted, is read differently: the ESV Study Bible thinks they pressed Jewish believers to eat separately; Wright's biography has them insisting that Gentiles be circumcised. Wright reads the works of the law as the badges of Sabbath, food laws and circumcision; the cultural backgrounds notes and the ESV Study Bible read the phrase more widely, and Carson, Moo and Morris insist that justification by faith rules out works, of the law or any other. The cultural backgrounds article Paul's Jewish Opponents sets out both views and suggests they may have been legalists in practice whatever their theology. Whether 2:16 speaks of faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ is also disputed, the ESV Study Bible taking the first and Wright the second.

ideas.s: Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

entries.title: Galatians 3:1-14, Who bewitched you? Abraham's blessing and the law's curse
entries.summary: Paul asks the Galatians who has bewitched them, since they received the Spirit by believing, then argues from Abraham that those who believe share his blessing, while Christ took the law's curse by being hung on a tree.
entries.plain: Paul asks the Galatians who has put them under a spell, since they saw Christ's crucifixion portrayed so plainly. They received the Spirit by believing the message, not by keeping the law, so why turn to the flesh now? Abraham was counted righteous for trusting God, which makes believers his true children and heirs of the promise that all nations would be blessed through him. The law brings a curse on those who rely on it, but Christ took that curse on himself by being hung on a tree, so that Abraham's blessing could reach the Gentiles.
entries.note: The word for bewitched refers to spells or the evil eye, "a jealous look with magical efficacy" (Keener); the ESV Study Bible says Paul borrows the language of pagan magic, and Wright sets the evil eye against Christ shown before their very eyes, while the Zondervan dictionary reads the word as a strong metaphor. Many Jewish sources tied the Spirit to merit, yet the Galatians had received it soon after leaving paganism (Keener). The rival teachers wanted the Galatians to complete their faith as full converts to Judaism did, by circumcision (Keener and his notes). Genesis 15:6 was a popular Jewish proof text for Abraham's faith as one of his works, and Jewish teachers saw Abraham as the model convert, though Genesis counts him righteous years before his circumcision (Keener and his notes). Paul links texts by shared key words, a standard Jewish method, and has chosen the only two Old Testament texts that join righteousness and faith, Genesis 15:6 and Habakkuk 2:4 (Keener and his notes). Heiser reads the good news announced to Abraham as delivered to him in person by the visible Word.

ideas.s: Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.
God's covenant set blessings for keeping it against curses for breaking it, and Deuteronomy spelled both out. Curses were also a familiar part of ancient religion, magic and everyday life.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

entries.title: Galatians 3:15-22, A will no one can change, and a law given through angels
entries.summary: Paul argues from the way a ratified will cannot be altered that the law, coming 430 years after the promise to Abraham and his seed, cannot cancel it, and says the law was added because of transgressions, put in place through angels by a mediator.
entries.plain: Paul uses the legal picture of a will: once ratified, no one can cancel it or add to it. God's promise to Abraham and his offspring, whom Paul takes to be Christ, came 430 years before the law, so the law cannot undo it. The law was added because of wrongdoing, delivered through angels by a mediator, and it was never against the promise; Scripture shut everyone up under sin so that the promise would be given through faith.
entries.note: Paul's word for covenant, diatheke, was the ordinary Greek word for a will, while the Greek Old Testament used it for covenant, and Paul plays on its legal sense (Keener and his notes). The ESV and CSB Study Bibles read 3:15 as an everyday illustration from human wills; Wright holds that the covenant of Genesis 15 is the point and the will only a passing analogy. The word for seed can be singular or collective, and Paul argues from the singular the way the rabbis argued (Keener and his notes). Jewish tradition after the Old Testament said that the law came through angels, and Josephus has Herod tell his army that "we have learned from God the most excellent of our doctrines, and the most holy part of our law, by angels or ambassadors." What because of transgressions means is disputed: the ESV Study Bible lists four readings and prefers revealing human sin; Heiser notes early readers who took it as restraining transgression and sets out the view that "the transgressions that prompted the giving of the law were those of the Watchers."

ideas.s: A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Galatians 3:23-29, The law as a guardian until faith came
entries.summary: Before faith came, Paul says, we were held in custody under the law, which served as a guardian until Christ; now all who have been baptized into Christ are God's children, one in him, Abraham's seed and heirs.
entries.plain: Paul describes the law as a guardian that kept God's people under watch until Christ came and faith was revealed. The guardian was the household slave who supervised a boy until he came of age, so now that faith has come that supervision is over. All who have been baptized into Christ are God's children and have put him on like clothing, and in him the divisions of Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female no longer define them; they are Abraham's offspring and heirs.
entries.note: Jewish traditions divided history into stages, and Paul makes the law a temporary stage until the promise (Keener and his notes). The guardian was the slave who walked a boy to school and watched his manners, not the teacher, and the role ended when a boy came of age at about thirteen or fourteen (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible); the King James Version's schoolmaster is the rendering Wright corrects. How the image sounds is weighed differently. The ESV Study Bible gives the guardian positive tasks, restraining transgressions and pointing ahead to Christ; Keener and his notes call the picture not demeaning in itself but shocking to Jewish thinkers, who called the law their teacher. Gentiles converting to Judaism were baptized, naked, and then reclothed, and writers spoke of being clothed with virtues (Keener and his notes). Some Greeks thanked the deity that they were not made animals, women or non-Greeks, and some Jewish teachers thanked God that they were not made Gentiles, women or ignorant, in some versions slaves (the cultural backgrounds notes). Some cults claimed to ignore social divisions but rarely did (Keener).

ideas.s: A trusted household slave walked a boy to school and back, watched his manners and kept him out of trouble until he came of age. He was neither the teacher nor anything like the father.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.

entries.title: Galatians 4:1-11, Heirs, slaves and the elements of the world
entries.summary: An heir who is still a child is no better off than a slave, Paul says; so we were enslaved under the elements of the world until God sent his Son to redeem us and his Spirit to cry Abba, and he asks why the Galatians want to go back to observing special days, months, seasons and years.
entries.plain: Paul compares God's people before Christ to an heir who is still a minor: though he will own everything, he lives under guardians until the date his father set, little better than a slave. In the same way they were enslaved to the elements of the world until, at the right time, God sent his Son, born under the law, to set them free and adopt them, and sent his Spirit so they could call God Father. Paul is dismayed that the Galatians, who once served beings that are not gods, now want to go back to those weak elements by observing special days and seasons.
entries.note: Under Roman law a minor under a guardian had roughly a slave's status, and estate managers were often slaves or freed slaves with real power (Keener and his notes). The Zondervan dictionary adds that a trustee ran a child's finances until he was twenty-five, while the cultural backgrounds notes say the heir waited until the will directed or until puberty, and Wright thinks the picture is bent to fit Genesis 15. Abba was rarely if ever used to address God in Judaism and was probably borrowed from Jesus (Keener and his notes); the dictionary questions the rendering Daddy, since adults used it, even respectfully of a rabbi. Arnold reads the elements of 4:3 and 4:9 as evil spirits that exploited both pagan religion and the law, so that taking up the law would be "trading one form of slavery to the powers for another." The days, months, seasons and years are read as the Jewish calendar (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Arnold), as astrology (Heiser), or as both (Keener). Wright adds that Paul may be hinting at the calendar of Caesar's cult.

ideas.s: A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

Paul twice says that people were enslaved under the stoicheia, the elements of the world. The word could mean basic rules, the stuff the world is made of, or the powers people worshiped in nature and the stars, and scholars still disagree which he meant.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.

entries.title: Galatians 4:12-20, Welcomed as an angel of God
entries.summary: Paul appeals to the Galatians as friends, reminding them that when he first preached to them in bodily weakness they did not scorn him but welcomed him as an angel of God, and asks whether he has now become their enemy by telling them the truth.
entries.plain: Paul begs them to become like him, since he became like them. They did him no wrong; they know he first preached to them because of a weakness of the body, and though his condition was a trial to them they did not scorn or despise him but welcomed him as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus himself, and would have torn out their own eyes and given them to him. Has he now become their enemy by telling them the truth? The rivals court them for no good end, wanting to shut them out so that they will court the rivals instead; he is in the pains of childbirth again until Christ is formed in them, and wishes he could be with them now and change his tone, for he does not know what to make of them.
entries.note: Paul here uses the themes of friendship letters (Keener and his notes). The weakness could be illness or injuries from persecution, and "Physical infirmities were quite often regarded as the curse or punishment of the gods" (Keener). What it was is not known (the ESV Study Bible). Proposals include malaria, prompting a move to the higher interior (the cultural backgrounds notes; the CSB Study Bible), eye trouble (the CSB Study Bible, though Keener and his notes call the giving of eyes a known figure of speech), and injuries from the stoning at Lystra (the CSB Study Bible), which Wright prefers. Wright suggests that people seeing a man so disfigured would have spat to ward off the evil eye. To welcome a guest as one would an angel of God was a sign of very great honor (Keener and his notes), and Carson, Moo and Morris report the suggestion that it recalls the Lystrans hailing Paul as Hermes (Acts 14:12). They add that I first preached can mean simply formerly, not the first of two visits. Teachers were often called fathers, but Paul takes a mother's part: labor pains were counted the worst pain people knew (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

ideas.n: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: Galatians 4:21-5:1, Hagar, Sarah and Sinai in Arabia
entries.summary: Paul reads the story of Abraham's two sons as a figure of two covenants: Hagar the slave stands for Sinai and the present Jerusalem, Sarah the free woman for the Jerusalem above, and he calls the Galatians to stand firm in freedom.
entries.plain: Paul turns to the law's own story for those eager to live under it: Abraham fathered a son by Hagar, a slave, in the ordinary way, and another by Sarah, a free woman, through God's promise. He reads the two women as two covenants, Hagar standing for Sinai and the present Jerusalem in slavery, Sarah for the free Jerusalem above, the mother of believers. As the slave's son troubled the free son then, the children of promise face hostility now, and Scripture says to send away the slave and her son; Christ has freed them, so they must not return to slavery.
entries.note: Some scholars suggest that Abraham and Sarah followed an ancient Near Eastern custom in using the barren wife's servant as a surrogate mother (Keener), and the Zondervan dictionary agrees. Philosophers often used allegory to deny a story's literal sense, while Jewish interpreters usually kept the literal sense and added an application; Philo made Sarah and Hagar advanced and elementary education (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The dictionary notes that Paul keeps the history and that many prefer to call his method typology. Arabia included Mount Sinai as well as the land near Damascus, and Jews of the period saw the Nabatean Arabs as Ishmaelites (Keener and his notes); Josephus says Ishmael's twelve sons "inhabited all the country from Euphrates to the Red Sea, and called it Nabatene." Because Paul rarely argues this way, some think he is answering rivals who likened God-fearers to Ishmael and law-keepers to Isaac (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Jewish texts looked for a Jerusalem in heaven that would descend to earth, and called Jerusalem our mother (Keener and his notes). Jewish teachers honored the yoke of the law, but a yoke also meant slavery (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.

entries.title: Galatians 5:2-12, Circumcision, the whole law and the knife
entries.summary: Paul warns that a man who accepts circumcision is bound to keep the whole law and is cut off from Christ, asks who cut in on their race, and wishes that the agitators would go further with the knife.
entries.plain: Paul warns that any Galatian man who accepts circumcision binds himself to the whole law and cuts himself off from Christ and grace. In Christ circumcision makes no difference either way; what matters is faith expressing itself in love. They had been running well until someone tripped them up, and Paul, using the proverb about a little yeast, says the false teaching will spread through them all; he ends with a harsh wish about the agitators and the knife, which most interpreters read as castration.
entries.note: Most Jewish teachers allowed that righteous Gentiles who kept the laws given to Noah could be saved, but a convert was bound to keep the whole law (Keener and his notes). The teachers were probably Jewish Christians like those who went from Judea to Antioch teaching circumcision (Acts 15:1), perhaps few in number, as the proverb about yeast hints, and verse 11 suggests they accused Paul of preaching circumcision when it suited him (Carson, Moo and Morris). Moral writers often compared the moral life to a race (Keener and his notes). Most commentators take 5:12 as castration, though it could mean cutting themselves off from the community (Keener); the King James Version's I would they were even cut off keeps the ambiguity. Many pagans thought circumcision a mutilation, Hadrian later outlawed it under a law against castration, and Jews abhorred eunuchs (Keener and his notes). People also mocked the Galli, the self-castrated worshipers of Phrygia's mother goddess (the cultural backgrounds notes). Lightfoot thought the Galatians' old religion of bodily mortification primed them for a ritual creed, which Carson, Moo and Morris call largely speculative.

D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 10, Galatians, Occasion

ideas.s: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.

entries.title: Galatians 5:13-6:10, Flesh and Spirit, burdens and teachers
entries.summary: Called to freedom, the Galatians are to serve one another in love, which fulfills the law; Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit and urges them to restore the fallen gently, carry each other's burdens, share with their teachers and keep doing good.
entries.plain: They were called to freedom, Paul says, but not as an opening for the flesh; through love they should serve one another, since the whole law is fulfilled in loving one's neighbor as oneself, and if they bite and devour each other they will be consumed. Walk by the Spirit, he urges, and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh; he lists the works of the flesh, whose doers will not inherit God's kingdom, and the fruit of the Spirit, against which there is no law. They are to restore anyone caught in a sin gently, carry each other's burdens and so fulfill the law of Christ, share good things with those who teach them, and remember that people reap what they sow.
entries.note: Other Jewish teachers also summed up the law with Leviticus 19:18 (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris see no second group of libertine opponents here: the warnings correct a misuse of Paul's own teaching on freedom. Jews spoke of walking in God's ways, and their moral rulings were called halakah, literally walking (Keener). The Dead Sea Scrolls traced every act to God's Spirit or the spirit of error (the cultural backgrounds notes). Philosophers taught that the wise needed no law, and Scripture promised a law written on the heart (Keener and his notes). Moralists used lists of vices and of virtues, and the two ways was a frequent image; Paul is sterner than pagan writers, who mostly warned against excess (Keener and his notes). Self-control was among the virtues philosophers stressed most (Keener and his notes). Carrying burdens was usually forced, on slaves or by soldiers impressing locals, so bearing them freely was an image of service (Keener and his notes). Many teachers charged fees, while early Christian teachers normally did not (Keener and his notes). Reaping what one sows was a common proverb (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.

entries.title: Galatians 6:11-18, Large letters in his own hand, and the marks of Jesus
entries.summary: Taking the pen himself, Paul writes in large letters that the rivals want the Galatians circumcised so they can boast in their flesh and avoid persecution, while he boasts only in the cross; he blesses those who follow this rule and the Israel of God, and says he bears the marks of Jesus.
entries.plain: Paul takes the pen himself and writes in large letters to underline his final point. The rivals want the Galatians circumcised so they can boast about it and escape persecution for the cross, though they do not keep the law themselves. Paul will boast only in the cross, through which he and the world are dead to each other, because circumcision means nothing and new creation is what matters. He blesses all who follow this rule and the Israel of God, and points to the marks of Jesus he bears on his body.
entries.note: Letters this long were dictated to scribes, and "not a scribe but Paul himself writes this section, as the handwriting shows" (Keener and his notes). Why the letters are large is read differently: eyesight (the CSB Study Bible, as one view), which Wright calls speculative; emphasis or an untrained hand (Keener and his notes); or, Wright suggests, dark humor against the rivals' fine showing in the flesh. Wright reads the pressure as coming from the Jewish community, the civic authorities or both: Jews were exempt from worshiping the city's gods, and uncircumcised Gentiles who stopped worshiping them put that exemption at risk. Pisidian Antioch styled itself new Rome (Wright); it was a Roman colony and garrison town and capital of southern Galatia (the Zondervan dictionary). Peace on Israel was a regular synagogue prayer, a fitting opposite to the curse of 1:8-9; scholars dispute whether the Israel of God means the faithful Jewish remnant or all believers, more favoring the latter (Keener). Paul's word for marks could mean any mark or wound and here probably means scars from persecution (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles); Carson, Moo and Morris read 6:17 as his last answer to attacks on his authority.

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.

entries.title: Ephesians 1:1-14, A circular letter opens with praise, a seal and a down payment
entries.summary: Paul greets God's holy people and launches one long blessing of God for choosing, adopting, redeeming and sealing a mixed people, with the Spirit as the down payment of their inheritance.
entries.plain: Paul greets the believers, though some early copies leave out the words naming Ephesus. He then pours out one long sentence of praise to God for what he has done in Christ: chosen and adopted a people, set them free through Christ's death, and shown them his plan to bring everything together under Christ. The Spirit is God's seal on them and a first installment of what they will inherit, which gave a mixed church firm ground to stand on.
entries.note: Where Paul was held is disputed: Rome, about AD 60 to 62 (Keener, his notes, the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), or Ephesus, about 55 (Wright; Wright and Bird); Carson, Moo and Morris also weigh Caesarea, find that the arguments for and against Ephesus "cancel each other out", and give a little more weight to Rome. Critics doubt that Paul wrote it, citing style, vocabulary and closeness to Colossians, and date it about 70 to 90; Carson, Moo and Morris and Wright hold it to be his. Some early manuscripts lack the words in Ephesus. Many take it as a circular (Keener and his notes; Wright, who suggests it was written from Ephesus rather than to it); the ESV Study Bible holds the words original, and Carson, Moo and Morris conclude that no one knows for sure. Ephesus was a trading city "that had few equals anywhere in the world" (the cultural backgrounds article). In one long sentence of praise, 1:3-14 gives Israel's titles to Jews and Gentiles together (Keener and his notes). The seal and the deposit were business words for ownership and a down payment (Keener and his notes; Wright); the ESV Study Bible stresses protection, Keener attestation.

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

entries.title: Ephesians 1:15-23, Far above every name that is invoked
entries.summary: Paul prays that the believers will know the hope, the inheritance and the power God showed when he raised Christ and seated him above every ruler, authority, power and name, in this age and the next.
entries.plain: Paul tells them he keeps thanking God for them and asks that they come to understand three things: the hope God has called them to, the wealth of what he will give, and how great his power is. That is the power that brought Jesus back to life and set him on the throne beside God, higher than every spiritual ruler and every name anyone could call on, now or later. For readers used to calling on many powers, this put Christ above every one of them, with the church as his body.
entries.note: Rule, authority, power and dominion were standard terms for the angelic powers thought to stand behind the nations (Keener and his notes); Arnold adds that some were Jewish words and others turn up in pagan magical and astrological texts. Heiser reads them as authority over geographical domains (Deuteronomy 32:8-9), while Arnold notes that Paul never ties the powers to a country. Magicians tried to control spirits by invoking their names, at Ephesus as elsewhere (Keener and his notes), and Arnold stresses that knowing the most powerful names lay at the heart of magic. He shows Artemis, the city's goddess, invoked by name in spells and argues that Ephesians gives a framework for answering her cult without naming her. Wright adds the imperial side: Ephesus was a center of imperial influence, and every ruler up to "the emperor himself" is put under Christ's feet (Psalm 8). To sit at a ruler's right hand was to hold the place of honor and authority (Psalm 110:1) (Keener and his notes). Jewish teachers held that the heavenly powers ruled every nation but Israel; Paul says those in Christ are raised above them (Keener).

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

Most people in Paul's world believed their lives were ruled by Fate, worked out through the stars, which many took to be heavenly beings. Few thought there was any escape, and cults that promised one drew followers.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

entries.title: Ephesians 2:1-10, The ruler of the kingdom of the air
entries.summary: Paul reminds his readers that they were once dead in sins, following the ruler of the kingdom of the air, until God in his mercy made them alive and seated them with Christ in the heavenly realms, saved by grace.
entries.plain: Paul reminds his readers what their life was before Christ: cut off from God by their wrongdoing, following the world's ways and an evil spiritual ruler, and driven by their own desires. Then God, out of mercy and love, brought them to life with Christ and gave them a place with him above. All of this is God's free gift received by trusting him, not something they earned, and it leads into a new life of doing good.
entries.note: Air was the usual word for the atmospheric heaven, and evil spirits were thought to rule this lowest level (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). A magical papyrus calls a spirit helper "the only lord of the air" (Arnold). Who the ruler is, is read in more than one way: Satan (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles, Arnold, Wright, the Zondervan dictionary), Satan or the chief angel of the nations (Keener), or, Heiser suggests, it may turn on whether Paul had Israelite or Greco-Roman cosmology in mind, since the verse names neither Satan nor the devil. Arnold declines a precise map: the air reflects "the common belief that demons inhabit the air." He rejects reading it as a spiritual climate, the picture Wright uses of ideas felt in the atmosphere of a place. For readers once afraid of Fate or the stars, being seated with Christ meant being enthroned above the powers (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Arnold). Most Jews held that God's grace, given through the covenant, had saved them, but they did not apply that grace to Gentiles (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

Most people in Paul's world believed their lives were ruled by Fate, worked out through the stars, which many took to be heavenly beings. Few thought there was any escape, and cults that promised one drew followers.
