entries.title: Ephesians 2:11-22, The dividing wall torn down, and a new temple
entries.summary: Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were once far off, shut out of Israel's citizenship and covenants, and tells them Christ has broken down the dividing wall and built Jews and Gentiles into one household and one temple.
entries.plain: Paul asks the Gentile believers to remember where they once stood: outside Israel, with no share in God's covenant promises and no hope. Through Christ's death they have been brought in, and the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile has been pulled down, so that the two make one new people at peace with God. They now belong to God's household and are being built together into a temple where God lives by his Spirit.
entries.note: Uncircumcised was an old insult for Gentiles, and made by hands was what Jewish writers said of idols (the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright). Without God in 2:12 is the word behind atheist, which pagans called Jews and later Christians, "since neither Jews nor Christians had statues of their gods" (Wright). Herod's temple barred Gentiles from its inner courts: Josephus describes a partition with an inscription that forbade any foreigner to go in "under pain of death," and a complete warning stone of this kind was found in 1871 (Price and House). Paul was in custody for allegedly taking an Ephesian past that line (Acts 21:28-29) (Keener and his notes). Whether Paul means that wall is debated: Keener, his notes and the CSB Study Bible think so, and Wright and Bird that he may; the ESV Study Bible, and Wright in his commentary, take the barrier to be the law in its use to keep Jew and Gentile apart. House meant both household and building, so the household of 2:19 becomes the temple of 2:21 (the cultural backgrounds notes); some Jewish writers called God's people his temple, but none included Gentiles in it (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

entries.title: Ephesians 3:1-13, The prisoner, the steward and the mystery shown to the powers
entries.summary: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, breaks off to explain the stewardship of grace given him: the mystery, now revealed, that Gentiles are co-heirs, made known through the church even to the rulers in the heavenly realms.
entries.plain: Paul starts to pray for the Gentile believers, then stops to explain his own role. God showed him a secret kept hidden for ages: Gentiles share fully with Israel in the inheritance, the body and the promise. His task is to announce it, so that through the church God's wisdom is shown even to the powers in the heavens, and his imprisonment for that work should not discourage them.
entries.note: Roman custody was normally a mark of shame, but Paul counts it an honor because of why he is held (Keener and his notes). Verses 2-13 are a digression, the thread taken up again at 3:14 (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Mystery was a word of the mystery cults, but Keener finds Paul's background in Daniel 2 and the Dead Sea Scrolls, God's plan once hidden and now revealed; the CSB Study Bible sets Paul's open mystery against the cults' secrets. No other New Testament book uses the word as often as Ephesians (Carson, Moo and Morris). Uncircumcised Gentile co-heirs would sound like heresy to many Jewish readers (Keener and his notes). Wright hears the Wisdom of Solomon, which told pagan rulers to seek wisdom from Israel's God. How the rulers of 3:10 take what the church shows them is read differently: the ESV and CSB Study Bibles see angels watching with interest; Heiser and Arnold hold that the hostile powers did not know the plan until it was revealed; and Wright, who reads earthly rulers and their heavenly counterparts, thinks them "unlikely to take this kindly".

ideas.s: Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Ephesians 3:14-21, Kneeling before the Father of every family
entries.summary: Paul kneels in prayer before the Father of every family, heavenly and earthly, and asks that they be strengthened by the Spirit and grasp the vast dimensions of Christ's love, closing with praise.
entries.plain: Paul takes up his interrupted prayer, kneeling before God, who is Father to every family, heavenly and earthly. He asks that the Spirit give them inner strength, that Christ make his home in their hearts, and that they grasp how vast Christ's love is, a love bigger than anyone can fully know. He closes by praising God, who can do far more than they could ever ask or picture.
entries.note: Jews usually prayed standing, though kneeling was used, especially in extreme situations, and Greeks rarely knelt to pray (Keener and his notes). Family translates patria, from pater, father, so the line is a play on words, and the Greek Old Testament often used patria for a family line from one ancestor (the cultural backgrounds notes). The Roman father held authority over all his descendants as long as he lived (Keener). Who the families in heaven are is read in more than one way: the guardian angels of the nations (Keener and his notes); every rank of angels, good and evil, taking its identity and authority from the Father (Arnold); or one household of God with members in heaven and on earth (Carson, Moo and Morris). The cultural backgrounds notes see in God as the source of every family a further blow to ethnic division. Breadth, length, height and depth almost certainly apply the language of divine Wisdom (Job 11:5-9) to God's love, Keener writes; some see the cube of the holy of holies, which the cultural backgrounds notes call much less likely. Jewish prayers often closed with praise and the hearers' Amen (Keener and his notes).

entries.title: Ephesians 4:1-16, The conqueror goes up and gives gifts
entries.summary: Paul urges unity, one body and one Spirit, then reads Psalm 68 as Christ ascending in victory and handing out gifts: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, to equip the church to grow up into him.
entries.plain: Paul turns from teaching to living and begins with unity. Because there is one body, one Spirit, one Lord and one God, the believers are to bear with one another humbly and keep the peace. He reads a psalm as a picture of Christ going up in victory and handing out gifts, and those gifts are people, apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, who equip the whole church to grow up together into Christ.
entries.note: Paul turns from praise to exhortation, and unity was a stock theme of ancient exhortation (Keener and his notes). Wright suggests that the list of unities in 4:4-6 may be a formula new converts learned. Paul adapts Psalm 68:18, which Jewish interpreters applied to God going up at Sinai and which Wright thinks a Jew might read of Moses; a later Aramaic paraphrase also has gave where the psalm has received (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). A conqueror took tribute and shared out the spoils (Keener and his notes). Who the captives are is disputed: defeated enemies (Heiser), most likely demons (the ESV Study Bible), the hostile powers (Arnold), or Christ's new followers (the CSB Study Bible). So is the descent of 4:9: to the realm of the dead (Keener; Arnold, who notes that Artemis and Hekate were thought to rule the underworld and that papyri give Hekate "the keys to Hades"), to earth at the incarnation (the ESV Study Bible), or Christ's coming in the Spirit (Heiser; Wright). Pastors are literally shepherds (Keener and his notes). Verse 14 joins a child, a storm-tossed boat and tricksters with loaded dice (Wright).

ideas.s: Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

Rome celebrated a great victory with a triumph, a parade of the general, his army and the spoils, with chained captives at the end who were killed or sold. Cities also staged shows in which condemned criminals fought or were thrown to beasts.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: Ephesians 4:17-32, No longer as the Gentiles live
entries.summary: Paul tells Gentile believers to stop living as the Gentiles do, to put off the old self and put on the new, to give the devil no foothold, to work with their hands and share, and not to grieve the Spirit who sealed them.
entries.plain: Paul tells Gentile believers to stop living the way their neighbors do, with darkened minds and lives given over to every impurity. Learning Christ means stripping off the old self like worn clothes and putting on a new one made to be like God. He spells it out in daily terms: tell the truth, deal with anger quickly, stop stealing and work so as to share, speak to build others up, and forgive as God forgave them, without grieving the Spirit who marked them as his.
entries.note: Jewish literature of the period described Gentiles in much the language Paul uses, and most Jews regarded most Gentiles as idol worshipers and sexually loose (Keener and his notes); the Testament of Reuben calls sexual sin the plague of Beliar (Arnold). Keener notes that Paul no longer calls Gentile believers Gentiles. Clothing was a natural picture for putting off and putting on behavior, and the new person probably recalls Adam (Keener and his notes); the CSB Study Bible links it with the baptismal custom of taking off old clothes. Verse 25 quotes Zechariah 8:16 and verse 26 Psalm 4:4 (Wright; Keener), and the Essenes and some philosophers required disputes to be settled the same day (Keener and his notes). Foothold is read two ways: a war picture, ground surrendered to the devil's side (Keener), or simply an opportunity, as in Romans 12:19 (Arnold). Arnold adds that the Testament of Dan ties unchecked anger to Beliar gaining control: "One text in particular links unchecked anger with the devil gaining a foothold." Judaism valued manual work, which the aristocracy disdained (Keener and his notes). Sealing attested that no one had tampered with the goods (Keener and his notes); Wright stresses ownership.

ideas.n: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
ideas.s: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

ideas.n: Manual work and the leisured class
ideas.s: The well-to-do despised people who worked with their hands. A respectable teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees or even on begging, so an apostle who made tents for his keep looked low class.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.

entries.title: Ephesians 5:1-20, Children of light, and wine or the Spirit
entries.summary: Paul calls believers to imitate God, to have nothing to do with sexual immorality, coarse joking or deeds done in the dark, and, instead of getting drunk on wine, to be filled with the Spirit, singing and giving thanks for everything.
entries.plain: Paul calls the believers to copy God as his loved children and to live in love, the way Christ gave himself for them. Sexual sin, greed and dirty talk have no place among them, because they have moved out of darkness into light and should expose what is done in the dark. He sets getting drunk against being filled by the Spirit, which shows itself in singing together and thanking God for everything.
entries.note: Sexual humor ran through Greek entertainment, and an inn wall at Pompeii could picture the prostitutes inside with their prices (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); the cultural backgrounds article on prostitution adds that most were slaves, many of them babies rescued from the rubbish heaps where infants were abandoned. Refusing the city's civic cults would get believers branded antisocial, as Jews were (Keener and his notes). Some mystery cults held night initiations and had immoral reputations (Keener and his notes; Wright). The saying of 5:14 is read as a paraphrase of Isaiah 60:1 or Daniel 12:2 (Keener), a combined allusion to Isaiah (the ESV Study Bible), or an early Christian song, which Wright thinks almost certain. Drunkenness was common at rich banquets and in poor taverns, and some linked it with possession by Dionysus, god of wine; Keener and Arnold see Dionysian revelry as a likely background, though Keener adds that not every drunkard was thought to be possessed. Only about fifty ancient musical scores survive, mostly in fragments (Wright), and Spirit songs may have been spontaneous (Keener). Only Jews and some Stoics urged thanks for everything (Keener and his notes).

ideas.n: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
ideas.s: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
Cults that a person entered by a secret initiation, often held at night. Some promised freedom from Fate, some had a name for drunken or immoral rites, and Rome distrusted them as foreign.

Most people in Paul's world believed their lives were ruled by Fate, worked out through the stars, which many took to be heavenly beings. Few thought there was any escape, and cults that promised one drew followers.

entries.title: Ephesians 5:21-33, Wives and husbands in the household code
entries.summary: Paul opens the household code with submitting to one another, asks wives to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, and asks husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, washing her and presenting her radiant.
entries.plain: Paul begins the household instructions by calling all believers to yield to one another out of respect for Christ. He then asks wives to yield to their husbands as to the Lord, and asks husbands to love their wives with the self-giving love Christ showed the church. He ties marriage to the joining of two into one flesh and says it points to Christ and the church.
entries.note: From Aristotle on, household codes told the male head of the house how to rule his wife, children and slaves, and minority groups used them to show they upheld Roman family values (Keener and his notes). The verb of 5:22 is borrowed from 5:21, so a wife's submission is one example of the general call (Keener; Carson, Moo and Morris). The cultural backgrounds article on marriage roles says nearly every Mediterranean society expected wives to submit; some contracts made a wife ask leave even to visit her family, Greek men commonly married at thirty, women at eighteen, and wives had more freedom in Macedonia and Rome than in Ephesus, "where Hellenistic culture dominated." Keener writes that "ancient household codes never list love as a husband's duty", and the article ranks Paul with the moderate minority, such as Xenophon and Musonius Rufus. The washing probably recalls the bride's bath (Keener and his notes). What submitting to one another means is disputed: Keener, his notes and Wright and Bird read a mutual submission that took in the head of the house, while the ESV Study Bible reads submission within the order the examples set out.

ideas.s: From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.
A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.

entries.title: Ephesians 6:1-9, Children, fathers, slaves and masters
entries.summary: The household code goes on to children and fathers, then to slaves and masters, asking something of each side and reminding masters that they and their slaves have the same Master in heaven.
entries.plain: Paul's household instructions move on to children and fathers, then to slaves and masters. Children are to obey their parents, as the commandment about honoring father and mother teaches, and fathers are to raise their children in the Lord's teaching without provoking them. Slaves are to serve wholeheartedly as if serving Christ, even when no one is watching, and masters are told to treat them the same way and stop threatening them, since both answer to one Master in heaven who plays no favorites.
entries.note: Codes told fathers how to govern children but did not normally address them; Wright notes that philosophers' codes ran only one way, while Paul gives children and slaves something owed to them (Keener and his notes; Wright). Paul sides with the minority who warned against harsh discipline (Keener and his notes). The cultural backgrounds article on slaves says household slaves faced the worst abuses, torture for evidence, beatings, sexual abuse and sale away from family, yet were "normally in better socioeconomic situations than free peasants", could earn money and often gained freedom, so Paul should not be read against slavery in the Americas. So far as is known only Paul tells masters to do the same for their slaves (Keener and his notes). What this implies about slavery is read differently. The article says "virtually no one was calling for the abolition of slavery", and Wright that Paul "could no more envisage a world without slavery" than we can a world without electricity; Keener and his notes find 6:9 pointing toward abolition; the ESV Study Bible says the system slowly died out through Christianity's influence, and the CSB Study Bible that Paul's words later fed the anti-slavery movement.

ideas.s: From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.
Children in the ancient world were loved but powerless. Status came with age, and a child had no rights or voice apart from the adults who provided for them.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.

entries.title: Ephesians 6:10-17, The armor of God
entries.summary: Paul calls the believers to stand firm in God's armor, because their struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.
entries.plain: Paul closes his teaching with a call to stand firm. The believers' real fight is with spiritual powers of evil, so they need the armor God supplies to hold their ground against the devil's schemes. He names each piece, truth, righteousness, readiness from the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and God's word, picturing each as part of a soldier's kit.
entries.note: The section works as a peroratio, the rousing close of a speech, much like a general's speech before battle (Keener and his notes). Where the armor comes from is read differently: most hearers in Asia Minor would first picture a Roman soldier (Keener and his notes), and the Zondervan dictionary thinks Paul drew on his Roman guards; the ESV Study Bible gives the Old Testament first place, and Arnold writes that "Most of the imagery comes straight from the book of Isaiah" (11:5; 52:7; 59:17), as Wright also notes. Only the sword can attack (the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright). The flaming arrows recall the darts of Eros, though Paul probably means slander and other attacks as well (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Struggle was "the typical term for the sport of wrestling", found on inscriptions for the games of western Asia Minor (Arnold), and philosophers spoke of wrestling with wicked ideas (Keener and his notes). Some pagan deities and star powers were called world rulers (Keener and his notes; Arnold). Heiser reads these words as rulers of geographical domains, while Arnold notes that Paul never names, ranks or places the powers.

ideas.s: The legionary was the most familiar picture of armed strength in the provinces: helmet, breastplate, boots, a big shield and a short sword, fighting shoulder to shoulder. Legions that held their ranks were thought almost unbeatable.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.

entries.title: Ephesians 6:18-24, An ambassador in chains, and the man who carried the letter
entries.summary: Paul asks for prayer that he may speak boldly, calling himself an ambassador in chains, and sends Tychicus to carry the letter and tell them his news.
entries.plain: Paul asks the believers to keep praying at all times, for all God's people and for him, so that he can speak the gospel boldly though he is in chains as Christ's ambassador. He is sending Tychicus, who will carry the letter, give them his news and encourage them. He ends by wishing them peace, love and grace.
entries.note: Chains, and being seen with anyone in chains, were humiliating (the cultural backgrounds notes). Envoys were to be received with the respect due to their sender, and as heralds "they were to be immune from hostility even if they represented an enemy kingdom" (Keener); chaining an envoy normally invited war (the cultural backgrounds notes). Wright calls the chained ambassador a deliberately bizarre picture: "An ambassador ought to be free to come and go." Philosophers prized frank speech (Keener and his notes), and Wright notes that Paul's word for boldly could almost mean brazenly. Mail traveled with travelers, and some news was safer spoken than written (Keener and his notes). Letters were usually carried by someone known to both sides who could explain them (the ESV Study Bible). Tychicus, a delegate of the province of Asia with the collection (Acts 20:4; the Zondervan dictionary), probably carried Ephesians and Colossians together, since the lines about him nearly match Colossians 4:7-8 (the CSB Study Bible; Wright); a circular, Carson, Moo and Morris note, would be filled out by his own comments. Wright pictures him on a round trip through the churches of the Lycus valley.

ideas.s: An ambassador spoke for one state to another, in Paul's day usually as the emperor's legate in the East. The way an envoy was received honored or insulted the one who sent him, and communities chose respected envoys to carry their gifts.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: Philippians 1:1-11, A letter between friends, and a partnership in the gospel
entries.summary: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Philippi with their overseers and deacons, thank God for their partnership in the gospel from the first day, and pray that their love will grow until the day of Christ.
entries.plain: Paul and Timothy write to the believers at Philippi and their leaders. Paul thanks God for the way this church has worked with him in spreading the gospel since the day they first believed, and he is sure God will finish what he started in them. He prays that their love will keep growing in wisdom, so that they can tell what matters most and be ready for the day Christ returns.
entries.note: No serious doubt is raised that Paul wrote the letter, but where he was held is disputed, and the answer moves the date between the mid fifties and the early sixties (Carson, Moo and Morris). Rome is the traditional view (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Wright, and Wright and Bird, prefer Ephesus, nearer for the journeys the letter implies, and Carson, Moo and Morris cite "inscriptions showing that a section of the praetorian guard was stationed at Ephesus". They set Caesarea aside, lean slightly to Ephesus, and call the place "an insoluble problem". Partnership, koinonia, was the normal word for a business partnership and here takes in the gift of 4:10-20 (Wright; Keener and his notes). Prisoners were not normally fed by their captors and had to rely on friends (Wright). Most people were "ashamed to be associated with anyone chained or in custody" of Rome, all the more in proud Roman Philippi (the cultural backgrounds notes). Overseers and deacons appear together again in 1 Timothy 3; the ESV Study Bible calls the level of church order uncertain (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

ideas.n: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.

entries.title: Philippians 1:12-26, Chains known to the whole palace guard
entries.summary: Paul tells how his imprisonment has carried the gospel through the palace guard and made other preachers bolder, some from rivalry, then weighs living against dying and expects to stay on for their sake.
entries.plain: Paul reassures his friends that his imprisonment has helped the gospel, since the guards now know why he is held and other believers have grown bolder. Some preach out of rivalry, but he is glad Christ is preached either way. He weighs living against dying: death would take him to Christ, but staying alive means more fruitful work for them, and he expects to stay.
entries.note: Stoics held that imprisonment and death did not matter, only one's attitude, and Paul partly agrees, for his own reasons (Keener and his notes). What the palace guard was depends on where Paul was: the Praetorian Guard, the emperor's elite troops counted as part of his household (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible; the Zondervan dictionary, which notes their triple pay); a governor's residence, as at Caesarea (Acts 23:35); or, for Wright, the guard found at "every major centre of Roman influence", Ephesus included. Wright adds that the soldiers knew the gospel of Caesar, news of a new emperor bringing peace. Who the rival preachers were is read differently: believers at odds with Paul (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Carson, Moo and Morris, since they preach Christ), or, Wright suggests, "ordinary pagans" gossiping about the prisoner. Deliverance follows the Greek of Job 13:16 and here means release (Keener and his notes), though the ESV Study Bible leaves room for final salvation. Keener thinks Paul was released in AD 62, when Nero freed the Jewish hostages Felix had sent to Rome.

ideas.s: Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

entries.title: Philippians 1:27-30, Live as citizens, contend like athletes
entries.summary: Paul tells a church in a Roman colony to conduct itself as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing firm and striving together, unafraid of opponents, in the same struggle they once saw him face.
entries.plain: Paul tells a church in a Roman colony to live as citizens whose conduct fits the gospel. Whether he visits or only hears news, he wants to know they are standing together, working side by side for the faith and unshaken by opponents. Suffering for Christ is part of what God has given them, and it is the same struggle they once watched Paul go through.
entries.note: Conduct yourselves, politeuesthe, was citizens' language (Keener and his notes). Philippi was a Roman colony on the Egnatian Way, which ran along the north side of its forum, and it held the ius Italicum, "rights legally equivalent to those of Italian cities" (the cultural backgrounds article). Who settled it is read differently: the victors' veterans after the battle of 42 BC (Wright; Wright and Bird; the ESV Study Bible), the defeated armies (the CSB Study Bible), or, after Actium, Antony's partisans unwanted in Italy (the Zondervan dictionary). How Roman it was is also read differently: Wright pictures a resented Latin-speaking elite over a Greek town, and the Zondervan dictionary calls the city "still more Greek in culture than Roman". Wright and Bird note a cohort of praetorians there and the cult of the deified Augustus. Striving together and struggle are athletic words, as of one team (Keener and his notes; Wright). Their opponents' destruction and their own salvation echo the hope that God would destroy his people's oppressors (Isaiah 66:14-16; Keener and his notes); Carson, Moo and Morris see these opponents as outsiders, unlike the rivals of 1:15.

ideas.s: Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.

The legionary was the most familiar picture of armed strength in the provinces: helmet, breastplate, boots, a big shield and a short sword, fighting shoulder to shoulder. Legions that held their ranks were thought almost unbeatable.

entries.title: Philippians 2:1-11, The form of a slave, a cross, and every knee
entries.summary: Paul urges humility and concern for others, then sets out Christ, who did not exploit his equality with God but took the form of a slave and died on a cross, and whom God exalted so that every knee will bow.
entries.plain: Paul asks the church to be united and humble, putting others' interests ahead of their own. He holds up Christ as the pattern: though he shared God's status, he did not use it for his own gain but gave it up, took the place of a slave and went all the way to death on a cross. So God raised him above all, and one day every being everywhere will bow and confess Jesus as Lord, to the Father's glory.
entries.note: Moral writers proved points with examples: here Jesus, then Paul, Timothy and Epaphroditus (Keener and his notes). Whether 2:6-11 is an earlier hymn Paul quotes is debated. Keener and his notes report the majority view that he does; Carson, Moo and Morris weigh the rare words and rhythm on both sides and judge "we should probably see it as coming from Paul", which the ESV Study Bible thinks just as likely; Wright leaves it open. Taking a slave's form ran against everything expected of persons of status (the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright and Bird). Wright sets the poem against Alexander, who suggested his own divinity, and Augustus, whom grateful subjects came to treat as divine, and against Adam's grasping. Isaiah 45:23, where every knee bows to Israel's God, is applied to Jesus (Keener and his notes). Who bows under the earth is read differently: the shadowy dead of Greek myth (Keener and his notes); the dead, saved and lost (the CSB Study Bible); or every spirit power, astral, earthly and underworld, which "will be forced to recognize Christ's sovereign lordship" (Arnold). On harpagmos, Wright and Bird and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles favor not exploiting what he already had.

Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: Philippians 2:12-18, Lights in a crooked generation, poured out like a drink offering
entries.summary: Paul urges the Philippians to work out their salvation without grumbling, shining like stars in a crooked generation, and pictures himself poured out like a drink offering on their sacrifice.
entries.plain: Paul urges the Philippians to keep obeying while he is away as they did when he was with them, carrying their salvation through to its end with reverent awe, since God himself is at work in them. They are to stop grumbling and quarreling, so that they stand out like lights in a twisted world and hold on to the message of life. Paul pictures his own life being poured out as an offering alongside their faith, and he invites them to share his joy.
entries.note: Letters were treated as standing in for the writer, and Jewish texts often paired fear and trembling (Keener and his notes; the cultural backgrounds notes). Grumbling recalls Israel in the wilderness, and the crooked generation comes from Deuteronomy 32:5 (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Wright). Shine like lights recalls Daniel 12:3, where the raised righteous shine like the stars (Keener and his notes; Heiser; Wright), and the cultural backgrounds article on resurrection reports Jews who pictured the raised body as fire, like the stars. Drink offerings were familiar from Old Testament worship (Leviticus 23:18, 37; Numbers 28:7-10) and among Gentiles, who poured them in memory of the dead and at banquets, usually wine (the cultural backgrounds notes; the Zondervan dictionary); Keener writes that "Ancient religions regularly poured out libations to the gods, usually wine but sometimes water". How the picture works is read differently: the CSB Study Bible makes Paul the substance poured out and the Philippians' faith the sacrifice, while Bailey stresses that poured is a word of worship, oil and wine being sacrificial elements.

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

entries.title: Philippians 2:19-30, Timothy and Epaphroditus, commended and sent
entries.summary: Paul commends Timothy as a son who serves with him and plans to send him soon, and sends home Epaphroditus, the church's messenger, who nearly died on their errand.
entries.plain: Paul plans to send Timothy soon and praises him as a helper who really cares for them and has worked beside Paul the way a son works with his father. Meanwhile he sends back Epaphroditus, whom the church had sent to help him and who fell ill and nearly died. Paul asks them to welcome him with joy and honor him, because he risked his life to serve Paul on their behalf.
entries.note: Travelers carried news and letters, and Paul waits for news of his trial before sending more (Keener and his notes; Wright). Superlative praise for more than one person was rare in letters of recommendation (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Teachers called close disciples sons (Keener and his notes), and Wright adds that most sons learned their father's trade by watching him. Whether the Philippians knew Timothy is read differently: Carson, Moo and Morris think the commendation suggests they did not know him well, while Wright and the Zondervan dictionary put him with Paul when the church was founded. Travel lowered resistance to typhoid and malaria, especially by sea near the dangerous winter season, mid-November to early March (Keener and his notes; the cultural backgrounds article on travel); Gentiles prayed to Asclepius, often hailed as savior, for healing (Keener and his notes; Arnold). Risked was a gamblers' word, and gamblers called on their goddess with the word epaphroditus, so a pun is possible (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The cultural backgrounds notes mention that he may be the Epaphras of Colossians 4:12; the Zondervan dictionary sees no reason to identify them.

ideas.s: A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

ideas.n: Roads, robbers and the dangers of travel
ideas.s: Travel by land was slow and risky. Robbers worked the lonely roads, rivers had to be forded, and news moved no faster than the people who carried it.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

entries.title: Philippians 3:1-11, Dogs, mutilators, and a pedigree counted as loss
entries.summary: Paul warns against teachers who press circumcision, calling them dogs and mutilators, lists his own credentials as a born Jew, a Pharisee and a zealous persecutor, and counts them all loss for the sake of knowing Christ.
entries.plain: Paul warns sharply against teachers who press circumcision on Gentile believers, using insulting names for them. If anyone could boast in Jewish credentials it was Paul, and he lists his birth, tribe, training as a Pharisee, zeal as a persecutor and strict keeping of the law. Yet he now counts all of it as loss compared with knowing Christ, being right with God through faith, sharing in Christ's sufferings and reaching the resurrection.
entries.note: Some scholars see two or three letters joined here, citing the sharp break at 3:1 and Polycarp's mention of Paul's letters to Philippi; Carson, Moo and Morris answer that Paul breaks off abruptly elsewhere and "It is better to see this as one letter", as Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes, the ESV Study Bible and Wright and Bird also hold. The targets are traveling teachers like those in Galatia (Keener and his notes; Wright); Carson, Moo and Morris list other proposals, from non-Christian Jews to perfectionists, and think Paul is "fighting on two fronts". Dogs was a stock insult: Jews viewed dogs as unclean, and some called Gentiles dogs, so Paul turns the insult back (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible); Wright notes that ancient dogs were mostly wild, seldom pets. Mutilation, katatome, puns on circumcision, and Wright hears in it the pagan cults that gashed the body. Eighth-day circumcision put Paul above any convert (Keener and his notes). Hebrew of Hebrews may mean a family that kept the Hebrew language and customs (the Zondervan dictionary), though Keener calls it unclear. Phinehas and the Maccabees, the models of zeal, used violence (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.

entries.title: Philippians 3:12-4:1, The race, citizens of heaven, and a Savior from there
entries.summary: Paul pictures himself as a runner straining toward the prize, warns against those whose god is their stomach, and reminds a Roman colony that its citizenship is in heaven, from where it awaits a Savior who will transform its lowly bodies.
entries.plain: Paul pictures himself as a runner who has not finished the race but keeps pushing toward the prize God calls him to. He asks the church to follow his example and warns against people whose lives deny the cross, ruled by appetite and focused on earthly things. To believers in a Roman colony he says their true citizenship is in heaven, and from there they await a Savior who will change their weak bodies to be like his glorious one.
entries.note: Greek runners ran a straight course, and heralds called the winner up for his prize (Keener and his notes). Sages admitted they were not yet perfect; Keener sets this above the mystery cults' use of perfection, while Carson, Moo and Morris and the Zondervan dictionary think Paul may be answering people who claimed perfection. Who the enemies of the cross were is read differently: the teachers of 3:2, with belly meaning food laws (the CSB Study Bible; some in Carson, Moo and Morris); people ruled by their passions (Keener and his notes; the Zondervan dictionary); or mainly pagans driven by appetite (Wright). Philippi's citizens were citizens of Rome, "citizens of a place they had never yet visited" (the cultural backgrounds notes), though not every resident was one (Keener and his notes). Wright notes that colonists were not meant to return to Rome, and in trouble hoped the emperor, called savior, would come to rescue them; Caesar's cult was the colony's latest Roman custom. Gods, rulers and the emperor were all called savior (Keener; the Zondervan dictionary), but the title for Jesus comes from Isaiah's language for God (Isaiah 43:11). A crown usually meant a victor's wreath (Keener and his notes).

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: Philippians 4:2-9, Two women at odds, names in the book of life, and whatever is true
entries.summary: Paul pleads with two women who worked beside him to agree, asks a companion to help them, notes that their names are in the book of life, and urges joy, prayer instead of worry, and thoughts fixed on whatever is true and excellent.
entries.plain: Paul urges two women who once worked hard beside him, Euodia and Syntyche, to settle their disagreement, and asks a trusted companion to help them. He calls the whole church to rejoice, to be gentle, and to replace worry with prayer and thanks, so that God's peace guards them. He closes by telling them to fill their minds with what is true and good and to practice what they saw in him.
entries.note: Euodia and Syntyche are Greek names in a Roman colony, perhaps merchants like Lydia, though that is a guess; some suggest they led separate house churches (Keener and his notes). Inscriptions show women active in Philippi's religious life (Keener and his notes). Their role is read differently: the ESV Study Bible thinks they ministered mainly among women, the CSB Study Bible that they were influential without a known office. Wright notes that the quarrel must have run for some time, since Paul heard of it from Epaphroditus. The loyal companion has been read as a proper name (the ESV Study Bible), for which the Zondervan dictionary finds no evidence, or as Epaphroditus or a known leader (Wright). Tradition links Clement with the author of 1 Clement (Keener and his notes), but the Zondervan dictionary adds that "most scholars think this is unlikely". Rejoice, Wright writes, meant public celebration in cities that held festivals for their gods and for Caesar. The Stoics held anxiety pointless because Fate could not be resisted (the cultural backgrounds notes), and Wright adds that "Anxiety was a way of life for many in the ancient pagan world", with gods who might be offended unawares.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Philippians, Situation, introduction to 4:2-9, and on Philippians 4:2, 4:3, 4:6-7 and 4:8

ideas.s: Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.
An old picture of God keeping a register of the names of those who belong to him. Jewish writers developed it, and the New Testament uses it from Luke to Revelation.
The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

entries.title: Philippians 4:10-23, A thank-you without a thank you, and Caesar's household
entries.summary: Paul acknowledges the Philippians' gift in the language of contentment and of business receipts and sacrifice, without a direct thank you, and closes with greetings from the saints of Caesar's household.
entries.plain: Paul thanks the Philippians for their gift without ever quite saying thank you. He explains that he has learned to be content whether he has plenty or little, because Christ gives him strength, yet he values their generosity, which has marked them out from the start. He describes the gift in the language of accounts and of sacrifice, promises that God will meet their needs, and sends greetings, including from believers in Caesar's household.
entries.note: Gratitude to benefactors was an essential virtue, and Keener reports that in Macedonia "an ungrateful man was said to have been liable to prosecution there"; yet a plain thank you could have cast Paul as a dependent client (Keener and his notes). Wright and Bird call the relationship a reciprocal partnership, and Wright adds that Paul had to avoid looking like the wandering teachers seen as "crooks and cheats". Carson, Moo and Morris think he had probably thanked them before. I have received full payment was "common language in ancient receipts" (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Philippi alone kept supporting Paul after he left, at Thessalonica and at Corinth (Wright). Caesar's household meant the emperor's slaves and freedmen, his civil service across the empire (the Zondervan dictionary), and carried great prestige (Keener). Keener and his notes think the guard is meant; the ESV Study Bible says soldiers, slaves or freedmen, and the CSB Study Bible civil servants. The Zondervan dictionary calls Rome the natural inference, while Wright and Bird and Carson, Moo and Morris point to the emperor's staff at Ephesus; Carson, Moo and Morris add that the Philippians' lack of opportunity (4:10) sits oddly with Rome.

ideas.s: Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: Colossians 1:1-14, Epaphras's report and a change of kingdoms
entries.summary: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Colossae, a church Paul has never visited, thank God for what Epaphras has told them, and pray that they grow in knowledge, having been rescued out of darkness into the kingdom of God's Son.
entries.plain: Paul and Timothy write to a church Paul has never visited, founded by Epaphras, who has told Paul about their faith and love. Paul says he keeps praying that they will understand God's will and live lives that please him and bear fruit. He reminds them that God has rescued them from the realm of darkness and moved them into the kingdom of his Son, where their sins are forgiven.
entries.note: Authorship is disputed: from Bultmann on, many have called the letter a follower's work, while Carson, Moo and Morris, the cultural backgrounds notes, the ESV and CSB Study Bibles and Wright and Bird hold it Paul's; Carson, Moo and Morris add that an imitator "would have selected a city of some importance". Where Paul wrote is disputed too: Rome, about AD 60 to 62 (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), or Ephesus in the mid fifties (Wright; Wright and Bird); Carson, Moo and Morris find that the Ephesus arguments "cancel each other out" and give a little more weight to Rome. Colossae lay in Phrygia's Lycus valley, about ten miles from Laodicea, and by Paul's day was the least of the three (Keener and his notes). It has never been excavated; its coins show Isis, the Ephesian Artemis, the Zeus of Laodicea and other gods (Arnold; Wright and Bird). An earthquake struck the valley about AD 60 or 61, and many date the letter before it (Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Moving from one kingdom to another suggested citizenship to Keener, deportation and colonization to Arnold, and the Exodus to the ESV Study Bible and Wright.

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: Colossians 1:15-20, Firstborn over creation, over thrones and powers
entries.summary: Paul describes the Son as the image of the unseen God and firstborn over all creation, through whom and for whom everything was made, thrones and powers included, and through whose cross God makes peace with all things.
entries.plain: In lines that read like a hymn, Paul presents the Son as the visible likeness of the unseen God and the one who holds first place over creation. Everything was made through him and for him, including every throne and spiritual power, and he keeps it all together. He is also the head of the church and the first to rise from death, and through his death on the cross God makes peace with all things. Whether Paul quotes an existing hymn or wrote the lines himself is debated.
entries.note: Paul describes Christ in the terms Judaism used for divine Wisdom, God's image through which he made the world, and Philo calls God's Logos his image and firstborn (Keener and his notes; the cultural backgrounds article). That article adds that "Many Gentiles deemed divine or partly divine a range of spirits", and Paul sets all such powers under Christ. Firstborn named rank and inheritance, not birth order (Keener and his notes; Wright and Bird; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Whether the thrones and dominions are good or evil is disputed: four classes of angels (the CSB Study Bible), ranks of angels with evil ones in view (the ESV Study Bible), or all hostile, the same rulers being defeated in 2:15 (Arnold); Heiser finds no agreed order. Keener writes that reconciling the powers "refers to their subordination rather than their salvation", and Arnold agrees: "They are subjected against their will." Whether verses 15-20 are an earlier hymn is debated: Keener reports a consensus short of proof, Carson, Moo and Morris note O'Neill's denial of hymnic form, the cultural backgrounds article that speakers turned to rhythmic prose when praising a deity, and Wright and Bird think Paul may have written it.

ideas.s: Greek thinkers spoke of the logos, the reason that ordered the world, and Jewish teachers spoke of God's Word and Wisdom, through whom he made everything. John opens his Gospel with that language and then says the Word became flesh.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Colossians 1:24-2:5, Sufferings for the body, and a steward of the mystery
entries.summary: Paul rejoices to suffer for the church, fills up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions, calls himself the servant entrusted with God's long hidden mystery, and tells churches he has never met how hard he struggles for them.
entries.plain: Paul says he is glad to suffer for the church, and he links his sufferings, in a much discussed phrase, with Christ's own sufferings for his body. God gave him the job of making known a secret hidden for ages, that Christ lives among the Gentiles and gives them hope of glory. He works hard for believers in Colossae and Laodicea he has never met, so that no one talks them out of what they have, and though absent he is with them in spirit.
entries.note: What is lacking in Christ's afflictions is disputed. Many Jewish traditions held that a set measure of suffering, sometimes called the Messiah's birth pangs, had to come before the end, and many scholars read Paul as taking on a share of it, as Wright and Bird and Wright's commentary do; Keener and his notes add that Paul plainly thinks Christ's own suffering enough for redemption. The ESV Study Bible reads it as the future suffering of all who suffer for the gospel, and the CSB Study Bible as Paul's sufferings spreading the message. The Dead Sea Scrolls speak of mysteries only the enlightened understand, and a mystery openly announced would answer anyone claiming private revelation (Keener and his notes); the cultural backgrounds article on mystery cults adds that "Converts to Christianity were not sworn to keep its tenets or practices a secret", and Arnold reads 2:2-3 as saying no initiation is needed for further wisdom. Absent in body, present in spirit was letter language for affection (Keener and his notes), and Wright thinks the good order of 2:5 probably sounded like soldiers in formation.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
Cults that a person entered by a secret initiation, often held at night. Some promised freedom from Fate, some had a name for drunken or immoral rites, and Rome distrusted them as foreign.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: Colossians 2:8-15, The philosophy, a cancelled IOU and a triumph
entries.summary: Paul warns against a philosophy built on human tradition and the elements of the world, tells Gentile believers they have already been circumcised in Christ, and pictures God cancelling their debt at the cross and leading the powers captive.
entries.plain: Paul warns the believers not to be taken in by an empty philosophy built on human tradition and the elements of the world instead of on Christ. All of God's fullness lives in Christ, and in him they already have everything, including a circumcision done by God in their baptism. At the cross God cancelled the record of their debts and stripped the hostile powers, leading them like captives in a victory parade.
entries.note: Outsiders sometimes took Jewish and Christian groups for philosophical schools (Keener and his notes), and the word was used broadly, even of magic (the ESV Study Bible; Arnold). Takes you captive could mean seized as a prisoner of war (Keener and his notes), and Wright hears a pun: the verb sylagogon "is very close to the word ‘synagogue’", a warning against being lured into the synagogue. Arnold reads two sources of the teaching: human tradition, and behind it the elemental spirits that "inspire this teaching". What the cancelled record was is read differently: "Paul intends his readers to think of an IOU before God," Keener writes; the law of Moses, for Wright, which the CSB Study Bible allows; or the written code with its regulations (Carson, Moo and Morris). In a Roman triumph the general led humiliated captives (Keener), and Wright adds that the defeated king came last and was executed as the climax, so every crucifixion of a rebel king was a small Roman triumph, here reversed. Arnold notes that the verb for making a public spectacle was used of disgracing an adulteress. Heiser reads the rulers as the rebel sons of God set over the nations.

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

Paul twice says that people were enslaved under the stoicheia, the elements of the world. The word could mean basic rules, the stuff the world is made of, or the powers people worshiped in nature and the stars, and scholars still disagree which he meant.

Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.
A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.

Rome celebrated a great victory with a triumph, a parade of the general, his army and the spoils, with chained captives at the end who were killed or sold. Cities also staged shows in which condemned criminals fought or were thrown to beasts.

entries.title: Colossians 2:16-23, Food, new moons, Sabbaths and the worship of angels
entries.summary: Paul tells the believers not to let anyone judge them over food, drink, festivals, new moons or Sabbaths, or disqualify them with self-denial, the worship of angels and visions, and calls rules about what not to touch or taste human commands with no power over the flesh.
entries.plain: Paul tells the believers not to let anyone judge them over food, drink, festivals, new moons or Sabbaths, which he calls a shadow of what came in Christ. Nor should they let anyone rule them out who insists on harsh self-denial, angel worship and visions. Rules about what not to touch or taste look wise but cannot curb the flesh. Who the teachers were, and what the worship of angels means, are both debated.
entries.note: The cultural backgrounds notes list "The three Jewish practices for which non-Jewish Romans especially mocked Jews": circumcision, food laws and holy days. What they have seen is the language of visions, and Arnold, following Ramsay, notes that the rare verb, literally entering, appears in inscriptions from Apollo's oracle at Claros for the climax of initiation, among visitors from Laodicea. The worship of angels is read as calling on angels for protection, close to magic (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible; Arnold), or as worship with the angels (the CSB Study Bible; Wright and Bird); Carson, Moo and Morris note that "The Jews did not worship angels, but they had quite an interest in them". Arnold links harsh treatment of the body with the cults of Cybele and Attis. Who the teachers were is the letter's oldest puzzle: a mystical Judaism (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), folk belief (the ESV Study Bible), Christianity plus initiation and magic (Arnold), a warning against Judaism with no false teachers inside (Wright, following Hooker), or "a blend of Jewish and Hellenistic teachings" that no one can pin down (Carson, Moo and Morris; the CSB Study Bible).

ideas.s: The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.
The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

Jewish visionaries told of being caught up through the heavens to see God's throne and paradise, and writers numbered the heavens differently. Paul's third heaven speaks that language, though he refuses to make it his credential.

Paul twice says that people were enslaved under the stoicheia, the elements of the world. The word could mean basic rules, the stuff the world is made of, or the powers people worshiped in nature and the stars, and scholars still disagree which he meant.

entries.title: Colossians 3:1-17, Things above, and no Greek, Jew, barbarian or Scythian
entries.summary: Raised with Christ, the believers are to set their minds on things above, put to death the old ways, take off the old self and put on the new, in which there is no Greek or Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, and above all put on love.
entries.plain: Since they have been raised with Christ, Paul tells the believers to fix their minds on heaven, where Christ reigns, and to kill off the old ways of sexual sin, greed, anger and lies. They have taken off the old self and put on a new one, being remade in their Creator's image, and in that new people the old labels of race, religion, culture and class no longer divide. Above all they are to clothe themselves with love, let Christ's peace rule among them, and do everything in the Lord's name.
entries.note: Philosophers were known for gazing upward, and Jewish apocalyptic writers stressed the purity of God's upper heavens; in Paul's version the one thing named in heaven is Christ (Keener and his notes). The vices of verse 5 were the ones Jews thought typical of Gentiles (Keener and his notes). The old self and the new probably allude to Adam and Christ, and image and Creator echo Genesis 1:26-27 (Keener and his notes). Putting off and putting on may borrow the moralists' image of armor or the Jewish image of being clothed with virtues. Keener notes that how churches outside Judea baptized is unknown, while Wright thinks the early custom by which "a candidate for baptism would take off the old suit of clothes" may well be in mind. Barbarian meant every non-Greek, and Scythians, nomads north of the Black Sea, were thought the most cruel of peoples (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible; the Zondervan dictionary), "the people furthest away from what they regarded as civilization" (Wright). Slave or free was a main social division, though some household slaves outranked many free people (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Jewish visionaries told of being caught up through the heavens to see God's throne and paradise, and writers numbered the heavens differently. Paul's third heaven speaks that language, though he refuses to make it his credential.

The Old Testament says little about Adam outside Genesis, but by Paul's day Jewish writers spoke often of his lost glory and of the sin and death he brought into the world. Each person, they added, became his own Adam.
Greeks split humanity into Greeks and barbarians, people whose speech sounded like babble. Jews split it into Israel and the nations. Paul uses both maps.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: Colossians 3:18-4:1, The household code
entries.summary: Paul addresses wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters in the form of an ancient household code, tells husbands to love and fathers not to embitter, and reminds masters that they too have a Master in heaven.
entries.plain: Paul uses a familiar ancient pattern of household instructions, speaking in turn to wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. Each side gets a duty: wives are to yield, husbands to love and not be harsh, children to obey, fathers to avoid crushing their children's spirit. Slaves are to work wholeheartedly, as for the Lord, even when unobserved, and masters are to be just and fair because they too answer to a Master in heaven. How far Paul reshapes the old pattern, and what that means for slavery, is debated.
entries.note: Minority religions suspected of undermining the family used household codes to show they upheld Roman values; Keener writes, "Paul takes over but modifies the codes considerably." The codes told husbands how to rule, while "Paul instructs husbands here how to love" (the cultural backgrounds notes). Wright notes that, unlike many pagan moralists, Paul balances every duty with one owed back. Law treated slaves as persons by nature but as property, and a master could legally execute his slaves, who "would all be executed if the head of the household were murdered" (the cultural backgrounds article on Philemon; Keener and his notes). Household slaves could earn money and often won freedom, though owners sometimes freed them in midlife to avoid keeping them in old age (the cultural backgrounds article on Ephesians 6). Wright likens slavery's place to that of engines and electricity now. How far Paul goes is disputed: Keener thinks his belief in equality before God shows he does not favor slavery; the ESV Study Bible says Scripture regulates servitude without commending it, the CSB Study Bible that Paul governed the structures with Christian principles, and Wright and Bird that later abolition may owe him its roots.

ideas.s: From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.
Children in the ancient world were loved but powerless. Status came with age, and a child had no rights or voice apart from the adults who provided for them.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: Colossians 4:7-18, Tychicus, Onesimus, Nympha's house and the letter from Laodicea
entries.summary: Paul sends the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus, passes on greetings from Jewish and Gentile co-workers, greets Nympha and the church in her house, asks for this letter to be read at Laodicea and the Laodicean letter at Colossae, and signs off in his own hand.
entries.plain: Paul sends the letter with Tychicus, along with Onesimus, a member of their own church. He passes on greetings from co-workers, among them Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke and Demas, and greets Nympha and the church that meets in her house. He asks for this letter to be swapped with one sent to Laodicea, then signs off in his own hand and asks them to remember he is in chains.
entries.note: Letters went whenever someone happened to travel, and Paul sends Tychicus on purpose (Keener and his notes), probably with Ephesians and Philemon (the ESV Study Bible; Wright). Onesimus is probably the slave of the letter to Philemon (Keener and his notes; Wright); where he had fled is read differently, Ephesus for Wright and Rome, "the frequent goal of such fugitives", for the Zondervan dictionary. Wright thinks the church may have numbered "no more than a dozen or so". Hierapolis had a large Jewish community (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), and Price and House cite an undated inscription there naming the community of the Jews of Hierapolis. Nympha may have been widowed or divorced, and the feminine form is probably original (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), though the Zondervan dictionary notes that the accent and some manuscripts leave it uncertain whether a man or a woman is meant. Whether the letter from Laodicea survives is debated: perhaps Ephesians sent as a circular (the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright and Bird; Wright; the CSB Study Bible; the Zondervan dictionary), or a lost letter (the ESV Study Bible; Keener; Carson, Moo and Morris, since no copy is addressed to Laodicea).

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10, Turned to God from idols
entries.summary: Paul, Silas and Timothy thank God for a young church that received the message in the middle of suffering, whose story is now told everywhere: they turned to God from idols to serve him and to wait for his Son from heaven.
entries.plain: Paul, Silas and Timothy thank God for a young church that took hold of the message with joy even while suffering for it. Their faith, love and hope have become an example across Macedonia and Achaia. Everyone is talking about how they left their idols to serve the true God and now wait for his Son, raised from the dead, to come from heaven and rescue them.
entries.note: No serious objection has been raised to Paul's authorship, and Carson, Moo and Morris place the letter at Corinth soon after Timothy arrived, probably in AD 50, among Paul's earliest letters, since Gallio, before whom Paul later stood there, came in about 51 (also the Zondervan dictionary and the atlas). Some read 3:6 as Timothy reaching Paul at Athens, but the spread of the church's fame "everywhere" (1:8) suggests more time (Carson, Moo and Morris). Thessalonica, founded in 315 BC by Cassander and named for his wife, was Macedonia's chief port and the province's capital, on the Via Egnatia, prosperous, with a large Roman element and a Jewish colony (the atlas; the Zondervan dictionary). Keener lists its cults, Serapis and Isis, Dionysus, and the Cabirus cult from Samothrace, and the cultural backgrounds notes add a significant temple for the emperor. Turning from idols cost family and civic ties, and Tacitus faulted Judaism for teaching converts to despise the gods (Keener and his notes). Acts names Jews and God-fearing Greeks, while 1:9 implies Gentiles; Carson, Moo and Morris think there were converts from both.
