ideas.s: The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 2:1-12, Gentle as a nurse, firm as a father
entries.summary: Paul reminds the church how he and his companions came to them after being mistreated in Philippi: no deceit, flattery or greed, gentle among them like a nursing mother, working night and day so as not to burden anyone, and urging each of them like a father.
entries.plain: Paul says their visit was not in vain: after being shamefully treated in Philippi, they dared to speak God's message in Thessalonica in spite of strong opposition. Their appeal did not come from error, impure motives or trickery; they spoke to please God, not people, never used flattery or cover for greed, and did not look for praise. Instead they were gentle among them, like a nursing mother caring for her children, sharing their own lives as well as the gospel, and working night and day so as not to be a burden. Like a father with his children, they urged each one to live in a way worthy of God, who calls them into his kingdom and glory.
entries.note: Wandering philosophers were often written off as frauds, and Keener, following Malherbe, notes that Dio Chrysostom accused most Cynics of the faults Paul denies here, while observing that "a true philosopher is gentle, like a nurse". Whether Paul answers real opponents is read differently: Keener and his notes think he need not be; the ESV Study Bible allows real or expected accusations; Carson, Moo and Morris and the Zondervan dictionary think Jewish opponents were slandering him as a man after money with a message of his own. The nurse could be a wet nurse or a nursing mother; Keener says the choice "does not affect Paul's point: gentleness". Some manuscripts read infants instead of gentle (the CSB Study Bible). A laborer could talk with visitors at the bench (Keener and his notes), and Malherbe, as Carson, Moo and Morris report, pictures the insula, shops on the street with families living behind, as a natural place to preach. How long Paul stayed is unclear: Acts names three Sabbaths, but work night and day and the Philippians' gift suggest longer, though Carson, Moo and Morris conclude that "Paul cannot have been in Thessalonica for more than a matter of months".

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

ideas.n: Manual work and the leisured class
ideas.s: The well-to-do despised people who worked with their hands. A respectable teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees or even on begging, so an apostle who made tents for his keep looked low class.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 2:17-3:13, Orphaned, blocked by Satan, crowned
entries.summary: Torn away from the church, Paul tells how he longed to come back but Satan blocked the way, how he sent Timothy from Athens, how Timothy's good news has revived him, and prays that the Lord will make them blameless at his coming with all his holy ones.
entries.plain: Paul explains why he has not come back: he was torn away from them, tried again and again to return, and says Satan blocked him. Unable to wait any longer, he sent Timothy from Athens to strengthen them under pressure. Timothy's good report of their faith and love has revived him, and he prays that God will make them holy and blameless at Jesus' coming, with all his holy ones.
entries.note: Keener writes, "Ancients sometimes spoke of Fate hindering them." What Satan's blocking was is not said: Jewish opposition or the city magistrates (Keener), "matters politically indiscreet to mention in a letter that would be read publicly" (the cultural backgrounds notes), persecution, illness or Jason's bond (the CSB Study Bible), threats to Paul's life (Wright), or unknown (the ESV Study Bible). Arnold lists similar guesses and adds that "Paul perceived Satan's hand as behind it", where in Acts 16:6-10 the Spirit redirects him. Thessalonica was a free city, so its politarchs' ban held only there and only while they were in office (the cultural backgrounds notes). Timothy may have reached Paul at Athens and been sent back, but Carson, Moo and Morris think 3:6 means his arrival at Corinth. The crown is a victor's wreath, and Jewish texts used crowns for future reward (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). The holy ones of 3:13 recall Zechariah 14:5: God's people, which Keener thinks Paul usually means, the angels, or, for Heiser, a returning army of divine beings and glorified people.

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
Some Greek cities, such as Thessalonica and Ephesus, kept a measure of self-rule under Rome, with their own officials and a citizen assembly. A riot could cost a city those privileges.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8, Holiness in the body
entries.summary: Paul reminds the church of the instructions he passed on from the Lord Jesus: God's will is that they be holy, avoid sexual immorality, control their own bodies in holiness and honor, and not wrong a brother in this matter.
entries.plain: Paul reminds the church of the way of life he taught them with the Lord's authority, and urges them to keep growing in it. God wants them holy, which means keeping clear of sexual sin, learning to manage this part of life with honor rather than lust, and never wronging a fellow believer in this area. To reject this is to reject God, who gives them his Holy Spirit. Whether the word for body here means one's own body or a wife is debated.
entries.note: Greek men often married at about thirty, women some twelve years younger, partly because more girls were abandoned at birth, and before marriage men commonly slept with prostitutes, slaves or other males (Keener and his notes; the cultural backgrounds article on prostitution). The article adds that "Gentiles did not punish married men’s affairs with unmarried women", and Roman law punished a man's sex before marriage only when an aristocrat did it with a woman of rank, the offense called stuprum (Keener and his notes). Wright and Bird suggest Paul may have had in mind the sexual side of mystery cults such as Cabirus, and Arnold quotes Livy on the night rites of Dionysus, where wine and the mixing of the sexes led to every kind of corruption. Vessel was a figure for the body and occasionally for a wife; Keener, his notes and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles lean toward the body, and Keener calls the matter not beyond dispute. Adultery was often called wife stealing, and a husband who learned of his wife's adultery had to divorce her or face a charge of pimping (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

ideas.n: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
ideas.s: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

A Jewish husband ended a marriage, or a betrothal, by handing his wife a written certificate before witnesses that left her free to marry again, and the teachers argued over the grounds. In Greek and Roman law either partner could end a marriage by leaving.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 4:9-12, A quiet life and your own hands
entries.summary: Paul praises the church's love for the whole family of believers in Macedonia and urges them to love more, to live quietly, mind their own business and work with their hands, so that outsiders respect them and they depend on no one.
entries.plain: Paul says they hardly need teaching on love, since they already love believers across Macedonia, but he urges them to love even more. He also asks them to live quietly, look after their own affairs and work with their hands, so that outsiders respect them and they rely on no one. Why some were not working is debated.
entries.note: Moralists wrote on love of family, and the word here is love of brothers; Paul treats all believers as one family (Keener and his notes), and Wright and Bird take the love as practical and financial support. Keeping aloof from public life was an Epicurean ideal, though "Only members of the upper classes followed Epicureanism" (the cultural backgrounds article on philosophies); for a persecuted minority a quiet life was wise, "inconspicuous, not monastic" in Keener's words. The elite despised manual work, but it was how most people lived, and Thessalonica, though rich, had unemployed men loitering in the marketplace (Acts 17:5; Keener and his notes). Some depended on wealthier benefactors (the cultural backgrounds notes). Why some were idle is not agreed: the Zondervan dictionary says they had given up work to wait for the Lord, and Carson, Moo and Morris see the problem growing in the second letter; the ESV Study Bible suggests wrong ideas about the future or exploiting wealthier members; Wright points to the strain of the church's family-style sharing; Keener suggests the begging of Cynic philosophers.

ideas.s: Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

ideas.n: Manual work and the leisured class
ideas.s: The well-to-do despised people who worked with their hands. A respectable teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees or even on begging, so an apostle who made tents for his keep looked low class.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, Grief with hope, and the welcoming party
entries.summary: Paul tells a grieving church that believers who have died are not lost: when the Lord comes down from heaven with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air.
entries.plain: Some in the church have died, and Paul writes so that the others will not grieve like people with no hope. Because Jesus died and rose, God will bring the believing dead with him. When the Lord comes from heaven with a shout and a trumpet call, the dead will rise first and the living will join them to meet him, and then they will be with him always. What the meeting in the air implies is debated.
entries.note: Consolation letters were common, but "rarely with the kind of hope Paul offers here" (the cultural backgrounds article on Jesus' teachings). Keener writes that "Most pagans believed in a shadowy afterlife in the underworld", though the Dionysus mysteries promised initiates bliss (Arnold). Martyrdom was probably rare around AD 50 (Keener and his notes); Carson, Moo and Morris think the survivors feared the dead would miss the Lord's coming. Word of the Lord probably means a saying of Jesus (Keener and his notes); the article finds these images clustered only in Jesus' teaching, while the ESV Study Bible thinks a revelation to Paul more likely. Parousia could mean a king's visit, and the word for meeting meant that "people welcoming him would go to form his escort en route to his destination" (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible). What follows is disputed. Keener, his notes, Wright and Wright and Bird read the welcoming party as turning back with the king; the CSB Study Bible and the Zondervan dictionary read a taking up of living believers, the dictionary listing three timings without choosing; and Keener notes that a rapture before the tribulation is first explicit around 1830.

ideas.s: Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11, A thief in the night, and peace and security
entries.summary: Paul reminds the church that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night: while people say peace and security, sudden destruction comes like labor pains, but they are children of the day who keep awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope.
entries.plain: Paul tells them they already know that the Lord's day will arrive without warning, like a burglar at night. When people are saying all is calm and safe, ruin will fall on them suddenly. The believers belong to the day, so they are to stay alert and sober, armed with faith, love and hope, since God has destined them for salvation, and they should keep encouraging one another. Who was saying peace and security is debated.
entries.note: Paul echoes Jesus on the unknown time (Acts 1:7; Keener and his notes). The thief in the night is another saying of Jesus (Matthew 24:43), a motif the cultural backgrounds article finds uncommon in earlier Jewish sources. Wilkins notes that thieves dug through clay walls and that, since "modern conceptions of police force were nonexistent", each householder guarded his own home. Who says peace and security is disputed. Keener and his notes hear the emperors' claim, Wright calls it "one of the comforting phrases that the Roman empire put out"; the ESV Study Bible thinks an echo of Jeremiah 6:14 more likely. These labor pains are sudden and final, as in Isaiah 13:8 (Keener and his notes), and the article notes that Jewish sources stressed "the destruction of the wicked far more than its unexpectedness". The armor recalls the Lord as warrior in Isaiah 59:17 (the cultural backgrounds notes; Arnold). Whether the day of the Lord means the end of history or can cover events within it is debated: the CSB Study Bible and the Zondervan dictionary tie it to the end, while Wright reads it as giving events within history their meaning.

ideas.s: The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

The legionary was the most familiar picture of armed strength in the provinces: helmet, breastplate, boots, a big shield and a short sword, fighting shoulder to shoulder. Legions that held their ranks were thought almost unbeatable.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:12-28, Leaders, prophets, a holy kiss and a letter read to all
entries.summary: Paul asks the church to honor those who work hard over them, to warn the idle and help the weak, to rejoice, pray and give thanks, not to quench the Spirit or despise prophecy but test everything, and to have the letter read to all.
entries.plain: Paul closes with a quick run of instructions for church life. They are to respect those who lead and care for them, warn the idle, encourage the fearful, support the weak and never repay wrong with wrong. They are to keep rejoicing, praying and giving thanks, to welcome prophecy while testing everything, and Paul asks that the letter be read to every believer.
entries.note: The word for those over the church was used especially of patrons, so Keener suggests the members who hosted and sponsored it, Jason probably among them; the ESV Study Bible takes it of elders and the CSB Study Bible of church leaders, while Carson, Moo and Morris find no officials yet, a sign to them of an early date. Social rank demanded honor, and Christian leadership was meant to be service (the cultural backgrounds notes). The idle are those who can work but will not (Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Even the strictest Jews did not pray all day, but they prayed regularly (Keener). Most Jews linked the Spirit with prophecy, and new churches without senior prophets had to test prophecy together (Keener and his notes). Spirit, soul and body is a Jewish way of naming the whole person (Keener and his notes). A light kiss was the usual greeting among family and close friends (Keener and his notes; the Zondervan dictionary). Most people could read very little, so the letter had to be read aloud (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: 2 Thessalonians 1:3-12, Suffering now, and the Lord revealed in blazing fire
entries.summary: Paul thanks God for a church whose faith and love keep growing under persecution, and promises that God will repay their persecutors and give them relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his powerful angels in blazing fire.
entries.plain: Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians' faith and love keep growing while they suffer persecution. He tells them their endurance shows God's justice at work: God will repay those who trouble them and give them rest when the Lord Jesus appears from heaven with his angels. Those who reject God will be punished and banished from the Lord's presence, while Paul prays that God will make the believers worthy of their calling. What everlasting destruction means is debated.
entries.note: More scholars doubt this letter than the first: critics point to its signs before the end, a lawless one found nowhere else in Paul, a colder tone and close imitation of 1 Thessalonians, and date it after Paul's death. Carson, Moo and Morris answer that apocalypses often join an imminent end with signs, that the first letter's warmth comes from its self-defense, and that 3:17 makes any other author a forger; with Keener, his notes, the ESV Study Bible, Wright and Bird and the Zondervan dictionary, they place it at Corinth a few months after the first letter, about AD 50 or 51, and they keep the traditional order of the two. God's reward for the righteous who suffer was a major Jewish theme, and most Jews expected intense suffering before the end of the age (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The blazing fire recalls Isaiah 66:15 (Keener and his notes). The powerful angels are God's army, and Heiser reads them with Jude 14-15 as a returning army of divine beings and glorified people. Everlasting destruction in Jewish writings sometimes meant complete destruction, sometimes eternal suffering, and sometimes both in one passage (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.

entries.title: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12, The man of lawlessness and the restrainer
entries.summary: Paul tells a church unsettled by claims that the day of the Lord has already come that the rebellion must come first and the man of lawlessness be revealed, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God; something holds him back for now, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth.
entries.plain: Some in the church have been told, by a prophecy, a report or even a letter said to be from Paul, that the Lord's day is already here. Paul says it cannot be, because a great rebellion must come first and a man of lawlessness must appear who sets himself up as God in God's temple. Something or someone is holding him back for now, but when he appears the Lord Jesus will destroy him, and those who refused the truth will be deceived. Who the restrainer is, which temple is meant and how the passage is fulfilled are all debated.
entries.note: Coming and gathering both come from Jesus' sayings (Matthew 24:3, 27, 31) (Keener and his notes), and the cultural backgrounds article finds the coming, parousia, uncommon in earlier Jewish sources, while lawlessness, apostasy and false prophets were stock items in Jewish lists of end-time sufferings. How anyone could think the day had come is not obvious: Keener and his notes suggest Greeks with no idea of a future resurrection took the future as fulfilled; Wright and Bird argue that the claim shows the day cannot have meant the end of the world. The abomination recalls Daniel, and Daniel came to mind again when Pilate brought the emperor's images into Jerusalem in AD 26 and when Caligula ordered his statue set up in the temple (Wilkins); even Romans normally deified rulers only after death (the cultural backgrounds article on the imperial cult). Only here is he called the man of lawlessness, and Carson, Moo and Morris write, "He is telling us something new". Who sends the delusion is read differently: Heiser has Satan empower the signs and God send the delusion, Arnold has God permit "evil spirits of deception to delude non-Christians", and Wright compares Pharaoh's hardened heart.

ideas.s: A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.
The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.

Daniel's king who exalts himself above every god and defiles the sanctuary became a pattern Jews saw again in Antiochus, Pompey and Caligula. Paul's man of lawlessness, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God, belongs to that line.
Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: 2 Thessalonians 2:13-3:5, Hold to the traditions, and let the word run
entries.summary: Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians, urges them to stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught by word or by letter, prays for them, and asks them to pray that the Lord's message will run swiftly.
entries.plain: Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians to be saved through the Spirit's work and their trust in the truth. He urges them to hold on to the teaching they received from him, whether in person or by letter, and prays that God will encourage and strengthen them. He asks them to pray that the Lord's message spreads quickly and that he is rescued from wicked people, confident that the Lord will guard them.
entries.note: In the Old Testament God chose Israel, and the New Testament often calls Gentile believers chosen (Keener and his notes). Whether God chose them from the beginning or as firstfruits is a textual question: Carson, Moo and Morris find the manuscripts divided and prefer from the beginning, since scribes were likelier to change it to Paul's familiar firstfruits, and they reject theories that the letter went only to the church's first, Jewish converts. Pharisaic Judaism stressed handing on earlier teachers' traditions, and Paul passed on Jesus' sayings (Keener and his notes). By letter points back to an earlier letter, which the ESV Study Bible and Carson, Moo and Morris take as a sign that 1 Thessalonians came first; after weighing the case for reversing the order, Carson, Moo and Morris conclude, "It is better to retain the traditional order." The prayer that the word may run probably borrows from the Greek of Psalm 147:15 (Keener and his notes). Arnold notes that protect recurs in the magical papyri in recipes for amulets against evil spirits, so 3:3 promises protection of another kind; the evil one recalls the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:13; the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.

entries.title: 2 Thessalonians 3:6-18, The idle, the busybodies, and a greeting in Paul's own hand
entries.summary: Paul tells the church to keep away from believers who are idle and will not work, recalls how he worked night and day to set an example, lays down that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and signs the letter in his own hand.
entries.plain: Paul tells the church to keep its distance from believers who refuse to work and live off others. He reminds them that he and his companions worked hard to support themselves while they were there, as an example, and repeats his rule that those who will not work should not be fed. Those who will not listen are to be warned as brothers, not treated as enemies, and Paul signs the letter in his own hand. Why some were idle, and whether Paul wrote the letter, are both debated.
entries.note: By this period the word translated unruly usually meant idle (Keener); the ESV Study Bible gives undisciplined, and Wright pictures a dancer stepping out of line. "Despite the prosperity of Thessalonica as a whole, many people were unemployed" (the cultural backgrounds notes). Why some were idle is not agreed: Keener weighs contempt for labor, a belief that the day had come, and, more likely, Cynic habits, since "unlike Paul, Cynics begged rather than worked"; the CSB Study Bible and the Zondervan dictionary point to the day of the Lord; the ESV Study Bible notes that the letters never link idleness to the end; Wright points to the strain of family-style sharing; and Carson, Moo and Morris find Ellis's supported church workers hard to square with the rebuke. Synagogues had graded discipline, and this is the lightest form (Keener and his notes). Most writers used scribes and signed at the end, and lawyers often argued that documents were forged (Keener and his notes); Carson, Moo and Morris note that no other letter of Paul explains its autograph, which suggests unusual circumstances at Thessalonica (2:2).

ideas.n: Manual work and the leisured class
ideas.s: The well-to-do despised people who worked with their hands. A respectable teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees or even on begging, so an apostle who made tents for his keep looked low class.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 1:1-11, Myths, endless genealogies and would-be teachers of the law
entries.summary: Paul greets Timothy, whom he left in Ephesus, and tells him to stop certain people teaching strange doctrines and spending themselves on myths and endless genealogies; they want to be teachers of the law without understanding it, while the law is meant for the lawless.
entries.plain: Paul writes to Timothy, whom he left in Ephesus to stop certain people from spreading strange teaching and getting lost in myths and endless family trees. The aim of his instruction is love that comes from a clean heart, a clear conscience and real faith. These would-be teachers of the law do not understand it, Paul says, because the law exists to restrain wrongdoers, and he lists the kinds he means. Who wrote this letter, and what exactly the opponents taught, are both debated.
entries.note: Authorship is disputed more than for any other letter of Paul (Keener). Carson, Moo and Morris report that most critics credit a later admirer, citing vocabulary (306 words absent from Paul's ten letters, on P. N. Harrison's count), style, church order and the heresy; they reply that on those figures the three letters differ from one another as much as from Paul, and that "there is no evidence that the church accepted any pseudonymous epistle". These verses show the problem: Moule judged 1:8-9 impossible for Paul, while Zahn cited them for him. Keener and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles argue for Paul; Wright and Bird print Dunn's view against. In Paul for Everyone Wright notes that writing in another's name was common and need not be forgery, but will "leave the question open", as this guide does. If Paul's, the date is about AD 62 to 66; Robinson's AD 55 has convinced few; deniers date the letters after AD 100 (Keener; Carson, Moo and Morris). The opponents' teaching is read as law-based self-denial (Keener), heading toward Gnosticism (Wright and Bird), or unidentifiable (the ESV Study Bible), and full Gnosticism came well into the second century (Carson, Moo and Morris).

ideas.s: A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.

Lists of ancestors that proved who you were: a true Israelite, a priest, an heir of David. Matthew opens with one. Some teachers also spun stories and family trees out of the Bible's lists, which 1 Timothy calls myths and endless genealogies.
Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 1:12-20, A blasphemer shown mercy, and two men handed over to Satan
entries.summary: Paul thanks Christ for taking a former blasphemer and persecutor into his service as an example of mercy, then charges Timothy to fight the battle well, as the prophecies about him foretold, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has handed over to Satan.
entries.plain: Paul thanks Christ for trusting him with service, though he was once a man who insulted Christ and persecuted his people. He calls himself the worst of sinners and says his rescue shows how patient Christ is, then breaks into praise of God as the eternal King. He charges Timothy to fight well and keep his faith and conscience intact, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has given over to Satan so that they learn to stop blaspheming.
entries.note: Ignorance lessened guilt in Jewish texts without removing it, and teachers used their own past as an example, sometimes a shameful one (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris doubt that a later admirer would have called Paul the chief of sinners or recalled his violence. Prophecy was rare in Judaism but common in the church, so the prophecies at Timothy's commissioning mattered (Keener and his notes). Wright notes that Jewish and pagan thinkers alike saw conscience as a kind of divine presence guiding people. Moralists described their work as a battle and used shipwreck as an image (Keener and his notes). Hymenaeus is probably the man of 2 Timothy 2:17 (Keener and his notes), and the dictionary keeps this Alexander apart from the Alexander of the Ephesus riot and the coppersmith of 2 Timothy 4:14. Synagogue exclusion was graded and aimed at repentance (the cultural backgrounds notes). Handing over to Satan meant, for Keener, leaving the men in the sphere they had chosen; for Wright and the ESV Study Bible, putting them out of the church, where the accuser alone has influence, so that they come back.

The legionary was the most familiar picture of armed strength in the provinces: helmet, breastplate, boots, a big shield and a short sword, fighting shoulder to shoulder. Legions that held their ranks were thought almost unbeatable.

A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 2:1-7, Prayers for kings and all in authority
entries.summary: Paul asks for prayers for everyone, kings and all in authority included, so that believers may live peaceful and quiet lives, because God our Savior wants all to be saved and there is one God and one mediator.
entries.plain: Paul asks that the church pray for everyone, including kings and all who hold power, so that believers can live quiet, peaceful and godly lives. Such prayer pleases God, who wants everyone to be rescued and to know the truth. A single God stands over all, with a single go-between for God and people, Christ Jesus, who gave himself to pay the price for all, and Paul was sent to tell the Gentiles.
entries.note: Rome let its peoples keep their gods but expected loyalty shown in worship of Roma and the emperor; because Jews worshiped one God, Rome let them pray and sacrifice for the emperor rather than to him (Keener and his notes; Wright). Josephus reports the Jews telling the governor Petronius, "We offer sacrifices twice every day for Caesar, and for the Roman people". In AD 66 Eleazar, captain of the temple, "persuaded those that officiated in the Divine service to receive no gift or sacrifice for any foreigner", which Josephus calls "the true beginning of our war with the Romans". Wright and Bird and Wright's commentary say the church took this Jewish stance, with Jeremiah 29:7 as its pattern. In Ephesus itself a large stoa was given over to the worship of the Caesars, beside a stoa of Roma (Price and House). Many gods and rulers were called saviors, while Jewish texts kept the title for Israel's God (Keener and his notes on 1:1), and Wright notes it was used of the emperor. Gentiles mostly believed in many mediators of revelation (Keener and his notes); Wright reads one God and one mediator as denying any ruler divine status.

ideas.s: Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 2:8-15, Lifted hands, braided hair, women learning, Eve and childbearing
entries.summary: Paul wants men to pray without anger or arguing and women to dress modestly; women are to learn quietly, and he does not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man, arguing from Adam and Eve, before a hard saying about being saved through childbearing.
entries.plain: Paul wants the men to pray without anger or quarrels and the women to dress modestly, marked by good deeds more than by costly hair, jewelry and clothes. He says a woman should learn quietly and that he does not allow her to teach or hold authority over a man, giving reasons from the story of Adam and Eve. He ends with a hard saying about women being saved through childbearing. Whether the limit was for Ephesus or for every church, and what saved through childbearing means, are both argued, and the sources below disagree.
entries.note: Moralists mocked dress meant to catch the eye (Keener and his notes); Wright takes good works as the stock phrase for a benefactor's public giving. Women were rarely trained in philosophy, rhetoric or the law, and "Women were teachers of adult men even more rarely than they were disciples." (the cultural backgrounds article). The sources part ways on 2:11-12, and this guide gives no verdict. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles ground the limit in creation, for every church; the ESV reads the rare verb as exercising authority and finds no evidence of women teaching error in Ephesus. Keener and his notes tie it to untrained women whom false teachers targeted: learn first. Wright translates "in full submission to God", hears the verb as being bossy or seizing control, and reads verse 12 as refusing a takeover like the Artemis cult, which he describes as run by women, so that both sexes may learn and lead (so too Wright and Bird). Saved through childbearing is read as persevering faith (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), godly living in women's role (reported by Keener), safe delivery (Keener), Eve's line continuing (Heiser), or a promise that childbirth is no curse (Wright).

ideas.s: Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.

In much of the eastern Mediterranean a respectable woman covered her hair in public, while fashionable rich women showed theirs off. Romans covered their heads to worship and Greeks did not, so in Corinth a covered or bare head sent several signals at once.

Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.
The great goddess of Ephesus, whose temple was one of the seven wonders of the world and a bank as well. Her cult was the city's pride and the living of its craftsmen.

The Old Testament says little about Adam outside Genesis, but by Paul's day Jewish writers spoke often of his lost glory and of the sin and death he brought into the world. Each person, they added, became his own Adam.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 3:1-13, Overseers, deacons and the women
entries.summary: Paul lists what is required of an overseer, above reproach, faithful in marriage, hospitable, able to teach, managing his household well, and then of deacons and of the women, who must also be worthy of respect.
entries.plain: Paul sets out what the church should look for in its leaders. An overseer must have a blameless reputation, be faithful in marriage, self-controlled, welcoming, able to teach, free of drink, violence and greed, and run his own household well, since that shows whether he can care for the church. Deacons and the women are held to a similar standard of respect, honesty and proven character. What faithful to his wife means, and who the women are, are both debated.
entries.note: Overseer was a title for officials of cities and associations, and Qumran had an equivalent (Keener). Most hold it the same office as elder (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Carson, Moo and Morris, who add that it soon became the single bishop); Wright leaves open whether it meant one leader or one of a team. A slandered minority needed a good name, and Arnold, citing Fee, reads the devil's trap as outsiders' scandal at leaders' conduct. Faithful to his wife is disputed: polygamy was illegal in Greek and Roman law and "in this period the practice was very rare" among Judeans (the cultural backgrounds article on marriage), so Keener, his notes and the CSB Study Bible read faithfulness; Wright holds that "Polygamy was common in Paul's world" and that the phrase bars men with several wives; the ESV Study Bible sets out three views. Wright notes that wine was the cheap drink where clean water was scarce. The women of verse 11 are deacons' wives or female deacons (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Wright and Bird; Wright, who leaves it open).

ideas.s: Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 3:14-16, God's household and the hymn
entries.summary: Paul writes so that, if he is delayed, Timothy will know how people ought to behave in God's household, the church of the living God, and quotes what seems to be a hymn about Christ.
entries.plain: Paul hopes to visit soon, but writes in case he is delayed, so that Timothy knows how God's people should behave in the church, God's household and the support of the truth. He then quotes what seems to be an early hymn that traces Christ's story from his coming in the flesh to his being taken up in glory, a confession of the mystery at the heart of their faith.
entries.note: Letters stood in for the writer's presence and often announced a visit (the cultural backgrounds notes). Political thought treated the household as a model of society, and the church met in homes, so Keener reads 3:1-13 as working like a household code. Pillars held up buildings, and the truth needed support against the false teachers (Keener). In the popular religions of Ephesus, Wright notes, a mystery was a secret for initiates, sometimes in verses repeated like a charm; here the mystery is announced openly. Some manuscripts begin the hymn with God, but "it is generally agreed that the former is correct", who (Carson, Moo and Morris). Vindicated by the Spirit points to the resurrection (Keener; Wright). Seen by angels means Christ shown in victory to heavenly beings (the ESV Study Bible) or gone ahead to where the angels live (Wright). Announced, Wright adds, is the word for summoning people to obey "a new emperor". Taken up in glory breaks the order of the lines if it is the ascension (the ESV Study Bible); Keener reports a proposal that it means his return; Wright holds that "The lines aren't meant to be in order" but balance in pairs.

ideas.s: A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 4:1-5, Deceiving spirits, no marriage, no foods
entries.summary: The Spirit warns that later on some will desert the faith for deceiving spirits and demonic teaching, banning marriage and certain foods, though God made food to be eaten with thanks.
entries.plain: Paul warns that the Spirit has foretold a time when some will leave the faith, misled by deceiving spirits and demonic teaching passed on by liars with dead consciences. These teachers ban marriage and tell people to stay away from certain foods. Paul answers that everything God made is good, and nothing should be turned away when God is thanked for it, because his word and prayer make it holy.
entries.note: The Spirit says works like thus says the Lord, and later times evokes the promised restoration, now applied to the age between the Messiah's comings (Keener and his notes). Some Jewish groups, Qumran among them, expected end-time apostasy stirred by evil spirits (Keener and his notes), and Arnold reads 4:1 as naming the spiritual source of the teaching, its liars "actually Satan's advocates". The branded conscience is read three ways: owned by evil spirits (Keener), no longer working (his notes), or, for Wright, scarred by past excess so that it now flinches from good things. Asceticism was rising, and though most teachers urged marriage, celibacy was gaining ground, with some Essenes practicing it (Keener and his notes), while Augustus gave tax incentives to marry (the cultural backgrounds article on celibacy). Whether the foods are those of the food laws (Keener; Wright, for whom nothing was unclean in itself) or an ascetic diet (his notes) is left open. Carson, Moo and Morris find nothing here that needs the second century, while Wright and Bird note that Marcion rejected these letters. Jews blessed God before meals, and God had called food and marriage good (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

Daniel's king who exalts himself above every god and defiles the sanctuary became a pattern Jews saw again in Antiochus, Pompey and Caligula. Paul's man of lawlessness, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God, belongs to that line.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.

Nearly everyone in the ancient world thought people should marry and have children. A few, from Cynic philosophers to some Essenes, refused marriage for a higher calling, and some in Corinth thought holiness meant giving up sex even within marriage.
The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 4:6-16, Training for godliness, and a young leader
entries.summary: Timothy is to train himself for godliness as an athlete trains his body, set an example despite his youth, devote himself to the public reading of Scripture and teaching, and not neglect the gift given when the elders laid hands on him.
entries.plain: Paul tells Timothy that a good servant of Christ feeds on sound teaching and shuns silly myths. Timothy is to train for godliness the way an athlete trains the body, since godliness pays off now and in the life to come. He should not let his youth undercut him but set an example in how he speaks and lives, give himself to reading Scripture aloud, preaching and teaching, and use the gift he received when the elders laid hands on him.
entries.note: Greek men exercised naked in the gymnasium, "the center of civic life in Hellenized towns", and moralists used training as a picture of moral discipline (Keener and his notes). First-century Ephesus built a new stadium and a complex for Olympic games (Price and House), and games were held in Artemis's honor (Arnold). Philosophers dismissed old women's tales as fit for children (Keener and his notes). Savior of all, especially believers, is read by Wright as a claim against Caesar, whose honorific savior was. Timothy was probably in his twenties or early thirties, young for office (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible), and Carson, Moo and Morris find him somewhat diffident. As in the synagogue, the reading of Scripture was followed by a sermon (Keener and his notes); Wright applies the verse to Timothy's own study. Prophecies had attested kings and officials, and Jewish teachers accredited successors by laying on hands (Keener and his notes). The dictionary dates the laying on of hands to Lystra, the elders with Paul; Carson, Moo and Morris note that the letter never calls it ordination. Progress was the philosophers' word for a disciple's advance (Keener).

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.

Hands laid on a person to bless, to heal, or to set someone apart for a task, the way Moses laid hands on Joshua. In the early church it went with prayer, the gift of the Spirit and sending people out.

Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 5:1-16, Older men as fathers, and the widows' list
entries.summary: Timothy is to treat older and younger believers as family; the church is to honor widows who are truly in need, families are to support their own, and only older widows of proven character are to be put on the list.
entries.plain: Paul tells Timothy to treat older and younger believers as fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters. The church should support widows who are truly alone and in need, while families must care for their own relatives first. Only older widows with a proven record of faithfulness and good works are to be enrolled; younger widows are encouraged to remarry, and believing women with widows in the family should help them so the church can support those who have no one. Whether the list was an order of widows serving the church, or simply those it supported, is debated.
entries.note: Respect for elders was standard, and Diaspora synagogues called honored members father or mother of the synagogue (Keener and his notes). With no state welfare, widows without family were often destitute, and converts were often disowned by their own families, so the church became an alternative family (the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright). The false teachers may have targeted widows because they often owned their homes (the cultural backgrounds notes). Since Augustus, who gave tax incentives for it, quick remarriage of younger widows was a Roman ideal and a Jewish one (Keener and his notes; the cultural backgrounds article on celibacy), and Wright and Arnold read verse 14 as guarding the church from outsiders' slander. Was there an order of widows? Keener thinks so, noting that commentators disagree; Wright calls enrollment "a commitment to make the Christian community one's primary family"; the ESV Study Bible thinks it unlikely. The danger with younger widows was a broken pledge or marriage to unbelievers (the CSB Study Bible). Wife of one husband means faithful (Keener), married once (the dictionary), or points help to those with the fewest relatives (the ESV Study Bible gives both of these).

ideas.s: Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

A good host set out water so arriving guests could wash the dust of the road off their feet. Doing the washing yourself was a slave's work, and a disciple was not expected to touch even his teacher's feet.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 5:17-25, Double honor, two witnesses, the elect angels and a little wine
entries.summary: Elders who lead well deserve double honor and pay; charges against them need two or three witnesses; Paul charges Timothy before God, Christ and the elect angels to act without favoritism, to lay hands on no one hastily, and to take a little wine.
entries.plain: Paul says elders who lead well, especially those who preach and teach, deserve double honor, and he backs this with the saying about not muzzling an ox and the saying that workers earn their pay. Accusations against an elder need two or three witnesses, and those who keep sinning are to be rebuked publicly as a warning. He charges Timothy before God, Christ and the chosen angels to act without favoritism, not to appoint anyone in haste, and to take a little wine for his stomach.
entries.note: Honor could include payment, and double pay was given to soldiers who served well (Keener and his notes); Wright holds that the word here "most naturally refers in this passage to money", and Carson, Moo and Morris that elders were to be paid. Paul joins Deuteronomy 25:4 to a saying of Jesus found in Luke 10:7; the CSB Study Bible takes this as treating Jesus' words as Scripture, while Wright calls it a reference to his teaching that only looks like a biblical quotation. Two or three witnesses were among the firmest rules of Jewish law, and public reproof came only after private attempts failed (Keener and his notes). Calling on witnesses, divine or angelic, made a charge binding, and the angels are elect as opposed to fallen (Keener and his notes; the CSB Study Bible). Laying hands on an untested elder made the ordainer answerable if he fell (Keener; Wright). Most people drank watered wine with meals; Timothy may have abstained to avoid the ascetics' criticism (Keener and his notes) or, Wright suggests, as a stern self-discipline. Carson, Moo and Morris cite this advice as a mark of a personal letter.

ideas.s: Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

Hands laid on a person to bless, to heal, or to set someone apart for a task, the way Moses laid hands on Joshua. In the early church it went with prayer, the gift of the Spirit and sending people out.

Nearly everyone in the ancient world thought people should marry and have children. A few, from Cynic philosophers to some Essenes, refused marriage for a higher calling, and some in Corinth thought holiness meant giving up sex even within marriage.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 6:1-10, Slaves under the yoke, and godliness as gain
entries.summary: Slaves are to respect their masters so that the faith is not slandered, and those with believing masters are to serve them all the more; then Paul turns on teachers who treat godliness as a way to get rich, and warns that the craving for money breeds every kind of harm.
entries.plain: Paul tells slaves to honor their masters fully, so that God's name and the faith are not brought into disrepute, and those whose masters are believers are to serve them all the more willingly. He then turns on teachers who argue over words and treat godliness as a way to make money. True gain is godliness with contentment, since we leave the world with nothing, while the urge to get rich traps people and leads to every kind of harm.
entries.note: Wright notes that "in Paul's day slaves formed up to one-third of the population" and that most free families owned one or two. A religion Romans thought might stir slave discontent would be branded subversive and persecuted (Keener and his notes), and Wright adds that Paul wanted no name for pointless provocation; the ESV Study Bible gives the motive as the faith's good name, the CSB Study Bible as love. The word for those who benefit was used of wealthy benefactors, so "Paul speaks of slaves as benefactors", picturing them as free in God's sight like Seneca (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Jewish teachers saw wealth as a blessing with dangers, and some philosophers used their teaching for profit (Keener and his notes); Wright suggests the grumblers meant to hawk the new faith as such teachers did. Contentment was a commonplace of the philosophers, the saying about bringing nothing in and taking nothing out was proverbial, Cynics and poor peasants owned one cloak, and the love of money as a root of evils was a proverb too (Keener and his notes). Wright and Bird note that Polycarp echoes these verses about AD 120.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introductions to 1 Timothy 6:1-2 and 6:3-10, and on 1 Timothy 6:3, 6:4, 6:5, 6:6, 6:7, 6:8 and 6:10

ESV Study Bible, study note on 1 Timothy 6:1

N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: The Pastoral Letters, comment on 1 Timothy 6:1-5

ideas.s: Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

entries.title: 1 Timothy 6:11-21, Fight the good fight, the King of kings, the rich, and the deposit
entries.summary: Timothy, as a man of God, is to flee greed and fight the good fight of the faith, keeping his charge until the appearing of the Lord, the King of kings; the rich are to be generous, and Timothy is to guard what has been entrusted to him.
entries.plain: Paul tells Timothy, as a man of God, to run from greed and chase after a godly life, fighting hard for the faith and holding on to eternal life. He charges him before God and Christ, who made his confession before Pilate, to keep his task faithfully until Christ appears, and he praises God as the only ruler and King over all kings. The wealthy are to trust God rather than riches and be generous, and Timothy is to protect what was put in his care and avoid false claims to knowledge.
entries.note: The good fight is a wrestling match or athletic contest for Keener and his notes, while Wright hears a soldier's enlistment, made with a public oath of allegiance to the emperor. A charge with gods as witnesses was as binding as an oath (Keener and his notes). Greeks spoke of a god's appearing (Keener and his notes), and Wright adds that the word named an emperor's staged visit, "a major spectacular state visit, and a moment of divine revelation". Greek-speaking Jews called God the Immortal (Keener and his notes); Wright reads only God has immortality against the belief that every soul is immortal. The very rich lived off rented land, and merchants grew rich in harbor cities like Ephesus (Keener and his notes), where the Artemis cult was the region's main savings and loan institution (Arnold). Entrusted is deposit language (Keener). False knowledge need not be Gnosticism (Keener; the ESV Study Bible; Carson, Moo and Morris), though Wright sees its small beginnings; some hear Marcion's Antitheses in 6:20, which the dictionary calls a verbal coincidence, and Wright and Bird judge the letters unlikely to answer him.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.

entries.title: 2 Timothy 1:1-7, Lois, Eunice and the laying on of hands
entries.summary: Writing from custody, Paul greets Timothy as his dear son, thanks God as he remembers him in prayer night and day, recalls the faith of Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and urges him to fan into flame the gift given when Paul laid hands on him.
entries.plain: Paul writes from custody to Timothy, whom he calls his dear son, and says he remembers him in prayer constantly and longs to see him. He recalls Timothy's sincere faith, first seen in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. He urges Timothy to stir up the gift God gave him when Paul laid hands on him, since God's Spirit brings power, love and self-control, not fear.
entries.note: Whether Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters is set out in the note on 1 Timothy 1:1-11. Carson, Moo and Morris call 2 Timothy, full of personal touches, "probably the hardest of the three Pastorals to claim as pseudonymous", as do Keener and his notes; Wright's biography says to start with it, and Wright and Bird report the proposal that it alone is Paul's. If Paul's, it comes from a second Roman custody shortly before his death: about AD 64 (Keener), 64 or 65 (the ESV Study Bible), about 66 (the Zondervan dictionary), 66 or 67 on Eusebius's date for the martyrdom (Carson, Moo and Morris), or 67 or 68 (the atlas). Wright notes that sons were often apprenticed to their fathers, learning by watching. A boy's mother was his main mentor until five or seven, and Jewish Scripture education began by five or six (Keener and his notes). Timothy's mother and grandmother were Jews, probably converted at Lystra on Paul's first journey (the dictionary); his father was a Gentile, perhaps a God-fearer (the cultural backgrounds notes). On the laying on of hands, Carson, Moo and Morris suggest it may be nearer the later confirmation than ordination.

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.

Hands laid on a person to bless, to heal, or to set someone apart for a task, the way Moses laid hands on Joshua. In the early church it went with prayer, the gift of the Spirit and sending people out.

entries.title: 2 Timothy 1:8-18, Not ashamed of my chains, the deposit, and Onesiphorus
entries.summary: Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord's testimony or of him as a prisoner, but to share his suffering and guard the good deposit; everyone in Asia has deserted him except Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found him.
entries.plain: Paul urges Timothy not to be ashamed of the message about Jesus or of Paul as a prisoner, but to share in suffering for the gospel with God's strength. He sums up the gospel as God's grace, now shown in Christ, who has broken death's power and brought life to light, and he tells Timothy to guard the teaching entrusted to him with the Spirit's help. Almost everyone in Asia has abandoned Paul, but Onesiphorus was not ashamed of his chains and searched Rome until he found him.
entries.note: People were often ashamed to be linked with a prisoner (the cultural backgrounds notes), and Wright explains why: a graded social order sneered at those out of favor, and Paul's gospel clashed with the proclamation of Caesar as Lord. The deposit was money or property handed over for safekeeping, and Jewish teachers passed a sacred deposit to their disciples (Keener and his notes). Wright suggests that turning away meant stopping support, since "People in jail in the first century were not provided for by the state." The dictionary allows either doctrinal defection or failing to stand by Paul at his trial. Refresh is the language of hospitality, and a well-to-do Ephesian patron could travel to Rome and find Paul through local believers (Keener and his notes). Wright notes that Acts leaves Paul under house arrest and apparently unchained, while this sounds much worse, perhaps a second imprisonment. Carson, Moo and Morris ask what a forger would gain by inventing the search. Some think Onesiphorus had died; Keener and the dictionary answer that he need not be dead, and the ESV Study Bible reads a prayer for his household now and for him at the judgment.

ideas.s: Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

entries.title: 2 Timothy 2:1-13, Soldier, athlete and farmer, and a prisoner in chains
entries.summary: Timothy is to pass on what he heard to reliable people who will teach others, and to endure hardship like a soldier, compete by the rules like an athlete and work like a farmer, remembering Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David, for whom Paul is chained like a criminal.
entries.plain: Paul urges Timothy to draw strength from grace and to pass on what he learned to trustworthy people who can teach others. He uses three pictures, the soldier who stays focused on his commander, the athlete who keeps the rules and the farmer who works hard, to show the endurance ministry needs. Timothy is to keep in mind Jesus Christ, risen and descended from David, for whose gospel Paul is chained like a criminal, though God's word is free, and Paul closes with a saying about dying and living with Christ.
entries.note: Pharisees and Greek schools alike stressed handing on tradition, and teachers expected chief disciples to pass it on (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Philosophers compared themselves to soldiers and athletes (Keener and his notes). Soldiers served about twenty years and could not marry while serving (Keener and his notes); Wright pictures a soldier keeping out of civilian life to please the officer who enlisted him, and notes that "Caesar's soldiers characteristically inflict suffering on others", while Jesus' troops receive it. Athletes swore to keep the rules and trained ten months before the Olympic games (Keener and his notes); breaking the rules brought whipping, fines or bans, and winners took a wreath and sometimes a statue (Price and House). Farm laborers were often tenants while the landlord owned the crop, so Paul appeals to folk wisdom that the worker should share first (Wright). Jews who expected a royal Messiah expected a son of David (the cultural backgrounds notes). Chains were heavy and chafing, and a prisoner's sweat could rust them onto his arm (the cultural backgrounds notes); Wright translates verse 9 as suffering like a criminal, even chained.

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

The legionary was the most familiar picture of armed strength in the provinces: helmet, breastplate, boots, a big shield and a short sword, fighting shoulder to shoulder. Legions that held their ranks were thought almost unbeatable.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: 2 Timothy 2:14-26, Gangrene, a resurrection already past, and vessels in a great house
entries.summary: Timothy is to warn the church against quarreling about words and to handle the word of truth correctly; the teaching of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened, spreads like gangrene, but God's foundation stands sealed, and in a great house some vessels are for honor and some for dishonor.
entries.plain: Timothy is to stop the church from fighting over words and to handle the message of truth faithfully. Paul names Hymenaeus and Philetus, whose claim that the resurrection is already past is spreading like gangrene and upsetting some believers' faith. Even so, God's foundation stands firm, and Paul uses the picture of a great house with fine and common vessels to urge Timothy to keep himself clean, avoid foolish quarrels and correct opponents gently, hoping God will lead them to repentance.
entries.note: Speakers fussed over turns of phrase and Jewish teachers over spelling, while others criticized such quibbling (Keener and his notes). Rightly handling the word recalled the study of God's law (Keener and his notes); Wright prefers the picture of "a pioneer hacking out a path through the jungle". Hymenaeus, named first here and in 1 Timothy 1:20, probably led the group (the dictionary). A spiritual resurrection already experienced suited Greek taste (Keener and his notes); Wright traces it to Paul's own language of dying and rising in baptism and notes that it "became popular in some circles about a hundred years after Paul", and the dictionary calls it akin to Gnosticism, while Carson, Moo and Morris place full Gnosticism well into the second century. Keener reads the vessels through Jewish purity rules, cheap vessels broken if made impure, and the CSB Study Bible takes the dishonorable ones as the false teachers; Wright hears honor and use instead, from fine ware to the floor rag. Arnold reads the captives of 2:26 as false teachers who are "in essence, Satan's instruments", yet still able to repent.
