ideas.s: Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: 2 Timothy 3:1-9, Terrible times, homes entered, and Jannes and Jambres
entries.summary: Paul warns that the last days will bring terrible times and people who love themselves, money and pleasure, having a form of godliness but denying its power; some worm their way into homes and win over gullible women, opposing the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses.
entries.plain: Paul warns Timothy that the last days will bring hard times, and he lists the vices of people who love themselves, money and pleasure more than God while keeping an outward show of religion. Timothy is to avoid them. Some of these teachers slip into homes and gain influence over women weighed down by sin who keep learning but never reach the truth, and Paul compares them to Jannes and Jambres, who opposed Moses and were exposed. How far Paul speaks of particular women here, and why they were open to these teachers, is read differently.
entries.note: Judaism pictured the end as a time of turmoil and apostasy, and Paul counts his own time in the last days (Keener and his notes). Most women in the traditional Greek culture of Ephesus kept out of public life, so these teachers went into homes, and widows often owned theirs (Keener and his notes). Juvenal mocked women's readiness to change religions, and women took up cults such as those of Isis and Serapis more readily than men (Keener); Ephesus had a temple of Serapis (the cultural backgrounds article on Ephesus). The sources read the women differently: lesser education (Keener and his notes, who stress particular women, not all) or guilt from past sins (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Jewish tradition named Pharaoh's magicians Jannes and Jambres (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Wright), a book bore their names (the dictionary), and the Damascus Document, as Heiser quotes Elgvin, says "Belial, with his cunning, raised up Jannes and his brothers". Wright and Bird wonder whether Paul alludes to the magic of Ephesus, which Arnold calls "a center of magical practices". Wright ties their failure to Exodus 7:12, where their serpents were swallowed.

ideas.s: Daniel's king who exalts himself above every god and defiles the sanctuary became a pattern Jews saw again in Antiochus, Pompey and Caligula. Paul's man of lawlessness, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God, belongs to that line.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

Lists of ancestors that proved who you were: a true Israelite, a priest, an heir of David. Matthew opens with one. Some teachers also spun stories and family trees out of the Bible's lists, which 1 Timothy calls myths and endless genealogies.

entries.title: 2 Timothy 3:10-17, Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and the sacred writings
entries.summary: Timothy has followed Paul's teaching, life and sufferings, as in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra; he is to continue in what he learned, knowing from whom he learned it and how from infancy he has known the sacred writings, for all Scripture is God-breathed.
entries.plain: Paul reminds Timothy that he has seen Paul's teaching, way of life and sufferings up close, including the persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and warns that anyone set on living a godly life in Christ will meet persecution. Timothy is to keep to what he learned, remembering who taught him and that he has known the holy writings since childhood. Those writings come from God's own breath and are useful for teaching, correcting and training, so that God's servant is ready for every good work.
entries.note: Timothy knew of Paul's sufferings in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra from his own region (Keener and his notes); the dictionary thinks his family was converted at Lystra, where Paul was stoned. The word for impostors often meant sorcerers or fake magicians, though by then swindlers generally (Keener and his notes). The ESV Study Bible says those Timothy learned from may include his mother and grandmother, and the dictionary credits his mother with teaching him the Scriptures from childhood. In pious Jewish homes boys learned the sacred writings from about five, a knowledge that amazed other peoples, and Josephus says the law commands teaching from infancy (Keener and his notes). Greek-speaking Jews used sacred writings of their Bible, and Josephus counts twenty-two books held divine (Keener). Belief in inspired poetry and prophecy was widespread, and Jews held their Scriptures inspired by God's Spirit and true (Keener and his notes). God-breathed occurs in no earlier Greek text, and the ESV Study Bible reads all Scripture as the Old Testament and by implication some New Testament writings, while Keener and Wright take it as Israel's Scriptures, the only Bible the first Christians had.

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

By the first century Jews held a known body of sacred writings, roughly the Old Testament, to be God's true word. They taught it to children from infancy, read it aloud in the synagogue and explained it, and Greek-speaking Jews called it the sacred writings.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

entries.title: 2 Timothy 4:1-8, Itching ears, a drink offering, and the crown
entries.summary: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus to preach the word in season and out of season, because people will gather teachers to suit their itching ears; he himself is already being poured out like a drink offering, has fought the good fight and finished the race, and awaits the crown.
entries.plain: Paul solemnly charges Timothy, before God and the Christ who will judge everyone, to preach the message whether the moment seems right or not, correcting and encouraging with patience. A time is coming when people will reject sound teaching and collect teachers who tell them what they want to hear. Paul knows his own death is near, pictures his life as an offering being poured out, and says he has finished the race and kept the faith, with the crown of righteousness waiting for him and for all who long for Christ's appearing.
entries.note: The letter reads like a farewell. Jewish testaments gave a dying leader's last wisdom, most under another's name, and Keener calls 2 Timothy "Paul's ultimate wisdom for young ministers"; Carson, Moo and Morris give it "the character of a testamentary charge", and the ESV Study Bible lists the farewells of Moses, Joshua, David and Jesus. Wright and Bird note that the testament shape leads some to read the letter as later veneration of Paul the martyr; Carson, Moo and Morris ask whether an admirer would record that no one stood by him (4:16). A charge witnessed by gods was as binding as an oath (Keener and his notes). The drink offering pictures his death (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Keener), poured, Wright suggests, on the faith of his churches as in Philippians 2:17; Keener doubts any atoning sense. The good fight is probably wrestling (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible), or "perhaps even the amphitheatre, for a gladiatorial contest" (Wright), and the crown is the victor's wreath. Wright sets the righteous Judge against Paul's human judges, among whom "Paul may very well number, as their chief, the emperor himself".

ideas.s: Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.

entries.title: 2 Timothy 4:9-22, The cloak, the scrolls, the first defense, and before winter
entries.summary: Paul asks Timothy to come quickly and bring Mark, the cloak he left at Troas and his scrolls; Alexander the metalworker did him great harm, no one stood with him at his first defense, but the Lord rescued him from the lion's mouth, and Timothy must come before winter.
entries.plain: Paul asks Timothy to come quickly, because Demas has left him and others have gone elsewhere, so that only Luke is with him. He asks for Mark, the cloak he left at Troas and his scrolls and parchments, and warns about Alexander the metalworker. At his first hearing no one stood by him, but the Lord gave him strength and rescued him, and he urges Timothy to come before winter, ending with greetings.
entries.note: Paul was held in Rome, where Onesiphorus found him (Carson, Moo and Morris; Wright), and not in the custody of Acts 28, since Timothy and Mark were with him then and he has lately been at Troas, Corinth and Miletus; Robinson's Caesarea must assume that Luke confused Tychicus with Trophimus (Carson, Moo and Morris). Clement of Rome says Paul reached the limit of the West, probably Spain (Carson, Moo and Morris). Keener writes that "Paul is cold and anticipates the approach of winter". The parchments may be codex notebooks (Keener), books in codex form, perhaps a gospel (Wright), or Paul's copies of the Old Testament (the dictionary). Wright thinks Alexander the coppersmith may be the Alexander of the Ephesus riot. The first defense was "a preliminary hearing, a prima actio, before a Roman magistrate" (Keener). The lion's mouth is a biblical figure for deadly danger (Keener and his notes), and Wright adds that a citizen died by the sword, not in the arena. The CSB Study Bible names the Mamertine Prison as Paul's, though Price and House give it as Peter's traditional last lodging.

ideas.s: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.

Outside winter, ships were the quickest and cheapest way to travel, but they were built for cargo, not passengers, and from mid-September the sea grew dangerous. The great grain ships of Alexandria fed Rome.

entries.title: Titus 1:1-9, Elders in every town, and God's steward
entries.summary: Paul greets Titus, whom he left in Crete to put in order what was unfinished and to appoint elders in every town, and lists what an elder must be: blameless, faithful to his wife, with believing children, a steward of God's household, hospitable and able to hold to sound teaching.
entries.plain: Paul greets Titus, whom he left in Crete to finish organizing the churches and to appoint elders town by town. He lists what an elder must be: of good reputation, faithful in marriage, whose children are believing and well behaved, and free of arrogance, temper, drink, violence and greed. As God's steward he must be welcoming, self-controlled and devoted to good, keeping a firm grip on reliable teaching so he can encourage others and refute opponents.
entries.note: On who wrote the letter, see the note on 1 Timothy 1:1-11. Wright and Bird give the style argument some weight, especially for Titus, and Wright's biography finds it hard to place in Paul's travels, while the ESV Study Bible holds that its claim, theology and fitting style favor Paul. Carson, Moo and Morris note that "Acts puts Paul neither in Crete nor in Nicopolis", so most place the letter after a release from Rome, in the mid 60s; Robinson dates it AD 57, with Titus sent to Crete as Paul left for Jerusalem; those who deny Paul usually date it to the second century. Titus, a Greek, had been a test case in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:1-3). Paul followed the pattern of synagogue elders, leaders for each town's house churches (Keener and his notes), and Wright and Carson, Moo and Morris take elder and overseer here as the same or overlapping office. These young churches could not insist on tested leaders (Keener and his notes), and whether the children must be believers or faithful is read both ways (the ESV Study Bible). Crete was known for drunkenness and for the drunken cult of Dionysus (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

ideas.n: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
ideas.s: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.

entries.title: Titus 1:10-16, The circumcision group, and Cretans always liars
entries.summary: Many rebellious talkers and deceivers, especially of the circumcision group, are upsetting whole households for dishonest gain; Paul quotes a Cretan prophet who called Cretans always liars, and warns against Jewish myths and human commands, for to the pure all things are pure.
entries.plain: Paul warns Titus about many rebellious and deceptive talkers, especially from the circumcision group, who are upsetting whole households for the sake of money. He quotes a Cretan's own saying that Cretans are liars and lazy, and tells Titus to correct them sharply so they turn from Jewish myths and human rules. Paul says that what makes things clean or unclean is the state of the person, and these people claim to know God while their actions deny him. Whether Paul here endorses a stereotype of a whole people, and where the line comes from, are read differently.
entries.note: The circumcision group were Jewish Christians, and the teaching had a strong Jewish element (the ESV Study Bible; Carson, Moo and Morris); Wright thinks "many people in Crete seem to have taken up with some kind of Judaism". A charlatan claiming to be Herod's son Alexander, Josephus writes, "deceived the Jews that were at Crete, and got a great deal of money of them for traveling in splendor". Upsetting households means subverting household order (Keener and his notes), or, for Wright, splitting families between circumcised and uncircumcised believers. The line about Cretans was often attributed to Epimenides (Keener and his notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; the dictionary), though Keener prefers Hesiod by way of Callimachus. Does Paul endorse the stereotype? Keener writes that "Paul is clearly not citing his own view," the ESV Study Bible and Carson, Moo and Morris that Paul agrees, and Wright that he is writing "tongue in cheek". Jewish myths were stories amplifying the Bible's narratives (Keener and his notes), books that Wright says mostly urged the laws separating Jews from Gentiles. To the pure all things are pure applies the food categories to moral purity (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.

Lists of ancestors that proved who you were: a true Israelite, a priest, an heir of David. Matthew opens with one. Some teachers also spun stories and family trees out of the Bible's lists, which 1 Timothy calls myths and endless genealogies.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.

entries.title: Titus 2:1-10, Older men, older women, young wives and slaves
entries.summary: Titus is to teach what fits sound doctrine to each group in the household of faith, older men, older women, younger women, younger men and slaves, so that outsiders have no cause to speak against God's message and the teaching about God is made attractive.
entries.plain: Titus is to teach a way of life that fits sound teaching, with a word for each group in the church: older men, older women, younger women, younger men and slaves. The qualities are self-control, respect, faithfulness and kindness, and Titus is to model them himself. Again and again Paul gives the reason as how outsiders see the faith, so that no one can speak ill of God's message and the teaching about God becomes attractive. How far these instructions answer the setting of their day, and how far they stand as lasting teaching, is read differently.
entries.note: Romans suspected Eastern religions of undermining family values, so such groups often followed the philosophers' household codes, which also covered duties to the state and the gods (Keener and his notes). Wright pictures a town watching its first Christians, who skip the sacrifices and festivals and are rumored to refuse the oath to the emperor. Some thought drunkenness on Crete worse than elsewhere (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Wright notes that older women might mean women from thirty, in households of two or three generations. Self-control in a woman meant sexual modesty, and Paul says subject rather than obedient (Keener and his notes). Owners stereotyped slaves as lazy and thieving (Keener and his notes), and Wright writes, "You could no more abolish slavery overnight in the first century" than invent space travel. Carson, Moo and Morris read such instructions as showing that the Cretans were unpromising material. Three times the aim is outsiders' view of the gospel (2:5, 8, 10; Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Keener reads the passage as addressing the Roman values of the day for the sake of witness, while the ESV Study Bible presents the wife's role as standing teaching.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Titus 2:1-14, and on Titus 2:1, 2:3, 2:5 and 2:9-10

ideas.s: From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.

Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Titus 2:11-3:8, Grace has appeared, be subject to rulers, and the washing of rebirth
entries.summary: God's grace has appeared, training believers to live with self-control now while they wait for Christ's glorious appearing; they are to respect rulers and be gentle to all, because God saved them by his mercy, giving them new birth and new life by the Holy Spirit.
entries.plain: Paul grounds his instructions in what God has done: his grace has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone and training believers to turn from godless living while they wait for Christ's glorious appearing. Titus is to remind the church to respect rulers, be ready for good work and be gentle with everyone. Paul recalls that they too once lived foolishly, but God in his kindness saved them by his mercy, not their good deeds, giving them new birth and new life through the Holy Spirit so they might inherit eternal life.
entries.note: Many Jews contrasted this age with the age to come (Keener and his notes). Greeks spoke of the appearing of gods, Jewish texts of God's glorious appearings, and Diaspora Jews called God the great God and Savior (Keener and his notes); Wright notes that in these letters Paul "regularly refers to Jesus with a title the Roman world used for Caesar". The likeliest grammar gives the title to Jesus (Keener; the ESV Study Bible). Eager is the word for zealous; Keener doubts any allusion to the Zealots, and Wright takes the good works as generous public help. Submission to rulers belonged with household duties, and with Judea moving toward revolt Paul keeps the movement clear of sedition (Keener and his notes); Wright calls the stance toward Caesar careful, not yet confrontational. God promised to cleanse his people and give his Spirit (Ezekiel 36:25-27), and some Jewish teachers spoke of converts reborn through immersion (the cultural backgrounds notes). The word for rebirth occurs only here and in Matthew 19:28 (the dictionary), "the one place in all Paul's letters" with new birth (Wright). The washing is baptism for Keener and Wright, a spiritual washing that baptism signifies for the ESV Study Bible.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Titus 2:15-3:8, and on Titus 2:12, 2:13, 2:14, 3:1 and 3:5

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.

entries.title: Titus 3:9-15, A divisive person, winter at Nicopolis, and Zenas and Apollos
entries.summary: Titus is to avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, and to warn a divisive person twice before having nothing more to do with him; Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis and asks Titus to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way with everything they need.
entries.plain: Titus is to steer clear of foolish disputes, genealogies and fights over the law, which do no good. A person who stirs up division should be warned twice and then avoided. Paul closes with travel plans, asking Titus to join him at Nicopolis for the winter and to supply Zenas the lawyer and Apollos well for their journey, and he urges the believers to give themselves to good works.
entries.note: Genealogies and disputes over the law were trifles (Keener), and Wright takes the quarrels as about reading the Jewish law as a Christian. Jewish ethics called for correction in private first, and expulsion was the last step (Keener and his notes; the ESV Study Bible). Nicopolis, built by Octavian to celebrate his victory over Antony (the Zondervan dictionary), lay on the Greek side of the Adriatic, and Paul would winter there because ships did not sail (Keener and his notes). Carson, Moo and Morris place Paul in or on the way to it after a release from Rome; Wright offers, as a maybe, that Paul was leaving Crete on his last voyage, meaning to winter there before Rome, until the winds of Acts 27 intervened. Keener thinks Zenas a jurist of Roman law, the cultural backgrounds notes and the dictionary more likely an expert in the Jewish law; the dictionary adds that the view that Titus was to bring him to Paul rests on the King James Version's mistaken Bring. The verse works as a small letter of recommendation, help meaning supplies for the voyage (Keener and his notes).

ideas.s: Lists of ancestors that proved who you were: a true Israelite, a priest, an heir of David. Matthew opens with one. Some teachers also spun stories and family trees out of the Bible's lists, which 1 Timothy calls myths and endless genealogies.

A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.

Outside winter, ships were the quickest and cheapest way to travel, but they were built for cargo, not passengers, and from mid-September the sea grew dangerous. The great grain ships of Alexandria fed Rome.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

entries.title: Philemon 1-7, The church in Philemon's house
entries.summary: Paul, a prisoner, and Timothy write to Philemon, to Apphia and Archippus, and to the church that meets in Philemon's house, and Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, his partnership, and the way he has refreshed the hearts of God's people.
entries.plain: Paul, writing as a prisoner, and Timothy greet Philemon, along with Apphia, Archippus and the church gathering in his house. Paul thanks God for Philemon's love for God's people and his faith in Jesus, and prays that their shared faith will bear fruit. He says Philemon's love has given him joy, because Philemon has lifted the spirits of the believers. Where Paul was held when he wrote is debated.
entries.note: Almost all accept the letter as Paul's (Keener; Carson, Moo and Morris), but where he was held is not agreed. The cultural backgrounds notes and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles say Rome, about AD 60 to 62; Wright and Wright and Bird say Ephesus, about 55, since the guest room of verse 22 suits a prison near Colossae. Carson, Moo and Morris grant the guest room but note that a slave might flee to Rome "because it was a long way away", and judge that "Rome is a little more likely". It filled "a single sheet of papyrus" (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener) and, though private in tone, was meant for the church in the house (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Carson, Moo and Morris). Apphia was a Phrygian name, and she was probably or possibly Philemon's wife; Archippus may have been a son, a slave or freedman, or no relation (the cultural backgrounds notes; the CSB and ESV Study Bibles; Carson, Moo and Morris), though Wright takes wife and son as settled. Partnership was a business word (Keener and his notes), and for Wright the key to the letter.

ideas.s: For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

ideas.n: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.

entries.title: Philemon 8-25, Onesimus sent home with a letter
entries.summary: Paul appeals to Philemon, on the basis of love, for Onesimus, the slave who became Paul's son in prison: he sends him back to be received as a beloved brother rather than as a slave, asks Philemon to welcome him as he would Paul, offers to repay anything he owes, and asks for a guest room.
entries.plain: Paul could simply order Philemon to do the right thing, but he appeals to him in love instead, on behalf of Onesimus, who became like a son to Paul while he was in prison. He says Onesimus, once useless to Philemon, is now useful to them both, and sends him back though he would rather have kept him as a helper. He asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother and as he would Paul himself, offers to pay any debt, and asks for a guest room to be readied. Whether Onesimus had run away, and what exactly Paul asks for him, are both debated.
entries.note: Most sources take Onesimus for a runaway, which Wright calls "a capital offence" in Philemon's world. Carson, Moo and Morris also allow an errand he failed to return from, or flight to "claim sanctuary at an altar, which might be a household altar", a Greek practice; the CSB Study Bible doubts the view that he sought Paul as an advocate. He fled to Ephesus (Wright) or Rome (the Zondervan dictionary); Carson, Moo and Morris cannot say. "Roman law required Paul to return Onesimus to his master" (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), and a master could legally execute his slaves (the cultural backgrounds article on Philemon). It was unthinkable to keep as a slave the son of one's spiritual benefactor (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). What Paul asks is read differently: Keener, his notes, the CSB Study Bible, the cultural backgrounds article and Wright, for whom more than I say "can only refer to giving Onesimus his freedom", read freedom; the ESV Study Bible is unsure; Carson, Moo and Morris say only that Paul urges a kind welcome, though calling him a brother "makes slavery meaningless". The cultural backgrounds notes judge that "Paul's letter is therefore more countercultural than Pliny's".

ideas.s: Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.
A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

entries.title: Hebrews 1:1-14, The Son above the angels
entries.summary: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has now spoken through a Son, heir of all things, who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty. A chain of Scripture quotations sets the Son above the angels, who worship him and are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.
entries.plain: Hebrews begins with no greeting and goes straight to its claim: God's earlier speech through the prophets has now reached its last and fullest word in his Son. The writer presents the Son as heir, maker and the shining of God's own glory, who dealt with sins and then took his seat beside God. A string of Old Testament texts follows to show that the Son outranks the angels, who serve while he rules. The author, date and first readers of the letter are all open questions.
entries.note: The letter names no author, and its writer, date and readers are open questions; the sources give both sides. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes find the Greek too unlike Paul's, and Wright and Bird call Pauline authorship "grossly improbable"; Carson, Moo and Morris add that in 2:3 the writer counts himself among those who heard the gospel second hand. Names put forward include Apollos, Barnabas, Luke, Clement of Rome and Priscilla, though Carson, Moo and Morris think the masculine self-reference of 11:32 rules her out, and conclude, "It is far better to admit our ignorance." Dates run from Wright and Bird's 50 to 95 to Keener's about AD 68; Carson, Moo and Morris find that "the preponderance of evidence favors a date before 70", with 1 Clement, which draws on this chapter, as a later limit. The readers were most likely Jewish believers, though the CSB Study Bible reports a Gentile view, living in Rome ("as good a guess as any", say Carson, Moo and Morris), in Macedonia, Asia or Syria (Keener), or near Jerusalem (Wright). Whether 1:6 quotes the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:43 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Heiser) or Psalm 97:7 (Wright) is debated.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Hebrews (Style, Date, Authorship, Audience, Genre), introduction to Hebrews 1:1-14, and on Hebrews 1:1-2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7 and 1:14

ideas.s: The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
Israel's Scriptures picture God presiding over an assembly of heavenly beings, the sons of God, and Psalm 82 calls its members gods. Who those gods are is one of the hardest questions behind John 10.

By the first century Jews held a known body of sacred writings, roughly the Old Testament, to be God's true word. They taught it to children from infancy, read it aloud in the synagogue and explained it, and Greek-speaking Jews called it the sacred writings.

entries.title: Hebrews 2:1-4, The message spoken through angels
entries.summary: The readers must hold to what they have heard, or drift away. If the message spoken through angels was binding and every breach was punished, there is no escape for those who neglect the greater salvation announced by the Lord and confirmed by God with signs.
entries.plain: Because the Son is greater than the angels, the writer says, his hearers must pay closer attention to what they have heard, so that they do not drift away. The message spoken through angels proved binding, and every breach and disobedience received its just penalty. How then will anyone escape who ignores so great a salvation, first announced by the Lord, confirmed by those who heard him, and backed by God with signs, wonders, miracles and gifts of the Holy Spirit?
entries.note: The message spoken through angels is the law of Sinai. A widely recognized Jewish tradition held that God gave the law through angels, as Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19 also assume, growing from Psalm 68:17 and above all the Greek of Deuteronomy 33:2 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). Heiser argues that in Hebrews the divine council is pictured present at Sinai. Josephus has Herod tell his army that the Jews learned the holiest part of their law "by angels or ambassadors" (Antiquities 15.5.3), wording that can be read either way. The argument runs from lesser to greater, the Jewish how-much-more pattern: if the law brought by angels punished every breach, rejecting the Son's word is worse (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Common Jewish thought shut out of the world to come any Israelite who willfully rejected the law (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Those who heard him, in 2:3, places the writer among those who heard Jesus only second hand (the ESV Study Bible; Wright), and Carson, Moo and Morris make it their strongest reason against Paul as author, given Galatians 1:11-12.

ideas.s: God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

By the first century Jews held a known body of sacred writings, roughly the Old Testament, to be God's true word. They taught it to children from infancy, read it aloud in the synagogue and explained it, and Greek-speaking Jews called it the sacred writings.

The law set sins done in ignorance apart from sins done in defiance, and sacrifice covered only the first. Many Jews held that someone who knowingly threw off God's law could not be restored, though teachers argued over who had gone that far.

entries.title: Hebrews 2:5-18, The world to come is not for angels
entries.summary: God did not put the world to come under angels. Psalm 8 promised rule to human beings; it is not yet seen, but Jesus, made a little lower than the angels for a while, is crowned with glory, and he shared flesh and blood to break the devil's power and become a merciful and faithful high priest.
entries.plain: The writer reads Psalm 8 as a promise that humans would rule God's world, and admits that the promise does not yet look fulfilled. His answer is Jesus, who took a place below the angels for a time, died, and has now been crowned. Jesus shared the full humanity of the people he came to rescue, so that his death would break the devil's grip and free them from their fear of dying. That shared humanity is what makes him a high priest who is merciful and can be trusted.
entries.note: Keener writes that "In Jewish thought, angels ruled the nations in this age", while the righteous would reign in the age to come (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Heiser reads the passage against Deuteronomy 32, where the nations were put under divine beings: the earth "wasn't created to be subject to the members of God's divine family", but to his human family. Arnold traces the same belief through the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:8, Daniel 10 and Jubilees 15:31, and reads 2:14 as Christ's death defeating the powers by "highlighting the leader of the powers, Satan." Where the Hebrew of Psalm 8:5 has elohim, the Greek has angels, and Hebrews follows the Greek (Keener; Heiser). Whether the son of man is simply a human being or already Daniel's figure is read differently: Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes take the ordinary Semitic sense and Wright and Wright and Bird allow the Messiah's sense too. Pioneer was used of founders who cut a path for followers, and the Greek Old Testament uses made perfect of consecrating a priest (Keener; the CSB Study Bible); for Carson, Moo and Morris perfection here is "essentially a matter of completion".
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Hebrews 2:5-18, and on Hebrews 2:5, 2:6-7, 2:8, 2:9, 2:10, 2:14-15 and 2:17-18

entries.title: Hebrews 3:1-4:13, Moses the servant, and the rest still open
entries.summary: Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant; Jesus is faithful over it as the Son. Psalm 95's warning not to harden hearts as in the wilderness still speaks today, because the rest God promised was never reached under Joshua and remains open for God's people.
entries.plain: The writer sets Jesus beside Moses, the most honored figure in Israel's story: both were faithful, but Moses served within God's household while Jesus rules it as Son. He then turns Psalm 95 into a warning, recalling the wilderness generation who refused to trust God and never reached the rest he had promised. Because Joshua did not bring that rest either, the writer argues, it is still on offer, and his hearers must not repeat Israel's unbelief, since God's word sees through every heart.
entries.note: Keener reads 3:2-6 as an unspoken commentary on Numbers 12:7-8, where God sets Moses above other prophets as faithful in all his house. Ancient sources often set a servant who managed a household against the son who would own it, and later rabbis read Numbers 12:7 the same way (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). From 3:7 the writer comments on Psalm 95, later a regular part of synagogue prayers, and like the Dead Sea Scrolls he applies its today to his own generation (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Some take turning away from the living God (3:12) to suit former pagans, but Carson, Moo and Morris note that Hebrews says it of Israel under Moses. Jewish teachers debated whether the wilderness generation was also barred from the world to come (Keener). Some Jewish writers pictured the world to come as the final Sabbath rest, and Hebrews links Psalm 95's rest with the seventh day by a shared key word (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The ESV Study Bible holds that the rest can be entered even now, while Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes stress its future completion.

entries.title: Hebrews 4:14-5:10, A high priest who can sympathize
entries.summary: Jesus is a great high priest who has passed through the heavens and was tested in every way, yet without sin, so his people can approach the throne of grace with confidence. Like every high priest he was appointed by God, not self-chosen, and God named him a priest for ever in the order of Melchizedek.
entries.plain: Here the writer opens the theme that fills the middle of his letter, Jesus as high priest. Because Jesus faced every kind of testing without sinning, his people can approach God's throne with confidence instead of fear. A high priest, the writer explains, must share the weakness of those he represents and must be appointed by God, and Jesus meets both conditions, called by God as a priest in the line of Melchizedek and made perfect through suffering.
entries.note: The ark stood for God's throne, but it sat out of reach in the holy of holies, which only the high priest entered, and he on a single day each year (Keener). Philo made the divine Word God's high priest and played down the human high priest's full humanity; Hebrews goes the other way, and its source is Psalm 110:4 (Keener). The ESV Study Bible draws three marks of a high priest from 5:1-4: he is human and deals gently with the weak, he offers sacrifices for others and for himself, and God appoints him. In Judea in the writer's day the office was a political favor granted by Rome, and later by Agrippa II (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Price and House write that before the revolt of 66 the Roman procurators "took over assigning the high priests". Rome had its own high priest, the pontifex maximus, but Keener holds that the model here comes from the Old Testament. The pun learned and suffered, emathen and epathen, was common in Greek writing (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener thinks the loud cries and tears of 5:7 more likely recall Gethsemane than a psalm.

entries.title: Hebrews 5:11-6:12, Milk, solid food and no way back
entries.summary: The readers should be teachers by now but still need milk, so the writer urges them past the elementary teachings. Those who have been enlightened and shared in the Holy Spirit and then fall away cannot be brought back to repentance, though he is confident of better things for his readers.
entries.plain: The writer breaks off his argument to scold his hearers for being slow learners who still need the basics when they should be teaching others. He urges them on toward maturity and then gives one of the sternest warnings in the New Testament, about people who have known God's gifts and then turn away. He ends warmly, sure that his readers are not in that position and urging them to keep going with patience and faith. Who is meant by those who fall away is debated.
entries.note: Philosophers told slow pupils they should be teachers by now, and Greek moralists used milk and solid food for basic and advanced instruction (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener takes the basics of 6:1-2 as the instruction given to converts to Judaism, and Carson, Moo and Morris count them among their reasons for Jewish readers; the CSB Study Bible reads the list as the Christian basics, baptism and the laying on of hands for leaders. The washings were Jewish ceremonial washings, the immersion of converts nearest to Christian baptism (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Most rabbis seem to have thought some could rebel past repentance, though Rabbi Meir held that the apostate Elisha ben Abuya could repent, and the Dead Sea Scrolls barred for ever a member of ten years who turned away (Keener). Who is in view in 6:4-6 is contested. Keener takes the terms as describing genuine converts; Wright and Bird lean toward people on the community's fringe; the CSB Study Bible lists four readings. Carson, Moo and Morris think the readers were drifting toward a Jewish Christianity that was in fact no Christianity at all, so that "apostasy is only a whisker away".

ideas.s: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.

Hands laid on a person to bless, to heal, or to set someone apart for a task, the way Moses laid hands on Joshua. In the early church it went with prayer, the gift of the Spirit and sending people out.

The law set sins done in ignorance apart from sins done in defiance, and sacrifice covered only the first. Many Jews held that someone who knowingly threw off God's law could not be restored, though teachers argued over who had gone that far.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.

entries.title: Hebrews 6:13-20, God's oath and the anchor behind the curtain
entries.summary: When God promised Abraham, he swore by himself, since there was no one greater. Promise and oath, two things in which God cannot lie, give a hope that holds like an anchor and reaches behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone ahead as high priest for ever.
entries.plain: To steady anxious readers, the writer points to the promise God gave Abraham and backed with an oath sworn on his own name, since no one greater existed. A promise plus an oath gave double assurance that God would not go back on his word. That hope, he says, holds like an anchor and reaches into the inner sanctuary, where Jesus has already gone ahead as a priest for ever.
entries.note: The weightiest human oaths called on God, and an oath God took on his own name left his word beyond doubt, above all in the few oaths that included a promise not to change his mind (Psalm 110:4; Isaiah 45:23) (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Philo said that God alone could bear witness to his own truthfulness (Keener). Oaths had legal force and were used in court, which explains the legal vocabulary here, and Jews and philosophers alike agreed that the true God did not lie (Keener). The two promises in view are the oath to Abraham (Genesis 22:16) and the oath to the priest like Melchizedek (Keener). The anchor was a common figure for a secure hope, and behind the curtain means the holy of holies, which only the high priest entered, once a year (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). The Zondervan dictionary describes that inner curtain as blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen worked with cherubim, hung on four gold-covered acacia posts. Forerunner was used of an army's vanguard and of the leading runner, and always implied that others would follow (Keener).

entries.title: Hebrews 7:1-10, Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem
entries.summary: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham, blessed him and received a tenth of the spoil. With no father, mother or genealogy recorded, he resembles the Son of God, and because Levi was still in Abraham's body when Abraham paid him, his priesthood ranks above Levi's.
entries.plain: The writer goes back to the brief story in Genesis 14 where Melchizedek, a priest who was also a king, blesses Abraham and takes a tenth of the spoils. He draws meaning from the name and title, and from the silence of the text about Melchizedek's family, birth and death, which he reads as a likeness of the Son. Because Abraham gave the tithe and received the blessing while Levi was not yet born, the writer argues that Melchizedek's priesthood ranks above the Levitical one. What verse 3 means is debated.
entries.note: Because Psalm 110 calls David's lord a priest like Melchizedek, a Jewish interpreter would naturally look in Genesis 14 for the likeness (Keener). Salem as Jerusalem is supported by Psalm 76:2 and Egyptian execration texts and assumed by Josephus, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the rabbis (Keener; the Zondervan dictionary); Rasmussen's atlas sets the meeting on Abram's way home from routing the eastern kings, after he met the king of Sodom in the King's Valley. Josephus says Melchizedek supplied Abram's army in an hospitable manner and accepted his tenth (Antiquities 1.10.2). Philo and Josephus explained the name as Hebrews does, king of righteousness (Keener; the ESV Study Bible). How to read without father or mother is disputed: an argument from silence of the kind Philo used (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), a genealogy simply not recorded (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), or a priesthood not inherited at all (Wright). Later rabbis claimed God gave Melchizedek's priesthood to Abraham, perhaps to answer the Christian reading (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). One Qumran scroll made Melchizedek a heavenly figure who atones and judges at the end (Wright and Bird), but Keener observes that Hebrews does not draw on it.

entries.title: Hebrews 7:11-28, A priest from Judah, by oath, for ever
entries.summary: If the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, no other priest would have been promised. Jesus comes from Judah, a priest by the power of an indestructible life and by God's oath, the guarantee of a better covenant; Levitical priests died and offered daily for their own sins, but he lives for ever and offered himself once for all.
entries.plain: The writer argues that God's promise of a priest like Melchizedek in Psalm 110 shows that the old priesthood from Levi could not bring people to completion. Jesus came from the tribe of Judah, which had no priestly role, so his priesthood rests on his risen life and on God's oath rather than on family descent. Levitical priests died and had to keep offering sacrifices, even for their own sins, but Jesus lives for ever and offered himself once, which makes him the guarantee of a better covenant.
entries.note: The writer faced Scripture's own word that the Levitical priesthood was perpetual (Exodus 40:15); his answer is that Scripture itself promised a newer one, sworn with an oath (Keener). Carson, Moo and Morris note that arguments like 7:11, which question whether the Sinai code's rules for worship were final, mattered only to readers tempted back to Judaism. The Dead Sea Scrolls expected two anointed figures, a king from Judah and a priest from Levi; Psalm 110 lets one figure fill both roles (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright and Bird). Josephus states the rule the writer sets aside: the high priesthood belonged to the blood of Aaron alone, "though he were a king" (Antiquities 20.10). Keener thinks the many priests of 7:23 means their mortality, though readers who knew Jerusalem politics would think of Rome appointing and deposing high priests. Before the Day of Atonement the high priest was guarded from defilement (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), and Josephus records a kinsman serving for one day when the high priest Matthias was defiled by a dream (Antiquities 17.6.4). Day after day in 7:27 may merge the priesthood's daily offerings with the high priest's yearly one (Keener).

entries.title: Hebrews 8:1-13, Copy and shadow, and a new covenant
entries.summary: The high priest believers have is seated in heaven and serves in the true tabernacle set up by the Lord. The earthly sanctuary was a copy and shadow built to the pattern shown to Moses, and Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant shows that the first was growing old and ready to disappear.
entries.plain: The writer sums up his case: the high priest believers have now serves in heaven, in the real sanctuary God himself set up. The tabernacle Moses built was only a copy, made to a pattern shown him on the mountain. To show that the first covenant was always meant to give way, the writer quotes Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, in which God puts his law within his people and forgets their sins.
entries.note: Parallels between heavenly and earthly were common in Judaism and in the older Near East, where Marduk's temple and Baal's had heavenly counterparts; Exodus 25:8-9 was read as pointing to a heavenly model (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Price and House note that the Hebrew word behind pattern, tabnit, can mean "either the original from which a replica is constructed or the actual replica", and list readings from the rabbis' miniature model to the heavenly sanctuary itself. The Dead Sea Scrolls community also saw itself as the people of Jeremiah 31's new covenant, but kept the law of Moses more strictly (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Why the writer speaks of the wilderness tabernacle rather than the temple is read differently: Wright and Bird suggest the temple may have seemed corrupt beyond repair, while Carson, Moo and Morris say the letter "is not so much antitemple" as showing the old worship obsolete in principle. On soon to disappear, Keener writes that in the late 60s many could see that Rome might soon crush Jerusalem; Carson, Moo and Morris argue that 8:13 and 10:1-2 assume the sacrifices were still running, while others answer that Hebrews never names the temple.

entries.title: Hebrews 9:1-10, The two rooms and their furniture
entries.summary: The first covenant had a sanctuary on earth: an outer room with the lampstand, the table and the bread, and behind the second curtain the most holy place with the golden altar of incense, the ark and the cherubim. Priests entered the first room daily and the high priest the second once a year with blood, a sign that access to the holy place had not yet been opened.
entries.plain: The writer walks through the layout of the wilderness tabernacle, from the outer room with its lampstand and table to the inner room with the ark and the cherubim. Priests served daily in the outer room, but the inner one admitted the high priest alone, once a year and carrying blood. For the writer this arrangement was itself a message: while the first tent stood, the way into God's presence stayed closed, and its gifts could not cleanse the worshiper's conscience.
entries.note: The writer follows the Old Testament tabernacle, not Herod's temple; by his day the manna and the staff were long gone (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes on 9:4). Josephus says the inner room of Herod's temple held "nothing at all" (War 5.5.5). The incense altar stood outside the curtain in Exodus, so Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes and the ESV Study Bible read 9:4 as saying it belonged to the inner room; the ESV Study Bible also allows that the jar and staff were later kept in the ark. The cultural backgrounds article on the tabernacle calls it "a portable temple"; most temples had lamps, since holy places were shut off from daylight, and an incense altar "to address the stench of burning sacrifices in closed spaces." Where other temples set the god's image, and even a bed for it, Israel's had neither (the article; Keener). Other Near Eastern priests went in daily to feed the image; Israel's high priest went in once a year (the cultural backgrounds notes on Leviticus 16:2). Josephus and Philo read the furniture as a map of the universe (Antiquities 3.7.7; Keener), while Wright reads the two rooms as two ages.

entries.title: Hebrews 9:11-22, Blood, ashes and a will
entries.summary: Christ entered the greater tent once for all with his own blood, not the blood of goats and calves. If the ashes of a heifer could make the unclean outwardly clean, how much more will his blood cleanse the conscience; and as a will takes effect only at a death, the new covenant was put in force by his.
entries.plain: The writer contrasts the high priest's yearly entry with Christ's single entry into the true sanctuary, made with his own blood rather than an animal's. If animal blood and a heifer's ashes could make people ritually clean, he argues, Christ's offering of himself does far more and cleanses the conscience. He links covenant and death, noting that even the Sinai covenant began with sprinkled blood and that under the law forgiveness came through blood. Whether 9:16-17 speaks of a covenant or a will is debated.
entries.note: On the Day of Atonement the high priest brought the blood of a bull for himself and a goat for the people (Leviticus 16) (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The heifer's ashes of Numbers 19 were mixed with water and sprinkled to cleanse corpse impurity (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). Water, scarlet wool and hyssop are not in Exodus 24; the writer seems to join that scene with the cleansing rites of Leviticus 14:6 or Numbers 19:6 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), and Josephus too adds that Moses "had sprinkled Aaron's vestments, himself, and his sons, with the blood of the beasts that were slain" (Antiquities 3.8.6). The Greek word for covenant also means a will, and the reading of 9:16-17 turns on it. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes see a deliberate play on words, since a will took effect only at death; the ESV Study Bible allows either a will or a covenant sealed by an animal's death; Wright calls the will sense daring. The Zondervan dictionary goes further: the Greek Old Testament chose a word whose main sense was a will, and that sense runs through 9:15-28.

ideas.n: The Day of Atonement and the mercy seat
ideas.s: Once a year the high priest went into the holy of holies with sacrificial blood, for his own sins and then the nation's. It was the one fast the law commanded, and the mercy seat on the ark was the place the blood was brought.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.
Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.

A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.

Jeremiah and Ezekiel promised a day when God would write his law on hearts instead of stone and put his own Spirit within his people. Some Jews of Paul's day believed the promise belonged to their own group.

entries.title: Hebrews 9:23-10:18, Once for all, and a seated priest
entries.summary: Christ entered heaven itself, not a copy, and offered himself once at the climax of the ages; as people die once and then face judgment, he will appear a second time to save. The yearly sacrifices only reminded people of sin, but his body offered once has made his people holy, and he has sat down, his offering finished.
entries.plain: Christ, the writer says, entered heaven itself rather than a man-made copy, and offered himself once at the climax of history, where the old high priest had to return every year. He will come again, this time to bring salvation to those waiting for him. The yearly sacrifices only kept sin in memory, because animal blood could never remove it, but Christ's single offering of his body has made his people holy for good. With sins forgiven, the writer concludes, no further offering is needed.
entries.note: When the high priest came out of the sanctuary on the Day of Atonement, the people knew the sacrifice had been accepted, and Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes compare Christ's second appearing; Wright pictures the high priest coming out to declare forgiveness, and Wright and Bird say Jesus will reappear not to sort out continuing problems but to save. Most first-century Jews expected one death, then resurrection and judgment, though Josephus and some others toyed with Plato's language of reincarnation (Keener). The yearly sacrifices may have reminded people of sin the way Passover reminded them of redemption (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Carson, Moo and Morris read 10:2, which asks whether the sacrifices would not have stopped, as written while they still went on: had they ended, "given the nature of his polemic, we expect noise." Where the Hebrew of Psalm 40:6 reads you have opened my ears, most Greek copies read a body you prepared for me, and interpreters generally chose the reading that made their point (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Priests stood to offer sacrifice, so a seated priest has finished (Keener; the ESV Study Bible).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Hebrews 9:23, 9:24-26 and 9:27-28, and on 10:1, 10:2-3, 10:4, 10:10, 10:11-14 and 10:18

ideas.n: The tabernacle and its heavenly pattern
ideas.s: The tent sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, with an outer room for the priests and an inner room, the holy of holies, for the ark. Moses built it to a pattern shown on the mountain, and many Jews thought of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.

ideas.n: The Day of Atonement and the mercy seat
ideas.s: Once a year the high priest went into the holy of holies with sacrificial blood, for his own sins and then the nation's. It was the one fast the law commanded, and the mercy seat on the ark was the place the blood was brought.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

entries.title: Hebrews 10:19-25, Through the curtain, bodies washed, meeting together
entries.summary: Because Jesus' blood has opened a new and living way through the curtain, believers may enter the most holy place with confidence. With hearts sprinkled and bodies washed with pure water, they are to hold fast, spur one another on, and not give up meeting together.
entries.plain: Here the writer turns his long argument about priesthood into a call to action. Because Jesus has opened the way into God's presence through his death, believers can come near to God with clean consciences and full confidence. They are to keep hold of their hope, push one another toward love and good works, and keep gathering together as the day of the Lord draws closer, since some had already stopped coming.
entries.note: Only the high priest could enter the holy of holies, on one day a year; the curtain had kept even the priests from the full holiness of God (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The ESV Study Bible and the Zondervan dictionary tie the curtain that is his flesh to the temple curtain torn at Jesus' death. Hearts sprinkled and bodies washed borrow the language of the Levitical rites, but the perfect tense of washed points to a single initiation, baptism (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Gentile converts to Judaism were immersed once, while the Qumran sect's first washing was the first of many (Keener; the cultural backgrounds article on baptism). Religious associations met about once a month, Diaspora Jews gathered especially on the weekly Sabbath, and Christians seem to have met at least weekly (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Romans distrusted private meetings, though in the East they were rarely investigated unless someone brought an accusation (Keener). Carson, Moo and Morris think the drift away from meeting together may mean the readers were a house church no longer meeting with the rest of the church.

ideas.n: The tabernacle and its heavenly pattern
ideas.s: The tent sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, with an outer room for the priests and an inner room, the holy of holies, for the ark. Moses built it to a pattern shown on the mountain, and many Jews thought of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.

entries.title: Hebrews 10:26-39, No sacrifice left; prison and plunder
entries.summary: For anyone who goes on sinning deliberately after knowing the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains. The readers once endured a hard contest: public insult, prison and the seizure of their property, which they accepted with joy. They must not throw away their confidence now.
entries.plain: The writer issues a second severe warning: anyone who knowingly turns from the truth and rejects the Son has no other sacrifice to fall back on, only judgment. He then softens his tone and reminds his hearers of their own past courage, when they faced public abuse, stood by those in prison and lost their property without bitterness. They must not throw that confidence away now, he says, because the one they wait for will soon arrive.
entries.note: Judaism distinguished intentional from unintentional sin (Numbers 15:29-31): sacrifices atoned for sins of ignorance, but none availed for one who knowingly rejected God's law, and later rabbis thought only death could atone for such rebels (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Trampling what was holy was the ultimate disrespect (Keener). Contest is an athlete's word, and with public spectacle it could suggest the arena, though Keener takes it as an image, since the readers were still alive (12:4). Prison brought shame, hunger and disease, and banishment could bring the confiscation of property (the cultural backgrounds notes). Tiberius expelled Jews from Rome, and Claudius did the same, "probably in AD 49", though probably not all left (the cultural backgrounds article on Rome); in Alexandria Jewish homes were looted in riots (Keener). Whose persecution this was depends on where the readers lived: Keener allows Macedonia but says the place is unknown, Wright and Bird suggest Rome under Claudius, and Wright's commentary thinks of persecution coming from Jerusalem. Carson, Moo and Morris add a reason the readers might drift back: "The religion of the Jews was recognized by the Romans; Christianity was not."
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Hebrews 10:26-31, and on Hebrews 10:26, 10:28, 10:29, 10:32-33 and 10:34

ideas.s: The law set sins done in ignorance apart from sins done in defiance, and sacrifice covered only the first. Many Jews held that someone who knowingly threw off God's law could not be restored, though teachers argued over who had gone that far.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: Hebrews 11:8-16, Strangers looking for a city
entries.summary: By faith Abraham left home without knowing where he was going and lived in tents in the promised land as a foreigner, waiting for a city with lasting foundations that God himself designed and built. He and Sarah and their family died still waiting, admitting they were strangers on earth and longing for a better, heavenly country.
entries.plain: Abraham is the writer's main example of faith: he left home at God's call without knowing his destination and lived in the promised land as a tent dweller, never owning it. Sarah too trusted God and bore a child when she was well past the age for it. The writer stresses that these ancestors died before they received what was promised, seeing themselves as outsiders on earth who longed for a better, heavenly homeland, and that God has a city ready for them.
entries.note: Chapter 11 is a historical retrospective, a survey of Israel's story told to make a point, like Acts 7 and Sirach 44-50, and it repeats by faith at the head of each account (Keener; Wright and Bird). The word often translated assurance in 11:1 appears in business documents meaning a title deed (Keener). Abraham's leaving home and family became a model for readers ready to lose their own families' favor (Keener). Diaspora Jews were often counted resident aliens in their cities, and Abraham called himself a foreigner in Canaan (Genesis 23:4) (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible); the Zondervan dictionary notes that the only land he ever owned there was the field of Machpelah, bought as Sarah's grave. Diaspora Judaism often called God architect and builder of the world; Philo called heaven the mother city, while others, the Dead Sea Scrolls among them, looked for a new Jerusalem in the age to come; Hebrews, like Philo, makes heaven the home of the righteous but looks for a future city (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Hebrews 11:1-31, and on Hebrews 11:1, 11:8, 11:9-10, 11:11 and 11:13-16

ideas.s: Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.

Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.

entries.title: Hebrews 11:32-40, Sawn in two, dressed in skins
entries.summary: Time fails to tell of the judges, David, Samuel and the prophets, who conquered kingdoms and escaped the sword. Others were tortured and refused release to gain a better resurrection; they were mocked, flogged, chained, stoned, sawn in two, and wandered in skins and caves, people the world was not worthy of.
entries.plain: Running out of room, the writer races through a list of judges, kings and prophets whose faith brought victories and rescues. He then turns to those whose faith brought no rescue at all, people who were tortured, imprisoned, killed and driven into the wilderness, too good for the world that rejected them. All of them were approved by God, yet none received the promise, because God meant them to reach completion together with the writer's own generation.
entries.note: Saying there is no time to tell while naming what one would tell was a standard rhetorical device (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The lions are Daniel's, the flames his three friends', and much of the language of 11:34 comes from 1 Maccabees, which Jews everywhere knew (Keener). Nearly all Jews knew the stories of the Maccabean martyrs, and the word for tortured comes from stretching on a wheel (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Josephus says the faithful under Antiochus "were whipped with rods, and their bodies were torn to pieces, and were crucified, while they were still alive, and breathed" (Antiquities 12.5.4). Sawn in two fits a Jewish tradition about Isaiah, and some traditions had Jeremiah stoned (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible); Charles, introducing the Martyrdom of Isaiah, retells how Manasseh "caused Isaiah to be sawn asunder with a wood saw", and notes that Origen tied the story to this verse. Carson, Moo and Morris list 11:37 among the verses whose wording is hard to settle. Skins were prophets' clothing, and Elijah, David's band and the Maccabean fighters hid in caves (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

entries.title: Hebrews 12:1-13, The race, the shame and the Father's discipline
entries.summary: Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every weight and run with endurance, eyes fixed on Jesus, who endured the cross and scorned its shame. Their hardships are a father's discipline, which only legitimate children receive.
entries.plain: Having listed the heroes of faith, the writer pictures them as spectators around a race and tells his hearers to drop whatever slows them and run with endurance. Jesus is the model runner, who bore the shame of the cross for the joy ahead and now sits beside God's throne. The writer then reads their present hardships through Proverbs as the training a loving father gives his true children, painful for now but producing holiness and peace. So they should take fresh heart and keep going.
entries.note: Athletic contests were a stock image for the moral struggle, and 4 Maccabees applied it to the martyrs (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Cloud was often used for a crowd, so the witnesses may be spectators, but Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes think rather of those who received God's testimony in chapter 11; the ESV Study Bible notes that the New Testament says nowhere else that saints in heaven watch, and Wright places them at the finishing line, cheering. Laying aside weights could mean training weights, but Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes think the Greek custom of stripping to run more likely. Not yet resisting to the point of blood may bear on the date: Carson, Moo and Morris note that if the readers were in Rome it would fall before Nero's persecution of 64, when, the cultural backgrounds article on Rome says, Christians were burned "alive as torches"; if they lived elsewhere it proves little. The word for discipline was the basic Greek word for education, which usually included beatings (Keener). Illegitimate sons lost inheritance rights and got little of a father's attention (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).
