ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.

Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.

entries.title: Hebrews 12:18-29, Sinai, Zion and the unshakable kingdom
entries.summary: Believers have not come to the burning, quaking mountain of Sinai but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, with myriads of angels, the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous, and Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel's. Since God will shake heaven and earth once more, they are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
entries.plain: The writer contrasts two mountains. Sinai, with its fire, darkness and terrifying voice, stands for the old meeting with God, while Mount Zion, the heavenly city full of angels and God's people, stands for the new one, where Jesus mediates the new covenant. If those who refused God's warning at Sinai did not escape, the writer argues, those who refuse the one speaking from heaven will fare worse, because God has promised to shake earth and heaven alike. What survives that shaking is the kingdom believers are receiving, and their fitting response is grateful, reverent worship.
entries.note: Zion, not Sinai, was to be the place where the new law went out in the end time (Isaiah 2:1-4), and everyone in antiquity counted a heavenly place of revelation greater than an earthly one (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Jewish tradition stressed the vast number of angels at the giving of the law, drawing on Psalm 68:17 and Deuteronomy 33:2 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The Greek Old Testament already used the word translated church for Israel's assembly, so the assembly led by Jesus stands against the one led by Moses (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Names enrolled recalls citizen registers and the Jewish idea of heavenly tablets and a book of life, and spirits of the righteous was a usual name for the righteous dead in texts such as 1 Enoch (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Abel's blood cried out against his murderer (Genesis 4:10) (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The writer quotes Haggai 2:6 for the shaking to come, reading its first shaking as Sinai (Keener). Wright and Bird call Sinai and the heavenly Jerusalem the final contrast in a letter of contrasts, a city in which believers are already citizens.

ideas.s: God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.
An old picture of God keeping a register of the names of those who belong to him. Jewish writers developed it, and the New Testament uses it from Luke to Revelation.
Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.

entries.title: Hebrews 13:1-6, Strangers, angels, prisoners
entries.summary: The writer turns to everyday duties: brotherly love, hospitality to strangers, since some have entertained angels without knowing it, care for prisoners as if in prison with them, honor for marriage, and freedom from the love of money.
entries.plain: As the letter draws to a close, the writer turns to the everyday shape of faithful life. He asks for continued love within the community, open homes for travelers, practical solidarity with prisoners and the mistreated, faithfulness in marriage and freedom from greed. Underneath all of it is trust that God will not abandon his people, so they need not cling to money or live in fear.
entries.note: Hospitality meant lodging and caring for travelers, and Jewish texts held up Abraham, who welcomed three visitors of whom at least two were angels, as its great example (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Josephus tells it so: Abraham "saw three angels; and thinking them to be strangers," greeted them and asked them to stay for a meal (Antiquities 1.11.2). Greek tales of gods visiting in disguise show how readily ancient readers took the point (Keener), and the ESV Study Bible adds that travel was hard and inns could be dangerous. Keener writes that "Roman law used prison as detention until punishment rather than as punishment itself", and prisoners depended on friends outside for food and clothing, with guards who sometimes demanded bribes for that much access (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Some philosophers counted prison visiting a virtue, and second-century Christians had a reputation for looking after prisoners (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The bed was a common way of speaking of intercourse; Greek men often married about thirty and before then used prostitutes, slaves or boys, which Jewish circles following Scripture counted immoral (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Hebrews 13:1-17, and on Hebrews 13:2, 13:3, 13:4, 13:5 and 13:6

ESV Study Bible, study notes on Hebrews 13:2 and 13:3

ideas.s: Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.

ideas.n: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
ideas.s: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.

entries.title: Hebrews 13:7-17, Foods, an altar and outside the camp
entries.summary: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever, so the readers must not be carried away by strange teachings about foods. Believers have an altar the tabernacle priests may not eat from; as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate, and they must go out to him, bearing his disgrace, seeking the city to come.
entries.plain: The writer asks his hearers to remember their former leaders, copy their faith and obey their present ones, because Jesus Christ does not change. He warns against unfamiliar teachings about food, saying grace rather than meals strengthens the heart. Drawing on the Day of Atonement, when the carcasses of the sin offerings were taken away and burned beyond the camp, he notes that Jesus died outside the city and calls believers to go out to him and share his disgrace, since their lasting city is still to come. What the strange teachings were is debated.
entries.note: What the strange teachings about food were is read differently: Keener takes them as the food laws of Leviticus 11, no longer necessary; Wright reads strange as ironic; the ESV Study Bible thinks of Jewish ideas perhaps in a syncretistic mix. Some see the Lord's Supper in the altar of 13:10 (the ESV Study Bible reports), and the Zondervan dictionary the cross. Burning outside the camp here is the Day of Atonement, whose sin offering could not be eaten (Leviticus 16:27) (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). Josephus' own summary says instead that the second goat was burned "within the limits of the camp" (Antiquities 3.10.3); no source read comments on the difference. The cultural backgrounds notes add that "Roman law also required that crucifixions occur outside the city gate." Going outside the camp may mean accepting expulsion from the Jewish community (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), leaving the world's approval (the ESV Study Bible), or leaving city and temple though called traitors (Wright). Carson, Moo and Morris think the readers "were tired of bearing the shame of living outside the mainstream" of their heritage, and perhaps afraid, since Rome recognized Judaism and not Christianity.

ideas.s: The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.

ideas.s: Once a year the high priest went into the holy of holies with sacrificial blood, for his own sins and then the nation's. It was the one fast the law commanded, and the mercy seat on the ark was the place the blood was brought.
Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.

A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.

entries.title: Hebrews 13:18-25, Timothy released, greetings from Italy
entries.summary: The writer asks for prayer so that he may be restored to his readers soon, blesses them in the name of the God of peace who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, calls the letter a brief word of exhortation, and reports that Timothy has been released. Those from Italy send greetings.
entries.plain: Hebrews opened with no greeting, but it closes like a letter. The writer asks for prayer so that he can rejoin his readers soon and offers a blessing that calls Jesus the great shepherd, raised by God by the blood of an everlasting covenant. He describes what he has written as a short word of encouragement, passes on the news that Timothy is free, and sends greetings, including some from people connected with Italy.
entries.note: In the Greek of Isaiah 63:11 Moses is the shepherd of the sheep whom God led up out of the sea, and the prophets promised a new exodus (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Philosophers and moralists gave words of exhortation, which could also be written, and speakers often claimed a brevity they did not practice (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Carson, Moo and Morris take the phrase to mean the whole book, a sermon sent as a letter. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes think Timothy was likely arrested under Nero and freed at Nero's death in 68; the ESV Study Bible says he was presumably released; the Zondervan dictionary reads him as simply away, perhaps touring churches. If he is Paul's companion, Carson, Moo and Morris add, the letter falls within his lifetime. Those from Italy could mean people in Italy sending greetings, which Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes think likely, or Italians abroad sending greetings home, which the ESV Study Bible and the Zondervan dictionary prefer: "If the writer had been in Italy, he would have named the precise place." The open questions of author, date and readers are set out in the note on 1:1-14.

ideas.s: Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: James 1:1-18, To the twelve tribes scattered
entries.summary: James greets the twelve tribes scattered among the nations, tells them to count their trials as joy and to ask God for wisdom, warns that the rich will wither like a wildflower, and insists that God tempts no one but gives every good gift from above, as the Father of lights.
entries.plain: James writes to the scattered people of God, whom he calls the twelve tribes. He tells them that trials met with joy build endurance, and that anyone short of wisdom should ask God with undivided trust. He turns ordinary status upside down, so the poor believer can boast of being raised and the rich of being humbled, and he insists that temptation grows from a person's own desires, never from God, who gives only good gifts. Who wrote the letter, when, and to whom are debated.
entries.note: Author, date and readers are all open questions. Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes, the ESV and CSB Study Bibles and Carson, Moo and Morris favor the Lord's brother: "The lack of elaboration points to a well-known James". Wright's commentary, though the name was common, sees "a strong chance" of the brother, the Jerusalem church's leader. Wright and Bird report that many scholars reject him and date the letter late, some to the second century, while finding the evidence "marginally favours authenticity". Dates run from the early to mid-40s (the ESV Study Bible; Carson, Moo and Morris) to near his death about 62 (the Zondervan dictionary) or late in the century. The readers may be believers in Palestine (Keener), Jerusalem believers scattered after Stephen, so that James "must minister to his scattered flock by mail" (the cultural backgrounds notes; Carson, Moo and Morris), or the church across the world as a new Israel (the ESV Study Bible; Wright's commentary). Jewish texts held that God tests people to strengthen them while Satan tests them to make them fall (Keener). Father of lights could mean Creator of the stars, which many feared ruled their fate (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

Most people in Paul's world believed their lives were ruled by Fate, worked out through the stars, which many took to be heavenly beings. Few thought there was any escape, and cults that promised one drew followers.

entries.title: James 1:19-27, Slow to anger, and the widows and orphans
entries.summary: James tells his readers to be quick to listen and slow to speak and to anger, to do the word and not merely hear it, and names the religion God accepts: care for orphans and widows in their distress and a life kept unstained by the world.
entries.plain: James presses his readers to listen more than they talk and to keep their anger in check, because anger does not bring about what God wants. Hearing God's word without doing it, he says, is like glancing in a mirror and forgetting your own face. Real religion shows in a controlled tongue, in care for orphans and widows who have no one to protect them, and in a life kept clean of the world's ways. Whether James has revolutionary anger in view or ordinary quarrels is debated.
entries.note: Quick to listen and slow to speak and to anger is among the commonest advice in Jewish wisdom from Proverbs on, and Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes read James as setting it against the revolutionary fervor in his land: Jewish nationalists thought that striking at the Romans and their aristocratic vassals would serve God's righteous anger. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles, Wright and Bird, and Carson, Moo and Morris read the letter's anger as quarrels within the churches, and Wright's commentary as any human anger that thinks it can help God's justice along; the readings are set out in the note on 3:1-4:10. No mirror gave an accurate image, and many people rarely saw themselves; Philo once compares the law to a mirror (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Orphans and widows had no direct means of support and no dependable legal defender; Greek society looked after freeborn orphans only, while Jews valued providing for widows and the fatherless (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The Zondervan dictionary adds that the law gave them the third-year tithe and gleanings (Deuteronomy 14:29; 26:12), and that, since inheritance passed through males, a widow without sons was in special distress.

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.
A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.
Giving to the needy was one of the three pillars of Jewish piety, with prayer and fasting. Greeks and Romans had nothing quite like it.

entries.title: James 2:1-13, The gold ring and the good seat
entries.summary: James forbids favoritism in the assembly. A rich man with a gold ring is given a good seat and a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand, though it is the rich who drag believers into court and slander the noble name; the royal law of love rules out partiality, and mercy triumphs over judgment.
entries.plain: James attacks favoritism in the Christian gathering, using the scene of a well-dressed rich visitor given a good seat while a poor one is sent to the floor. He points out that God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while it is the rich who oppress believers and haul them before judges. Showing partiality breaks the command to love one's neighbor, and those who show no mercy will receive none.
entries.note: The word for meeting is literally synagogue, used either because James addresses the whole Jewish community or because Jewish Christian congregations thought of themselves as messianic synagogues (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright and Bird); the ESV Study Bible says it is probably a Christian house church. At Rome gold rings marked the equestrian or the senatorial class (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The cultural backgrounds article on dress calls the tunic "The only item of clothing the poorest people may have owned", often dirty. The best synagogue seats were on raised platforms (the cultural backgrounds notes); the nearer the front, the greater the honor (the Zondervan dictionary). Roman law openly favored the rich (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The royal law may recall an imperial edict, which outranked the justice of the aristocracy (Keener), or, probably, the law King Jesus himself endorsed (Wright's commentary). Who drags them into court and slanders the name is read differently: Sadducean aristocrats, one of whom later had James executed (the cultural backgrounds notes), the Jewish aristocracy (Wright and Bird), the rich who feared the new messianic movement (Wright's commentary), or rich unbelievers in general (the ESV Study Bible).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to James 2:1-13, and on James 2:1, 2:2, 2:3, 2:4, 2:6, 2:7, 2:8 and 2:9-10

ideas.s: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.

entries.title: James 2:14-26, Faith that shudders, Abraham and Rahab
entries.summary: Faith without deeds is dead, James argues. Wishing a hungry brother well helps no one, the demons believe that God is one and shudder, and Abraham and Rahab were counted righteous by what they did.
entries.plain: James argues that a faith that never acts is no faith at all. Kind words to a hungry, poorly clothed believer, with no help given, are useless, and even demons hold correct beliefs about God and tremble. He points to Abraham offering Isaac and Rahab sheltering the spies as people whose trust in God showed in what they did. How James's words sit beside Paul's on faith and works is debated.
entries.note: There is one God is the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4, which Jews recited every day; it was the cornerstone of Jewish faith (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). That demons recognized the truth about God and trembled at his name was widely held, even in the magical papyri (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Heiser notes that the word for the messengers Rahab welcomed is the Greek word also used for angels. Whom James is answering is read in several ways: a garbled form of Paul's teaching heard secondhand, before James had met Paul (Carson, Moo and Morris), a later stage of Paul misunderstood, after James's death (Kümmel, as they report), a strain of Jewish piety feeding the revolutionary mood (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), or mere intellectual assent (the Zondervan dictionary). The ESV Study Bible, Wright and Bird, and Wright's commentary see no real contradiction: for Wright, faith here is the bare Jewish confession that God is one, and James is "on the same page as Paul" (Galatians 5:6). Luther called James an "epistle of straw", yet "he quoted James approvingly many times" (Carson, Moo and Morris).

ideas.s: Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: James 3:1-4:10, The tongue on fire, zeal and wars
entries.summary: James warns would-be teachers that the tongue is a small fire set alight by hell, contrasts bitter envy and selfish ambition with the peaceable wisdom from above, traces fights and quarrels to desires at war within, calls friendship with the world enmity with God, and tells his readers to resist the devil.
entries.plain: James warns that teachers face stricter judgment and then turns to the tongue, a small thing that steers a whole life and can set it ablaze. He contrasts a wisdom marked by jealousy and rivalry, which he calls earthly and demonic, with God's wisdom, which is pure and makes peace. Conflicts among the readers, he says, grow from desires fighting within them, and he calls them to stop loving the world, yield to God, stand against the devil and return in humility. Whether James means revolutionary violence or quarrels in the church is debated.
entries.note: That the tongue's fire is lit by Gehenna shows where it leads, since Jewish pictures of Gehenna typically included flame (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Heiser pairs James 3:6 with 1 Enoch 48:7. The word for envy in 3:14 was the word for zeal used by those who wanted to overthrow Roman rule, after Phinehas and the Maccabees (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The Testament of Simeon warns, "beware of the spirit of deceit and envy", and promises that for one who flees to the Lord "the evil spirit will quickly depart from him" (Arnold, who does not cite James). The setting is disputed here most of all. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes read James as answering poor Jews tempted to violent revolt; Carson, Moo and Morris trace this reading to Ralph Martin and warn "not to be more definite than the text allows us to be". The ESV Study Bible reads the killing of 4:2 as a metaphor, and the CSB Study Bible, Wright and Bird, and Carson, Moo and Morris think of quarrels in the church. Wright's commentary reads jealous fault-finding that breeds the fear and suspicion in which fighting starts, and does not mention rebels.

ideas.s: The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.

ideas.n: Zeal for God and the law
ideas.s: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.
In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.

ideas.n: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: James 4:13-5:6, Merchants, landowners and the wages that cry out
entries.summary: James rebukes traders who plan a year of business without God, then turns on rich landowners whose hoarded wealth is rotting, whose withheld wages cry out to the Lord of hosts, and who have fattened themselves for a day of slaughter and condemned the righteous one.
entries.plain: James first rebukes merchants who map out a year of travel and profit as if their lives were their own, reminding them that life is brief and every plan depends on God's will. He then turns on wealthy landowners in the manner of the old prophets, announcing that their hoarded riches are already rotting and that the unpaid wages of their field workers cry out to God. They have lived in luxury while condemning and killing the innocent. Who these rich were, and who the righteous one is, are debated.
entries.note: After Pompey and Herod's taxes many peasants worked as tenants on large estates, while "others became landless day laborers in the marketplaces, finding work only sporadically" (Keener; the cultural backgrounds article on poverty, in the same words). The law forbade holding back wages overnight (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15). Ananias, who had been high priest, "was a great hoarder up of money", and his servants seized the tithes so that poorer priests "died for want of food" (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.2). A day of slaughter was a feast, and the rich are cattle fattened for their own slaughter, as in 1 Enoch 94:8-9 (Keener; Charles). Who the righteous one is, is read differently: the poor killed by judicial oppression, or James himself, whom Ananus had stoned (Antiquities 20.9.1; Keener), though Hegesippus says he was thrown from the temple pinnacle (Price and House); a believer or an innocent (the ESV Study Bible); or Jesus, an explanation Wright and Bird report and Wright's commentary adopts, naming the rich as the Jerusalem elite, the Sadducees and chief priests, fat on the pilgrims' offerings. Keener and Wright's commentary place these landowners in Judea, the ESV Study Bible across much of the empire.

ideas.s: Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.

ideas.n: Chief priests, elders and the council
ideas.s: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.

The law of Moses named stoning as the penalty for blasphemy, but under Rome Jewish courts could not execute without the governor. In practice stoning was what angry crowds did, in Jewish and Gentile towns alike.

ideas.n: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
ideas.s: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.

entries.title: James 5:7-12, Early and late rains, Job, and no oaths
entries.summary: James tells the oppressed to be patient until the Lord comes, as a farmer waits for the autumn and spring rains, to stop grumbling, to remember the prophets and Job, and above all not to swear.
entries.plain: James tells believers suffering under the rich to wait patiently for the Lord's coming, as a farmer waits through the seasons for rain and harvest. They must stop complaining about one another, since the judge is near. He offers the prophets and Job as examples of endurance, and ends by forbidding oaths, because their plain word should be enough.
entries.note: Keener reads the call to patience as the answer for the oppressed: they were to wait for God rather than take matters violently into their own hands, and the cultural backgrounds article on poverty adds that believers elsewhere might be suspected as Jewish rebels. Wright's commentary links the grumbling of 5:9 to the persecution believers in and around Jerusalem had faced since Stephen's death, as fear outside bred quarrels inside. Harvest was an image of the day of judgment in later Jewish writing such as 4 Ezra (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The autumn rains came in October and November and the spring rains of March and April just before harvest (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible); four or five dry weeks in winter could ruin a crop (Rasmussen's atlas). The Testament of Job enlarged Job's endurance (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Josephus writes of the Essenes that "swearing is avoided by them, and they esteem it worse than perjury" (War 2.8.6). What swearing James means is read differently: Keener thinks impatient swearing more likely than a Zealot-type oath; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles see a call to truthfulness, not a ban on every oath.

ideas.s: The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.
Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.

entries.title: James 5:13-20, Elders, oil and Elijah's prayer
entries.summary: The suffering should pray and the cheerful sing; the sick should call the church's elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah's was, and whoever turns a sinner back covers a multitude of sins.
entries.plain: James closes with prayer for every situation: the troubled should pray, the cheerful should sing praise and the sick should call the church's elders to pray and anoint them with oil. Prayer, healing and forgiveness belong together, so believers should confess sins to one another and pray for one another. Elijah, an ordinary man whose prayers stopped and restarted the rain, shows what a righteous person's prayer can do, and anyone who brings a straying believer back rescues that person from death.
entries.note: Elders had ruled Old Testament villages and still led, usually as a group (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible). The oil is read several ways, set out under anointing with oil: medicine joined with a sign of God's Spirit (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), a symbol of the Spirit (the ESV Study Bible), a cure-all with the healing placed in the prayer (the CSB Study Bible), a household remedy given with prayer, not a church ritual (the Zondervan dictionary), or a sign of God's longing to heal that the church still uses (Wright's commentary). Jewish literature often linked sin and sickness, though neither the Old Testament nor James ties every illness to sin (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Only a few holy men were thought able to bring rain, chief among them Honi the Circle-drawer, whom Josephus calls Onias, "a righteous man he was, and beloved of God" (Antiquities 14.2.1; Keener). A cultural backgrounds article notes that these rain stories were embellished centuries later. James applies that standard of prayer to every believer (Keener). The three and a half years are later tradition (Keener) or half of seven, a symbol of judgment (the ESV Study Bible).

ideas.s: Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.
Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.

entries.title: 1 Peter 1:1-12, To the exiles of the dispersion
entries.summary: Peter writes to God's chosen exiles scattered through five provinces of Asia Minor, blesses God for a new birth into a living hope and an inheritance kept in heaven, and tells them their trials test their faith as fire tests gold. The prophets searched for this salvation, and angels long to look into it.
entries.plain: Peter writes to believers scattered across five regions of Asia Minor, calling them God's chosen people living as exiles. He praises God for giving them new birth, a living hope through Jesus' resurrection and an inheritance kept safe in heaven. Their present troubles, he says, test their faith the way fire proves gold, and the salvation they have was searched for by the prophets and is something even angels long to see. Who wrote the letter, when, to whom, and what kind of suffering they faced are all debated.
entries.note: Author, date and readers are all open questions. Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes, the ESV and CSB Study Bibles, Carson, Moo and Morris and Wright's commentary hold that Peter wrote it; Wright and Bird report that many take it as written after 70 or by a Petrine school, and judge Peter's authorship plausible but unproven. Dates run from about 60 to 64 if Peter wrote it to 80 to 110 if not (Wright and Bird; Carson, Moo and Morris). The readers were mainly Gentiles (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Carson, Moo and Morris; Wright's commentary: ex-pagan converts in rural Turkey), a mix (Keener), or uncertain (Wright and Bird). What they suffered is read as Nero's attack after the fire of 64 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), local abuse and ostracism (the ESV Study Bible; Wright and Bird; Carson, Moo and Morris), or such abuse with some official action by local authorities (Wright's commentary). Exile may be literal (Elliott, reported by Wright and Bird) or figurative (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Wright's commentary: a dual citizenship). The provinces are listed "in the order in which a messenger might visit them" (Hemer, cited by Carson, Moo and Morris).

ideas.s: Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

entries.title: 1 Peter 1:13-25, Minds girded, foreigners, and the lamb
entries.summary: Peter calls his readers to be ready and sober, holy as God is holy, and to live as foreigners in reverent fear, since they were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish. Born again of imperishable seed, the living word, they must love one another deeply.
entries.plain: Peter turns from praise to how his readers should live. With their hope fixed on Christ's return, they are to be clear-headed and holy, because the God who called them is holy. They were bought out of an empty inherited way of life at the cost of Christ's own blood, so they should live in reverent awe as strangers in the world and love one another from the heart, since God's word has given them a new and lasting life.
entries.note: Men wore long robes and tucked them into the belt to move quickly, so girding the mind meant being ready; Keener hears the first Passover, eaten dressed to leave (Exodus 12:11) (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener writes that "Jewish communities throughout the empire generally enjoyed a resident alien status", and the cultural backgrounds notes that "cities did not treat them as well as they did local citizens". Josephus records the Ionians asking Agrippa to keep citizens' rights for themselves, since if Jews shared them "they might be obliged to worship the gods they themselves worshipped" (Antiquities 12.3.2). Keener notes that a way of life handed down from the ancestors could mean either paganism or Judaism; Carson, Moo and Morris think it plainly pagan: "That Gentiles are addressed seems clear from 1 Pet. 1:18". Redemption by a lamb's blood recalls Passover, and sacrifices had to be without blemish (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Carson, Moo and Morris report van Unnik's argument that the comparison has its full force only while the temple stood. Children were taken to inherit their father's nature, which is the point of the imperishable seed (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 1 Peter 1:13, 1:14, 1:15-16, 1:17, 1:18, 1:19-21, 1:22, 1:23 and 1:24-25

Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 12.3.2, trans. William Whiston
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 19, Peter, Destination, and note 15

ideas.s: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

entries.title: 1 Peter 2:1-10, Living stones and a royal priesthood
entries.summary: Like newborn babies the readers should crave pure milk. Coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, they are being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood; Peter strings together Scripture's stone texts and calls them a chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation.
entries.plain: Peter urges his readers to put away malice and deceit and to hunger for spiritual nourishment like infants. He gathers several Old Testament texts about a stone to describe Christ as the rejected stone God has made the cornerstone, and believers as living stones built into a new temple and priesthood. Then he gives his readers titles once given to Israel, a chosen people and holy nation, who were once no people and now belong to God.
entries.note: The Qumran community also saw itself as a living temple and applied Isaiah 28:16 to its own leaders; philosophers and Jews alike spoke of spiritual sacrifices (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). House could mean a building such as the temple or a household such as the house of Israel, and Peter plays on both (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Peter joins Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14 by their shared word stone, the method Jewish teachers called gezerah shavah (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Wright's commentary adds a Hebrew wordplay: stone is eben and son is ben, which Jesus seems to have used when his parable about a son ended on the rejected stone (Mark 12:1-12). Psalm 118 was sung in the Passover season, and some Jews described the deliverance from Egypt as a call from darkness into light (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). About half of 2:9 quotes Exodus 19:6, which gives all believers, Gentiles included, a share in God's covenant with Israel (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), and Carson, Moo and Morris observe that, unlike Paul in Romans 9-11, Peter shows no struggle over Israel's place.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 1 Peter 2:4-12, and on 1 Peter 2:2, 2:3, 2:5, 2:6, 2:7-8, 2:9 and 2:10
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 1 Peter 2:2, 2:5, 2:6, 2:7-8, 2:9 and 2:10
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 19, Peter, Author and The Contribution of 1 Peter
N. T. Wright, Early Christian Letters for Everyone, comment on 1 Peter 2:4-10

ideas.s: Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

By the first century Jews held a known body of sacred writings, roughly the Old Testament, to be God's true word. They taught it to children from infancy, read it aloud in the synagogue and explained it, and Greek-speaking Jews called it the sacred writings.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

entries.title: 1 Peter 2:11-17, Foreigners among the nations; honor the emperor
entries.summary: As foreigners and exiles the readers must keep their conduct good among the Gentiles, who slander them as wrongdoers. They are to submit to every human authority, the emperor and his governors, and so silence ignorant talk; they are free people, but slaves of God. Honor everyone, love the believers, fear God, honor the emperor.
entries.plain: Peter tells his readers, who live as outsiders in their own towns, to keep their conduct so good that pagan neighbors who slander them will end up praising God. They are to accept the authority of the emperor and his officials, since doing good will silence foolish accusations. They are free, but their freedom is for serving God, and they should honor everyone, love fellow believers, fear God and respect the emperor.
entries.note: The usual sense of the words for foreigners and exiles is resident aliens; Philo called souls strangers in their bodies, but Peter's point is conduct, not escape from the body (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Gentiles readily slandered converts to what they saw as a Jewish sect, and the household code that follows answers the charge that such faiths undermined public order and family values (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). As Keener writes, "the household mirrored the government of a city-state". The king is probably the emperor, technically princeps, the leading citizen; governors covers both the legates of imperial provinces and the proconsuls of senatorial ones (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener calls Asia Minor "the stronghold of emperor worship"; the cultural backgrounds article on the imperial cult adds that Rome welcomed such worship in the East as a bond of loyalty, but that "unless they were accused of disloyalty, no one would hunt down nonparticipants." Carson, Moo and Morris read the favorable words about rulers in 2:13-17 as unlikely while the whole church faced state persecution; the trouble came from private slander (2:12). Brief lists of public duties like 2:17 appear in other moralists (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 1 Peter (Provenance and Audience), introduction to 1 Peter 2:13-17, and on 1 Peter 2:11, 2:12, 2:13, 2:14, 2:15, 2:16 and 2:17
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on 1 Peter 2:11, 2:12, 2:13-17, 2:14, 2:15, 2:16 and 2:17
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article The Imperial Cult
D. A. Carson, Douglas J. Moo and Leon Morris, An Introduction to the New Testament, ch. 19, Peter, Author

ideas.s: In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: 1 Peter 2:18-25, Household slaves and a harsh master
entries.summary: Peter tells household slaves to submit to their masters, the harsh as well as the kind, because suffering unjustly while doing good is commendable before God. Christ suffered for them, leaving an example: insulted, he did not insult in return, and by his wounds they have been healed.
entries.plain: Peter speaks directly to household slaves, telling them to submit to their masters, cruel ones included, and saying that patient endurance of unjust suffering pleases God. He grounds this in Christ, who suffered without returning insult or threat and left them an example to follow. Drawing on Isaiah's picture of the suffering servant, Peter says Christ carried their sins in his body so that they could be healed and brought back like strayed sheep to their shepherd.
entries.note: Peter speaks to slaves in households, whose economic and social prospects were frequently better than those of free peasants; field slaves were worse off, and slaves in the mines would never hear the letter (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The cultural backgrounds articles on slavery add the harsher side: slaves could be beaten, sold away from family and tortured for testimony, and "slaveholders sometimes freed them in midlife to avoid caring for them in old age." Wright's commentary adds sexual abuse. Peter does not address the institution itself; no ancient slave war had ever succeeded and abolition was virtually impossible, but his sympathy is plainly with the slave, whom he sets beside the suffering Christ (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Speaking to slaves at all was unusual: "relatively few writers cared to even provide advice directly to slaves" (the article on Ephesians 6). In a culture of honor an insult was answered with an insult, an option slaves did not have (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The passage runs through Isaiah 53; Carson, Moo and Morris report Selwyn's view that 2:20-25 carries an eyewitness's memories of the passion, and Diaspora Jews called God the Overseer (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 1 Peter 2:18-25, and on 1 Peter 2:18-20, 2:21, 2:22, 2:23, 2:24 and 2:25

N. T. Wright, Early Christian Letters for Everyone, comment on 1 Peter 2:18-25

ideas.s: Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: 1 Peter 3:1-7, A wife who does not share her husband's gods
entries.summary: Wives are to submit to their husbands so that husbands who do not believe may be won without a word, by their conduct. Their beauty should be a gentle and quiet spirit rather than braided hair and gold, like Sarah, who obeyed Abraham and called him lord. Husbands must be considerate and honor their wives as co-heirs of the gracious gift of life.
entries.plain: Peter tells wives to accept their husbands' authority, hoping that unbelieving husbands may be won over more by their wives' conduct than by argument. Their beauty should lie in a gentle, quiet spirit rather than in costly hairstyles, jewelry and clothes, after the example of Sarah and other holy women. Husbands in turn must live with their wives considerately and honor them as fellow heirs of God's gift of life, or their prayers will be hindered.
entries.note: Wives were expected to adopt their husbands' religion, and Jewish or Christian women who refused the family's gods could be charged with atheism (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The ESV Study Bible quotes Plutarch: it is "proper for a wife to recognize only those gods whom her husband worships". Pagan households often exposed a second or later baby girl; Christians, like Jews, refused, so marriageable Christian women were plentiful, and wives winning husbands was a main way the faith spread (Wright's commentary). Well-to-do women braided their hair after costly fashions (the cultural backgrounds article on dress), and moralists condemned such display and praised a gentle, quiet spirit (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Many writers complained of women's weakness, and Roman law assumed it; Peter uses the word only as a reason for consideration and calls wives co-heirs (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), "a radical break with normal culture" (Wright and Bird). Sarah calling Abraham lord is read differently: Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say little should be read into it, since Abraham also obeyed Sarah; the ESV Study Bible sees a wife following her husband's leadership; the CSB Study Bible stresses that Sarah's daughters do not fear.

ideas.s: From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.
A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.

In much of the eastern Mediterranean a respectable woman covered her hair in public, while fashionable rich women showed theirs off. Romans covered their heads to worship and Greeks did not, so in Corinth a covered or bare head sent several signals at once.
Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.

entries.title: 1 Peter 3:8-22, A defense, and the spirits in prison
entries.summary: Peter calls for harmony and for blessing in return for insult, and tells his readers to be ready to make a defense of their hope. Christ suffered once for sins, was put to death in the body and made alive in the Spirit, and went and made proclamation to the spirits in prison who disobeyed in Noah's day; the flood that saved eight people prefigures baptism, and Christ has gone into heaven, where every angelic authority and power is subject to him.
entries.plain: Peter calls for unity and humility and tells his readers to answer insult with blessing, ready to explain their hope gently when questioned. If they suffer for doing right, they follow Christ, who died for sins once, the just for the unjust, and was raised to life. Peter connects this to the spirits imprisoned since Noah's time, to the flood as a picture of baptism, and to Christ's rule over every angelic power. Who the spirits in prison are, and when and what Christ proclaimed to them, is one of the most debated questions in the New Testament.
entries.note: The word for answer in 3:15 normally means a legal defense, which the readers might one day need (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The spirits in prison are read three ways. First, Christ preached to the dead in Hades between death and resurrection, the view of many church fathers, resting on 4:6 (Keener; the Zondervan dictionary). Second, Christ preached through Noah to Noah's generation (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Third, Christ proclaimed his triumph to fallen angels, the view of most scholars today (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright and Bird; the Zondervan dictionary; Wright's commentary, after the resurrection); Heiser finds that "The reference to the spirits being imprisoned is decisive." Arnold joins the third reading to the first's timing: on a descent to the underworld before the ascension, "he likely proclaimed his victory over all the fallen angels and spirits". A Jewish tradition had Enoch sent to proclaim judgment to the imprisoned angels (Keener; Heiser). Wright's commentary adds that Jews and pagans in ancient Turkey held that the ark landed on a mountain near them. Authorities and powers were the angelic rulers over the nations, now subject to Christ (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Arnold).

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.

ideas.n: The Watchers, the flood and the bound angels
ideas.s: Most Jews of the period read the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4 as angels who took human wives before the flood. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, had the guilty angels bound under the earth in darkness until the judgment, and 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude speak of that prison.
Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

entries.title: 1 Peter 4:1-11, The neighbors' parties and their abuse
entries.summary: Armed with Christ's attitude, the readers have done with the life of the Gentiles, its debauchery, drinking parties and idolatry, and their old companions are surprised and heap abuse on them; they will give account to God. The end of all things is near, so they must be sober, love one another, be hospitable without grumbling, and use their gifts as stewards of God's grace.
entries.plain: Peter tells his readers to share Christ's readiness to suffer and to break with the pagan habits of their past, such as drunken parties and idol worship. Their old friends find the change strange and insult them, but those friends will answer to God, who judges everyone. Because the end is near, believers should stay clear-minded in prayer, love one another, open their homes without complaint and use whatever gift God has given them to serve others.
entries.note: Dinners at patrons' homes and at social clubs ran far into the night, with heavy drinking; hosts poured libations to the gods, and the worship of the gods ran through clubs, household cults and almost all of life (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Pagan neighbors portrayed Jews, who kept out of all this, as lawless and subversive, and the same charges fell on Christians; Nero accused the Christians he killed of hating humanity (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Josephus complains that Apollonius Molon "sometimes reproaches us as atheists, and man-haters" (Against Apion 2.15). Carson, Moo and Morris note that here, as in 2:12, private neighbors, not the state, made the trouble. The day of judgment was pictured as a trial, at which the accusers would have to give account (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Those who are now dead in 4:6 are read by Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes, and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles as believers who heard the gospel in life and have since died; the Zondervan dictionary notes that this verse, with 3:19, is the main basis of the creed's descent into hell. Hospitality meant taking in travelers, especially fellow believers (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 1 Peter (Situation), and on 1 Peter 4:1-2, 4:3, 4:4, 4:5, 4:6, 4:7, 4:9 and 4:10-11

ideas.s: At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.

ideas.n: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
ideas.s: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

entries.title: 1 Peter 4:12-19, The fiery ordeal and the name Christian
entries.summary: The readers should not be surprised at the fiery ordeal, but rejoice to share Christ's sufferings. No one should suffer as a murderer, a thief or a meddler, but anyone who suffers as a Christian should not be ashamed; judgment begins with God's household, so those who suffer should commit themselves to their faithful Creator.
entries.plain: Peter tells his readers not to be shocked by the painful trial they are facing, as if something unheard of were happening. Suffering for Christ's name is a share in his sufferings and a sign that God's Spirit is with them, so it is no cause for shame, provided they are not suffering as wrongdoers. Judgment is starting with God's own household, and those who suffer should trust their lives to the Creator who keeps faith, and go on doing good. What the fiery ordeal was is debated.
entries.note: What the fiery ordeal was is read differently. The cultural backgrounds notes recall Nero's burning Christians to light his gardens; Keener thinks the image of gold tried by fire (1:7) more likely, and Wright's commentary hears Zechariah 13:9, where those left after the shepherd is struck are refined like silver and gold; Wright and Bird think of a local persecution in Asia Minor; Carson, Moo and Morris note that "There is no martyr piety in this letter." The cultural backgrounds article on Nero says he was the first emperor to declare a state persecution of Christians, but in Rome only, and the Zondervan dictionary quotes Tacitus on Christians "set on fire in order to serve as torches by night". The name Christian was an outsiders' nickname, here set beside charges like murderer and thief (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the Zondervan dictionary). Some read suffering for the name as a sign of Domitian's or Trajan's day; Carson, Moo and Morris answer that Christians "could rarely look to government officials with confidence for protection" long before. Pliny, governing Bithynia, one of Peter's provinces, from 111 to 113, asked Trajan whether to punish "the name itself, even without offenses" (Wright and Bird).

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

ideas.n: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
ideas.s: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: 1 Peter 5:1-14, Elders, the roaring lion, and greetings from Babylon
entries.summary: As a fellow elder Peter urges the elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for gain, until the Chief Shepherd gives them an unfading crown. All must be humble, for their adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion. Peter writes through Silvanus and sends greetings from she who is in Babylon and from his son Mark.
entries.plain: Peter, writing as a fellow elder, tells the church's leaders to care for God's flock willingly and by example, without greed or domineering, and promises them a lasting reward when Christ returns. Younger members should respect the elders, and everyone should practice humility and hand their worries to God. They are to stay alert, because the devil hunts like a lion, and stand firm, knowing believers everywhere suffer the same way. The letter closes with word of Silvanus's help and greetings from Babylon and from Mark.
entries.note: Elders, older men skilled in judging cases, ruled most Israelite towns and held a respected place in the synagogues, and the churches took the office over (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Wright's commentary notes that outside a narrow strand of Jewish tradition no one had counted humility a virtue. Devil means slanderer, and Jewish tradition had Satan accuse God's people day and night (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Under Nero, Keener writes, some Christians were fed to real lions. Whether Silvanus wrote the letter down or carried it is debated: Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes and Carson, Moo and Morris take him as the scribe, the last noting that Peter says I wrote, not I sent, while the ESV and CSB Study Bibles, Wright and Bird, and Wright's commentary think him the carrier. She who is in Babylon is widely read as the church in Rome (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Wright and Bird); the city on the Euphrates is unlikely, say Carson, Moo and Morris, since "the Jews were chased out of that city well before this time", and "Rome is usually accepted, and rightly so." Wright's commentary is less sure that Babylon is code for Rome.

ideas.s: Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

ideas.n: Babylon as a name for Rome
ideas.s: Babylon burned Jerusalem's first temple and carried Judah into exile. By the first century Jews were calling Rome by its name, and Christians did the same for the city that ruled and scattered them.

entries.title: 2 Peter 1:1-21, A reminder before the tent is folded
entries.summary: Simeon Peter writes to those who share a faith as precious as his, through whom they may share in the divine nature, and urges them to add virtue to virtue. Knowing his death is near, he means to remind them, for he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, and the prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place until the morning star rises.
entries.plain: The writer, naming himself Simeon Peter, reminds his readers that God has given them all they need to share in his own life and escape the world's corruption, and urges them to build one virtue upon another. Aware that he will soon die, he wants to leave them a lasting reminder. His message rests on what he saw with his own eyes when God's voice honored Jesus on the mountain, and on the prophets, whose words came from God and give light until Christ's day dawns. Who wrote the letter, and when, is one of the most disputed questions in the New Testament.
entries.note: Author and date are open questions; the Zondervan dictionary says it has "the poorest external attestation of any book in the canon". Wright and Bird list eight reasons for doubt, among them the use of Jude, Paul's letters called Scripture and very different Greek, and with Bauckham read it as a farewell testament in Peter's name, a transparent fiction. Carson, Moo and Morris ask why, if so, the early church argued over it, and with Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles accept Peter. Wright's commentary takes a middle line: it is meant to come from Peter in some sense, even if he did not physically write it. Dates run from 64 to 68 (the study Bibles) to 80 to 90 (Bauckham) or 150 to 200 if 2 Peter used the Apocalypse of Peter (Wright and Bird, reporting Grünstäudl); Carson, Moo and Morris think the Apocalypse used 2 Peter, making about 150 the latest date. The star rising from Jacob (Numbers 24:17) was widely read as the Messiah, and may lie behind the morning star (1:19) (Wright's commentary). The holy mountain was probably a spur of Hermon, not Tabor (the Zondervan dictionary; Rasmussen's atlas).

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

entries.title: 2 Peter 2:1-10, Angels in Tartarus, Noah, Sodom and Lot
entries.summary: As there were false prophets in Israel, so false teachers will come, greedy and denying the Master who bought them. God punished the angels who sinned, keeping them bound in darkness in Tartarus for judgment; he swept away the ancient world but kept Noah; he burned Sodom and Gomorrah but rescued righteous Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and keep the unrighteous for judgment.
entries.plain: Peter warns that false teachers will arise in the church as false prophets once did in Israel, greedy men who deny the Master who bought them and lead many astray. He offers three examples from the past: the angels who sinned and were imprisoned in Tartarus, the ancient world swept away by the flood while Noah was kept safe, and Sodom and Gomorrah burned while Lot was rescued. The lesson cuts both ways, since God can rescue the faithful and also hold the wicked for judgment.
entries.note: The verb behind sent them to hell is formed from Tartarus, in Greek myth the prison of the Titans, which Jewish writers borrowed for the fallen angels (Keener; the CSB Study Bible; the Zondervan dictionary). Heiser writes that "Tartarus was part of the underworld (biblical Sheol)", and that the angels' punishment comes from 1 Enoch, where, Arnold notes, "the good angels, Raphael and Michael, have bound those angels" until the judgment. The Zondervan dictionary instead reads 2:4 as a fall of angels before Adam's. Jewish tradition made Noah a preacher of repentance (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Who borrowed from whom between 2 Peter 2 and Jude is debated: Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes and Wright and Bird say 2 Peter used Jude; the CSB Study Bible prefers the reverse or a common source; Carson, Moo and Morris find "only 78 words are common to the two accounts" and say "we cannot say for certain which of the two borrowed from the other." The false teachers are read as Hellenized Diaspora Jews (Keener), unidentifiable and not Gnostics (the ESV Study Bible; Carson, Moo and Morris), or a range of currents (Wright and Bird).

ideas.s: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

ideas.n: The Watchers, the flood and the bound angels
ideas.s: Most Jews of the period read the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4 as angels who took human wives before the flood. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, had the guilty angels bound under the earth in darkness until the judgment, and 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude speak of that prison.

The cities of the plain that God destroyed with fire in Lot's day. The prophets and later Jewish teachers made Sodom the byword for wickedness and sudden judgment, and its burned ruins by the Dead Sea were still pointed out in the first century.
The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.

entries.title: 2 Peter 2:10-22, The glorious ones, the way of Balaam, a dog and a sow
entries.summary: The false teachers slander the glorious ones, which even angels do not dare to do. Like unreasoning animals they carouse in daylight, with eyes full of adultery; they have followed Balaam, who loved profit gained by wrongdoing and was rebuked by a donkey. They promise freedom while slaves of corruption, and they are like a dog returning to its vomit and a washed sow to the mud.
entries.plain: Peter goes on to describe the false teachers in harsh terms. They insult heavenly beings that even angels treat with respect, indulge themselves openly and chase profit like Balaam, the prophet whose own donkey rebuked him. They promise others freedom while they themselves are enslaved to corruption, and having once known the right way, they are worse off for turning back, like a dog going back to its vomit.
entries.note: Who the glorious ones are is read in several ways. Heiser takes them as divine beings of God's council close to his glorious presence, noting that 2 Enoch 21:3 calls Gabriel one of the glorious ones of the Lord. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes think of angelic powers, whom some Jews cursed along with Satan, and suggest the teachers reviled earthly rulers and the angelic authorities behind them; Arnold notes that Jewish titles for ranks of angels were also used of human officials, though he does not discuss this verse. The ESV Study Bible says they are probably evil angels. The straight way and the way of Balaam draw on the common picture of two paths (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Bosor, Balaam's father's name here, stands in nearly every manuscript where the Old Testament has Beor; the Zondervan dictionary reports that some call it "simply an ancient blunder that spread through virtually the whole MS tradition", others original. The dog comes from Proverbs 26:11, and the sow, the cultural backgrounds notes say, from the story of Ahiqar, whom Price and House place at the Assyrian court of Sennacherib and Esarhaddon.

ideas.s: Israel's Scriptures picture God presiding over an assembly of heavenly beings, the sons of God, and Psalm 82 calls its members gods. Who those gods are is one of the hardest questions behind John 10.

The seer from beyond the Euphrates whom Moab's king hired to curse Israel, who could only bless, and who then, Numbers says, showed Midian how to lead Israel into sin. Jewish tradition remembered him as the greatest prophet of the Gentiles and a byword for greed.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

entries.title: 2 Peter 3:1-18, Scoffers, the flood and the day of fire
entries.summary: Scoffers will ask where the promised coming is, since everything goes on as it has since creation. Peter answers that the world once made by God's word was destroyed by water and is now kept for fire on the day of judgment; the Lord does not count time as people do, and he delays out of patience. The day will come like a thief, and the readers wait for new heavens and a new earth, as Paul too wrote in letters some twist like the other Scriptures.
entries.plain: Peter answers scoffers who say the promised return of Christ will never come because nothing has changed since creation. He replies that the world God made by his word was once destroyed by water and is now being kept for judgment by fire, and that God measures time differently and delays out of patience, wanting people to repent. The day will arrive suddenly, so believers should live holy lives as they wait for a renewed heaven and earth, and beware of those who twist Paul's letters. Whether the world is to be destroyed or renewed is debated.
entries.note: Who the fathers of 3:4 are is read two ways: the first Christian generation, which would point to a later date (reported by Wright and Bird), or, as Carson, Moo and Morris argue, the Jewish patriarchs. The scoffers' world had rival accounts: Epicureans that God does not act in the world, Stoics that "the universe would be resolved into periodic fire" and remade (Keener; the cultural backgrounds article on ancient philosophies). Jewish tradition held that the next destruction would be by fire (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), and Jews before Jesus already explained God's delay as room for repentance (Wright's commentary). Whether the world is destroyed or renewed is read differently: Keener and Carson, Moo and Morris take Peter to mean destruction; the cultural backgrounds notes say Jewish thought more often looked for renewal; the ESV Study Bible prefers the earliest reading, will be found, and transformation, though Westcott and Hort thought that reading a corruption (Carson, Moo and Morris); Wright and Bird read laid bare. Wright's commentary takes will be found as original, from two of the best manuscripts, calls a burned-up world closer to Stoicism, and reads the elements as probably the sun and moon.
