ideas.s: The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.

ideas.n: The Watchers, the flood and the bound angels
ideas.s: Most Jews of the period read the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4 as angels who took human wives before the flood. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, had the guilty angels bound under the earth in darkness until the judgment, and 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude speak of that prison.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

By the first century Jews held a known body of sacred writings, roughly the Old Testament, to be God's true word. They taught it to children from infancy, read it aloud in the synagogue and explained it, and Greek-speaking Jews called it the sacred writings.

entries.title: 1 John 1:1-4, What our hands have touched
entries.summary: The letter opens with the Word of life, which was from the beginning and which the writer and those with him heard, saw and touched. They announce the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to them, so that the readers may share their fellowship with the Father and the Son.
entries.plain: The writer opens with eyewitness testimony: he and others heard, saw and touched the one who is the Word of life, present from the beginning and now made visible. They proclaim this so that the readers can share their fellowship, which is fellowship with God the Father and his Son. Writing it down will make their joy complete. Who the writer was, and whether this is really a letter at all, the sources answer in more than one way.
entries.note: Who wrote the letter is debated. The cultural backgrounds notes, the ESV and CSB Study Bibles and Carson, Moo and Morris name the apostle John, and Carson, Moo and Morris argue that the John the elder of Papias was the apostle himself. Wright and Bird think John the elder, whom Papias and Eusebius distinguish from the apostle, more likely. Dates run from AD 85 to 95 (the cultural backgrounds notes) to the early nineties, after the Gospel (Carson, Moo and Morris), while Wright and Bird say the letters "might, however, quite easily be earlier". Ephesus is the likeliest place on either view: the tradition that John moved there in the Jewish War "is not overwhelming, but it is consistent" (Carson, Moo and Morris), and the readers were probably churches around it, though Wright's commentary thinks them Jewish Christians. The form is a homily or letter-essay (Keener) or a pastoral letter (Carson, Moo and Morris). Eternal life means the life of the coming age, from the Jewish division of history into the present age and the age to come (Wright's commentary). Philosophers and Jewish teachers spoke of a divine Word, Keener writes, but none of the Word becoming human.

ideas.s: Greek thinkers spoke of the logos, the reason that ordered the world, and Jewish teachers spoke of God's Word and Wisdom, through whom he made everything. John opens his Gospel with that language and then says the Word became flesh.

Late in the first century a group left the churches John wrote to, taking a different view of Jesus with them. Some may have denied that he was the Messiah; others that he truly became human, as the Docetists and Cerinthus later taught.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

entries.title: 1 John 1:5-2:17, God is light, an advocate, and a world passing away
entries.summary: God is light with no darkness in him, so to claim fellowship with him while walking in darkness is a lie; the blood of Jesus cleanses, and those who confess are forgiven. Anyone who sins has an advocate with the Father, the atoning sacrifice for the whole world. The old command of love is new, the darkness is passing, and the world is passing away.
entries.plain: The writer's starting point is that God is light, so anyone claiming fellowship with God while living in darkness is lying. He refuses both extremes: believers must not deny that they sin, but when they confess, God forgives, and Jesus speaks for them as the sacrifice that deals with sin for the whole world. Knowing God shows in obeying him and loving fellow believers, and the readers must not love the world, which is already passing away. The Greek word behind atoning sacrifice is read in more than one way.
entries.note: Whether the opponents claimed to be sinless or simply did not count their sins as sins is read both ways: Keener thinks the second likelier, while Carson, Moo and Morris and Wright and Bird read a claim that sin did not touch them at all. Advocate meant an intercessor or a defending attorney, and Jewish tradition made God's mercy or Israel's merit an advocate for Israel (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The word behind atoning sacrifice is read in different ways. The ESV Study Bible takes it as propitiation, a sacrifice that turns God's wrath to favor; the Zondervan dictionary explains that propitiation is done with reference to a person, while "Expiation is done with reference to crimes or evil deeds", and that translations divide; the cultural backgrounds notes hear the Day of Atonement; Wright and Bird speak of the purifying power of Jesus' death. The Day of Atonement was for Israel alone, where this sacrifice is for the whole world (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Wright's commentary hears a word to Jewish Christians who might have thought the Messiah's sacrifice was for them alone.

ideas.s: Jewish writers, the Dead Sea Scrolls above all, divided people into children of light and children of darkness, and pictured the present age as darkness that the coming age of light would end. John, Paul and Jesus use the same contrast.

ideas.n: The Day of Atonement and the mercy seat
ideas.s: Once a year the high priest went into the holy of holies with sacrificial blood, for his own sins and then the nation's. It was the one fast the law commanded, and the mercy seat on the ark was the place the blood was brought.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

entries.title: 1 John 2:18-27, The last hour and many antichrists
entries.summary: It is the last hour: the readers heard that antichrist is coming, and many antichrists have already come. They went out from the community, which shows they never belonged; whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ is the liar and the antichrist. The readers have an anointing from the Holy One and need no one else to teach them.
entries.plain: The writer tells his readers that they are living in the last hour, shown by the many antichrists who have already appeared. These were people who left the community, and their leaving proved they had never truly belonged; to deny that Jesus is the Messiah marks the liar. The readers, by contrast, have been anointed by God and know the truth, so they should hold to what they heard from the start. What the departed group believed, and what the anointing is, are both read in more than one way.
entries.note: John alone in the New Testament uses the word antichrist (Keener), and Heiser quotes Horbury that its first uses are Christian, in these letters. Whether anti means against or in place of is read both ways: Keener and Heiser think against; the cultural backgrounds notes and the CSB Study Bible allow a figure seeking to replace Christ. What the denial that Jesus is the Christ meant is read differently: Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes allow a Jewish objection, which would let believers stay in the synagogues, or the teaching of Cerinthus that the Christ-Spirit came on Jesus without being identical to him; Carson, Moo and Morris take it as denying that the human Jesus was the Christ, and conclude that John faces "an embryonic Docetism or Cerinthianism". Wright's commentary reads rival messianic movements, which filled first-century Judaism and were as political as religious; some believers left to follow them, and any such movement had to deny that Jesus was the Messiah. The secessionists probably left after failing to win more of the congregation (Carson, Moo and Morris). Whether the anointing is the Spirit or the gospel message is open (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles).

ideas.s: Late in the first century a group left the churches John wrote to, taking a different view of Jesus with them. Some may have denied that he was the Messiah; others that he truly became human, as the Docetists and Cerinthus later taught.

Daniel's king who exalts himself above every god and defiles the sanctuary became a pattern Jews saw again in Antiochus, Pompey and Caligula. Paul's man of lawlessness, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God, belongs to that line.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.

entries.title: 1 John 2:28-3:24, Children of God, Cain, and love in deed
entries.summary: Those who do right are born of God, whose love makes them his children, and when he appears they will be like him. Whoever keeps on sinning belongs to the devil, who has sinned from the beginning, and the Son came to undo his work. The readers are not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother, but to love in deed and in truth, as Christ laid down his life.
entries.plain: The writer marvels at God's love in making believers his children and promises that when Christ appears they will be like him. Children of God show their parentage by doing right and do not go on in sin, while habitual sin marks those who belong to the devil, whose work the Son came to destroy. Cain, who killed his brother, is the opposite pattern; believers are to love as Jesus did, with practical help for those in need rather than words alone. How no one born of God sins fits the earlier warning that everyone sins is read in more than one way.
entries.note: Keener writes, "It was an ancient commonplace that children inherited the natures of their fathers", and some thinkers spoke of a divine seed in humans (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). How no one born of God sins fits 1:8-10 is read several ways: a settled life of sin set against occasional failure (Wright and Bird; the CSB Study Bible), an ideal type, or John turning the opponents' claim to sinlessness against them, which Keener favors. What God's seed is also varies: the Holy Spirit (Heiser), the gospel message (the CSB Study Bible), or the Spirit working through the word (the ESV Study Bible). Jewish tradition often read the serpent of Genesis 3 as the devil (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), and Arnold calls this "the unanimous early Christian (and Jewish) interpretation"; he reads the devil's works destroyed in 3:8 as "a definite loss of authority by Satan over the world". Cain was a stock figure of wickedness, and Josephus makes him a man who "was wholly intent upon getting" (Antiquities 1.2.1); Heiser reads him as the serpent's spiritual offspring. Keener notes that "Murder of a brother was considered one of the most hideous crimes" in antiquity.

ideas.s: The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.
Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.
Giving to the needy was one of the three pillars of Jewish piety, with prayer and fasting. Greeks and Romans had nothing quite like it.

entries.title: 1 John 4:1-6, Test the spirits
entries.summary: The readers must test every spirit instead of trusting each one, since many false prophets are now abroad. A spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as truly come in the flesh is from God, and one that refuses is the spirit of the antichrist. God in them is greater than the power in the world, and this is how the Spirit of truth is told from the spirit of error.
entries.plain: The writer warns that many false prophets are abroad, so believers must test every spirit rather than accept every claim to inspiration. The test is a confession that Jesus Christ has truly come in the flesh; any spirit that will not make it comes from the antichrist. The readers belong to God and have already won, because God in them is stronger than the power at work in the world. What the confession of Jesus come in the flesh was meant to rule out is read in more than one way.
entries.note: Jewish tradition tied prophecy to God's Spirit and often tied false prophecy to evil spirits (1 Kings 22:22-23) (the cultural backgrounds notes); the Zondervan dictionary adds the law's sentence on a prophet who urged other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1-4). Many Jews, especially the elite, doubted that prophets still flourished, while early Christians believed prophecy renewed and, "Just as in the OT, such prophecy needed to be evaluated" (the cultural backgrounds article on prophecy). Keener writes that John does not deny the opponents were inspired: "he merely denies that the spirit working in them is God's Spirit." What come in the flesh rules out is read two ways: a Docetic denial that Jesus was truly human and truly died (Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Wright and Bird; Carson, Moo and Morris; Wright's commentary, which hears an early branch of Gnosticism but warns the group may be unknown to us), or a view of Jesus as a mere prophet, which would let believers stay in the synagogue (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener as an option). Irenaeus quotes 4:3 as "every spirit which separates Jesus Christ is not of God", against those who divided Jesus from the Christ.

ideas.s: Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

Late in the first century a group left the churches John wrote to, taking a different view of Jesus with them. Some may have denied that he was the Messiah; others that he truly became human, as the Docetists and Cerinthus later taught.

Jewish writers, the Dead Sea Scrolls above all, divided people into children of light and children of darkness, and pictured the present age as darkness that the coming age of light would end. John, Paul and Jesus use the same contrast.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

entries.title: 1 John 5:1-12, Water, blood and three witnesses
entries.summary: Whoever believes Jesus is the Christ is God's child, and loving the parent means loving the child. Faith overcomes the world. Jesus Christ came by water and blood, not by water only, and three testify, the Spirit, the water and the blood; God's testimony is that he has given eternal life in his Son.
entries.plain: The writer ties faith, love and obedience together: whoever believes Jesus is the Christ is God's child, and loving God means loving his children and keeping his commands. This faith is what overcomes the world. He insists that Jesus came by water and blood, and he names three agreeing witnesses, Spirit, water and blood, whose testimony is that God gives eternal life in his Son. What water and blood stand for is read in more than one way.
entries.note: Some scholars think water and blood answer Cerinthus, who reportedly said that the Christ-Spirit came on Jesus at his baptism and left before his death, or Docetists who denied a real death; and since "Instead of blood Greek gods had ichor, which looked like water", some may have taken the water and blood of John 19:34 for a demigod's (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the Zondervan dictionary). Carson, Moo and Morris add, with Marshall, that much known of Cerinthus is absent from the letters. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles take water as Jesus' baptism and blood as his death. Scripture required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and John offers three (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The words about three witnesses in heaven, in the King James Version at 5:7, are not original: Keener counts three late manuscripts drawn from the Latin Vulgate; Wright and Bird call them "the work of a pious medieval scribe"; Carson, Moo and Morris call them "certainly a gloss", absent from every Greek manuscript earlier than the 1300s apart from two with a much later marginal addition, and from every ancient version.

ideas.s: Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.

Late in the first century a group left the churches John wrote to, taking a different view of Jesus with them. Some may have denied that he was the Messiah; others that he truly became human, as the Docetists and Cerinthus later taught.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.

entries.title: 1 John 5:13-21, The sin that leads to death, the evil one and idols
entries.summary: John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life, and that God hears them. They are to pray for a brother or sister whose sin does not lead to death, though there is a sin that does. Those born of God are kept from the evil one, while the whole world lies under his power; the letter ends with a warning to keep away from idols.
entries.plain: The writer states his purpose: he wants believers to be sure that they have eternal life and that God hears their prayers. They should pray for a fellow believer who sins in a way that is not deadly, though some sin is. Those born of God are kept safe from the evil one even though the world lies in his grip, and the letter ends abruptly with a warning against idols. Which sin leads to death, and what idols means here, are both read in more than one way.
entries.note: Some Jewish texts, the Dead Sea Scrolls among them, called a grave offense "a matter of death", enforced by expulsion (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Which sin leads to death is read in several ways: the secessionists' hatred and false view of Jesus (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright's commentary, tentatively, denying that Jesus came in the flesh), unrepented rejection of Christ (the ESV Study Bible); apostasy, left to God (the CSB Study Bible); or cutting oneself off from the Son (Wright and Bird). Judaism held all the nations but Israel to be under Satan and his angels (Keener), and Arnold reads the whole world lying under the evil one as a world that "stands apart from God", Satan's rule reaching its institutions. Idols flourished in John's world (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes): the cultural backgrounds article on the imperial cult notes Ephesus's imperial temple, and that "Christians expelled from synagogues might well lose their exemption." Keener thinks a literal meaning makes good sense in Asia Minor; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles and Wright and Bird read any rival to God, and Wright's commentary a false god called God by some who called themselves Christians.

ideas.s: The law set sins done in ignorance apart from sins done in defiance, and sacrifice covered only the first. Many Jews held that someone who knowingly threw off God's law could not be restored, though teachers argued over who had gone that far.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: 2 John 1-6, The elder to the chosen lady
entries.summary: The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in the truth. He is glad that some of her children walk in the truth, and he asks for no new command but the old one, that they love one another, which means walking in God's commands.
entries.plain: The elder writes to a chosen lady and her children, whom he loves because of the truth they share. He is glad that some of her children are living by the truth, and he reminds her of the command they have had from the start, to love one another. Love, he explains, means living by God's commands. Who the elder was, and whether the lady is a woman or a church, are both read in more than one way.
entries.note: Who the elder was is debated. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles and Carson, Moo and Morris take him for the apostle John: "there is nothing anomalous about an apostle designating himself as an elder" (1 Peter 5:1); Wright's commentary calls elder a title some gave the aging apostle. Wright and Bird think John the elder, whom Papias and Eusebius distinguish from the apostle, the more likely author. Readings of the lady vary. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles, Wright and Bird, Carson, Moo and Morris and Wright's commentary take her as a congregation, since "the universal church has no sister" (verse 13); Keener thinks a congregation more likely but, with the cultural backgrounds notes, leaves open a woman, and the Zondervan dictionary notes that Kyria could be a proper name. Wright's commentary guesses that the family language was a cover, with danger at hand, and that both churches might lie within Ephesus, then a city of tens of thousands. Wright and Bird and Carson, Moo and Morris think 2 John may be a covering note for 1 John. Ephesus, late in the first century, is the likeliest setting (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Carson, Moo and Morris).

ideas.s: Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.

entries.title: 2 John 7-13, Deceivers at the door, paper and ink
entries.summary: Many deceivers who refuse to confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh are abroad in the world; such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist. Whoever runs ahead and does not keep to Christ's teaching does not have God, and the readers are not to take such a person into the house or greet him. The elder would rather not use paper and ink, and hopes to talk face to face.
entries.plain: The elder warns that deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh are at large, and calls any such person the antichrist. Anyone who goes beyond Christ's teaching does not have God, so the readers must not give these teachers hospitality or a welcome, since that would make them partners in their work. He ends by saying he would rather speak in person than write, and passes on greetings from her sister's children. How far the refusal of welcome reaches is read in more than one way.
entries.note: Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes take the deceivers to be the secessionists of 1 John, for whom Jesus was a great prophet but not the Lord come in the flesh; Wright and Bird call them Docetists outright. The Didache rules that an apostle may stay a day, or two if needed, "but if he remain three days, he is a false prophet". The Dead Sea Scrolls community expelled anyone who supported an apostate, so that, Keener writes, "Housing or blessing a false teacher was thus seen as collaborating with him." How far the refusal reaches is read differently: the ESV Study Bible limits it to caution about false teachers, since a welcome in a house church looked like endorsement; the CSB Study Bible reads withholding support from their mission; Wright and Bird read turning away any itinerant without the apostolic teaching; Wright's commentary would not even greet such a teacher in the street, since a greeting could be taken as approval. Irenaeus, telling how John fled a bathhouse where Cerinthus was, concludes that the apostles would not even speak with corrupters of the truth.

Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.

entries.title: 3 John 1-8, Gaius and the traveling brothers
entries.summary: The elder writes to his dear friend Gaius, praying that he is in good health and glad to hear that he walks in the truth. Gaius has been faithful in what he does for the brothers, strangers though they are; he should supply them for the next stage of their journey in a way that honors God, since they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from the pagans.
entries.plain: The elder writes a short personal note to Gaius, wishing him good health and rejoicing at reports that he lives by the truth. Gaius has been looking after traveling believers he did not know, and the elder asks him to keep supplying them for their journey in a way that honors God. These travelers went out on behalf of the Name and took nothing from outsiders, so believers who support them become partners in the truth.
entries.note: On the elder, see the note on 2 John 1-6; Carson, Moo and Morris place all three letters near Ephesus in the early nineties. Gaius was "one of the most frequent Roman names" (the cultural backgrounds notes), so he need not be any other Gaius in the New Testament; Carson, Moo and Morris call him "not to be associated with Gaius of Corinth", noting that only the late Apostolic Constitutions link him with Gaius of Derbe, and Wright and Bird think him a leader of a nearby church. Hospitality was a key virtue, inns were poor and often doubled as brothels, and Jewish travelers carried letters of recommendation, a practice Christians took over (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). To send someone on often meant supplying the next stage of the journey (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Traveling speakers who lived off their hearers were often suspected of greed (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), and the Didache rules that a departing apostle takes only bread, "but if he ask money, he is a false prophet". Wright and Bird write that "The third Johannine letter is about hospitality".

A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.

God gave his name to Moses at the burning bush as I AM, and in Isaiah he says I am he. To make God's name known was to show who he is, and when Jesus uses those words in certain settings, his hearers can take them as God's own name.

Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.

entries.title: 3 John 9-15, Diotrephes and Demetrius
entries.summary: The elder wrote to the church, but Diotrephes, eager to be first, refuses to receive him; he spreads malicious talk, refuses to welcome the brothers and puts out of the church those who do. Gaius is not to imitate evil. Demetrius is well spoken of by everyone, and the elder adds his own testimony; he hopes to come soon and talk face to face.
entries.plain: The elder reports trouble with Diotrephes, a man who wants to be in charge, rejects the elder's authority, spreads accusations against him, refuses to receive traveling believers and expels those who do. The elder promises to deal with this when he comes and urges Gaius to copy good rather than evil. He commends Demetrius, says he would rather talk in person than write, and sends greetings. Why Diotrephes acted as he did is read in more than one way.
entries.note: Diotrephes apparently led another house church and refused hospitality to missionaries carrying the elder's letters of recommendation (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Why Diotrephes refused is read in different ways. Wright and Bird write, "This is likely to represent a clash of ecclesiastical authority rather than of theological dogma." Käsemann argued that the writer was an early single bishop and Diotrephes the defender of older local freedom; Carson, Moo and Morris answer that he simply "loved to be first", and suggest he may have used the danger of heresy to build his power. 3 John itself may be a letter of recommendation for Demetrius (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), probably its carrier (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; Wright and Bird), since "apart from official business of the empire, no public postal service existed" (the cultural backgrounds article on the seven churches). The wish to talk face to face was a standard thing to say in letters (Wright's commentary). The ink of verse 13 was usually black, carbon mixed with a natural gum, on papyrus sheets made from strips of the Egyptian plant (the cultural backgrounds article on writing materials, written for this verse).

ideas.s: For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.
A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.

ideas.n: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
ideas.s: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.

entries.title: Jude 5-7, Israel in the desert, the angels who left their place, and Sodom
entries.summary: Jude reminds his readers that the Lord who saved a people out of Egypt later destroyed those who did not believe; that the angels who did not keep their position are held in darkness, bound in everlasting chains, for the judgment of the great day; and that Sodom and Gomorrah serve as an example of the punishment of eternal fire.
entries.plain: Jude explains that he set aside the letter he had planned in order to urge his readers to defend the faith, because ungodly intruders have slipped in and are using God's grace as an excuse for immorality. He reminds them of three warnings from the past: the generation saved from Egypt and then destroyed for unbelief, the angels who left their proper place and are held in chains for judgment, and Sodom and Gomorrah, punished with fire. Who wrote the letter, who the angels were, and what other flesh means are all read in more than one way.
entries.note: Who wrote the letter, and when, is open. Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes and Carson, Moo and Morris argue that no one writing under another's name would choose this Jude, since "Jude the brother of Jesus had no great reputation in the early church", so the author is most likely the Lord's brother; Wright's commentary, not absolutely sure, agrees, noting that he calls himself a slave of Jesus, not his brother. Kümmel and many recent scholars think it pseudonymous, and Wright and Bird hold it open. Dates run from the 50s (Bauckham) to 65 to 80 (the cultural backgrounds notes; the CSB Study Bible; Carson, Moo and Morris) and about AD 100 (Kümmel). The angels who left their place were, in most Jewish traditions and in 1 Enoch, the sons of God of Genesis 6 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Heiser); the ESV Study Bible also gives an original fall, and Wright's commentary a revolt against their assigned ranks and duties, known from later Jewish tradition, not the Bible. Going after other flesh is read as lust for the angelic visitors (Wright and Bird; Keener) or attempted homosexual rape (the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV Study Bible).

ideas.s: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

ideas.n: The Watchers, the flood and the bound angels
ideas.s: Most Jews of the period read the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4 as angels who took human wives before the flood. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, had the guilty angels bound under the earth in darkness until the judgment, and 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude speak of that prison.

The cities of the plain that God destroyed with fire in Lot's day. The prophets and later Jewish teachers made Sodom the byword for wickedness and sudden judgment, and its burned ruins by the Dead Sea were still pointed out in the first century.

entries.title: Jude 8-13, Michael and the body of Moses, and hidden reefs at the love feasts
entries.summary: The intruders claim dream visions, defile the body, despise authority and slander the glorious ones, though the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, did not dare to slander him but left the rebuke to the Lord. They have taken the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah; they are hidden reefs at the love feasts, waterless clouds, wild waves and wandering stars.
entries.plain: Jude turns on the intruders, who claim visions, defile their bodies, reject authority and insult the glorious ones. He contrasts them with the archangel Michael, who would not pass judgment even on the devil in their dispute over Moses' body but left it to the Lord. Jude places them in the line of Cain, Balaam and Korah and piles up images from nature, such as rainless clouds, dead trees, foaming waves and wandering stars, to show how dangerous and empty they are, hidden reefs at the community's love feasts. Who the glorious ones are, and where Jude found the story of Michael, are both read in more than one way.
entries.note: The glorious ones are read as the ranks of angels set over nations and nature (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); divine beings close to God's glory (Heiser); probably evil angels (the ESV Study Bible); or angels the intruders cursed in healing spells (Wright and Bird). Charles pieces the lost story together from later fragments: "Michael was commissioned to bury Moses", and Satan opposed it. Most commentators, Wright's commentary among them, hear Zechariah 3 behind the Lord rebuke you. Heiser disagrees: the Old Testament is not the source, but "it is the inspiration for it". Moses died outside the land, and Michael, guardian of the Lord's own domain, contends with the devil, lord of the dead, to bring the body there; he will not curse the devil, who even in rebellion is one of the divine beings. Whether the love feasts included the Lord's Supper (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles) or it "properly followed, but was distinct from, the love feast" (the Zondervan dictionary) is debated. Wandering stars were the planets, which most people took to be "spirits, gods and supernatural powers" (Arnold), or star-angels imprisoned in 1 Enoch (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

The seer from beyond the Euphrates whom Moab's king hired to curse Israel, who could only bless, and who then, Numbers says, showed Midian how to lead Israel into sin. Jewish tradition remembered him as the greatest prophet of the Gentiles and a byword for greed.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

ideas.n: The Watchers, the flood and the bound angels
ideas.s: Most Jews of the period read the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4 as angels who took human wives before the flood. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, had the guilty angels bound under the earth in darkness until the judgment, and 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude speak of that prison.

entries.title: Jude 14-25, Enoch's prophecy, scoffers, and a closing doxology
entries.summary: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about such people that the Lord comes with his countless holy ones to judge all and convict the ungodly. The apostles foretold scoffers in the last times; the readers are to build themselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love and show mercy, snatching some from the fire. Jude closes with praise to the one able to keep them from stumbling.
entries.plain: Jude quotes a prophecy from Enoch that the Lord will come with countless holy ones to judge the ungodly, and applies it to the intruders, whom he describes as grumblers driven by their own desires. He reminds his readers that the apostles predicted such scoffers. The faithful are to build up their faith, pray in the Spirit, stay in God's love and show mercy, rescuing those they can, and the letter ends in praise of the God who can keep them from falling. What Jude's quotation of Enoch says about that book's standing is read in more than one way.
entries.note: Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles), from the Book of the Watchers (Wright and Bird); a cultural backgrounds chart dates the Enoch literature 200 to 63 BC. Carson, Moo and Morris record that "some in the early church were sure that no canonical writer would do this", which cost the letter acceptance for a time. Heiser notes that Second Temple readers took Enoch for God's spokesman because he carried God's judgment to the fallen sons of God. Heiser reads the holy ones who come with the Lord as the armies of heaven, not saints, and Wright's commentary hears Zechariah 14:5, where the Lord comes with all his holy ones. The cultural backgrounds notes suggest the intruders used 1 Enoch while ignoring its judgment. Wright and Bird and Carson, Moo and Morris answer the argument that the apostles' words in verse 17 point to a late date. Praying in the Holy Spirit is read as inspired prayer, perhaps including tongues (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), or prayer led by the Spirit (the ESV Study Bible).

ideas.s: A collection of Jewish writings in the name of Enoch, who walked with God and was taken, composed over the last centuries before Christ and widely read in the first. It tells of the fallen Watchers and the coming judgment, and Jude quotes it by name.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.

entries.title: Revelation 1:1-8, a revelation sent as a letter
entries.summary: The book opens as a revelation God gave Jesus, sent by his angel to his servant John, with a blessing on the one who reads it aloud and on those who hear. It then greets seven churches in Asia like a letter, from the one who is, was and is to come, and from Jesus, ruler of the kings of the earth, who is coming with the clouds.
entries.plain: The opening tells the reader what kind of book this is: a vision handed from God to Jesus, passed through an angel to John, and meant to be read out loud to gathered believers, who are blessed for heeding it. It then turns into a letter, greeting seven congregations in the Roman province of Asia from God, from the Spirit, and from Jesus, praised as the one who loved them, set them free and made them a royal priesthood. Its first theme is announced at once: Jesus will return in full view of the world, and God holds the beginning and the end. Who this John was, and when he wrote, are both debated.
entries.note: Who wrote it is open. Keener holds that one author wrote the Fourth Gospel and Revelation, and Carson, Moo and Morris "attribute both books to John the apostle", noting that Melito of Sardis and Irenaeus of Smyrna, early witnesses, came from its cities. Dionysius of Alexandria denied it on grounds of style, and so, Carson, Moo and Morris report, do most scholars today; Wright and Bird call the author John the Seer. Irenaeus dates the vision to the end of Domitian's reign (Against Heresies 5.30.3), and Keener, the study Bibles, Beale and Carson, Moo and Morris favor about 95; a date just after Nero, 68-69, is the main alternative, argued partly from 11:1-2 (Carson, Moo and Morris), and Wright and Bird write that "No agreement is in sight". On genre, Carson, Moo and Morris call the book a prophecy in apocalyptic form sent as a letter, and hesitate to call it an apocalypse; the Zondervan dictionary calls it apocalyptic. The broken grammar of verse 4 is deliberate for Carson, Moo and Morris and for Heiser, who hears Exodus 3:14 in it; the dictionary blames Hebrew idiom and haste. One reader read the book aloud to each church (Keener).

ideas.n: Apocalypses, visions and numbers that mean something
ideas.s: Jewish books of visions, usually written in the name of a hero from long ago, in which a heavenly guide shows a seer what heaven sees in the present trouble and how God will end it. They spoke in pictures and in numbers that carried meaning, and Revelation is the one that calls itself an apocalypse.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

entries.title: Revelation 1:9-20, Patmos, the Lord's day, lampstands and stars
entries.summary: On the island of Patmos, in the Spirit on the Lord's day, John hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to write to seven churches. He turns and sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, holding seven stars, who holds the keys of death and Hades and explains what the stars and lampstands mean.
entries.plain: John, a fellow sufferer with the churches, is on the small island of Patmos for his loyalty to God's message about Jesus when, on the Lord's day, a voice orders him to write down his vision for seven named congregations. He turns and sees the risen Jesus standing among seven lampstands, a blazing and overwhelming figure, and collapses before him. Jesus lifts his fear by saying he once died, now lives for ever and controls death itself, and he explains that the lampstands are the churches and the stars are their angels. Why John was on Patmos, which day the Lord's day was, and who the angels of the churches are are all debated.
entries.note: A governor could banish without loss of property, relegatio; deportatio was the emperor's (Keener). Origen's tradition and the Zondervan dictionary say the emperor sent John, Carson, Moo and Morris and Wright and Bird a local official. Patmos too is disputed. The CSB Study Bible and the dictionary call it a penal colony, the dictionary with mines; the ESV Study Bible an island of political exile, as Pliny attests (Carson, Moo and Morris); Wright and Bird write that "Patmos was a military garrison, not a penal colony", and Heiser, after Aune, pictures John under house arrest there. The seven-branched lampstand was Judaism's most common symbol (the cultural backgrounds notes). Jewish sources gave the keys of death and Hades to God alone (Keener), against magical papyri that gave them to Hekate (Arnold). Gentiles took stars for gods, Jews for angels (Keener); a coin of Domitian shows seven stars around his deified son (Price and House). The angels of the churches are read as guardians (the cultural backgrounds notes; the CSB), personifications (the ESV) or heavenly beings (Beale); Heiser's book allows a human reading, but in his podcast he follows Aune: nearly every angel in Revelation is supernatural, so these are too.

ideas.s: The day early Christians kept for Jesus, most likely Sunday, the weekday of the resurrection. In the cities of Asia one day a month was already given to honoring the emperor.

Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, proud cities of the Roman province of Asia, strung along a road a courier could walk. Each letter in Revelation 2 and 3 speaks into its own city's history, trades and temples.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

Most people in Paul's world believed their lives were ruled by Fate, worked out through the stars, which many took to be heavenly beings. Few thought there was any escape, and cults that promised one drew followers.

entries.title: Revelation 2:1-7, Ephesus and the Nicolaitans
entries.summary: To Ephesus the one who holds the seven stars praises a church that tested false apostles and hates the works of the Nicolaitans, but warns that it has abandoned its first love and may lose its lampstand. The one who conquers will eat from the tree of life in God's paradise.
entries.plain: Jesus praises the Ephesian believers for hard work, endurance and for exposing false teachers and rejecting the group called the Nicolaitans. Yet they have let their early love grow cold, and unless they turn back he will take away their place as a light among the churches. Whoever holds out to the end is promised food from the tree of life in God's garden. Who the Nicolaitans were is debated.
entries.note: Ephesus was the province's leading city (Keener), named guardian of the imperial cult, where a new cult of the emperors opened about five years before Revelation (the cultural backgrounds notes); the atlas names its temple, the Sebastos, for Vespasian, Titus and Domitian. Says this is the prophets' messenger formula (Keener), and the seven letters resemble emperors' edicts, but the prophets' oracles on the nations more closely (the cultural backgrounds article Letters to the Seven Churches). The Cayster silted the harbor, but the lampstand threat is to the church (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); the Zondervan dictionary instead finds a dying city's "lassitude" in the letter, and Heiser suggests removing the lampstand means withdrawing the church's guardian angel. Heiser, following Beale, reads the lost first love as a failing mission, not cooled devotion, since verses 2-3 commend them. The Nicolaitans are unknown (the cultural backgrounds notes). Some fathers tied them to Nicolas of Antioch, a link the dictionary finds unsupported and Heiser, with Aune, calls legend; Beale and Heiser read the name as he conquers the people, a match for the rabbis' Balaam. The tree of life is Eden's language, and the Artemis estates had tree-shrines (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, proud cities of the Roman province of Asia, strung along a road a courier could walk. Each letter in Revelation 2 and 3 speaks into its own city's history, trades and temples.
The great goddess of Ephesus, whose temple was one of the seven wonders of the world and a bank as well. Her cult was the city's pride and the living of its craftsmen.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.

entries.title: Revelation 2:8-11, Smyrna, poor and slandered
entries.summary: To Smyrna the risen Jesus says he sees their hardship and poverty and the abuse they suffer from local opponents claiming to be the true Jews, whom he condemns in harsh terms. Some will be jailed for a short time; if they stay loyal even to death he will reward them with life.
entries.plain: Smyrna's believers are poor and harassed, and Jesus, who himself died and rose, tells them he sees it and that in his eyes they are rich. Local opponents who claim the name of Jews are slandering them, and Jesus answers with a fierce label for that gathering. Prison is coming for some, but only for a brief, limited time, and those who stay loyal to death will be given life and will escape the final judgment. What lay behind the slander, and how that harsh label should be heard, are debated.
entries.note: Keener calls Smyrna and Ephesus the oldest imperial-cult centers; the atlas and the Zondervan dictionary make Smyrna's emperor temple of AD 26 the second in Asia, after Pergamum's. Judea offered sacrifice to God for the emperor instead of to him, and "Christians expelled from synagogues might well lose their exemption" (the cultural backgrounds article The Imperial Cult; Keener); Carson, Moo and Morris suggest instead that some Christians sheltered in the synagogue. Cases came through informers, delatores, and Jews of Smyrna later joined against Polycarp (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). How harsh the pressure was is read differently: the CSB Study Bible has Domitian make emperor worship mandatory; the article says no one was hunted down unless accused; Beale sees no widespread demand, Wright and Bird local pressure, and Carson, Moo and Morris no solid evidence of persecution in Asia. Synagogue of Satan echoes the Dead Sea Scrolls' polemic, an intra-Jewish debate and no model for Gentile speech (the cultural backgrounds notes); Heiser, calling an antisemitic reading nonsense, takes it as a faction working with the pagan rulers. The crown was the athlete's and the martyr's garland (Keener); the dictionary hears Smyrna's ring of porticoes, the atlas perhaps its citadel.

ideas.s: A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.

ideas.n: The games and the victor's wreath
ideas.s: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.

entries.title: Revelation 2:12-17, Pergamum, where Satan's throne is
entries.summary: To Pergamum Jesus, who wields the sword of judgment, says they have stayed loyal in a city he calls Satan's seat, even after the martyrdom of Antipas. But some follow teaching like Balaam's that leads to idol meals and immorality. The faithful are promised hidden heavenly food and a white stone carrying a new name.
entries.plain: Pergamum's church lives in a city Jesus calls the seat of Satan, and it has kept faith even after one of its own, Antipas, was killed. But some members have accepted teaching that, like the old story of Balaam luring Israel, draws them into idol feasts and sexual sin, and Jesus warns he will come against them with the word of his mouth. To those who overcome he promises secret bread from heaven and a white stone inscribed with a name of their own. What Satan's seat refers to, and what the white stone means, are debated.
entries.note: The sword of Jesus' mouth answers the governor's right of the sword to execute (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Wright calls Pergamum the governor's seat; Price and House and the atlas place the capital at Ephesus by then. Satan's throne is read as the imperial cult (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), the cult with the altar of Zeus (Wright and Bird), Asclepius' serpent (Wright), or all at once (the ESV Study Bible; the atlas); Price and House report many scholars for the altar, and Heiser tentatively favors it. Balaam is probably a local teacher's nickname (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); he led Israel into sexual sin and idol food (Numbers 25:1-2; 31:16). Beale, the cultural backgrounds article Sacrificed Food and Heiser take the issue as eating at idol worship, not market meat. Jewish tradition hid the ark and its manna until the end (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); the Zondervan dictionary ties the hidden manna to the messianic banquet, Heiser to angels' food (Psalm 78:25). The white stone may be a festival token, a medicinal stone or a juror's acquittal (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Heiser, with Aune, reads acquittal, and the name as God's or Christ's (3:12).

ideas.s: Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.

The seer from beyond the Euphrates whom Moab's king hired to curse Israel, who could only bless, and who then, Numbers says, showed Midian how to lead Israel into sin. Jewish tradition remembered him as the greatest prophet of the Gentiles and a byword for greed.

Most meat in a Greek city had passed through a sacrifice at a temple. Eating it at the temple's table, buying it in the market or meeting it at a friend's dinner raised the question of whether a believer was sharing in the worship of the god.

entries.title: Revelation 2:18-29, Thyatira, the guilds and Jezebel
entries.summary: To Thyatira the Son of God, with eyes like fire and feet like bronze, praises a growing church but rebukes it for tolerating Jezebel, a self-styled prophetess who leads his servants into immorality and idol food. Those who hold fast are promised authority over the nations and the morning star.
entries.plain: Jesus, pictured with piercing eyes and gleaming feet, commends Thyatira for growing love, faith and service. But the church puts up with a self-appointed prophetess he nicknames Jezebel, who is leading members into idol meals and sexual sin, and he warns of judgment on her and her followers so that every church will know he sees into the heart. Those who have refused her teaching need only hold firm, and the faithful are promised a share in his rule and the morning star. Whether her immorality is literal or figurative is debated.
entries.note: Thyatira's records name more trade guilds than any other Asian city (the Zondervan dictionary). Each guild met for meals, usually monthly, dedicated to its patron god (Keener), often in its temple (the dictionary); "To refuse to share the meal was tantamount to refusing connection" with members one needed to make a living (the cultural backgrounds notes). Metalworking led its trades, so bronze feet would strike home (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Wright notes that the bronze trade's patron, Apollo Tyrimnaeus, appeared on coins with the emperor as son of god, which sharpens the only Son of God in Revelation. Jezebel led Israel into idolatry; here the name labels a local prophetess (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), chosen, the dictionary suggests, because Ahab's marriage sealed a trade alliance, and perhaps standing for a group. Whether her immorality is literal is debated: both may be present (the cultural backgrounds notes), probably spiritual (Keener), mainly idolatry (Wright); Heiser reads her as a figure for pagan religion. The morning star was Venus, and Numbers 24:17 was read of the Messiah (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Heiser says the fallen gods now ruling the nations "will be displaced and replaced" by believers.

ideas.s: Craftsmen of one trade lived and worked in the same streets and banded together in guilds, which set standards, defended their interests and met for meals in honor of a patron god.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

Most meat in a Greek city had passed through a sacrifice at a temple. Eating it at the temple's table, buying it in the market or meeting it at a friend's dinner raised the question of whether a believer was sharing in the worship of the god.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

entries.title: Revelation 3:1-6, Sardis, alive in name only
entries.summary: To Sardis the one who holds the seven spirits and seven stars says the church has a reputation for being alive but is dead, and warns that he will come like a thief if it does not wake up. A few have not soiled their clothes; the one who conquers will walk with him in white and will not be blotted out of the book of life.
entries.plain: Sardis has a name for being lively, but Jesus says the church is spiritually dead. They must wake up and turn back, or he will arrive without warning, like a burglar. A few have kept themselves clean, and they and every overcomer will wear white, stay in the book of life and be owned by Jesus before his Father. What the city's reputation alludes to is debated.
entries.note: Sardis had a large, respected Jewish community (Keener) that later built one of antiquity's largest synagogues (the cultural backgrounds notes; the atlas). Its reputation for being alive may allude to a renewal cult, the burial ground facing the acropolis or, most plausibly, the faded glory of Croesus (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), whom the Zondervan dictionary calls a byword for wealth and pride; the CSB Study Bible, death and Artemis. The earthquake of AD 17 ruined it, and despite ten million sesterces of Roman relief it never recovered (the dictionary). Its acropolis was twice taken by stealth through lax guards (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), by Cyrus and, the dictionary says, later by the Romans; but coming like a thief most directly recalls Jesus' saying. Temples barred worshipers in soiled clothes (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), and the atlas hears Sardis's textile trade in the white garments; for Heiser, white denotes "membership or belongingness for those who overcome". Cities struck names from citizen rolls (Keener). On the book of life, Beale sees no threat of losing salvation; the dictionary stresses assurance but says being blotted out means perdition; Heiser, with Aune, argues an erasable name rules out a predestinarian reading.

ideas.s: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, proud cities of the Roman province of Asia, strung along a road a courier could walk. Each letter in Revelation 2 and 3 speaks into its own city's history, trades and temples.
The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
An old picture of God keeping a register of the names of those who belong to him. Jewish writers developed it, and the New Testament uses it from Luke to Revelation.

entries.title: Revelation 3:7-13, Philadelphia and the key of David
entries.summary: To Philadelphia the one who holds the key of David sets before a weak but faithful church an open door no one can shut. Those of the synagogue of Satan will bow at their feet, and the one who conquers will be a pillar in God's temple, bearing the name of the new Jerusalem.
entries.plain: Jesus, who controls the door to God's kingdom, tells the small, weak church in Philadelphia that he has opened a door for them that no one can close, because they have stayed true to him. He promises that the local opponents who deny them the name of God's people will one day have to admit that he loves this church, and that he will protect them in the coming time of testing. The overcomer will become a permanent pillar in God's temple, marked with the names of God, his city and Jesus himself. Who the church's opponents were, and how large the city's Jewish community was, are debated.
entries.note: The key of David comes from Isaiah 22:22, the royal steward's control of the palace door, so Jesus, not the synagogue's leaders, decides who belongs (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Heiser, after Beale and Carson, reads this key and the keys of 1:18 as one claim: Jesus alone opens a new Eden without death. Expulsion could expose believers to Roman persecution (Keener), since they might lose the Jewish exemption (the cultural backgrounds article The Imperial Cult). On the city's Jews, Keener cites a third-century synagogue inscription and the ESV Study Bible one from a nearby town; the CSB Study Bible finds little evidence, and the Zondervan dictionary, citing none, pictures a bitterly nationalistic synagogue. Falling at their feet reverses Isaiah 60:14 (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; Heiser). After the earthquake of AD 17 the city took new names, for a time Neocaesarea (the ESV Study Bible; the cultural backgrounds notes). Temple pillars often carried inscriptions, as at the temple of Zeus at Euromos (the atlas), but the main background is Isaiah 56:5 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Heiser reads the hour of trial as final judgment, not freedom from suffering.

ideas.s: A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.

Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, proud cities of the Roman province of Asia, strung along a road a courier could walk. Each letter in Revelation 2 and 3 speaks into its own city's history, trades and temples.
Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.

entries.title: Revelation 3:14-22, Laodicea, lukewarm and rich
entries.summary: To Laodicea the faithful and true witness says the church is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm, and he will spit it out. It thinks itself rich but is poor, blind and naked; he counsels it to buy gold, white clothes and eye salve, and stands at the door and knocks.
entries.plain: Laodicea's church is comfortable and pleased with itself, and Jesus says its half-hearted faith disgusts him, like a drink that is neither refreshing nor warming. They think they are wealthy, but he calls them poor, blind and exposed, and urges them to get true riches, proper clothing and healing for their sight from him instead. He corrects them because he loves them, and pictures himself knocking at their door, ready to share a meal with anyone who lets him in. What the hot and cold imagery stands for is debated.
entries.note: Laodicea, a banking city, rebuilt after the earthquake of AD 60 (Keener; AD 61 for Wright), refusing relief offered, in differing accounts, by Rome (Keener), the emperor (the cultural backgrounds article Laodicea), Nero (the atlas) or the Senate (the Zondervan dictionary). Its black wool, medical school and eye salve make verse 18 a reply to the city's boasts (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright); the dictionary thinks the salve was probably made from Hierapolis's thermal mud. Keener writes that "Laodicea lacked a natural water supply"; piped water arrived lukewarm and full of sediment (the cultural backgrounds notes; the article). Its source is disputed: hot springs six miles south (Keener); springs to the south, temperature unstated (the article; the atlas); or Hierapolis, which the others place to the north, with warm, soda-laden water (the dictionary). With Hierapolis's hot springs and Colossae's cool water nearby (the atlas; the cultural backgrounds notes), Keener, the cultural backgrounds notes, the ESV Study Bible and Wright read hot and cold as both useful and lukewarm as useless; Beale reports hot as zeal and cold as rejection, and blames an ineffective witness. A shared meal bound host and guest (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener).

ideas.s: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, proud cities of the Roman province of Asia, strung along a road a courier could walk. Each letter in Revelation 2 and 3 speaks into its own city's history, trades and temples.
Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.

ideas.n: The banquet of the age to come
ideas.s: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.

entries.title: Revelation 4:1-11, the throne room and the twenty-four elders
entries.summary: Through an open door John is called up to heaven and sees God on a throne, ringed by a rainbow, with twenty-four elders on thrones, four living creatures and a sea of glass. The creatures cry holy, holy, holy, and the elders lay down their crowns, saying the Lord and God is worthy because he created all things.
entries.plain: John is summoned up into heaven and sees God enthroned in dazzling light, surrounded by twenty-four elders on their own thrones and by four strange living creatures full of eyes. The creatures praise God's holiness without pause, and the elders bow and set down their crowns, declaring that God deserves all honor because he made everything. Before any judgment on earth is shown, the reader is shown who really rules. Who the twenty-four elders are is debated.
entries.note: Come up here and the open door recall Moses' summons and other apocalypses (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Some Jewish mystics fasted and kept vigils to win a throne vision, but John, like Ezekiel, is simply caught up (the cultural backgrounds notes and article on Paul's third heaven; Keener). Heiser reads chapters 4 and 5 as a divine council scene shaped as a covenant lawsuit and built on Daniel 7. On the elders, Keener writes that "it almost certainly alludes to the twenty-four orders of priests" (Josephus, Antiquities 7.14.7), the Zondervan dictionary sees the church's heavenly priesthood, and Wright, Beale and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles the tribes with the apostles. Heiser's book leans to council members; his podcast, answering Beale, makes them council members, glorified believers and star imagery at once. The sea of glass recalls Solomon's bronze sea in a temple-like throne room (Keener; the cultural backgrounds article Heaven as a Temple in Revelation); the ESV Study Bible makes it heaven's floor, the dictionary the lavers or the waters above. The scene answers Caesar's court (Wright): Domitian demanded the title lord and god, apparently as a loyalty test (Carson, Moo and Morris, citing Suetonius).

ideas.s: Jewish visionaries told of being caught up through the heavens to see God's throne and paradise, and writers numbered the heavens differently. Paul's third heaven speaks that language, though he refuses to make it his credential.
Israel's Scriptures picture God presiding over an assembly of heavenly beings, the sons of God, and Psalm 82 calls its members gods. Who those gods are is one of the hardest questions behind John 10.

ideas.n: Priests on duty: the twenty-four courses
ideas.s: Israel's ordinary priests were divided into twenty-four courses that took turns at the temple, a week at a time. Most lived in the country and came up to Jerusalem when their turn came round.

ideas.n: The tabernacle and its heavenly pattern
ideas.s: The tent sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, with an outer room for the priests and an inner room, the holy of holies, for the ark. Moses built it to a pattern shown on the mountain, and many Jews thought of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: Revelation 5:1-14, the sealed scroll and the Lamb
entries.summary: In God's right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and no one is worthy to open it until the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, appears as a Lamb that looks slain. The living creatures, the elders, countless angels and all creation worship him.
entries.plain: God holds a sealed scroll, and John weeps because nobody anywhere is fit to open it. He is told that the promised royal heir from Judah has won the right, but what he actually sees is a Lamb bearing the marks of slaughter, who takes the scroll. The whole of heaven, then every creature, breaks into worship, praising the Lamb because his death has bought a people for God from every nation. What the scroll is, and what its seals stand for, are debated.
entries.note: A scroll written on both sides, an opisthograph, was rare; this echoes Ezekiel 2:9-10 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; the ESV and CSB Study Bibles). Witnesses pressed seals into the wax over a legal document's threads (the cultural backgrounds article Sealing Documents and Revelation 5): often seven (Keener), seven for a Roman will (Beale), though the article says "usually about six in number". A will could not be opened until its maker's death was attested, so the slain Lamb opens it (Keener). The scroll is read as a covenant inheritance in the form of a will (Beale), a will or covenant (the ESV Study Bible), a will, perhaps the book of life (Keener), God's sealed plan (Wright) or his plan of judgment and redemption (the CSB Study Bible). The article and Heiser agree that the seals' judgments are not the scroll's contents, which stay shut until the seventh seal; Heiser adds that John never reveals these. Lion of Judah and Root of David were Davidic titles, and the slain Passover lamb shocks beside the reigning lion (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Heiser, with Aune, sees the Lamb's investiture, not enthronement: "the lamb never occupies the throne" until 22:1.

ideas.s: A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.

A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
Israel's Scriptures picture God presiding over an assembly of heavenly beings, the sons of God, and Psalm 82 calls its members gods. Who those gods are is one of the hardest questions behind John 10.

entries.title: Revelation 6:1-8, four horsemen
entries.summary: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders go out: a crowned archer on a white horse bent on conquest, a rider on a red horse who takes peace from the earth, a rider with scales on a black horse while wheat sells at famine prices, and Death on a pale horse with Hades following.
entries.plain: As the Lamb breaks the first four seals, four horsemen ride out one after another. They bring conquest, bloodshed, food prices so high that a day's pay buys only bread, and finally death on a massive scale through war, hunger, disease and wild animals. None of them rides out until the Lamb opens the seal. Who the first rider stands for is debated.
entries.note: The riders adapt the patrolling horsemen of Zechariah 1:8-11 and 6:1-8 (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; Wright), and Heiser, with Beale, reads them, like Zechariah's, as sent out from God's throne in the council scene of chapters 4 and 5. Keener reads each seal as a witness to the document, which could not be opened until every seal was broken. An archer on a white horse evoked the Parthians, Rome's most feared enemy (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); "Romans admitted that they could not defeat the Parthians to the east" (the cultural backgrounds article Parthia). The first rider is read differently: conquest, with Parthia in view (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); an evil, deceiving force (Beale); more likely conquering kings than the Messiah (Wright); and destructive conquest, wearing a victor's wreath, not diadems (the CSB Study Bible). Famine prices ran more than ten times normal (Keener) or five to fifteen times (the cultural backgrounds notes), and readers may have recalled Domitian's vineyard edict of AD 92 (Beale; Keener). Heiser, after Beale, hears in the fourth rider's list Ezekiel 14:21's four judgments on an unfaithful nation.
