ideas.s: A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.

The empire east of the Euphrates, Rome's most feared enemy, famous for mounted archers who could shoot backward as they rode. Its armies had destroyed a Roman army and once marched into Judea to put their own man on the throne.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Revelation 6:9-17, souls under the altar and the great day of wrath
entries.summary: At the fifth seal the souls of those killed for God's word cry out from under the altar, how long, and are given white robes and told to wait. At the sixth a great earthquake shakes the world, the sky rolls up like a scroll, and kings and slaves alike hide in the caves from the wrath of the Lamb.
entries.plain: At the fifth seal John sees the martyrs beneath heaven's altar, crying out to God to ask how long before he puts things right; they are given white robes and told to rest a little longer. At the sixth seal the whole universe seems to come apart, with earthquake, a darkened sun and falling stars. Everyone from kings to slaves runs for the caves, begging to be hidden from God and the Lamb on the day of their anger. Whether this pictures the literal end of the world or a great upheaval in history is debated.
entries.note: Sacrificial blood was poured at the altar's base (Leviticus 4:7), so the martyrs are sacrifices, as in 4 Maccabees (Keener); Heiser hears the Lord avenging his own, the vengeance of Deuteronomy 32:43 (after Bandy). In 4 Ezra, of about the same decade, the righteous dead ask how long and must wait until their number is complete (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener reads comfort against the emperor and governors who judged them, though Carson, Moo and Morris, who note that most scholars see unusual persecution behind 6:9, think the evidence for one under Domitian exaggerated. Earthquakes had wrecked Asian cities in living memory (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Heaven rolled up is Isaiah 34:4 in the terms of a reader rolling up a scroll (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Whether this is the end of the age is read differently: Keener says the cosmic language fits the end most naturally; Wright reads vivid symbol for political upheaval; Carson, Moo and Morris hold that "Revelation is about eschatology, not history" but set against John's own day; and Heiser, after Beale, reads stock imagery, chiefly Isaiah 34:4, for judgment on heavenly powers as well as earthly ones.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to Revelation 6:9-11 and 6:12-17, and on 6:9, 6:10, 6:12-13, 6:14 and 6:15-16

ideas.s: Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.

Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.

ideas.n: Apocalypses, visions and numbers that mean something
ideas.s: Jewish books of visions, usually written in the name of a hero from long ago, in which a heavenly guide shows a seer what heaven sees in the present trouble and how God will end it. They spoke in pictures and in numbers that carried meaning, and Revelation is the one that calls itself an apocalypse.
The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.

entries.title: Revelation 7:1-17, the sealing of the 144,000 and the crowd in white
entries.summary: Four angels hold back the winds until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, who have come out of the great tribulation and whom the Lamb will shepherd.
entries.plain: The storm of judgment is held back until God marks his servants as his own, and John hears their number, 144,000, counted tribe by tribe from Israel. When he looks, he sees instead a vast, uncountable crowd from all over the world, dressed in white and celebrating God's rescue. An elder explains that they have come through great suffering and that the Lamb will now shelter, feed and guide them, ending their pain. Who the 144,000 are, whether they are the same people as the crowd, and why the tribe of Dan is missing are all debated.
entries.note: God's servants are marked as his, like sealed goods; the mark is the taw of Ezekiel 9:4-6, set on the righteous before judgment (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Heiser), and Heiser adds that the seal is God's name, mirroring the beast's mark. The list resembles a military census (the cultural backgrounds notes; the CSB Study Bible). Why Dan is missing is read differently: a warning about apostasy (Keener); unexplained, since Jewish sources criticize every tribe (the cultural backgrounds notes); and for Heiser, who will not dismiss the patristic Antichrist from Dan, perhaps suspicion of Gentile mixing in the tribe, which he calls probably unanswerable. The 144,000 are the whole people of God or a remnant of ethnic Israel, which "remains debated" (Keener); the whole redeemed community (Beale; Wright); symbolic (the ESV Study Bible); a future converted Israel (the CSB Study Bible). Heiser, in his Revelation 7 and question-and-answer episodes alike, reads Jews who follow the Lamb, distinct from the crowd. The great tribulation is a definite future period (the Zondervan dictionary) or perhaps the whole era between Jesus' comings (the cultural backgrounds article Time in Revelation). Palm branches belonged to Tabernacles (Keener) and came to mean victory (the dictionary).

ideas.s: A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.
Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.

ideas.n: Apocalypses, visions and numbers that mean something
ideas.s: Jewish books of visions, usually written in the name of a hero from long ago, in which a heavenly guide shows a seer what heaven sees in the present trouble and how God will end it. They spoke in pictures and in numbers that carried meaning, and Revelation is the one that calls itself an apocalypse.

The autumn pilgrim feast, eight days long, when men lived in leafy shelters, priests poured water at the altar and torches lit the temple courts. It carried hopes of rain, of resurrection and of a coming king.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: Revelation 8:1-13, silence, incense and the first four trumpets
entries.summary: The seventh seal brings half an hour of silence in heaven. Seven angels receive trumpets, an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people at the golden altar and hurls fire to the earth, and the first four trumpets bring hail and fire, a burning mountain into the sea, the star Wormwood and a darkening of sun, moon and stars.
entries.plain: When the last seal opens, heaven falls quiet for a short time, and the prayers of God's people rise with incense before him. An angel then flings fire from the altar to the earth, and seven trumpets begin to sound. The first four strike a third of the land, the sea, the fresh water and the lights of the sky, and an eagle warns that worse is coming. What the silence means is debated.
entries.note: What the silence means is read differently: awe or fear before judgment (the cultural backgrounds notes); awe or the silence of the guilty (Keener); suspense (the ESV Study Bible); awe and expectation (Wright). Heiser, with Beale, prefers the appalled hush before judgment of Habakkuk 2:20, Zechariah 2:13 and Zephaniah 1:7, finding a silence so the prayers can be heard less persuasive. Judaism then counted seven archangels before God (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Trumpets warned of invasion and sounded in the temple (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The angel does a priest's task at the incense altar, where incense stood for prayer (the Zondervan dictionary; Keener), and Keener and Heiser both read the martyrs' prayers of 6:9-11 as what sets off the judgments that follow. The first four trumpets follow the plagues on Egypt: hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Beale; Wright). Wormwood is evidently Artemisia absinthium, a bitter herb (the dictionary); Heiser, rejecting modern headline readings, calls it the Old Testament's stock image of bitter judgment. The eagle could be a messenger, an omen, a legion's emblem or, as Keener thinks likeliest, a vulture signaling doom (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

ideas.n: The tabernacle and its heavenly pattern
ideas.s: The tent sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, with an outer room for the priests and an inner room, the holy of holies, for the ark. Moses built it to a pattern shown on the mountain, and many Jews thought of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.
Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
The blows God struck on Egypt before the exodus, from water turned to blood to the death of the firstborn, while Israel was spared. Revelation's trumpets and bowls replay them on the whole world.

entries.title: Revelation 9:1-21, the Abyss opened and the armies from the Euphrates
entries.summary: At the fifth trumpet a fallen star is given the key to the Abyss, and from its smoke come locusts like horses with human faces, women's hair and scorpions' stings, under a king called Abaddon and Apollyon. At the sixth, four angels bound at the Euphrates are released with a cavalry of two hundred million that kills a third of humanity, yet the survivors do not repent.
entries.plain: The fifth trumpet opens the pit of the Abyss, and a nightmarish swarm of locusts pours out to torment, for five months, those who lack God's mark, led by a king whose names mean destruction. The sixth trumpet unleashes a vast cavalry from beyond the Euphrates, the empire's eastern frontier, which kills a third of humanity. Even so the survivors keep worshiping idols and keep up their violence, witchcraft, immorality and theft. Whether the star and the king are evil angels, and how far the armies draw on fear of Parthia, are debated.
entries.note: Jewish traditions held evil angels imprisoned until their time, with angels holding the keys (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes), and the Zondervan dictionary calls the Abyss the prison of evil spirits. Heiser reads its opening as "the release of the fallen Watchers before their ultimate destruction with Satan", the rebels of Genesis 6 whom 1 Enoch has bound there. The star and the king are evil for Beale and the cultural backgrounds notes; Heiser, "skeptical of his skepticism", makes the star a good angel, perhaps 1 Enoch's Uriel. The hordes are demonic for the ESV and CSB Study Bibles, and Abaddon an evil angel in one dictionary entry but a title of Satan in another. The locusts recall the eighth plague, amplified by Joel's army (Keener; Heiser). Some link Apollyon with Apollo, whose emblems included the locust and whom emperors claimed: possible but unclear (Keener), seen by many (Beale). The Euphrates divided Rome from Parthia (Keener; Wright), and Jewish traditions had God's angels summon a Parthian invasion (1 Enoch 56:5-8; the cultural backgrounds article Parthia). Most keep the four bound angels apart from those of 7:1 while Beale links them (Beale); the CSB Study Bible and Heiser call them evil.

ideas.n: The Watchers, the flood and the bound angels
ideas.s: Most Jews of the period read the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4 as angels who took human wives before the flood. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, had the guilty angels bound under the earth in darkness until the judgment, and 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude speak of that prison.
The blows God struck on Egypt before the exodus, from water turned to blood to the death of the firstborn, while Israel was spared. Revelation's trumpets and bowls replay them on the whole world.

The empire east of the Euphrates, Rome's most feared enemy, famous for mounted archers who could shoot backward as they rode. Its armies had destroyed a Roman army and once marched into Judea to put their own man on the throne.

The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.

entries.title: Revelation 10:1-11, the mighty angel and the little scroll
entries.summary: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.
entries.plain: Between the sixth and seventh trumpets a towering angel, standing astride sea and land, holds a small open scroll. John is not allowed to record what seven thunders say, but the angel swears that God will wait no longer and that his long-hidden plan will be finished at the last trumpet. John is told to eat the scroll, which tastes sweet but turns bitter inside him, and then to prophesy again to many nations and rulers.
entries.note: Jewish literature pictured giant, sun-bright angels, meant to awe hearers with the God greater than any angel (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Heiser's chapter episode argues for "the second person of the Trinity appearing as a man", the Old Testament angel of the Lord, whose oath by God suits the Son serving the Father; his question-and-answer episodes call Christ a real option. A raised hand was an oath gesture in Greek practice as in the Old Testament (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The angel echoes Daniel 12:7, where an angel swears that three and a half years remain; here he swears the waiting is over (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Sealing up the thunders recalls Daniel 12:4, and some mysteries stay hidden until the end (Deuteronomy 29:29) (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Eating the scroll follows Ezekiel 2:8-3:3, sweet as God's word and bitter as the judgment John must announce (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Heiser, reporting Aune in his Revelation 5 episode, calls this open scroll not likely the sealed one of chapter 5, though some link them. John's commission to many nations recalls Jeremiah's, where Ezekiel was sent to Israel alone (the cultural backgrounds notes).

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.
Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.
Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.

entries.title: Revelation 11:1-14, the measured temple and the two witnesses
entries.summary: John is told to measure God's temple and its worshipers but to leave out the outer court, given to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Two witnesses in sackcloth prophesy with the powers of Elijah and Moses, are killed by the beast from the Abyss and left unburied in the great city, then raised and taken up to heaven.
entries.plain: John is told to measure God's temple and count its worshipers, while the outer court is left to the nations for a set time. Two witnesses, clothed for mourning and armed with powers like those of Moses and Elijah, preach until a beast from the Abyss kills them and their bodies are left exposed in the city where Jesus died, to the world's delight. After a short while God brings them back to life and takes them up to heaven, and a great earthquake shakes the city into giving God glory. What temple is meant, who the two witnesses are, and which city is the great city are all debated.
entries.note: Measuring marked a building for praise or preservation (Ezekiel 40-42; Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); Heiser, with Aune, says protection. Gentiles were kept to the outer court by pillars warning "no foreigner should go within that sanctuary" (Josephus, War 5.5.2), and one found in 1871 survives (Price and House). The temple is read as a rebuilt one (the ESV Study Bible's dispensationalists), God's persecuted people (Beale), the church (Wright), the heavenly temple (Keener). Early-date readers see Jerusalem's temple before its fall (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles); the Zondervan dictionary calls that obvious yet prefers Domitian; Carson, Moo and Morris grant that the argument "is not without force" but allow a rebuilt or metaphorical temple; Heiser sets out both cases, notes each camp turns literal or symbolic to suit its date, and leaves it open. Daniel's forty-two months may describe the kind of time, not its length (the cultural backgrounds article Time in Revelation). The witnesses are Enoch and Elijah (Hippolytus), a new Moses and Elijah or the church (Keener), the church's witness (Wright; Beale), or, for Heiser, after Zechariah 4, God's redeemed people. The great city is Jerusalem (Keener; the dictionary), Rome or the world (the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.s: Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

ideas.n: Apocalypses, visions and numbers that mean something
ideas.s: Jewish books of visions, usually written in the name of a hero from long ago, in which a heavenly guide shows a seer what heaven sees in the present trouble and how God will end it. They spoke in pictures and in numbers that carried meaning, and Revelation is the one that calls itself an apocalypse.

Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Revelation 11:15-19, the seventh trumpet and the ark
entries.summary: At the seventh trumpet heaven announces that rule over the world now belongs to God and his Messiah for ever. The elders worship, the angry nations meet God's judgment, and the heavenly temple opens to reveal the ark of the covenant.
entries.plain: The seventh trumpet brings a shout from heaven that the world's rule has passed for good to God and his anointed king. The elders bow and thank God for taking up his power, saying the time has come to judge the dead, reward his faithful servants and destroy those who ruin the earth. Heaven's temple then opens to show the ark of God's covenant, with storm and earthquake around it.
entries.note: Trumpets hailed a new king (1 Kings 1:34) (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The seventh trumpet brings no event of its own, only hymns (Carson, Moo and Morris); Heiser takes it as the day of the Lord itself, not AD 70. Keener notes that the world's kingdom was then Rome, to be handed to God's people (Daniel 7:17-18). The Messiah and the raging nations of verse 18 echo Psalm 2 (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; Heiser), and Heiser counts the fallen gods among the destroyers destroyed. The ark's fate is uncertain: the Zondervan dictionary says in one entry there is no evidence, and in another, citing Josephus's empty holy of holies, that it was evidently destroyed in 586 BC. Many Jews expected God to restore it at the end (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Once seen only by the high priest, it is now open to view; in Near Eastern symbolism it matched a throne, fitting a heaven drawn as throne room and temple (Keener; the cultural backgrounds article Heaven as a Temple in Revelation). Lightning and thunder recall Sinai (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Heiser, for whom God again makes a covenant people).
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Revelation 2:17, 11:14-15, 11:17, 11:18 and 11:19

ideas.s: Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
Israel's Scriptures picture God presiding over an assembly of heavenly beings, the sons of God, and Psalm 82 calls its members gods. Who those gods are is one of the hardest questions behind John 10.

ideas.n: The tabernacle and its heavenly pattern
ideas.s: The tent sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, with an outer room for the priests and an inner room, the holy of holies, for the ark. Moses built it to a pattern shown on the mountain, and many Jews thought of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.

entries.title: Revelation 12:1-6, the woman, the child and the dragon
entries.summary: A radiant woman, crowned with twelve stars and standing on the moon, labors to give birth while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, destined to rule the nations, is caught up to God's throne, and the woman escapes to the wilderness, where she is kept safe for 1,260 days.
entries.plain: A sign appears in the sky: a woman dressed in sunlight and crowned with stars, about to give birth. A monstrous dragon, with many heads and horns, drags down a third of the stars and waits to devour her baby as soon as it arrives. Her son, who is destined to rule the nations, is taken up to God's throne, and she flees to a safe place God has prepared for her in the desert. Who the woman is, what the third of the stars are, and whether the 1,260 days are symbolic or a future span are all debated.
entries.note: Hearers knew the myth of Python hunting pregnant Leto until her son Apollo killed it, or Typhon pursuing Isis (Keener; Beale; the cultural backgrounds article Symbolism in Revelation 12:1-6). Emperors posed as Apollo, putting the emperor on the dragon's side (Keener). Keener thinks Scripture and Jewish texts could supply every detail; Heiser, with Beale, roots the birth in Genesis 3:15; for Beale, John retells the pagan story as the true one. The article holds that "John's signs do not, however, communicate astrological meaning"; Heiser's Reversing Hermon reads 12:1-7 as a real sky sign. Joseph's dream (Genesis 37:9) and Zion in labor (Isaiah 66:7-10) make the woman Israel for most; for Heiser, God's people; for the CSB Study Bible, a Jewish remnant in a future tribulation. The third of the stars are angels fallen at the first rebellion (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; the Zondervan dictionary), the revolt against Jesus (Keener), or the faithful struck down, after Daniel 8 (Beale; Heiser). The 1,260 days span the age between Jesus' comings (Keener; the article Time in Revelation, which calls this debated), a future tribulation's second half (the CSB Study Bible), or, for Heiser, both: begun at the ascension, persecution still ahead.

ideas.s: The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.

entries.title: Revelation 12:7-17, war in heaven and the accuser thrown down
entries.summary: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him out of heaven, and a voice celebrates the fall of the accuser of the brothers, defeated by the Lamb's blood and the witnesses' testimony. On earth the dragon chases the woman, who is given eagle's wings, and when the earth swallows the river he spews after her, he turns to make war on her other children.
entries.plain: The archangel Michael and his forces defeat the dragon, revealed as the devil, and throw him and his angels out of heaven. A voice celebrates that the one who accused believers before God has lost his place, beaten by the Lamb's death and by believers who would not abandon their witness even to save their lives. Enraged, the dragon hunts the woman on earth, but she is carried to safety and the ground swallows the flood he sends, so he turns on her other children. When this war takes place, at the cross or at some other moment, is debated.
entries.note: Jews knew Michael from Daniel 10-12 as the prince who guards Israel, and the cultural backgrounds notes say "Jewish thinkers recognized Michael as Israel's guardian prince"; each nation had its angelic prince (Keener), and Arnold finds in Daniel "a direct correspondence between the outcome of the angelic battles and the fortunes" of nations. The War Scroll sends Michael's princely angel to help Israel at the end (Beale; Arnold). Satan accused the faithful in God's court (Job 1; Zechariah 3), so the war is a lawsuit too (Keener; Beale), and Heiser dates his fall to the kingdom's start, marked at Luke 10:18: "Satan has no claim on you". Arnold calls the serpent's identification with Satan, made in verse 9, unanimous among early Jews and Christians. The war's timing is disputed: at Christ's death and exaltation (Keener; Beale; the cultural backgrounds article Time in Revelation), still in the future (Arnold; the Zondervan dictionary; the CSB Study Bible), or the original fall (one ESV Study Bible option). In one Leto story Earth was Python's mother, so the earth helping the woman turns the myth around (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Heiser, with Beale and McDonough, hears Exodus 15:12, where the earth swallows Egypt.

ideas.s: God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

ideas.n: Rulers and powers over the nations
ideas.s: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.

The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.

Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.

entries.title: Revelation 13:1-10, the beast from the sea
entries.summary: A beast with ten horns and seven heads rises from the sea, built from Daniel's leopard, bear and lion, and the dragon gives it his power. One head seems to have had a fatal wound that healed, the whole earth follows it in awe, and it is allowed to blaspheme and to make war on God's people for forty-two months.
entries.plain: A beast rises from the sea, a composite of the animals in Daniel's vision, and the dragon hands it his power and rule. One of its heads appears to recover from a death blow, and the amazed world worships both the dragon and the beast, thinking no one can resist it. For a limited time it is allowed to mock God and overpower his people, and everyone whose name is missing from the Lamb's register of the living bows to it, so believers are called to patient faith. Whether the healed wound alludes to the rumor of Nero's return is debated.
entries.note: The beast gathers Daniel's four beasts into one, and Jews then read the fourth as Rome (Keener; Wright; Beale; the Zondervan dictionary). Rome reached Asia by sea (Keener; 4 Ezra), and for Beale "Roman ships literally seemed to be rising out of the sea". Heiser adds Job 40-41, the one Old Testament pair of sea and land beasts, Leviathan and Behemoth, as a minority background beside Daniel. The blasphemous names fit emperors' titles, son of god and, for Domitian, lord and god (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Nero killed himself in AD 68 (Josephus, War 4.9.2), rumor said he would return, and in Armenian his name came to mean Antichrist (the cultural backgrounds article A New Nero). Keener says most commentators see that legend behind the healed head, though the article says John need not have expected Nero literally; Beale allows the allusion but reports doubts; Carson, Moo and Morris find the legend not very close to the beast; Wright and the ESV Study Bible read the empire's near-collapse in 68-69; Heiser hears a counterfeit of Christ's death and resurrection. War on the saints recalls Nero burning Christians as torches after the fire of 64 (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes).

ideas.n: Daniel's four beasts and the fourth kingdom
ideas.s: Daniel 7 pictured four empires as four beasts rising from the sea, the last with ten horns, judged before one like a son of man receives the kingdom. In the first century many Jews read the fourth beast as Rome.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.

Daniel's king who exalts himself above every god and defiles the sanctuary became a pattern Jews saw again in Antiochus, Pompey and Caligula. Paul's man of lawlessness, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God, belongs to that line.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
An old picture of God keeping a register of the names of those who belong to him. Jewish writers developed it, and the New Testament uses it from Luke to Revelation.

entries.title: Revelation 13:11-18, the beast from the earth, the mark and 666
entries.summary: A second beast, harmless-looking like a lamb but speaking like the dragon, rises from the earth and drives everyone to worship the first beast, working wonders and making its statue speak. Trade is barred to anyone without its mark on hand or forehead, a mark tied to the beast's name and number, 666.
entries.plain: A second beast comes up from the land, lamb-like in appearance but dragon-like in speech, and it works on the first beast's behalf to bring the world to worship it. It dazzles people with wonders, has a statue of the first beast made and brought to life, and puts to death those who will not bow. Everyone, whatever their rank or wealth, must bear its mark on hand or forehead to trade at all. The wise reader is told to work out the beast's number, 666; whether that points to Nero, and whether the mark is a literal brand, are debated.
entries.note: Most link the land beast to Asia's imperial cult and its elites (Keener; Wright; Beale); futurists see a religious leader (the study Bibles) or, says the Zondervan dictionary, the Antichrist. Domitian set up a statue nearly 25 feet high at Ephesus, and a governor executed Christians who refused to worship it (the cultural backgrounds notes), yet "no one would hunt down nonparticipants to ensure their participation" unless accused (the cultural backgrounds article The Imperial Cult). The mark is read as a brand or imperial stamp (Keener; Beale), a parody of Deuteronomy 6:8 (Beale; loosely, says Heiser), a mark of doom as in Psalms of Solomon 15, "visible only to God and his angels" (the article The Mark of the Beast), or a literal brand for trade (the CSB Study Bible); Heiser, after Imes, reads it as bearing a name (Numbers 6:27). Counted in Hebrew letters, Nero Caesar gives 666, or 616, a manuscript variant (Keener; Wright), "as if some knew the riddle's answer but calculated it differently" (the article). Beale objects, reading 666 as short of 777; Heiser says nobody knows, and that Nero needs juggled spellings: "it just feels like cheating at some point".

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.
Craftsmen of one trade lived and worked in the same streets and banded together in guilds, which set standards, defended their interests and met for meals in honor of a patron god.

ideas.n: Apocalypses, visions and numbers that mean something
ideas.s: Jewish books of visions, usually written in the name of a hero from long ago, in which a heavenly guide shows a seer what heaven sees in the present trouble and how God will end it. They spoke in pictures and in numbers that carried meaning, and Revelation is the one that calls itself an apocalypse.

entries.title: Revelation 14:1-5, the Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
entries.summary: The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name and his Father's on their foreheads, singing a new song only they can learn. They have kept themselves pure, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are offered as firstfruits to God and the Lamb.
entries.plain: In contrast to the beast and its marked followers, John sees the Lamb on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who carry the names of the Lamb and his Father instead. Heaven resounds with music, and they sing a song only they can learn. They are described as pure and truthful, loyal followers of the Lamb, offered to God as the first of the harvest. Who the 144,000 are, and what their virginity stands for, are debated.
entries.note: Mount Zion, the temple mount and loosely Jerusalem, lay mostly in ruins after AD 70 but was promised restoration (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); the Zondervan dictionary reads it as where Christ will stand at his return. The Lamb's name against the beast's mark is a stark contrast (Keener; Wright), and the numbers contrast too: "Whereas 666 is a doubly triangular number, 144 is a square number" (the cultural backgrounds notes). Their virginity suggests holy-war purity, when soldiers kept from women (1 Samuel 21:5; Deuteronomy 23:9-11), or priestly purity (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Heiser, against Aune and Bauckham, finds holy war a weak fit, since soldiers abstained but were not virgins. Firstfruits went to God (Exodus 23:19) and promised more (Wright; Keener; the ESV Study Bible). The 144,000 are read as the church as Israel renewed (Wright and Bird), new Jerusalemites (the cultural backgrounds notes), Jewish believers in a future tribulation (dispensationalists, in the ESV Study Bible), or, for Heiser, in his Revelation 7 episode and his question-and-answer episodes, Jewish followers of Jesus. His Reversing Hermon reads them as a reversal of the Watchers' sin; the podcast says it "has more explanatory power" but may not be right.

ideas.s: Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.

A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.

Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.
Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.

entries.title: Revelation 14:6-20, Babylon fallen, the harvest and the winepress
entries.summary: Three angels announce an eternal gospel, the fall of Babylon and the undiluted cup of God's wrath for those who worship the beast, and a voice blesses those who die in the Lord. Then one like a son of man reaps the earth's grain with a sickle, and an angel gathers its grapes into the great winepress, from which blood flows as high as the horses' bridles.
entries.plain: Three angels speak in turn: one calls all peoples to honor their creator, one announces the fall of Babylon, and one warns that those who worship the beast will face God's undiluted anger. A heavenly voice declares that believers who die faithful from this point are blessed and will find rest. Then two harvests follow, a grain harvest reaped by a heavenly Son of Man figure and a grape harvest crushed in the winepress of God's anger, with a flood of blood flowing from it. Whether both harvests mean judgment, or one of them the gathering of God's people, is debated.
entries.note: Fallen, fallen echoes Isaiah 21:9. Jews called Rome Babylon and counted it Daniel's fourth kingdom (the cultural backgrounds notes and article Babylon and Rome; Keener). Heiser reports Aune's point that every Jewish text equating Babylon with Rome comes after AD 70, which would favor a later date, notes that the argument cuts both ways, and will not settle the date. Wine was usually mixed with water; God's is poured undiluted, from the old cup of wrath (Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15; the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Rest for the righteous dead was standard Jewish hope, and over half the Jewish epitaphs found in Rome say in peace (Keener). Blood up to the bridles was stock battle exaggeration, as in 1 Enoch (Keener; Heiser, after Aune), and 1,600 stadia is forty times forty (Keener). Keener and Heiser read both harvests as judgment, after Joel 3:13; the cultural backgrounds notes call only the vintage certainly judgment; the ESV Study Bible reads the grain as believers gathered; Wright reads both as "images of salvation, not of condemnation". The one like a son of man is Jesus (the ESV Study Bible; Heiser) or perhaps an angel, since he takes an order from another angel (Keener).

ideas.n: Babylon as a name for Rome
ideas.s: Babylon burned Jerusalem's first temple and carried Judah into exile. By the first century Jews were calling Rome by its name, and Christians did the same for the city that ruled and scattered them.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.

entries.title: Revelation 15:1-16:11, the song of Moses and the first bowls
entries.summary: Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Seven angels dressed like priests come out of the heavenly temple with seven golden bowls of God's wrath, and the first five bring sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, scorching sun and darkness on the beast's throne.
entries.plain: Those who have defeated the beast stand by a glassy, fiery sea and sing a song like Moses' victory song, praising God's just deeds. Seven angels in priestly clothing then come out of the heavenly temple and are handed seven bowls filled with God's anger. The first five are poured out in turn, bringing sores, a sea and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat and darkness on the beast's kingdom, yet people curse God and refuse to change.
entries.note: The victors sing by the sea as Israel did after crossing it (Exodus 15), in words drawn mostly from Psalm 86:9-10 (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the CSB Study Bible); Heiser hears the sea of glass first as the Red Sea of a new exodus. Angels in linen with golden sashes act as temple priests (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), and Heiser, after Aune, takes their bowls as vessels that carried waste out of sacred space, suggesting that pouring them cleanses the earth for its king. Smoke and glory barring the doors recall the dedication of the tabernacle and of Solomon's temple (Exodus 40:35; 1 Kings 8:10-11). The bowls repeat Egypt's plagues, and John's hearers, like Israel, are spared (Keener). Jewish tradition said the Nile turned to blood to repay Egypt for drowning Israel's sons (Wisdom of Solomon 11:5-7), hence blood for blood (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The bowls are read as a future sequence (the ESV Study Bible), as spanning the age between Christ's comings with the end at the last two (Beale), or, for Heiser after Aune, as no literal events: they strike earth, water, sun and air, the four elements, to mean the whole world.

ideas.s: The blows God struck on Egypt before the exodus, from water turned to blood to the death of the firstborn, while Israel was spared. Revelation's trumpets and bowls replay them on the whole world.
The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.

ideas.n: The tabernacle and its heavenly pattern
ideas.s: The tent sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, with an outer room for the priests and an inner room, the holy of holies, for the ark. Moses built it to a pattern shown on the mountain, and many Jews thought of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Revelation 16:12-21, the Euphrates dried and Armageddon
entries.summary: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to make way for the kings from the east, and three frog-like spirits from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet gather the kings of the world to battle at the place called Armageddon. The seventh bowl brings a voice saying it is done, the greatest earthquake ever, the splitting of the great city and hundred-pound hailstones.
entries.plain: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates, clearing a road for eastern kings, and three frog-like demonic spirits go out from the dragon and his two allies to gather the world's rulers for war at a place called Armageddon. In the middle of this Jesus warns that he will come unannounced and blesses those who stay alert. The seventh bowl brings God's declaration that it is finished, a record earthquake that splits the great city, Babylon's judgment and enormous hail, but people still curse God. What place Armageddon names, a battlefield or a mountain, is debated.
entries.note: Informed hearers took the kings from the east as Parthians (Keener; Wright; Wright and Bird; the cultural backgrounds notes). Pompey had made the Euphrates the frontier, Parthians crossed it only to fight Rome, and a later writer said "only a river separated these two most powerful empires" (the cultural backgrounds article Parthia). Stories had Nero returning with a Parthian army (Carson, Moo and Morris), and a false Nero won Parthian backing less than a decade before Revelation (the article A New Nero). Heiser hears them as Babylon, the old Mesopotamian enemy. Jews hoped God would dry the river for the exiles (Isaiah 11:15-16; 4 Ezra 13; the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The frogs recall Exodus 8 (Keener). In the Jezreel Valley below Megiddo, which guarded the main pass, Deborah, Gideon, Saul and Josiah fought, and Thutmose III before them (the Zondervan dictionary; the atlas; Keener). Keener calls Mount Megiddo the commonest reading, a plain made a symbolic mountain; the ESV Study Bible insists "Megiddo was a plain, not a mountain", though the dictionary writes of Mount Megiddo and its low hills. Heiser reads the Hebrew behind the name as har mo'ed, the council's mountain of Isaiah 14:13, which is Zion.

ideas.s: The empire east of the Euphrates, Rome's most feared enemy, famous for mounted archers who could shoot backward as they rode. Its armies had destroyed a Roman army and once marched into Judea to put their own man on the throne.
Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.
Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.
The blows God struck on Egypt before the exodus, from water turned to blood to the death of the firstborn, while Israel was spared. Revelation's trumpets and bowls replay them on the whole world.

entries.title: Revelation 17:1-6, the woman on the scarlet beast
entries.summary: An angel carries John into a wilderness to see the great prostitute who sits on many waters, riding a scarlet beast full of blasphemous names. Dressed in purple and scarlet and glittering with gold and pearls, she holds a golden cup of filth, bears the name Babylon the great on her forehead and is drunk with the blood of God's people.
entries.plain: An angel takes John into the desert to show him the judgment of a powerful prostitute, a figure for a city that has seduced the world's rulers and intoxicated its peoples. She rides a scarlet beast covered in insults to God, wears royal colors and jewels, and holds a gold cup full of her corruption. Her forehead bears the name Babylon, and she is drunk on the blood of Jesus' faithful witnesses, a sight that leaves John stunned. Whether she stands for Rome alone or for something wider is debated.
entries.note: Gentiles pictured a homeland as a woman: coins showed a city as an enthroned goddess, and Roma seated on seven hills (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Rome's own Judea Capta coins showed "a Jewish woman (symbolizing Judea) seated, bound, and mourning" (Price and House). The prophets used harlot language for Tyre's trade and Nineveh's sorceries (Nahum 3:4; the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener), and Heiser takes those two as the models, reading the harlotry as idolatry. Purple and scarlet were costly dyes, and drunk with blood recalls Nero's killings and the arena (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Carson, Moo and Morris report that most scholars build the case for unusual persecution partly on verse 6, but find the evidence for it under Domitian exaggerated; the Zondervan dictionary ranks him with Nero. Many waters repeats Jeremiah 51:13 on the old Babylon (Heiser). The woman is read as Rome (Keener; Wright; Wright and Bird; Heiser, for John's day); a world system including Rome (the ESV and CSB Study Bibles; the cultural backgrounds article Babylon and Rome); a future body or rebuilt Babylon (futurists); apostate Israel within Babylon (Beale); or Jerusalem (some early-date readers). Heiser rejects Jerusalem: Israel is seduced, Babylon seduces.

ideas.n: Babylon as a name for Rome
ideas.s: Babylon burned Jerusalem's first temple and carried Judah into exile. By the first century Jews were calling Rome by its name, and Christians did the same for the city that ruled and scattered them.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

Rome celebrated a great victory with a triumph, a parade of the general, his army and the spoils, with chained captives at the end who were killed or sold. Cities also staged shows in which condemned criminals fought or were thrown to beasts.

Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.

entries.title: Revelation 17:7-18, seven hills and seven kings
entries.summary: The angel explains the woman and the beast: the beast once was, now is not and will come up from the Abyss; its seven heads are seven hills and also seven kings, five fallen, one living and one still to come, and the beast is an eighth who belongs to the seven. Its ten horns are ten kings who will make war on the Lamb, and in the end the beast and the horns turn on the woman, the great city that rules the kings of the earth, and burn her.
entries.plain: The angel decodes the vision of the woman and the beast she rides. The beast is a power that existed, vanished and will return from the Abyss only to be destroyed; its heads stand both for the hills of the woman's city and for a line of kings, with the beast itself as a final eighth ruler, and its horns are allied kings who will fight the Lamb and lose. In the end the beast and its allies turn on the woman, the city that dominates the world's rulers, and destroy her. How to count the kings, and whether the eighth recalls Nero, are debated.
entries.note: Rome was famous as the city on seven hills (Keener; Wright; the study Bibles), and Carson, Moo and Morris call the allusion "unmistakably a reference to Rome"; Heiser agrees. Beale reads the mountains first as kingdoms, and the CSB Study Bible warns against being dogmatic. An eighth king who is one of the seven fits the rumor that Nero would return, perhaps with Parthian armies (Keener; Wright and Bird); the cultural backgrounds article A New Nero says John need not have expected Nero literally, and Carson, Moo and Morris think the legend not very close to the beast. Counting from Augustus makes Galba the sixth and the date 68-69 (Carson, Moo and Morris, who still prefer Domitian); others start from Julius Caesar or Caligula, or skip the three brief emperors, and "None of these questions can be answered certainly." Beale reads the seven as world government in every age. The ten horns are probably Rome's client kings (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Heiser reads Daniel's horn-kings, their one hour echoing Nebuchadnezzar's time as a beast in Greek Daniel 4. Rome ruled the peoples around the sea "because it is a maritime power" (the cultural backgrounds article Babylon and Rome).

ideas.n: Babylon as a name for Rome
ideas.s: Babylon burned Jerusalem's first temple and carried Judah into exile. By the first century Jews were calling Rome by its name, and Christians did the same for the city that ruled and scattered them.

ideas.n: Daniel's four beasts and the fourth kingdom
ideas.s: Daniel 7 pictured four empires as four beasts rising from the sea, the last with ten horns, judged before one like a son of man receives the kingdom. In the first century many Jews read the fourth beast as Rome.

Daniel's king who exalts himself above every god and defiles the sanctuary became a pattern Jews saw again in Antiochus, Pompey and Caligula. Paul's man of lawlessness, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God, belongs to that line.

The empire east of the Euphrates, Rome's most feared enemy, famous for mounted archers who could shoot backward as they rode. Its armies had destroyed a Roman army and once marched into Judea to put their own man on the throne.
Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.

entries.title: Revelation 18:1-8, come out of her, my people
entries.summary: A shining angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons and unclean birds, because the nations drank her wine and the merchants grew rich on her luxury. A voice calls God's people to come out of her, and to pay her back double, since she boasts that she sits as a queen and will never be a widow.
entries.plain: A glorious angel announces that Babylon has fallen and become a ruin haunted by demons, because she seduced the nations and their rulers and made traders rich on her luxury. A second voice urges God's people to leave her so they are not caught up in her guilt or her punishment, since God has not forgotten her crimes. Because she boasted that she was a queen beyond the reach of grief, her ruin will come suddenly, in a single day, with death, mourning, famine and fire.
entries.note: Mocking laments over doomed cities were a known form (Isaiah 21:9; Jeremiah 51), and orators wrote speeches praising cities, as Aelius Aristides did for Rome; John writes a eulogy that curses (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The genre was risky: "Romans regarded as subversive those who prophesied Rome's fall" (the cultural backgrounds article Babylon and Rome). The Greek Old Testament puts demons among the creatures haunting ruined Babylon (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14; the cultural backgrounds notes), and Arnold notes "a strong connection between wild animals and evil spirits throughout antiquity". Come out of her follows Jeremiah 51:6 and 45 (Keener; Wright). Paying double follows the law for a thief (Exodus 22:4), and queen and never a widow comes from Isaiah 47:7-8; Rome called itself the eternal city and spread the worship of the emperor and the goddess Roma (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible), whose temple with Augustus stood at the heart of Herod's Caesarea (Price and House). Heiser reads the fall as Psalm 82 fulfilled, the death of the empire's gods. Keener takes Babylon as Rome with later embodiments, Wright as every such city, the CSB Study Bible as the world system from Babel to Jerusalem.

ideas.n: Babylon as a name for Rome
ideas.s: Babylon burned Jerusalem's first temple and carried Judah into exile. By the first century Jews were calling Rome by its name, and Christians did the same for the city that ruled and scattered them.

Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.

ideas.n: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
ideas.s: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.

entries.title: Revelation 18:9-24, kings, merchants and the cargo list
entries.summary: The kings, the merchants and the sea captains stand far off and mourn as Babylon burns, because no one buys their cargoes any more, a long list of luxuries that ends with human beings. An angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, and the sounds of music, craftsmen, the mill, the lamp and the wedding fall silent in the city where the blood of prophets and saints was found.
entries.plain: Rulers, merchants and seafarers stand at a safe distance and lament as Babylon burns, because the trade that made them rich has collapsed. The list of lost cargo runs from luxury goods and food to livestock and, at its end, enslaved human beings. An angel hurls a huge stone into the sea as a sign that the city will vanish just as completely, with all its music, work, light and weddings gone, because it deceived the nations and is guilty of killing God's prophets and people.
entries.note: The mourners are those who profited: kings, merchants and shipowners (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). John reworks Ezekiel 27's cargo list for Tyre, fifteen of his twenty-nine items appearing there (Beale; the study Bibles), and the cultural backgrounds article Rome's Imports says he "updates it accurately for the trade realities of first-century Rome"; Wright and Bird, after Bauckham, see Babylon as Rome's political power and Tyre as its economic power. Keener and the article differ on origins: gold from North Africa or mostly from Spain, where mine slaves rarely lived long; cinnamon from China or most probably Somalia. About 200,000 families in Rome got grain free while children starved in some of the lands that grew it (the article; Keener). The list ends with human beings, "the gravest injustice of the empire" (the cultural backgrounds notes); "Asia exported a large quantity of humans to Rome", probably through Ephesus (the article). Beale reads bodies and souls as one phrase for slaves; Keener separates human lives, perhaps kept for the arena. Heiser sees a power that controls trade, with "a more sinister intelligence" behind it that wants worship. The silenced mill, lamp and wedding reverse Jeremiah 25:10 (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener).

ideas.s: Craftsmen of one trade lived and worked in the same streets and banded together in guilds, which set standards, defended their interests and met for meals in honor of a patron god.

Outside winter, ships were the quickest and cheapest way to travel, but they were built for cargo, not passengers, and from mid-September the sea grew dangerous. The great grain ships of Alexandria fed Rome.
Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Revelation 19:1-10, the marriage supper of the Lamb
entries.summary: A vast heavenly crowd shouts hallelujah because God has judged the great prostitute, and again because the Lamb's wedding day has arrived and his bride stands ready in fine linen. The angel declares those invited to the wedding feast blessed, and when John bows to him, tells him to worship God alone.
entries.plain: Heaven erupts in praise because God has judged the corrupt city and avenged the blood of his servants. The celebration turns to a wedding announcement: God reigns, the Lamb's marriage has come, and his bride is dressed in clean linen that stands for the faithful deeds of God's people. When John falls down to worship the angel who shows him this, the angel refuses, calling himself a fellow servant and pointing John to God, since true prophecy bears witness to Jesus.
entries.note: Ancient writers set funeral against wedding, so the dirges over Babylon give way to a wedding, and the prostitute to the bride (the cultural backgrounds notes). Heiser keeps two suppers apart: this wedding feast and the carrion supper of 19:17, the two sides of the day of the Lord. Kings marked victories with banquets, an image passed to God's end-time feast (the Zondervan dictionary), above all Isaiah 25:6-8, a feast for all peoples where death is swallowed up (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; the ESV Study Bible); Heiser reads its setting, Zion with God's elders (Isaiah 24:23), as the divine council. Some Jewish teachers said Leviathan would be served (Keener; 2 Baruch), which Heiser reads as chaos itself consumed. Betrothal already counted as marriage (Keener; Beale). Pure linen, the high priest's dress, is set against the prostitute's purple and scarlet (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes); whether it is the bride's own deeds (the Zondervan dictionary) or God's gift of vindication is argued both ways (Beale; the ESV Study Bible). Some Jews in Asia Minor called on angels with amulets, which may be why the angel refuses worship (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener); Arnold thinks Colossians 2:18 may attack such invocation.

ideas.s: A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.

ideas.n: The banquet of the age to come
ideas.s: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.
God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.

entries.title: Revelation 19:11-21, the rider on the white horse
entries.summary: Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse, named Faithful and True and the Word of God, leads heaven's armies, his robe stained with blood and a sword coming from his mouth, his title King of kings. Birds are summoned to feast on the fallen, the beast and the false prophet are seized and cast into the fiery lake, and their armies fall to the rider's sword.
entries.plain: Heaven opens and a royal warrior rides out on a white horse, known as trustworthy and true and as the Word of God, his robe stained with blood, with heaven's armies behind him. He fights with justice and strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth, and his robe declares him the supreme king and lord. Birds are summoned to a grim feast on the defeated, the beast and its lying prophet are captured and thrown into the burning lake, and the rest fall to the rider's word. Who the armies are, and whether this is the same battle as the one in chapter 20, are debated.
entries.note: Keener writes that "Roman princes customarily rode white horses in military triumphs", and Domitian rode in the Judean one behind Vespasian and Titus (Josephus, War 7.5.5), whose capture of Judea the Flavians celebrated on coins and monuments (Price and House). White horses and King of kings could also mean the Parthian king (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Magicians claimed power over spirits whose names they knew, so an unknown name means no one controls him (Keener; Arnold); Heiser takes it as most likely the divine name. The robe follows Isaiah 63:1-6. Where the Scrolls and Zealots expected war on Rome, Jesus fights alone, the divine warrior (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). The armies are angels (Keener), believers (the CSB Study Bible), both (the cultural backgrounds notes) or, for Heiser, Zechariah 14's holy ones with glorified believers. The birds' feast follows Ezekiel 39:17-20 (Keener). Whether this is the battle of 20:7-10 divides amillennialists and premillennialists (the ESV Study Bible). The beast lies in the lake before Gog comes, so, Heiser notes, a linear reading cannot make Gog the beast; after Kline he reads chapters 16, 19 and 20 as one battle, since only Ezekiel 39 summons birds to such a feast.

ideas.s: Rome celebrated a great victory with a triumph, a parade of the general, his army and the spoils, with chained captives at the end who were killed or sold. Cities also staged shows in which condemned criminals fought or were thrown to beasts.

The empire east of the Euphrates, Rome's most feared enemy, famous for mounted archers who could shoot backward as they rode. Its armies had destroyed a Roman army and once marched into Judea to put their own man on the throne.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.

entries.title: Revelation 20:1-6, Satan bound and the thousand years
entries.summary: An angel with the key to the Abyss and a great chain seizes the dragon, binds him for a thousand years and seals him in the Abyss so that he cannot deceive the nations. Those beheaded for their witness, who refused the beast and its mark, come to life and reign with Christ for the thousand years, the first resurrection, over which the second death has no power.
entries.plain: An angel comes down with a key and a chain, seizes the dragon, Satan, and locks him away in the Abyss for a thousand years so that he can no longer mislead the nations, though he will later be released briefly. John then sees thrones of judgment and the martyrs who refused the beast brought back to life to reign with the Messiah for that thousand years. This is called the first resurrection, and those who share in it are blessed, serve as priests and are safe from the second death. When the thousand years fall, and what the binding means, are read in several ways.
entries.note: Jewish texts bound wicked angels until judgment: in 1 Enoch 10 Raphael and Michael bind them under the earth (Arnold; Beale), Jubilees 48 binds Mastema, and Isaiah 24:21-22 shuts the host of heaven in a pit (Beale). Chapters 20-22 follow Ezekiel 37-48 (Keener). Papias and Irenaeus expected a reign on earth, but by Eusebius's day such readers were a minority (the cultural backgrounds article The Millennium), and Dionysius denied apostolic authorship to discredit the literal reign (Carson, Moo and Morris). For a future reign, "it follows the logic of the narrative": Satan is not bound in chapters 12-13, and the beast is still in the lake at 20:10; against it, no such interim appears elsewhere in the New Testament, and Revelation retells its judgments in cycles (the article). Beale reads the binding as restraint of Satan's deceiving since the cross (Mark 3:27, where Arnold too sees Satan tied up at the cross). Heiser, after Kline, takes the binding's thousand years as the church age, granting that the reign of verse 6, after the first resurrection, does not fit it; he rejects Beale's binding: Satan is kept only from what he does when loosed, when "he leads the nations against Zion".

ideas.n: The Watchers, the flood and the bound angels
ideas.s: Most Jews of the period read the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4 as angels who took human wives before the flood. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, had the guilty angels bound under the earth in darkness until the judgment, and 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude speak of that prison.

Several Jewish apocalypses expected an in-between kingdom, a reign of the Messiah or an age of peace between the present age and the final judgment, of varying length. Revelation 20 gives it a thousand years, and Christians have read that span in three main ways ever since.

In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.

Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: Revelation 20:7-15, Gog and Magog and the great white throne
entries.summary: Released at the end of the thousand years, Satan gathers Gog and Magog, the nations from the four corners of the earth, around the camp of God's people, but fire from heaven consumes them and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. Before a great white throne the dead, given up by the sea, death and Hades, are judged from the books, and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.
entries.plain: At the end of the thousand years Satan is freed and rallies the nations from every corner of the world, called Gog and Magog, against God's people and his beloved city, but fire from heaven destroys them and the devil is cast into the burning lake for ever. John then sees a great white throne before which heaven and earth flee, and all the dead, raised from sea and grave, are judged by their deeds as recorded in God's books. Death and the grave are themselves destroyed in the lake of fire, along with all whose names are missing from the book of life. Who Gog is, and whether this battle is the one already told in chapter 19, are debated.
entries.note: Gog is Israel's last enemy in Ezekiel 38-39; Josephus writes that "Magog founded those that from him were named Magogites, but who are by the Greeks called Scythians" (Antiquities 1.6.1). Many identify Gog with Gyges of Lydia, whose capital, Sardis, was one of the seven churches (the Zondervan dictionary; the atlas, whose gazetteer calls Magog uncertain). In Jewish texts Gog stood for all nations massed against Israel (Keener; the dictionary). Heiser's Unseen Realm reads Gog as a supernatural figure from the cosmic north, and the dictionary calls him "the demonic and sinister leader of ungodly peoples"; Keener reads human nations. Books of deeds recall Daniel 7:10 and Enoch (Keener), and the book of life Israel's registers of citizens (the dictionary). The drowned, unburied, were thought barred from Hades (the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright), hence the sea giving up its dead. The lake of fire recalls Daniel 7:10's river of fire, the Greek underworld and 1 Enoch 90 (the cultural backgrounds notes); Heiser's Reversing Hermon traces the fire prepared for the devil's angels to 1 Enoch, while his podcast finds fiery judgment already in Isaiah 33:14 and 66:24. Heiser leaves open whether the second death is annihilation or endless torment.

ideas.s: An old picture of God keeping a register of the names of those who belong to him. Jewish writers developed it, and the New Testament uses it from Luke to Revelation.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.
Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.

entries.title: Revelation 21:1-8, new heaven, new earth, no more sea
entries.summary: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride dressed for her husband. A voice announces that God's dwelling is now with people, that he will wipe away every tear, and that he makes all things new; the thirsty will drink freely, while the cowardly, the faithless, murderers, sorcerers, idolaters and liars have their place in the lake of fire.
entries.plain: The old creation is gone and John sees a new heaven and earth, with no sea, and the holy city descending from God, beautiful as a bride on her wedding day. A voice announces that God now lives among his people, and that tears, death and pain are over for good. God declares that he is renewing everything, offers free water of life to the thirsty and an inheritance to those who overcome, while those who persist in evil are shut out in the second death. Why the sea is gone, and whether creation is renewed or replaced, are debated.
entries.note: New heavens and earth come from Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. Jewish texts spoke of the world purified, transformed or replaced; Keener thinks Revelation means replacement, and the ESV Study Bible weighs both. Beale notes that the word new means new in kind, Wright stresses heaven and earth joined, the Zondervan dictionary says "the old universe will be marvelously regenerated", and Heiser notes that Isaiah gives the new creation and the new Jerusalem together. The missing sea is read as chaos, home of Leviathan, for Heiser, who writes, "When Eden comes, there is no more sea"; a hostile element removed (the dictionary); no place left for monsters to rise (Wright); five senses at once, from evil to trade (Beale). Keener doubts that John's hearers knew the old Canaanite sea stories, and the cultural backgrounds notes think the river of life replaces the sea. God dwelling with his people is tabernacle language (Leviticus 26:11-12; Ezekiel 37:27; Keener; Wright); Heiser hears the verb of John 1:14 and promises to Israel now reaching every believer. Magic was widespread in Roman Asia (Acts 19; Keener) and counted antisocial, done secretly for the magician's own good (the cultural backgrounds article Magic in the New Testament).

ideas.n: This age and the age to come
ideas.s: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.

ideas.n: The tabernacle and its heavenly pattern
ideas.s: The tent sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, with an outer room for the priests and an inner room, the holy of holies, for the ark. Moses built it to a pattern shown on the mountain, and many Jews thought of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.

entries.title: Revelation 21:9-27, the city of gold and twelve stones
entries.summary: An angel carries John to a high mountain to show him the bride, the holy city Jerusalem, shining with God's glory, with twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and twelve foundations named for the Lamb's apostles. The city is a cube of pure gold, its foundations set with twelve precious stones and its gates each a single pearl; it has no temple, since God and the Lamb are its temple, and its gates never shut as the nations bring their glory into it.
entries.plain: An angel shows John the bride of the Lamb, which turns out to be the holy city, glowing with God's glory, its gates named for Israel's tribes and its foundations for the Lamb's apostles. Measured, it forms a vast perfect cube of gold, gems and pearl. It has no temple, because God and the Lamb are present everywhere in it, and no need for sun or moon; its gates stay open as the nations bring their treasures in, but nothing unclean ever enters. Whether the city and its measurements are literal or symbolic is debated.
entries.note: Jewish writers after Ezekiel pictured the new Jerusalem: Tobit 13, a Qumran blueprint, the Temple Scroll's twelve gates (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). The bride is shown as the prostitute was (17:1-3), but from a high mountain, not a wilderness (Keener; Beale). The city's "cubic shape recalls the Most Holy Place" (the cultural backgrounds notes), so it needs no temple; Heiser notes the prophets already merged temple and city (Jeremiah 3:16-17). Ezekiel's city was 18,000 cubits around (Ezekiel 48:35); John's, some 1,400 miles a side, is "nearly 2,000 times larger", granting "What the world could not accomplish in Babel" (the cultural backgrounds article Dimensions of the New Jerusalem). Keener, Beale, Wright and Heiser read the size as symbolic; the ESV Study Bible allows a literal city, which premillennialists, says the Zondervan dictionary, set above Jerusalem. The twelve stones largely match the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:17-20; Keener; Beale); Heiser hears Ezekiel 28's stones of Eden instead. Josephus tied the twelve to the zodiac (Antiquities 3.7.7), and Ephesian Artemis wore the zodiac as a necklace (Arnold), but John avoids astrology (Keener; Beale). The CSB Study Bible keeps Israel and the church distinct in the gates and foundations; Heiser reads one people.
