Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.

The head of Israel's priests, from Aaron's line, who offered for his own sins and then the people's and alone went into the holy of holies, once a year. By the first century Herod and Rome named and removed him at will.
Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.

entries.title: Revelation 22:1-5, river and tree of life
entries.summary: The angel shows John a clear, life-giving river running from God's throne through the middle of the city, with the tree of life on both banks, fruiting every month and healing the nations with its leaves. Nothing cursed remains; God's servants will see him face to face, carry his name and reign for ever in his light.
entries.plain: John is shown a sparkling river of life flowing from the shared throne of God and the Lamb through the center of the city, with the tree of life growing on both sides, fruiting all year and bearing leaves that heal the nations. Nothing under God's curse remains. God's servants will live in his presence, see him face to face and bear his name, ruling for ever in a city that needs no lamp or sun because God himself is its light. Whether the tree is one or many, and what the healing of the nations means, are debated.
entries.note: The river joins Ezekiel 47's river from the temple with Eden's river in Genesis 2:10 and the living waters of Zechariah 14:8 (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener; Beale; Wright). At the Feast of Tabernacles priests poured water at the altar to signify that "rivers of living water would flow from the temple", and Ezekiel 47 and Zechariah 14 were read on its last day (the cultural backgrounds article Tabernacles and the Promise of Living Water). Later Jewish texts pictured the end as Eden restored (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). Ezekiel 47:12 has trees fruiting every month, and some traditions counted twelve trees (the cultural backgrounds notes; Keener). One tree or many is read differently: one source of life (the cultural backgrounds notes), a collective singular for Ezekiel's trees (Beale), or trees in profusion (Wright). Heiser reads the healing of the nations as Babel undone: in his book God reclaims the nations given to lesser gods (Deuteronomy 32:8-9), and in the podcast they become one family, with no disease to cure. No more curse echoes Zechariah 14:11 and undoes Genesis 3 (Keener; the ESV Study Bible), and Jewish hope included seeing God's face (Keener).

Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.
God's covenant set blessings for keeping it against curses for breaking it, and Deuteronomy spelled both out. Curses were also a familiar part of ancient religion, magic and everyday life.

entries.title: Revelation 22:6-21, I am coming soon
entries.summary: The angel confirms that the words are trustworthy, and Jesus says he is coming soon. John is told not to seal up the prophecy, since the time is near; those who wash their robes may enter the city while dogs, sorcerers and liars stay outside. The book closes with the Spirit and the bride saying come, a warning against adding to or taking from it, and the prayer, come, Lord Jesus.
entries.plain: The book closes by insisting that its message is reliable and urgent: Jesus repeats that he is coming soon, and John is told to leave the prophecy open for all to read. Jesus names himself the beginning and end of all things and the promised heir of David, invites in those who have been washed clean and warns that the unrepentant remain outside. The Spirit and the church call out for him to come, anyone thirsty is invited to drink freely, readers are warned not to alter the book, and John ends with a prayer for the Lord Jesus to come.
entries.note: The echoes of chapter 1 bracket the book (Keener). Daniel sealed his words, the end being far off; John's stay open for his own generation and later ones (Keener). Heiser holds that all Christ's return required was in place in that first generation, so every generation could expect him. Verses 8-9 would refute any Asian Jewish Christians who exalted angels (Keener). Dogs probably means the sexually immoral, "specifically unrepentant prostitutes" (Deuteronomy 23:17-18; Keener). The root of David comes from Isaiah 11:1 and the morning star, Venus, from Numbers 24:17, which the Dead Sea Scrolls also gave a conquering messiah (Keener); magical recipes offered to the star of Venus (Arnold). The thirsty drink freely as in Isaiah 55:1 (Keener). "The words of a divinely instituted covenant or book were not to be altered" (Deuteronomy 4:2), and Josephus and the Letter of Aristeas said as much of the Septuagint (Keener); the CSB Study Bible notes the warning concerns this book, not the canon, which Revelation entered late in the East (Carson, Moo and Morris). Marana tha, a common early prayer, shows early recognition of Jesus' deity (Keener); the Zondervan dictionary prefers it, with most scholars, to our Lord has come.

ideas.n: Apocalypses, visions and numbers that mean something
ideas.s: Jewish books of visions, usually written in the name of a hero from long ago, in which a heavenly guide shows a seer what heaven sees in the present trouble and how God will end it. They spoke in pictures and in numbers that carried meaning, and Revelation is the one that calls itself an apocalypse.
The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.

Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.
Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
